TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.crossin.text:
The time $2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$ forming the right endpoint of the crossing bracket. Lean calls the successor ratio `next`. This is a real-valued definition for arbitrary arguments, so positivity and nonzero denominator are hypotheses of the theorems that use it. The finite-return theorem assumes both ratios positive and places this horizon within the prescribed normalized interval.

Default-value audit (b5): Real.sqrt is zero for nonpositive products, and division by zero is zero, so the horizon becomes zero there. The crossing theorems require both ratios strictly positive and a small successor ratio.

TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.eight_d.text: The crossing horizon is at least $8/\varepsilon$ under `hε : 0 < ε`, `hn : 0 < next`, and `hsmall : next ≤ ε / 32`. Since the horizon is twice $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}$, this is the manuscript's bound $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}\ge4/\varepsilon$. It places the upper bracket endpoint strictly after every $\tau_m\le3/\varepsilon$.
TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.eight_d.summary: The crossing horizon lies beyond the turning range

TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.exists_.text: A continuous ratio with $1/(4x)\le\rho\le3/(2x)$ has a crossing strictly inside the bracket from $\tau_m$ to the horizon. The hypotheses `hε`, `hn`, `hsmall`, `hτm`, and `hT` give the positive ratios, successor size, turning range, and available interval; `hρ` and `hbounds` give continuity and the late bounds. Every crossing in $[\tau_m,T]$ also satisfies $1/(4\varepsilon_+)\le x\le3/(2\varepsilon_+)$.
TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.exists_.summary: A continuous coupling ratio crosses the prescribed value

TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.exists_.text: For positive successor ratio at most epsilon divided by 32, a continuous ratio between one half and three halves of the reference cosine crosses that successor value strictly inside the peak-to-horizon interval. Every later crossing also has explicit tangent bounds. The old docstring numbers refer to the earlier manuscript; the current application is Proposition 2.8 using Lemma 2.7.

If a continuous real ratio on $[a,b]$ reaches `next` somewhere, it reaches it at a least time in that interval. The proof makes the level set compact and takes its minimum. It requires neither monotonicity nor uniqueness of crossings, and it does not locate the first crossing outside the chosen interval.
TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.exists_.summary: A nonempty compact crossing set has a first point

TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.x_cross.text: At the crossing horizon, $x=2/\varepsilon_+$. The assumptions `hε : 0 < ε` and `hn : 0 < next` justify cancellation of the square root in $x(2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+})$. This exact identity gives the upper-end coupling estimate needed to put the target ratio strictly below its value at the turning time and above its value at the horizon.
TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.x_cross.summary: The clock value at the upper crossing endpoint

TorusEuler.AuxiliaryTerminalSmoothness.text: The combined proposition for Auxiliary Theorem 1.1 and Auxiliary Lemmas 1.2 and 1.3. Its existential parameters `b`, `threshold` and `N₁` precede the choice of initial frequency. For each admissible frequency it asks for one `c : ScheduledEulerConstruction P`, both families of estimates for its stages, and an Euler singularity witness with the terminal extension. These are requirements of a proposition; the theorem `auxiliaryTerminalSmoothness` supplies them. The displayed predicate does not itself state convergence of these stages to the chosen velocity.
TorusEuler.AuxiliaryTerminalSmoothness.summary: Auxiliary conclusions on one chosen schedule

TorusEuler.BoundedSpatialJet.text: An order `m` jet is a bounded continuous function of the spatial variable with values in continuous `m` linear maps. The norm is the uniform operator norm. This type alone does not say that the function is a derivative of any velocity; that compatibility is imposed by later hypotheses.
TorusEuler.BoundedSpatialJet.summary: A uniformly bounded spatial derivative field

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.DeformationOn.text: This proposition packages an actual flow on $[0,T]$, compatibility with all lattice translations, inverse identities, and differentiability with norm bound `C` for the transitions from and to zero. The bounds are imposed at every spatial point of the lift. It records geometric regularity of a supplied velocity and flow, without imposing Euler's equation.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.DeformationOn.summary: A periodic flow with bounded forward and inverse deformation

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.DeformationOn.congr.text: If two velocity fields agree as spatial functions at every slab time, a `DeformationOn` certificate for one is also a certificate for the other. The same flow family, lattice property, and derivative bounds are retained. Only the trajectory equation is rewritten, so no new flow or estimate is introduced.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.DeformationOn.congr.summary: Transfer a flow certificate across slabwise velocity equality

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.DeformationOn.fderi.text: From `DeformationOn` and membership of `t` in the slab, the forward derivative at `x` and reverse derivative at the transported point compose to the identity in both orders. Differentiability and inverse-map identities are already fields of the structure. The theorem differentiates those identities, giving actual inverse matrices without a totalized inverse construction.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.DeformationOn.fderi.summary: The two deformation matrices are mutual inverses

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.PhaseState.text:
The enlarged particle space is the product of a three-dimensional label and one real phase variable. The phase graph is imposed later; this abbreviation does not restrict points to that graph or quotient the phase modulo one.

Default-value audit (b5): The type is an unrestricted Euclidean label and real phase pair. There is no exceptional default or graph membership assertion; phase periodicity and restriction to the transported graph are additional hypotheses or constructions.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.PhaseState.summary: Labels and an independent phase coordinate

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.childVelocity.text: Add to the parent velocity the oscillatory profile evaluated through the reverse parent transition, together with the Eulerian correction `v`. This defines the physical child field used in the deformation theorem. The formula does not itself assert divergence freedom, smoothness, or that the child solves Euler; those require the construction's separate hypotheses.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.childVelocity.summary: The parent velocity with its transported perturbations

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.contDiffOn_pullback.text: The perturbation pulled back by the actual parent flow is jointly smooth.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.contDiffOn_pullback.summary: The pulled-back perturbation is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.defect_scaledField.text: Applying the phase-defect functional to the scaled particle field gives zero when both scales are nonzero. The cancellation is algebraic: the phase velocity is the wave vector paired with the label velocity. This tangency is valid at every enlarged state, so the defect is conserved along the constructed trajectories.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.defect_scaledField.summary: The lifted velocity is tangent to the phase graph

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.defect_scaledGraph.text: When both scaling parameters are nonzero, every point produced by the scaled graph embedding has phase defect zero. The identity records compatibility of the embedded phase with the initial linear phase. It provides the invariant constraint used when a trajectory in the enlarged space is converted back to labels.

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.exists_childFlow_of.text: Given a smooth parent flow, forward and inverse deformation bounds, the twisted divergence identity, phase periodicity, and scaled oscillatory and mean jet bounds, construct the physical child flow with deformation bounded by the specified frequency-quarter-power budget. The numerous smallness and scale hypotheses are explicit inputs; this helper does not establish them for the hierarchy.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.exists_childFlow_of.summary: Child deformation from oscillatory and mean bounds

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.exists_childFlow_of.text: Assume a smooth periodic parent with both Jacobians bounded by `D`, positive scales, the prescribed frequency relations, and the explicit step smallness `hsmall`. Smooth bounded pullback data with periodic graph field and the two derivative bounds `hLabel` and `hPhase` yield a physical child flow with `DeformationOn` bound $\Gamma D^b\mathrm{freq}^{1/4}$. The hypotheses carry the profile estimates; this theorem assembles their geometric consequences.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.exists_childFlow_of.summary: Constructing the child flow from scaled derivative bounds

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.graphDerivative_app.text: A derivative on the phase graph splits into its label and phase components. For a linear derivative `D : PhaseState →L[ℝ] Vec3`, Lean expands its composition with `labelPhaseSlope ell h k` as a label term plus $h^{-1}\langle k_*,v\rangle D(0,1)$. The factors $\ell_*^{-1}$ and $h^{-1}$ occur because the domain is scaled. Applied to the projected displacement, this is the paper’s formula for $D\mathcal A_t-\operatorname{Id}$.

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.graphField.text: Evaluate the independent-phase field `c` at the label `a` and phase $\langle k,a\rangle$. The result is an ordinary time-dependent label velocity. The definition imposes neither periodicity nor divergence freedom; those are proved later from the profile's lattice rule and combined label-phase divergence identity.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.graphField.summary: Restricting the label velocity to its phase graph

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.graphField_pullback.text: A periodic parent flow, periodic Eulerian perturbation, and the skew label-phase lattice rule `hW` imply spatial periodicity of the graph-restricted pullback velocity. The phase shifts together with the label by the pairing with `k`. No integrality assumption on `k` is needed because the combined lattice rule handles arbitrary wave vectors.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.graphField_pullback.summary: The profile lattice rule gives a periodic label velocity

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.hasFDerivAt_labelPr.text: For nonzero envelope radius, the derivative of the projected scaled field is exactly the derivative `C` of the rescaled label velocity. The reciprocal envelope factor in the lifted field cancels with the projection. This preserves the smaller projected-displacement estimate even when the full scaled-field gradient has larger scaling factors.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.hasFDerivAt_labelPr.summary: Projecting removes the envelope reciprocal from the derivative

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.hasFDerivAt_labelTr.text: If the projected displacement of an enlarged transition has derivative `D` at the embedded label, then the unscaled label transition minus the identity has derivative `D` composed with the graph slope. Nonzero envelope radius permits cancellation of the initial label. This formula tracks the scale cost before estimating the full transition derivative.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.hasFDerivAt_labelTr.summary: The label displacement derivative factors through the graph

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.hasFDerivAt_scaledF.text: Given derivatives `C` and `G` of the rescaled label velocity and scalar phase velocity, the derivative of the lifted field is their product with reciprocal envelope and phase factors. The theorem preserves the separately estimated scalar derivative. It therefore retains the longitudinal cancellation instead of replacing it immediately by a wave-vector norm bound.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.hasFDerivAt_scaledF.summary: The scaled field derivative keeps label and phase separate

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.isLabelFlowOn_label.text: Start with a scaled trajectory family satisfying the initial and trajectory equations, with nonzero label and phase scales. Its projection from the embedded graph is an `IsLabelFlowOn` for the graph-restricted label field. Conservation of phase defect identifies the projected right-hand side, so the result is an actual flow equation on the slab.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.isLabelFlowOn_label.summary: The invariant phase graph produces an actual label flow

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.isLabelFlowOn_physi.text: For a $C^2$ periodic parent and an actual label flow of the graph-restricted pullback field, conjugating by the parent transitions gives a flow of `childVelocity`. The theorem differentiates both the parent trajectory and the evolving label. It proves the correct physical ODE, without asserting that the resulting velocity already satisfies Euler's equation.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.isLabelFlowOn_physi.summary: Conjugating the label flow gives the child flow

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelProjection.text: Multiply the first component of a label-phase state by the envelope radius `ell`. This continuous linear map returns the physical label from the scaled coordinate when that scale is nonzero and the point lies on the chosen graph. The definition does not inspect the independent phase coordinate.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelProjection.summary: Recovering the label from its scaled coordinate

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelProjection_sca.text: For a state with zero phase defect, projecting the scaled velocity gives `graphField` evaluated at its recovered label. Only the envelope radius is assumed nonzero in this identity. It identifies the differential equation satisfied by a projected trajectory once conservation of the defect has placed that trajectory on the graph.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelProjection_sca.summary: On the graph the projected velocity is the label field

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelProjection_sca.text: With nonzero envelope radius, projecting `labelPhaseSlope` by `labelProjection` returns the original label. The phase width need not be nonzero because the projection discards the phase component. This identity supplies the correct initial value for the label flow obtained by restricting the enlarged scaled flow.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelProjection_sca.summary: Projecting the scaled graph recovers the label

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelTransition.text: The label transition obtained by starting the scaled particle flow on $s=k_*\cdot a$ and then projecting to the unscaled label. The input `Φ` is a two-time flow, and `labelPhaseSlope ell h k a` inserts the initial label into the scaled graph. This definition corresponds to $\mathcal A_t(a)=a+\eta_a(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ once the lifted flow is written as identity plus displacement.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelTransition.summary: The label transition obtained from the invariant graph

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_fderiv_labelTr.text: A derivative bound `hB` on the projected displacement, together with positive scales, gives the derivative of the label transition as the identity plus that displacement derivative composed with the graph slope. Its norm is bounded by $1+(\ell^{-1}+\|k\|h^{-1})B$. The statement supplies both the derivative identity and its quantitative estimate.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_fderiv_labelTr.summary: Projected displacement bounds the full label deformation

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_fderiv_scaledF.text: With positive scales and derivative bounds `A` and `B` for the rescaled label and scalar phase velocities, the full scaled-field derivative is bounded by $\ell^{-1}A+h^{-1}B$. The actual derivative identifications `hC` and `hG` are assumed. This is the quantity made small before applying flow stability.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_fderiv_scaledF.summary: The scaled gradient has two distinct costs

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_fderiv_scaledP.text: For a smooth profile whose weighted coordinate derivatives through order one are bounded by nonnegative `M`, the derivative after label-phase rescaling has norm at most $4M$. The factor counts the enlarged space's four coordinates. This converts the component estimates supplied by the profile calculus into the operator norm needed for ODE stability.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_fderiv_scaledP.summary: Four weighted coordinates control the first derivative

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_scaledField_le.text: For positive scales, a bound `A` on the label velocity at the rescaled point controls the enlarged field by $\ell^{-1}A+h^{-1}\|k\|A$. This is a value-level estimate, not a derivative estimate. It supplies the boundedness needed to extend the scaled ODE across the entire time slab.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_scaledField_le.summary: A label-velocity bound also bounds the lifted field

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_scaledGraph_le.text: For positive envelope radius and phase width, the graph embedding has operator norm bounded by $\ell^{-1}+\|k\|h^{-1}$. This is the scale conversion needed to apply a derivative estimate from the enlarged coordinates to the original labels. The theorem itself concerns one fixed linear embedding and makes no flow assumption.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.norm_scaledGraph_le.summary: The graph slope costs envelope and wave-number factors

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseDefect.text: The functional returns the unscaled phase minus the initial wave vector paired with the recovered label. Its zero set is the original phase graph after rescaling, provided both scales are nonzero. Applying it to the lifted particle velocity gives zero, which is the mechanism preserving that graph under the flow.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseDefect.summary: The difference between phase and linear label phase

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseDefect_transit.text: The quantity $s-k_*\cdot a$ is preserved by the lifted particle flow in either time direction. The hypotheses `hell` and `hh` make the coordinate scales nonzero; `hinit` and `htraj` specify a flow of `scaledField`. The result applies to every initial point `z`. A point with zero phase defect therefore stays on the graph $s=k_*\cdot a$, which is the graph used to recover the physical label flow.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseDefect_transit.summary: The lifted flow preserves phase minus label phase

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseMean_pullbackF.text: The cutoff tail shifts the phase mean by its label-dependent pullback.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseMean_pullbackF.summary: The cutoff tail changes only the phase mean

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseOscillation_pu.text: The phase-independent cutoff tail contributes no oscillatory term.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseOscillation_pu.summary: The cutoff tail leaves the oscillation unchanged

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition.text: The physical transition obtained by conjugating a label transition with the parent flow. It is defined by $Y(s,t,x)=X(0,t,\mathcal A(s,t,X(s,0,x)))$. At initial time zero this becomes $Y(t,a)=X(t,\mathcal A_t(a))$. The definition itself assumes no flow equation; `isLabelFlowOn_physicalTransition` proves that it is the flow of the parent plus the transported correction and perturbation.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition.summary: The physical flow from the parent and label flows

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.text: The physical forward and reverse transition derivatives are bounded by the product of the parent and label derivative bounds. The assumptions `hXf`, `hXr`, `hAf` and `hAr` give differentiability and bounds $D$ and $B$ for both directions. The parent flow hypothesis `hX` identifies its initial map with the identity. The chain rule then yields $\|DY\|\le DB$ and the same estimate for the inverse transition.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.summary: Parent and label derivatives bound the physical deformation

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.text: For a parent flow with time zero in its slab, the physical transition from zero is the parent transition applied after the label transition. The reverse parent map at the initial time becomes the identity. The algebraic formula holds for arbitrary target `t`; the theorem does not assert a flow equation at that unrestricted time.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.summary: Starting at zero simplifies the physical transition

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.text: When parent and label flows both have uniform spatial Lipschitz bounds, conjugated forward and reverse physical transitions are left and right inverses for every allowed time. The result follows from the restart identities of the two component flows. No derivative estimate or volume-preservation conclusion is part of this statement.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.summary: Reverse physical transitions are two-sided inverses

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.text: The physical transition back to time zero is the reverse label transition applied after the reverse parent transition. The parent transition from zero to zero disappears by the initial-value property. The identity is algebraic for arbitrary `t`; analytic flow and inverse claims later restrict that time to the slab.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_.summary: Returning to zero simplifies the inverse transition

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.pullbackField.text:
The label velocity $c=(D_aX)^{-1}(W+v\circ X)$ before restricting to the phase graph. The arguments `X`, `W` and `v` are the parent flow, label–phase correction and Eulerian perturbation. The inverse derivative is written `fderiv ℝ (X t 0) (X 0 t z.1)`. Its application to the correction converts the physical velocity increment into motion of the parent labels.

Default-value audit (b5): The derivative operator fderiv is total and defaults to zero at points where differentiability fails. The intended inverse-deformation interpretation requires the supplied smooth flow and inverse identities; these are not encoded in this definition alone.

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.pullbackField_skewP.text: The pulled-back velocity is unchanged by $(a,s)\mapsto(a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)$. The assumptions `hXf` and `hXr` give lattice equivariance of the forward and inverse parent flows, `hW` gives the profile’s combined translation rule, and `hv` makes the perturbation periodic. The proof also differentiates the inverse flow’s lattice identity, so its coframe has the required periodicity.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.pullbackField_skewP.summary: The label velocity respects combined lattice shifts

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledCutoffTail_ph.text: If `v` has spatial Hölder regularity of order two and norm at most `ε`, then the scaled phase-independent field $G(a)\bigl(v(A(a))\bigr)$ has first jet bounded by $\max\{G_0,G_0A_1+G_1\}\,\varepsilon$. The hypotheses bound the forward derivative, coframe, and coframe derivative, and require $|\ell| \le  1$. No phase-derivative cost appears.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledCutoffTail_ph.summary: A cutoff tail contributes a controlled first jet

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledField.text: The independent label–phase particle field in coordinates $(a/\ell_*,s/h)$. At a scaled point `z`, Lean first evaluates $c$ at `labelPhaseScale ell h z`, then returns $(c/\ell_*,k_*\cdot c/h)$. The definition makes no assumption that the phase already equals $k_*\cdot a$. The subsequent conservation of `phaseDefect` shows that a trajectory started on that graph remains there.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledField.summary: The particle field in scaled label and phase

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledGraph_labelPr.text: If an enlarged state has zero phase defect and both scales are nonzero, recovering its label and embedding that label again gives the original state. This is the converse of the graph's zero-defect identity. It ensures that preserving the scalar defect keeps a trajectory on the intended graph, rather than merely in a larger constraint set.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledGraph_labelPr.summary: Zero phase defect reconstructs the graph point

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledPerturbation_.text: A phase-independent perturbation costs at most one derivative of the inverse deformation and one derivative of the forward map.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledPerturbation_.summary: The pulled-back tail costs one geometric derivative

TorusEuler.ChildFlow.slope_divergence_pu.text: The pulled-back particle field satisfies $(\nabla_a+k_*\partial_s)\cdot c=0$. The hypotheses `hX`, `hU`, `hper`, `hK` and `hUdiv` give the smooth volume-preserving parent flow, while `hdiv` is the total divergence identity for $W+v\circ X$ before the pullback. Differentiability assumptions `hX₂`, `hc` and `hW` justify Piola and the phase derivative. The conclusion is an identity in the independent label and phase variables.
TorusEuler.ChildFlow.slope_divergence_pu.summary: Piola converts solenoidality into label–phase divergence

TorusEuler.CommutesTorusLineDerivatives.text: Requires `P` to preserve every actual derivative relation along each translated torus line $a+s v$. The premise and conclusion use `HasDerivAt` at every real parameter, so they assert existence of the derivative, not just an equation involving a total derivative function. Both the field and its derivative are half-Hölder torus fields.
TorusEuler.CommutesTorusLineDerivatives.summary: Projection commutes with derivatives along torus lines

TorusEuler.CommutesTorusLineDerivatives..text: If `P` commutes with actual derivatives along all torus lines, its directionwise extension has the same property on linear-map-valued fields. The proof differentiates each coordinate evaluation, applies `hP`, and reconstructs the derivative by a finite sum. This lets the same commutation argument be repeated at successive Fréchet derivative orders.

TorusEuler.ComplexEuclideanVec3.text:
This abbreviation is the three-dimensional complex Euclidean target used for Fourier synthesis. Real velocity fields are embedded coordinatewise and recovered by taking their real parts.

Default-value audit (b5): This is a type abbreviation for the source type displayed here. It does not by itself assert a PDE, nonvanishing, smoothness or an existence theorem.
TorusEuler.ComplexEuclideanVec3.summary: Complex Euclidean space for Fourier synthesis

TorusEuler.ComplexPressureTensor.text: This finite function type stores the nine complex entries of a three-dimensional tensor. It is the input space for the scalar pressure symbol. The coordinates use the ordinary finite product norm; symmetry and reality are not encoded in the type and are only present for tensors constructed from real velocities.
TorusEuler.ComplexPressureTensor.summary: Complex coordinates for the velocity tensor

TorusEuler.ComplexVec3.text: This abbreviation represents a complex vector as a function from the three coordinate indices to complex numbers. It is convenient for componentwise Fourier algebra. It is not the Euclidean $L^2$ normed wrapper; conversion to `EuclideanSpace` is made explicitly when orthogonality or contractive operator norms are needed.

TorusEuler.ContinuousOnSlabInSpatialNorm.text: This predicate requires `norm (f r - f t)` to tend to zero as `r` approaches each `t ∈ Icc 0 T` from within the slab. It expresses endpoint continuity using differences of spatial fields. The supplied `norm` is just a real-valued function at this level; its analytic norm properties are not assumed by the definition.
TorusEuler.ContinuousOnSlabInSpatialNorm.summary: Continuity in a spatial norm along a closed slab

TorusEuler.DistinctPairs.text: This subtype consists of pairs whose two coordinates are unequal. It excludes the diagonal before the half-Hölder difference quotient is formed. In a genuine metric space, distinctness makes the distance strictly positive, so its square root has a nonzero reciprocal in the quotient construction.
TorusEuler.DistinctPairs.summary: Pairs of distinct points for difference quotients

TorusEuler.EndpointBoundedTest.text: This subtype packages a measurable scalar function together with existence of a global bound on its norm. It does not demand smoothness or continuity. Such tests can include measurable-set indicators, allowing vanishing integral pairings to detect almost-everywhere zero time means or spatial pairings.

TorusEuler.EndpointCoefficientC1Bound.text:
The coefficient assumptions used by Theorem A.1: nonnegative constants $C_0,C_1$, continuity in time into the spatial half-Hölder space, and differentiability of the periodic lift at every time in $[0,1]$. The lift and its first derivative have norms at most $C_0$ and $C_1$. These are fields of a predicate. They neither assert symmetry nor impose continuity in the stronger $C^{1,1/2}$ norm.

Default-value audit (b5): This is a predicate on the supplied objects. It makes the recorded equalities or bounds assumptions; it does not construct objects satisfying them. The relevant existence and regularity hypotheses are carried by its callers.
TorusEuler.EndpointCoefficientC1Bound.summary: Uniform coefficient and first derivative bounds

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexTimeL2.text: The complex time-path space is L² of complex Euclidean three-vectors over the restriction of Lebesgue measure to $(0,T]$. It receives complex extensions of real time-path operators for the Fourier analysis in labels. No frequency, divergence, or zero-mean restriction is built into this abbreviation.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexTimeL2.summary: Complex velocity paths on the restricted time interval

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.text: A complexification consists of a real embedding, real and imaginary projections, compatibility with multiplication by $i$, reconstruction, and a squared-norm splitting identity. These fields are assumptions carried by the structure. They encode the Hilbert-style real/complex relationship needed to extend coefficient operators with unchanged norm.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.summary: Real and imaginary parts reconstruct the complex space

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Bundle the componentwise extension of `A` as a complex continuous linear map. Complex linearity follows from the real and imaginary decomposition of scalars, and continuity uses the original norm bound. The construction applies to any bounded real endomorphism; no coercivity or invertibility is imposed here.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: The real operator extends complex linearly

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Package extension itself as a real continuous linear map from real bounded endomorphisms to complex bounded endomorphisms. Its continuity certificate uses the norm bound one, with exact norm preservation established separately. This lets smoothness and derivative estimates for operator-valued symbols pass through complexification by composition.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: Complex extension is a bounded map between operator spaces

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Applying `extendOperatorCLM` to a real operator gives exactly `extendOperator A`. This is a definitional compatibility between the convenient continuous-linear-map packaging and the previously constructed extension. It lets later smoothness estimates use the bundled map while algebraic proofs continue to use the component formulas.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: The operator space map evaluates to complex extension

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Package extension as a unital ring homomorphism on bounded endomorphisms. It preserves zero, addition, identity, and composition by the previously proved identities. This algebraic form is used to transport units and their inverses; boundedness and smooth dependence are supplied by the separate continuous-linear-map packaging.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: Complex extension preserves the endomorphism ring

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Complex extension commutes with addition of real bounded operators. Both real and imaginary components receive the sum, so linearity of the embedding rearranges the result into two extended operators. This algebraic equality is later bundled as part of a real-linear map between operator spaces.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: Extending a sum adds the extended operators

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Evaluation of the complex-linear extension is the embedding of `A` applied to the real component plus $i$ times the embedding of `A` applied to the imaginary component. Although the bundled scalar field has changed from real to complex, the underlying function is the same componentwise construction.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: The complex extension applies the operator to both parts

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Complexifying the real frozen operator $rBr+I-r$ gives the same polynomial expression in the extended projection and coefficient. The identity is algebraic and requires no projection, coercivity, or symmetry assumptions on `r` and `B`. Those hypotheses enter the later invertibility and norm estimates for this symbol.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: The frozen operator formula survives complexification

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: The extension of `A * B` equals the product of their extensions, where multiplication of endomorphisms means composition. The real and imaginary projection formulas show that applying `B` then `A` acts componentwise in the expected order. This property is used in frozen-symbol formulas and inverse compatibility.

Applying the extended complex operator to `X.ofReal x` equals embedding `A x`. The imaginary component of the embedded input is zero, so the extension restricts to the original real action. This is the compatibility used to transfer identities obtained with complex Fourier methods back to the real space.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: The extension agrees on embedded real vectors

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: Extending the identity real operator gives the identity complex operator. The proof is precisely the reconstruction axiom of `X`: real part plus $i$ times imaginary part recovers every vector. This identity is required to make extension a unital ring homomorphism on bounded endomorphisms.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: The identity operator remains the identity

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: If `hA : IsUnit A`, extending `Ring.inverse A` equals taking the ring inverse of the extended operator. The proof represents `A` by a unit and maps that unit through the extension homomorphism. The unit assumption is essential: the theorem does not justify interpreting a totalized inverse of a singular operator as a genuine inverse.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: Extension commutes with the inverse of an invertible operator

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.text: For a real scalar `c`, the extension of `c • A` is `c` times the extension of `A`. The real scalar restriction matters because the input operator space is over the real field. Combined with additivity and norm preservation, this gives a real continuous linear map on operator spaces.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.exte.summary: Real scalar multiples extend with the same scalar

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.im_e.text: The imaginary projection of the extended operator is `A` applied to the imaginary projection of the input. Thus the same real operator governs both components. This equality supports norm splitting and coercivity arguments without assuming that the complex input itself is the embedding of a real vector.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.im_e.summary: Imaginary projection commutes with the complex extension

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.norm.text: The norm of `X.extendOperator A` equals the norm of `A`. The upper bound follows from squared-norm splitting; the lower bound tests the extended operator on embedded real vectors, whose norms are unchanged. This exact equality keeps frozen-coefficient constants uniform under complexification.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.norm.summary: Complex extension preserves the operator norm exactly

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.norm.text: For any complexification `X`, the norm of `X.ofReal x` equals the norm of `x`. Apply the squared-norm splitting and use that its real part is `x` and imaginary part is zero. This isometry is later used to prove equality, rather than just an upper bound, of extended operator norms.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.norm.summary: Embedding a real vector preserves its norm

TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.re_e.text: The real projection of `X.extendOperator A z` is `A (X.re z)`. This identifies the real component of the complex-linear operator with the original real coefficient action. It is later used when transferring Fourier multiplier identities back to real-valued velocities and real test functions.
TorusEuler.EndpointComplexification.re_e.summary: Real projection commutes with the complex extension

TorusEuler.EndpointMeanRecoveredWords.text: Records a finite family of spatial derivative words for the same recovered label velocity `g`. The empty word agrees with `g` only on the time slab; derivatives and smoothness are required through order `N`. Each word also has a mixed representation fixed by the Leray projection and satisfies its differentiated projected equation, including the coefficient correction.
TorusEuler.EndpointMeanRecoveredWords.summary: Exact spatial derivatives of one recovered velocity

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.text:
Record equality of the labelwise temporal L2 path and the evaluated time curve for almost every label and almost every time. This predicate asserts no time continuity; continuity is supplied when a representative must be unique at every time.

Default-value audit (b5): The predicate is only almost-everywhere in both variables. Exceptional-time values can differ; at zero duration it is vacuous. Equality at all times requires a positive duration and continuous representatives.

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.add.text: If two mixed fields represent two time curves, their sum represents the pointwise sum of those curves. The proof intersects the almost-everywhere sets for both input representations with the representative identity for $L^2$ addition. This propagates compatibility through the finite source sums in the differentiated endpoint equation.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.add.summary: Represented fields remain compatible under addition

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.coeff.text: A represented mixed field stays represented after multiplication by compatible mixed and time-slice coefficients. The hypothesis `hC` requires the mixed coefficient’s temporal action to equal pointwise multiplication almost everywhere for every input path. Applying it to the path at the current label transfers the representation to the product.

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.eqOn.text: Two continuous time curves representing the same mixed field agree at every time of a positive closed interval. Their primitives agree, and uniqueness of within-interval derivatives identifies their endpoint values as well.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.eqOn.summary: Continuous representatives of one mixed field coincide

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.integ.text: Integrating a mixed field in time represents the primitive of its continuous half-Hölder time curve, provided the duration is nonnegative. The proof uses almost-everywhere equality of the paths, invariance of the primitive under that equality, and commutation of evaluation with integration. This handles the Volterra term in differentiated residuals.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.integ.summary: Time integration preserves the spatial representation

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.norm_.text: If a mixed field represents a continuous half-Hölder time curve bounded by a nonnegative $M$, then its mixed norm is at most $\sqrt T\,M$ for $T\ge0$. The proof constructs the canonical mixed source and identifies it with the given representative through the joint-space embedding. This is a time-$L^2$ conversion, not a pointwise recovery estimate.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.norm_.summary: A continuous source bounds its mixed representative

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.of_sp.text: A continuous half-Holder curve whose L2 image agrees with almost every spatial slice of a mixed field represents that mixed field labelwise almost everywhere. The theorem changes the order of the slice description.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.of_sp.summary: Recovering path representation from spatial slices

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.spati.text: Compatible representatives of lower-order velocity words and coefficient actions give a time-curve representative for the mixed Leibniz correction. The result is assembled from coefficient multiplication and a finite sum.

A continuous time curve representing a mixed field has its L2 value equal to the mixed field's spatial slice for almost every time. The proof constructs a canonical mixed source from the curve and identifies their joint L2 images.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.spati.summary: Spatial slices of a represented mixed field

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.sub.text: The difference of two mixed fields represents the difference of their spatial time curves whenever each original pair satisfies the representation relation. Equality is tracked almost everywhere in both variables rather than assumed pointwise. It supplies compatibility for residuals and commutator corrections containing negative terms.
TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.sub.summary: Represented fields remain compatible under subtraction

TorusEuler.EndpointMixedRepresents.zero.text: The zero mixed field represents the identically zero spatial half-Hölder curve. The statement uses the almost-everywhere representative relation in label and time, since even the zero $L^2$ class is compared through its chosen representative. It provides the base case for linear combinations of represented commutator terms.

TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalJets.text: Collects spatial half-Hölder jets for $F^*F$, $F^*(M^*-M)F$ and the source, together with mixed time-path realizations. Proof fields identify their actions almost everywhere, preserve all spatial derivative edges, and give spatial Lipschitz bounds for the zeroth coefficients. The structure contains regularity and compatibility data, not ellipticity, a flow equation or a solution of the endpoint problem.
TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalJets.summary: Compatible physical coefficients and source in both function spaces

TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery.text: Records that a specified label velocity is the lift of one solenoidal curve with the actual kinetic, vorticity and integrated-force jets. It retains recovered words at every finite order, the projected integrated equation, and both coercivity inequalities. This record links later quantitative estimates to the velocity already returned by the existence construction.
TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery.summary: The recovered mean retains its exact derivative data

TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery..text: For a supplied mean recovery, smooth deformation lift, and smooth periodic force, this constructs half Hölder words for the pulled force $F^*f$. The recovered source words equal their negative time primitives. At order $n+1$, the projected kinetic operator acts on the highest derivative of the same recovered velocity, while the right side uses velocity and force only through order $n$, with explicit binomial coefficient terms.
TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery..summary: The recovered mean obeys the higher time equation

TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery..text: For the actual recovery and its supplied spatial words, `hgEq` identifies source words as negative primitives of a continuous forcing family. With `T ≤ 1`, the fixed-time and mixed inverse bounds, coefficient control, positive label radius, and force bound $G$, every word of length at most $N$ is bounded uniformly in time by $\mathrm{Cap}(1+2^N\mathrm{Kcost})^NG$. “Initial” here means time derivative order zero, not evaluation at time zero.
TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery..summary: The recovered mean has a bound at time order zero

TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery..text: Reuses every field and every exact jet of `rec` while replacing its inverse deformation bound $D_0$ by any $D\ge D_0>0$. Both reciprocal coercivity constants decrease, so their inequalities remain valid. The assumption `hL` ensures the mixed denominator is positive. No new solution is chosen, which preserves the link between existence and the later estimate.
TorusEuler.EndpointPhysicalMeanRecovery..summary: Increasing the inverse bound preserves the recovered mean

TorusEuler.EndpointRealTimeL2.text: This abbreviation is the real vector-valued L² space for Lebesgue measure restricted to $(0,T]$. It is the Hilbert space on which mixed endpoint coefficient operators act. The type contains all square-integrable time paths; zero time mean is a separate projection or subspace condition.
TorusEuler.EndpointRealTimeL2.summary: Real velocity paths on the restricted time interval

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.text:
Package the actual spatial derivative words of a periodic lift as half-Holder curves, including smooth time dependence, evaluation identities, spatial derivative relations, and finite uniform norms for each word.

Default-value audit (b5): This structure stores actual smooth curves and their compatibility proofs. It does not choose default derivatives; existence for a smooth periodic lift is a separate theorem requiring positive duration. Its fields place no claims outside the closed slab.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.summary: Spatial derivative words as smooth Holder curves

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.ba.text: For a smooth periodic lift on a positive-duration slab and a compatible half-Hölder jet package, the zeroth torus curve has a common spatial Lipschitz bound. Compactness and periodicity first bound the lifted gradient; controlled representatives of two torus points then give the factor-two metric conversion. The constant is existential and depends on the underlying field.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.ba.summary: Smooth periodic data give a uniform spatial Lipschitz bound

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.ev.text: For a smooth lifted field and its `EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets`, evaluating the time derivative of the recovered word equals the actual spatial derivative word of the field’s Eulerian time derivative. The time lies in $[0,T]$ and `0 < T`. Evaluation commutes with time differentiation, and the strong spatial derivative relation is preserved at every order.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.ev.summary: Recovered word time derivatives equal derivatives of the lift

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.mu.text: For exact quotient jets of a smooth slab field and a positive label scale, bounds the weighted closed-time half-Hölder norm by $\sqrt2$ times the lifted Hölder jet supremum. The explicit `hB : BddAbove ...` hypothesis prevents using a supremum without finiteness. The jet evaluation identity ensures this estimates the actual spatial derivative word.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.mu.summary: Lifted word bounds control the half Hölder curve

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.mu.text: For a smooth periodic field with recovered half Hölder words, the scaled norm of any length-$N$ word of its $i$th time derivative is bounded by four times the unweighted label norm at order $N+1$, divided by $\sqrt\ell$. This requires $0<\ell\le1$ and `0 < T`. Periodicity and smoothness provide boundedness of the suprema used in the label norm.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.mu.summary: A label norm bounds each recovered time word

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.mu.text: Assume raw derivatives of the selected time derivative have bounds $C(n)AD^{pn}$, with $D\ge1$, nonnegative $A,C$, positive $\ell$, and $\ell D^p\le1$. Then a recovered word of length $n$ has scaled half Hölder norm at most $6(C(n)+C(n+1))AD^p$. The spatial-order dependence is absorbed by the label scale, leaving one fixed parent-scale factor.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.mu.summary: Raw mixed derivative bounds control half Hölder words

TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.sl.text: If all recovered words of a given time derivative through length $n$ satisfy the common scaled norm bound $C$, its finite unweighted label norm is at most the number of admissible words times $C$. The hypotheses include joint smoothness, `0 < T`, and nonnegative $\ell,C$. The proof bounds each word supremum using evaluation in the half Hölder space.
TorusEuler.EndpointSlabHalfHolderJets.sl.summary: Recovered half Hölder word caps bound the label norm

TorusEuler.EndpointSmoothPotential.text:
Package a real-valued smooth function on Euclidean label space together with lattice periodicity. No zero-mean normalization is part of this structure; only its gradient is relevant to the solenoidal test space.

Default-value audit (b5): Smoothness and periodicity are explicit structure fields. Constants and nonzero-mean potentials are allowed; adding a constant does not change the gradient used in the weak solenoidal tests.

TorusEuler.EndpointSobolevEnergyBound.text:
The lower energy bound on the normalized interval. The velocity is `v : Path`, an $L^2$ path, with `endpointIntegral 1 v = 0`; its displacement is $Jv$. For every label, the predicate requires $\mu\|v\|^2$ to be bounded by the integral of $Kv\cdot v+\Omega v\cdot Jv$. This is the derivative representation of the paper’s zero trace Sobolev test paths, and is an assumption of the inverse theorem.

Default-value audit (b5): This is a predicate on the supplied objects. It makes the recorded equalities or bounds assumptions; it does not construct objects satisfying them. The relevant existence and regularity hypotheses are carried by its callers.

TorusEuler.EndpointTorusL2.text:
The joint Hilbert space consists of vector fields square integrable over time restricted to the chosen interval and normalized Haar measure on the label torus. Its elements are almost-everywhere classes.

Default-value audit (b5): For nonpositive T the time measure is zero and this L2 space is trivial. Its elements are equivalence classes, so pointwise values must not be interpreted without separate slice or representative lemmas.

TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness.text:
The full collection of properties for one chosen $u_0,T,u,p$. It requires smooth periodic odd divergence-free initial data, an odd maximal smooth Euler solution with $u(0)=u_0$, two infinite time integrals, bounded velocity and vorticity magnitude tending to infinity at the origin. Both $u$ and its time derivative must have the stated off-origin spatial limits. The integrals take values in $[0,\infty]$ and equal `⊤`; no conversion to a real number occurs. The witness includes maximality, but the later Paper.Statement.theorem_1_1 separately quantifies over other maximal solutions and asserts their equal lifetime and velocity.

Default-value audit (b4): The embedded IsMaximalEulerSolution supplies 0<T and smooth periodic velocity and pressure on the nonempty slab. The initial datum is separately ContDiff, so its divergence is an actual derivative trace. Both divergent integrals are lintegrals with values in ℝ≥0∞ and are compared directly with ⊤: they are not Bochner integrals and never use toReal ⊤=0. The finite-velocity clause uses ENNReal.ofReal C; if C is negative it becomes the stronger bound by zero, not a way to hide an unbounded velocity. The fixed cell is nonzero measure. Central curl divergence is a genuine limit because the terminal filter is nonbottom. Smooth slices are essential when relating pointwise curl to essential supremum. Off-origin derivative limits retain the regularity guards described for HasOffOriginLimits. These observations do not constitute a full independent proof of the singularity theorem.
TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness.summary: Initial data and terminal singularity properties

TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientCoordinatePo.text: Requires smooth coefficient slices, a positive table of order constants, boundedness of every coordinate-derivative supremum set, and the corresponding power estimate for their finite sum. The explicit `BddAbove` clause is part of the mathematical content. It makes this encoding comparable with actual operator-norm derivative bounds under $D\ge1$.
TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientCoordinatePo.summary: Bounded coordinate versions of coefficient powers

TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientMultiIndexPo.text: This library predicate records smooth spatial slices and bounds $|c|_m\le C_mD^{a(m+1)}$ using one word per multi-index. It existentially chooses a sequence $C_m\ge1$ after the fixed parameter and coefficient. Consequently the predicate itself does not encode independence of these constants from a varying $D$ or field. The current Paper vocabulary supplies the constants as inputs, allowing the statement of Lemma D.2 to make that uniformity explicit.
TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientMultiIndexPo.summary: Polynomial coefficient bounds at every derivative order

TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientPower.text: Encodes smoothness of every spatial coefficient slice and one order-indexed table $C_m\ge1$ such that $\|D^m c(t,x)\|\le C_mD^{a(m+1)}$ for all indices and points. The derivative is measured in operator norm. Uniformity is over `t` and `x` after `D,a,c` are fixed; the definition alone does not make the table uniform over different families.

TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientPower.mono.text: If the coefficient derivatives satisfy `FiniteCoefficientPower D a c`, then they also satisfy the predicate with exponent `b` whenever $D\ge1$ and $a\le b$. The same smoothness and prefactor table work. Monotonicity of nonnegative powers supplies the comparison; no new coefficient regularity is constructed.

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.text:
Package solvers for admissible mean and zero-mean transverse sources, their pressure equations, and a divergence completion preserving zero mean. This is abstract input to the ordered recursion, not a proof of analytic solvability.

Default-value audit (b5): Solvers are supplied functions with equations and source admissibility proofs. This structure does not assert their existence for arbitrary analytic data; the physical realization provides them later. Its completion operator need not independently carry a divergence theorem in this abstract structure.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.summary: The mean and transverse solvers for a finite hierarchy

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text:
Construct the finite hierarchy from the supplied mean and transverse solvers, leading wave, completion switch, and phase-independent parent residual. The recursion determines each mean before the corresponding oscillation; positive-depth index behavior is proved separately.

Default-value audit (b5): The recursion is defined for every natural depth, including zero. The theorem that profiles vanish at index zero or beyond the retained depth assumes positive depth; the prescribed leading level is treated specially by the recursion. Do not extrapolate the positive-depth zero statement to depth zero.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: The finite profiles produced by ordered solves

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: At every index $p$, the average of the constructed mean `B p` equals that mean. The proof projects `average_B` from the recursive level. This is an operator-level phase-independence statement; interpreting it as independence of the phase variable uses the concrete periodic profile realization.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Every constructed mean is fixed by averaging

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: At each retained oscillatory level, including the leading level, the constructed completion equals the supplied completion operator applied to that oscillation. The library stores completion at its input level, whereas the paper names the output C at the next level.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Every retained oscillation receives its completion

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: Given a linear `divergence`, assume completed transverse outputs have zero divergence and every mean-solver output does too. The finite constructed velocity then has zero divergence. The theorem uses the actual selected completion at each retained index and treats the leading mean as zero; it does not derive the supplied solver divergence properties.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: The constructed finite velocity is divergence free

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: For positive retained depth, all five stored profile sequences vanish at index zero and beyond that depth. The named hypotheses `hP` and `hp` require positive depth and an unused index. The solvers, the mean-valued residual and the leading transverse output are inputs. The library stores the correction made from $V_p$ as `u.C p`; in the current paper that is $C_{p+1}$. Thus `u.C 0 = 0` corresponds to the paper's $C_1=0$, not a claimed paper convention for $C_0$. This is a finite-sequence convention and contains no assertion about an infinite hierarchy.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Hierarchy profiles vanish at unused indices

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: The constructed profiles satisfy both correction equations at every retained level specified by `hp`. The solver package `S` already provides mean and transverse solves, and `hR` states that the parent residual is a mean. The oscillatory source is minus the centered source and the mean-phase interaction; the mean source also includes the parent residual at level two. This declaration is abstract linear-operator algebra: identifying those operators with material derivatives, pressure gradients, and covectors requires the physical instantiation.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Mean and oscillatory equations at each retained level

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: The constructed hierarchy starts with the supplied leading velocity and pressure, while its first mean velocity and pressure are zero. The binder `S` supplies the abstract finite hierarchy solvers, and `leading` supplies a transverse leading output. The hypothesis `hR` says the parent residual is fixed by averaging. This is an algebraic fact about the construction; the identity of `leading.V` with a physical switched wave is established separately.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Finite hierarchy keeps its prescribed leading wave

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: Proves by strong induction that the actual selected finite construction has the velocity and pressure memberships at every index. It requires depth at least one, compatible initial data, operator closure and separate preservation by the chosen mean, transverse and completion solvers. Out-of-range levels use the construction’s proved zero values; retained levels follow the mean-before-transverse order.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Every selected hierarchy level preserves the required classes

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: If every selected mean solve satisfies the supplied seminorm estimate with one additional source derivative, then each constructed level from two through `P` satisfies the corresponding measured mean bound. The forcing is identified using the actual ordered construction. The theorem transports a solve estimate into level notation rather than proving the analytic inverse bound.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: A selected mean estimate becomes a level estimate

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: At each retained correction level, the constructed mean and pressure equal the selected mean solver's outputs for the prescribed averaged source. The hypothesis `hp : p ∈ Finset.Icc 2 P` fixes the retained level, while `hR` says the parent residual is phase independent. The parent residual enters only at level two. This identity follows from the ordered recursion with `S : FiniteHierarchySolvers A`; the concrete analytic solvers are supplied separately by `physicalSolvers`.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: The constructed mean is the selected mean solve

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: For a hierarchy with at least one retained level, the level-one oscillatory source, mean source and mean profile have zero measured size, as does completion level zero. This uses the seed values built into the ordered construction and the fact that a seminorm vanishes at zero. It does not assert that the leading oscillation vanishes.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: The initial mean and source entries vanish

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: For a retained correction level, the measured mean and transverse sources equal the supplied norm functions applied to the corresponding material-plus-pressure left-hand sides. The construction’s exact equations justify the substitution. These measuring functions need only be nonnegative here; no triangle inequality or genuine norm interpretation is asserted by this lemma.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Measure the actual solved left-hand sides at correction levels

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: For `hP : 2 ≤ P`, a supplied leading momentum equation and mean-invariant parent residual give the complete algebraic residual identity. All retained mean and transverse sources cancel, leaving the hierarchy remainder plus the leading and completion switching terms. Analytic realizations of the operators and solvers remain explicit inputs through `A` and `S`.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Cancel every retained source in the finite expansion

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: Assume nonnegative numerical coefficients, the leading weighted estimate, selected mean and completion estimates, the transverse solve estimate, and `HierarchySourceTermBounds` for the actual constructed profiles. Then the measured levels satisfy `HierarchyNormRecurrence` through the supplied derivative reserve `H`. Each analytic ingredient remains an explicit premise; the proof assembles them and handles the prescribed zero seed entries.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: The constructed profiles satisfy the quantitative recurrence

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: For the actual finite hierarchy constructed by `S`, obtains `HierarchyNormRecurrence` from a leading-wave bound, a mean solver estimate from `Uforce` to `U`, a completion estimate, oscillatory solver estimates, and `HierarchySourceTermBounds`. It assumes positive depth, mean residual, and nonnegative frequency and constants. The mean-source measurement remains separate throughout, so its residual hypothesis can use a lower time order. The theorem does not establish those analytic input estimates itself.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: The selected finite hierarchy obeys the separate mean force recurrence

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: For every index, the constructed oscillation and completion have zero average, and phase advection by the oscillation annihilates every second input. These properties come directly from the level records, including their zero branches. The theorem does not assert support, differentiability, or bounds for the profiles.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Every constructed oscillation is transverse and mean zero

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: The constructed transverse velocity and pressure equal the selected solver's outputs for $f_p+f_p^S$ at every retained correction level. The hypotheses `hp : p ∈ Finset.Icc 2 P` and `hR` fix the level and phase-independent parent residual. The source first removes the phase mean from $H_p$, then adds the negative mean-advection sum. The theorem also supplies the source's zero phase mean. The new mean has already been inserted before the transverse solver is called.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: The constructed oscillation is the selected transverse solve

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.text: Subtracting the average from the constructed finite velocity leaves the sum of its oscillatory velocities and completions. The result uses only the zero-average and fixed-average proofs stored in each level. It identifies the oscillatory part of the expansion without imposing a positivity condition on the depth.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr.summary: Recover the sum of all completed oscillations

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.remain.text: Bounds the actual hierarchy remainder by an explicit constant times $\lambda^{\mathrm{hierarchyOscExponent}(P+1)}$. Besides `P ≥ 1`, frequency and parent factor at least one, and nonnegative constants, it requires $L^6\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, spatial monotonicity of the velocity norms, retained level bounds, and separate linear and quadratic tail estimates. The proof uses the exact identities $V_{P+1}=B_{P+1}=0$ and $Y_{P+1}=C_P$ at the end of the retained expansion.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.remain.summary: The finite depth remainder keeps the next level decay

TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.veloci.text: For the exact selected hierarchy, assumes level bounds at spatial order `n`, frequency and parent factor at least one, and `C ≥ 0`. The oscillatory velocity sum is at most $2P C L^2\lambda^{-5/4}$ and its phase average at most $P C L^6\lambda^{-5/2}$, with `P` represented by the cardinality of the retained index set. The separate mean-source measurement does not alter these velocity measurements. No infinite sum or limiting solution is asserted.
TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.veloci.summary: Summed oscillations and means retain their two decay rates

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.text: The central covector and amplitude of the first wave, together with a positive initial amplitude scale. The structure records the two affine wave equations, transversality, initial directions $\lambda e_1$ and $e_2$, and attainment of the peak $\lambda^{-3/4}$ on $[0,T]$. These are fields required of a value `w : FirstWaveOrigin s T freq`; existence is proved separately.

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.amplitude_eq_.text: On $[0,T]$, the amplitude stored in `FirstWaveOrigin` equals the explicit smooth seed at label zero with scale `w.scale`. The assumptions are nonnegative lifespan and nonzero frequency. Linear-ODE uniqueness matches the common equation and initial value, so the explicit label extension inherits the central solution’s attained-maximum normalization.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.amplitude_eq_.summary: The smooth seed retains the central peak normalization

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.child_T4_cent.text: Given the actual first primary wave, differentiable oscillatory and mean corrections, and a second-order Hölder cutoff-tail budget, the child gradient has the prescribed rank-one splitting with error at most `freq^(-1/4)`. The first crossing occurs at time zero, and the normalized seed supplies the coupling and strength bounds. The approximation and tail estimates remain explicit hypotheses.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.child_T4_cent.summary: The first child satisfies the central and crossing bounds

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.covector_eq_t.text: On a nonnegative time interval, the covector stored in a `FirstWaveOrigin` agrees at the origin with the explicit inverse-transpose transport formula. Both solve the same linear ODE and have identical initial data. The conclusion is equality only on $[0,T]$, so arbitrary extensions of the stored curve outside that interval are irrelevant.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.covector_eq_t.summary: The central ODE uses the actual transported covector

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.exists_seed_a.text: For each label, constructs an amplitude with the central seed’s initial value and the label-dependent constant shear coefficient. It remains nonzero and perpendicular to the actual transported covector throughout $[0,T]$. The hypothesis `hT` permits a degenerate interval; this theorem gives separate existence for each label and does not yet establish joint smoothness in the label.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.exists_seed_a.summary: Every label admits a transverse affine seed

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.first_couplin.text: The first moving-frame coupling of the stationary shear is at least $\pi$ throughout $[0,T]$. Lean assumes `hf : 0 < freq`, `hs : |s| ≤ 1`, the small-slab condition `hsmall`, and `ht : t ∈ Icc 0 T`. The proof estimates the frame’s variation from its coordinate-frame value at time zero.

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.hasFDerivAt_c.text: The actual completed localized first-wave velocity has precisely the normalized affine seed’s rank-one derivative at the origin at time zero. The statement concerns the completed wave, not only its leading profile. Nonzero frequency and the support and phase-scale hypotheses come from the explicit initial-wave derivative theorem.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.hasFDerivAt_c.summary: At time zero completion leaves the exact central gradient

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.hasFDerivAt_h.text: The Eulerian graph readout of the hierarchy’s leading velocity has the same rank-one derivative at the origin as the normalized first-wave pair. The graph identity reduces it to the actual localized transported wave. The time belongs to the slab, the frequency is positive, and the smooth localization hypotheses are explicit.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.hasFDerivAt_h.summary: The profile graph has the normalized first-wave gradient

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.hasFDerivAt_l.text: At every time in the first slab, the centered-periodized transported primary wave has derivative `rankOne ℝ (w.amplitude t) (w.covector t)` at the origin. Positive frequency and the radial-support and phase-scale hypotheses are required. The scalar wave vanishes at zero phase, eliminating derivatives of its slowly varying coefficient.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.hasFDerivAt_l.summary: The actual localized first wave has the prescribed central gradient

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.initial_coupl.text: The first central wave has couplings $\nu(0)=2\pi$ and $\eta(0)=2\pi s$ under `hf : 0 < freq`. Its positive amplitude scale and positive frequency make its initial normalized frame exactly $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The declaration calculates both frame entries of the stationary shear gradient, rather than assuming the coupling values.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.initial_coupl.summary: Initial shear couplings of the first wave

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.initial_cross.text: For a normalized `FirstWaveOrigin`, positive frequency and small shear-time product imply the initial coupling ratio equals the shear parameter. The first coupling lies between $\pi$ and $4\pi$, and the strength lies between `C⁻¹*freq^(1/4)` and `C*freq^(1/4)*L²` when `C ≥ 2` and `L ≥ 1`.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.initial_cross.summary: The first crossing has the required couplings and strength

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.initial_profi.text: If $0<h\le1$ and the spatial envelope equals one near the origin, the initial leading profile has derivative $a(0)\otimes k(0)$ there. The scalar wave profile has derivative one at zero, while the locally constant envelope contributes no derivative. This is a statement about the leading wave; the completed curl velocity is treated separately.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.initial_profi.summary: The initial leading wave has the prescribed rank one gradient

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.initial_proje.text: The initial transverse projection leaves the first-wave amplitude unchanged at every label. The binders are a normalized wave `w`, an interval condition `hT : 0 ≤ T`, and a label `a`. The covector is $\lambda e_1$ at time zero, and its inner product with the initial amplitude is zero by the transversality field of `w`.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.initial_proje.summary: The initial transverse projection changes nothing

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.initial_stren.text: The initial product $|\kappa(0)|\,|a(0)|$ lies between $\lambda^{1/4}/2$ and $\lambda^{1/4}$. The inputs are `w : FirstWaveOrigin s T freq`, `hf : 0 < freq`, and `hsmall : T * ‖stationaryShearGradient s‖ ≤ 1 / 8`. The attained peak and amplitude propagation bound control the initial amplitude; its covector has length $\lambda$.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.initial_stren.summary: The initial strength lies at the prescribed scale

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.localized_cen.text: For the first shear wave with positive frequency, $|s|\le1$, and $T\|B_s\|\le1/8$, every amplitude solution has forward growth relative to the distinguished amplitude bounded by any $D\ge2$. The distinguished wave also has raw central coupling at least $D^{-1}$ times its norm product. These are the two center hypotheses needed to localize the initial wave.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.localized_cen.summary: The first wave supplies stability and positive coupling

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.nextSlabData.text: The first wave restricted to a shorter slab retains nonzero perpendicular data and its affine equations over the stationary shear. For positive frequency and the small-time hypothesis, its initial first coupling is $2\pi$, its coupling ratio is `s`, and its strength lies between half and all of $\mathrm{freq}^{1/4}$. The second wave activates at zero.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.nextSlabData.summary: The first wave supplies the successor data at time zero

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.scale_le_cent.text: For `w : FirstWaveOrigin s T freq`, a nonzero frequency and a time in $[0,T]$ with $t\le1$ identify the chosen amplitude with the explicit seed. The positive normalization scale is then bounded by $[1+(2\pi)^2]\|w.amplitude\ t\|$. This transfers the explicit coordinate estimate to the abstract first-wave data.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.scale_le_cent.summary: The chosen first wave controls its normalization

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.strength_boun.text: The first wave’s sharper initial strength bounds imply the same lower and upper constants used for later crossings, once the next gain `L` is at least one. Positive frequency and the small stationary-shear interval assumption are retained. This unifies the base case with the numerical convention used by subsequent induction steps.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.strength_boun.summary: The first wave fits the common strength constants

TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.weighted_forw.text: For a normalized wave `w`, every solution `b` of its linear amplitude equation satisfies $|b(v)|/\gamma(v)\le D|b(u)|/\gamma(u)$ between ordered times in $[0,T]$. Lean assumes positive frequency, `hsmall`, `hD : 2 ≤ D`, and the derivative hypothesis `hb`. No transversality hypothesis on `b` is required. Here $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|a|$.
TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.weighted_forw.summary: Weighted propagation along the first wave

TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.continuousOn_.text: With continuous nonzero wave paths and continuous strain, additionally assumes `hν` that the first normalized coupling never vanishes. It then proves continuity of the second coupling divided by the first. Positivity is not needed for this continuity statement, but the amplification construction later supplies the stronger lower bound $\varepsilon/2$, making the ratio well-defined throughout the window.
TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.continuousOn_.summary: The coupling ratio is continuous away from a zero denominator

TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.continuousOn_.text: For continuous nonzero wave-vector and amplitude paths and a continuous strain, proves continuity of both normalized couplings. The scale $S$ is a fixed real parameter and need not be positive here. No transversality or trace-free hypothesis is needed for continuity of the formulas; those conditions establish their geometric meaning and bounds in the application.

TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.couplingNumer.text: The pair contains the two polynomial numerators before division by wave and amplitude norms. Its scalar argument `r` represents $S^{-2}$, not the growth rate. The amplitude ratio is `w=U/V=-q` in the paper’s notation, so the middle term in the second numerator has the corresponding minus sign.
TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.couplingNumer.summary: Numerators for the two new-wave couplings

TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.couplingNumer.text: Substituting $X=x$, $Q=-\varepsilon\tau$, $Z=1$, $w=Y$, $z=xY+\varepsilon\tau$, and $S^{-2}=0$ into the coupling numerators gives $x+\varepsilon+2\varepsilon\tau Y$ and $-1+\varepsilon x+2(1+x^2)Y^2+2\varepsilon\tau xY$. The variables `ε`, `τ`, and `y` are arbitrary reals. This is an exact algebraic reference calculation; it does not assign a finite real shear parameter with inverse square zero.
TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.couplingNumer.summary: Reference values of the two coupling numerators

TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.coupling_conc.text: Given the reference representation `hform`, the deviation bound $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$, and uniform coupling errors controlled through $\kappa\le CT^p\delta$, sufficiently large `C₀` absorbs the polynomial losses. The first normalized coupling is at least $\varepsilon/2$ throughout $[0,T]$. For $t\ge\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, it lies within $\varepsilon$ of one and the coupling ratio divided by $s$ lies within $1/2$ of one.
TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.coupling_conc.summary: A small polynomial error gives positive successor couplings

TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.forcing.text: The three quantities obtained by applying a strain matrix to an amplitude with normalized components $(-w/S,1,z/S)$. The first and third outputs are multiplied by $S$, matching the paper's $f_1,f_2,f_3$. The argument `A : Entries` is the complete strain matrix in the frame; its $(1,0)$ entry includes the rank-one shear when that strain is substituted. The definition itself imposes no equation or size condition.
TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.forcing.summary: Scaled strain components acting on the amplitude

TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.forcing_sub_r.text: Assume $S\ge1$, box radius $R\ge4$, $|w|\le2$, $|z|\le6R$, and $|w-y|\le\kappa$. If every scaled strain entry differs from reference by at most $d\ge0$, each forcing coordinate differs from $(1/2,-y,\varepsilon/2)$ by at most $\kappa+7Rd$. The estimate retains the growing size of the third amplitude coordinate.
TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.forcing_sub_r.summary: Forcing coordinates follow the scaled strain errors

TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.normalizedEta.text:
Define twice shear times the inner product of the cross-product direction with the normalized-strain image of the normalized amplitude. Perpendicularity and nonvanishing are hypotheses of its physical interpretation, not of this total formula.

Default-value audit (b5): A zero wave or amplitude vector makes the normalized direction and coupling zero. Parallel nonzero vectors also give zero cross product. The new-wave interpretation requires the separately proved perpendicular nonzero data and orientation.
TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.normalizedEta.summary: The second coupling of the normalized strain

TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.normalizedNu.text:
Define twice shear times the inner product of the normalized wave direction with the strain applied to the normalized amplitude direction. When the strain is divided by the growth rate and physical parameters hold, this is the first physical coupling divided by the preceding first coupling.
