TorusEuler.continuous_realBanachFourierC.summary: Continuity of the real convolution output

TorusEuler.continuous_realVectorFourierC.text: The real vector cutoff of any torus function is continuous because its output is a finite Fourier sum followed by a continuous real-part map. No measurability or integrability hypothesis is asserted for the input. This regularity of the reconstructed output must be distinguished from a classical integral interpretation of its coefficients.

TorusEuler.coordinateCurl_rankOne.text: The coordinate curl of the rank-one derivative $a\otimes k$ is $k\times a$. The vectors `a` and `k` are arbitrary elements of three-dimensional Euclidean space. In Lean, `(innerSL ℝ k).smulRight a` is the linear map $v\mapsto\langle k,v\rangle a$. This identity determines the orientation of the curl contribution used in the projection argument; no orthogonality assumption is required.

TorusEuler.coordinateDirection.text:
The Eulerian coordinate directions in the lift.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.

TorusEuler.couplingRatioOfGain.text: The ratio $\varepsilon=L^{-2}$ prescribed from the logarithmic gain. Lean writes it as `(L ^ 2)⁻¹`, with real input $L$. This definition alone permits zero or negative inputs; the subsequent schedule and crossing lemmas establish positivity of the gains where the physical ratio is used. The schedule associates $\varepsilon_{j-1}$ with $L_j$, so the frequency and coupling indices differ by one.
TorusEuler.couplingRatioOfGain.summary: Coupling ratio prescribed by the logarithmic gain

TorusEuler.couplingRatioOfGain_step.text: For `hL : 0 < L` and `hstep : 640 * L ≤ LNext`, the next prescribed ratio equals $(L/L_{\rm next})^2$ times the preceding one and is at most its thirty-second part. The same theorem gives $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}=LL_{\rm next}\le L_{\rm next}^2$. These are algebraic consequences of defining the ratio as the inverse squared gain.

TorusEuler.cross3.text:
Define the standard Euclidean cross product by transporting the coordinate cross product to the Euclidean-space type. It fixes the orientation of the third moving-frame vector and of curl-based constructions.

Default-value audit (b5): The coordinate cross product is bilinear and total, including zero and parallel vectors. It gives a unit third frame vector only when the first two vectors satisfy the separate normalization and perpendicularity assumptions.
TorusEuler.cross3.summary: The oriented cross product in three dimensions

TorusEuler.cross3Left.text:
This continuous linear map sends v to κ × v in three-dimensional Euclidean space. The construction transfers the coordinate cross product through the Euclidean-space equivalence.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.

TorusEuler.cross3Left_apply.text: Applying the bounded linear cross-product map to v gives the ordinary vector cross product κ × v. This identifies the operator packaging used in the divergence completion.
TorusEuler.cross3Left_apply.summary: The linear cross-product map has the expected value

TorusEuler.cross3_cross3.text: In three-dimensional Euclidean space, expands $\kappa\times(u\times v)$ as $\langle\kappa,v\rangle u-\langle u,\kappa\rangle v$. The formula is unconditional and fixes the sign convention used by the wave potential. The proof transfers the coordinate cross-product identity through the Euclidean-space wrapper; no nonzero or orthogonality hypothesis enters.

TorusEuler.cross3_neg_inv_norm_sq_smul.text: For nonzero $\kappa$ and a transverse vector $v$, proves that applying $\kappa\times$ to $-\|\kappa\|^{-2}(\kappa\times v)$ returns $v$. The transverse hypothesis removes the longitudinal term in the triple product, while `hκ` justifies cancellation of the squared norm. This is the algebraic inversion used before integrating the wave potential in phase.

TorusEuler.crossingClock_le_endpointHalf.text: The upper crossing time $2(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}/r$ is at most $\mu^{-1/8}L_{\rm next}^3$. Lean assumes positive `μ`, `c`, and `L`, gain growth `hstep`, the rate lower bound `hr`, and `hlarge : 2 / c ≤ LNext`. This is the scalar conversion from normalized time to the physical endpoint half length.
TorusEuler.crossingClock_le_endpointHalf.summary: The crossing bracket fits before the midpoint

TorusEuler.crossingHorizon_eq_of_gains.text: For positive `L` and $640L\le L_{next}$, the abstract crossing horizon at the two inverse-square gain ratios equals $2LL_{next}$. These assumptions select the appropriate horizon branch and justify the reciprocal-square-root simplification. The theorem is an exact scalar identity, preceding any choice of a physical crossing.
TorusEuler.crossingHorizon_eq_of_gains.summary: The crossing horizon is twice the product of gains

TorusEuler.curl.text:
The vorticity of v at x is curlOfDerivative applied to fderiv ℝ v x. On a differentiable field this is the usual three-dimensional curl with the orientation used in the paper. The bare definition imposes no regularity on v; the smoothness of an Euler solution is supplied by its surrounding predicate.

Default-value audit (b4): A nondifferentiable v has default derivative zero at the offending point, and hence curl v x = 0 there. This can make an isolated curl equation misleading. The main witness requires smoothness on the physical slab, and IsEulerSolution.contDiff_velocity_slice exposes the guard. Its terminal curl limit uses actual smooth slices before T; no derivative at T is assumed.
TorusEuler.curl.summary: Vorticity from the spatial velocity derivative

TorusEuler.curlIntegral_eq_top_of_activa.text: For monotone activation times and a gain sequence tending to infinity, eventual positive-frequency, normalized-delay, rate, and central-curl bounds force the curl integral on $[0,T)$ to be infinite. The velocity slices must be spatially continuously differentiable. Each eligible interval already carries mass proportional to its gain; the proof does not sum disjoint intervals or require activation times to converge to `T`.
TorusEuler.curlIntegral_eq_top_of_activa.summary: Unbounded interval mass forces the total curl integral to diverge

TorusEuler.curlIntegral_eq_top_of_activa.text: The direct interval-mass conclusion remains valid when the central curl lower bound contains the errors $B\mu_j^{1/32}+B$, provided the frequency sequence and gain sequence both tend to infinity. Activation times are monotone, relevant intervals lie in $[0,T)$, and spatial slices are continuously differentiable. The errors are absorbed into half the positive leading coefficient before applying the exact-bound theorem.
TorusEuler.curlIntegral_eq_top_of_activa.summary: Lower-order curl errors preserve divergence of the integral

TorusEuler.curlIntegral_eq_top_of_induct.text: With diverging frequencies, monotone activation times below `T`, continuously differentiable spatial slices, and eventual strength and coupling bounds, actual growing crossings from `activation (j + 2)` to `activation (j + 3)` supply the normalized delays needed for integral divergence. The curl lower bound uses `freq (j + 1)` with lower-order errors. These crossings and intervalwise curl bounds are hypotheses; neither an Euler equation nor convergence of activation times is required.
TorusEuler.curlIntegral_eq_top_of_induct.summary: Actual scheduled crossings force the terminal curl integral to diverge

TorusEuler.curlIntegral_lower_bound_on_i.text: If every slice on $[0,T)$ is spatially continuously differentiable and its central curl is at least $m\ge0$ on $[a,b)$, with $a\ge0$ and $b\le T$, the total curl integral is at least $m(b-a)$. The statement does not require $a\le b$; in the reversed case the extended-nonnegative lower bound is zero.
TorusEuler.curlIntegral_lower_bound_on_i.summary: A central curl lower bound forces interval integral mass

TorusEuler.curlOfDerivative.text:
Given an actual continuous linear map D : Vec3 →L[ℝ] Vec3, take its three columns D e₀, D e₁, D e₂. The output is ((D e₁)₂−(D e₂)₁, (D e₂)₀−(D e₀)₂, (D e₀)₁−(D e₁)₀) in zero-based indexing. When D=Dv this is (∂₂v₃−∂₃v₂, ∂₃v₁−∂₁v₃, ∂₁v₂−∂₂v₁) in the paper’s indexing. This operation only reads the antisymmetric part; it does not itself differentiate a field.

Default-value audit (b4): Finite linear algebra only: subtraction, application to three basis vectors and a Euclidean wrapper. There is no denominator or derivative computation. If the caller obtained D from fderiv of a nondifferentiable function, the zero-default risk belongs to that caller, especially curl.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.curlOfDerivative.summary: The antisymmetric derivative entries giving curl

TorusEuler.curlOfDerivativeCLM.text:
Curl as a bounded linear function of the velocity gradient.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.curlOfDerivativeCLM.summary: Curl as a bounded linear map of the gradient

TorusEuler.curlOfDerivative_add.text: The vector obtained by taking the antisymmetric coordinate combinations of a derivative matrix is additive in that matrix. This is a finite-coordinate linear identity. It permits the curl of the transported profile derivative to split into its label contribution and its rank-one phase contribution.

TorusEuler.curlOfDerivative_smul.text: The algebraic curl of cD is c times the algebraic curl of D. No differentiability hypothesis is needed because D is already supplied as a continuous linear map.

TorusEuler.curl_planeWave.text: If `hF` gives the scalar profile derivative at $k\cdot x$, the curl of $F(k\cdot y)a$ at `x` is that derivative times $k\times a$. The wave vector and amplitude are constant here. The explicit derivative hypothesis prevents relying on totalized differentiation of an arbitrary profile.
TorusEuler.curl_planeWave.summary: The plane wave curl follows the frequency cross amplitude

TorusEuler.curl_transportedProfile.text: The Eulerian curl of a profile graph is the sum of the pulled-back label curl and $\kappa\times\partial_sQ$. The derivative hypothesis `hA` identifies the inverse-label differential, and `hQ` assumes joint differentiability of the potential in label and phase at the graph point. The theorem spells out both parts using `curlOfDerivative` and a cross product. It is a local chain rule and does not require phase periodicity or a support assumption.

TorusEuler.curl_transportedWavePotential.text: Assume `hA` differentiates the inverse label, `hκ` identifies its transported covector, `hk` excludes zero covector, and `htrans` gives phasewise transversality. With phase continuity `hV` and joint potential differentiability `hQ`, the transported potential curl equals the evaluated oscillation plus its slow label curl. Periodicity is not required for this local identity.
TorusEuler.curl_transportedWavePotential.summary: The potential curl recovers the wave plus its slow correction

TorusEuler.curl_transportedWavePotential.text: The curl of the transported potential equals the transported oscillation plus its slow curl taken with the phase held fixed. The hypothesis `hκ` identifies the covector with the adjoint inverse-label derivative, while `hk`, `hV`, and `htrans` supply nonvanishing, continuity, and transversality. The regularity assumptions `hA` and `hQ` make both differentiated terms meaningful. This theorem supplies the first completed-velocity identity in Eulerian coordinates rather than an independent formal operator notation.
TorusEuler.curl_transportedWavePotential.summary: Completed oscillation is an exact Eulerian curl

TorusEuler.currySlab.text: Jointly continuous data on a closed slab define, for every parameter, a continuous time path obtained by fixing that parameter. The continuity proof is stored with the path. This definition only constructs the path-valued function; its continuity or smoothness in the parameter is proved by subsequent results.
TorusEuler.currySlab.summary: View joint data as parameterized time paths

TorusEuler.currySlabWithin.text: For a parameter belonging to `S`, this constructs its continuous time path from joint continuity on the slab times `S`. For parameters outside `S`, it returns the zero path. The later continuity and smoothness statements are within `S`, so the arbitrary total extension does not supply behavior across its boundary.
TorusEuler.currySlabWithin.summary: Restrict parameterized time paths to their valid domain

TorusEuler.currySlabWithin_apply.text: If `hp : p ∈ S`, evaluation of the restricted curried path at a slab time gives the original value $X(t,p)$. The membership hypothesis selects the nondefault branch of the definition. There is no corresponding equality outside `S`, where the constructed path has deliberately been set to zero.
TorusEuler.currySlabWithin_apply.summary: Inside the parameter domain the path is exact

TorusEuler.cutoffHolderTailConstant.text: Defines the loss-`k` tail constant as the absolute kernel moment, with an additional one when `k=0`. For positive loss the Taylor remainder supplies the bound directly; for zero loss the identity term in $f-S_\Lambda f$ must be included alongside the convolution norm. The distinction is intentional.
TorusEuler.cutoffHolderTailConstant.summary: The tail constant includes the order-zero identity term

TorusEuler.cutoffHolderTailUniformConsta.text: Defines $(M+1)$ times one plus the sum of absolute kernel moments through order `M`. The finite sum covers every possible loss of derivatives, and the prefactor covers the number of derivative levels in the Hölder norm. The constant depends on the fixed Schwartz kernel and input order, never on the cutoff scale or field.
TorusEuler.cutoffHolderTailUniformConsta.summary: One cutoff constant for a fixed input order

TorusEuler.cutoffKernelAbsoluteMoment.text: Defines the `k`th absolute spatial moment $\int\|y\|^k\|K(y)\|\,dy$ of a complex Schwartz kernel. These constants measure the cost of the Taylor remainder after convolution. The kernel is bundled as a Schwartz map, so every polynomially weighted norm is integrable and the constant is finite.

TorusEuler.cutoffMomentumTensor.text: The two continuous torus vector fields `g` and `h` are combined pointwise by the continuous bilinear map `momentumTensor`. The result is bundled as a continuous torus tensor field. Keeping the inputs separate allows the time Leibniz formula to pair jets of different orders before applying the tensor Fourier cutoff.
TorusEuler.cutoffMomentumTensor.summary: Form the momentum tensor of two torus fields

TorusEuler.cutoffPressureDifferenceSourc.text: Defines the scalar source as the negative trace-square difference minus the trace of `DR`. With velocity-gradient and residual-gradient representations and the later momentum and pressure-Poisson hypotheses, it equals $\Delta(p-\Pi)$. The definition itself accepts arbitrary half-Hölder operator fields; the later residual theorem establishes that differential interpretation.
TorusEuler.cutoffPressureDifferenceSourc.summary: Include the residual divergence in the pressure source

TorusEuler.cutoffPressureDifferenceSourc.text: Expands the scalar source into the negative difference of the traces of two operator squares and the negative trace of the residual operator. This fixes both signs before the Fourier multiplier is applied. It is valid for arbitrary supplied operator fields, independently of any velocity or pressure equation.
TorusEuler.cutoffPressureDifferenceSourc.summary: Evaluate the complete pressure difference source

TorusEuler.cutoffSchwartzKernel.text: Defines the inverse Fourier transform of a smooth symbol vanishing outside the ball of radius two, viewed as a complex Schwartz function. Compact support makes the original smooth symbol Schwartz, so its inverse Fourier transform has rapidly decaying derivatives. This is the kernel denoted by $\check\psi$ in Appendix B. The definition supplies the kernel; its mass, moments and convolution identity are separate theorems.
TorusEuler.cutoffSchwartzKernel.summary: The inverse Fourier kernel of the cutoff symbol

TorusEuler.derivWithin_endpointTimeParit.text: On a positive closed time slab, identifies the actual `derivWithin` of the selected field with the selected derivative field. Joint smoothness provides differentiability, and `hT : 0 < T` gives uniqueness of within derivatives even at the endpoints. Those hypotheses distinguish this operator equality from a merely formal differentiation rule.
TorusEuler.derivWithin_endpointTimeParit.summary: The chosen time derivative commutes with parity selection

TorusEuler.derivWithin_kineticForm_sub_v.text: The coefficients satisfy $K_t-\Omega=2F^*F_t$ wherever the deformation obeys $F_t=MF$. The binder `hF` is the derivative equation and `hs : UniqueDiffWithinAt ℝ s t` allows the derivative within the time set to be identified with its prescribed value. This handles closed slab endpoints as well as interior times. The statement is an operator identity on any complete real inner product space.

TorusEuler.derivWithin_waveCompletion_ad.text: Given the time derivative of the potential’s label jet and the reverse equation for the coframe, adding the material and pressure terms to the actual derivative of the correction yields `hierarchyLinearRelayAt`. Unique differentiability of the time set is required to recover `derivWithin`. The theorem assumes mixed-derivative compatibility through `hJet` rather than proving it here.
TorusEuler.derivWithin_waveCompletion_ad.summary: The differentiated correction equals the four-term relay

TorusEuler.deriv_waveProfile_bounds.text: For every phase, the constructed derivative lies in $[-h/2,1]$. The hypotheses `hh` and `hle` impose $0<h\le1$, and the phase binder `s` is unrestricted. This gives the paper's lower bound $-Ch$ with the explicit constant $C=1/2$. The upper bound remains one, allowing a narrow region of strong positive shear while keeping the negative slope uniformly small.
TorusEuler.deriv_waveProfile_bounds.summary: Wave slope lies between negative half scale and one

TorusEuler.deriv_waveSwitch.text: The derivative of the switch equals the derivative of the base smooth transition at $r(t-t_0)$, multiplied by $r$. This is the scalar chain rule, valid for every real rate and activation time. The positive-rate assumption used in activation estimates is unnecessary for this identity.

TorusEuler.det_flow_eq_one.text: On an order-connected time set `J`, a variational curve initially equal to the identity keeps determinant one if its coefficient has zero trace everywhere. The assumptions `hF`, `htr`, and `h₀` supply the ODE, trace condition, and normalization. The conclusion is volume preservation along that entire interval, with no independent invertibility hypothesis.

TorusEuler.differentiableAt_relayPotenti.text: Assume the full potential-time profile and the potential of `F` are differentiable at `x`, and both input slices are continuous. Their difference is the zero-forcing potential-time profile, hence it is differentiable there. The theorem transfers existing differentiability; it does not prove either of the two input differentiability assumptions.
TorusEuler.differentiableAt_relayPotenti.summary: Subtracting the force potential gives homogeneous differentiability

TorusEuler.dist_le_torusEuclideanDistanc.text: The default product distance on the three-torus is no larger than the Euclidean norm of the three coordinate circle distances. Each coordinate is bounded by that square root, so the product supremum is bounded as well. This implication lets vanishing on a product-metric ball yield vanishing whenever the auxiliary Euclidean torus distance is small.
TorusEuler.dist_le_torusEuclideanDistanc.summary: Product distance is bounded by Euclidean distance

TorusEuler.divergence.text:
Defines the divergence of a vector field as the sum of its three diagonal spatial derivatives. The Fréchet derivative is applied to the coordinate unit vectors, and the matching output coordinates are summed. This is the usual divergence in Euclidean coordinates. Applied separately to each row, it supplies the matrix-field convention in the introduction; the declaration itself takes a vector field, not a matrix field.

Default-value audit (b4): If v is not differentiable at x, fderiv ℝ v x takes the default zero linear map, so this definition returns zero there. Thus divergence v x = 0 alone is not a sufficient definition of a differentiable incompressible field. IsEulerSolution includes joint smoothness and has a proved smooth-slice accessor; EulerSingularityWitness separately assumes ContDiff for u₀. Those are the guards in the headline use.

Default-value audit (b5): The definition uses fderiv, whose default value at a nondifferentiability point is zero. Thus the equation divergence=0 alone is not a classical incompressibility claim without regularity.
TorusEuler.divergence.summary: Divergence as the trace of the derivative

TorusEuler.divergenceMode.text: The divergence symbol contracts a complex vector coefficient with the three coordinate derivative multipliers $2\pi i k_i$. It returns a scalar coefficient. This is a complex-linear algebraic definition, whose agreement with the Euclidean divergence of finite Fourier polynomials is established later in the module.

TorusEuler.divergenceMode_eq.text: The vector divergence multiplier equals $2\pi i$ times the frequency contraction. The common scalar factor is pulled out of the finite coordinate sum. This identity translates transversality into zero divergence and fixes the normalization shared by the pressure and Leray symbol calculations.
TorusEuler.divergenceMode_eq.summary: Divergence is the frequency contraction times two pi i

TorusEuler.divergenceMode_gradientMode.text: Applying the divergence symbol to the gradient of a scalar coefficient gives the Laplacian symbol times that coefficient. The proof sums the coordinate squares and uses $i^2=-1$. This identity checks both the negative sign and the $2\pi$ normalization in the periodic Poisson calculation.
TorusEuler.divergenceMode_gradientMode.summary: Divergence after gradient gives the Laplacian symbol

TorusEuler.divergenceMode_lerayMode.text: For any frequency and vector coefficient, applying divergence after the Leray symbol gives zero. The result follows by expressing divergence through the frequency contraction and using transversality of the projected coefficient. It is a modewise statement; spatial divergence freedom follows after finite synthesis.
TorusEuler.divergenceMode_lerayMode.summary: The Leray symbol produces zero divergence

TorusEuler.divergenceMode_real_smul.text: Multiplying a complex vector coefficient by a real scalar multiplies its divergence symbol by the same scalar. This elementary identity is the exact algebraic property required when a real cutoff symbol rescales each coefficient. It is valid at every frequency, including zero.
TorusEuler.divergenceMode_real_smul.summary: Real coefficient scaling commutes with divergence

TorusEuler.divergenceMode_zero.text: The divergence symbol at zero frequency vanishes on every vector coefficient. This is the frequency-space expression of the fact that constant vector fields are divergence free. It allows the pressure correction to omit the zero mode while still recovering the full divergence source.
TorusEuler.divergenceMode_zero.summary: Constant vector coefficients have zero divergence

TorusEuler.divergence_advection_eq_trace.text: For a twice continuously differentiable divergence-free field, the divergence of $u\cdot\nabla u$ is $\operatorname{tr}((\nabla u)^2)$. The assumptions are `hv : ContDiff ℝ 2 v` and `hdiv : ∀ x, divergence v x = 0`. The second derivative term vanishes after differentiating the zero-divergence identity. The remaining product of first derivatives is written as the trace of a composition of continuous linear maps.
TorusEuler.divergence_advection_eq_trace.summary: Divergence of advection is the gradient-square trace

TorusEuler.divergence_affineWaveVelocity.text: At a fixed time and spatial point, the divergence of $Dx+\mathbf aF(k\cdot x)$ is $\operatorname{tr}D+(k\cdot\mathbf a)F'(k\cdot x)$. The only regularity assumption is the indicated derivative of the profile. Zero trace and perpendicularity then make this quantity vanish. The declaration itself gives the general formula, with neither cancellation assumed.

TorusEuler.divergence_closedSlab_momentu.text: For a jointly smooth solenoidal velocity on a positive closed slab and a smooth pressure slice satisfying the trace-square Poisson equation, proves zero divergence of the actual momentum residual. Time differentiation preserves divergence at slab endpoints, and the advection divergence cancels the pressure Laplacian. The conclusion concerns the residual of these same fields.
TorusEuler.divergence_closedSlab_momentu.summary: The Poisson equation makes the true residual solenoidal

TorusEuler.divergence_completedWaveOn.text: The graph of a transverse profile plus its slow curl correction is divergence free on an open chart. The binders `hU` and `hx` locate the point, `hA` and `hQ` provide $C^2$ regularity, and `hκ` identifies the nonzero covector with the inverse-label derivative. Continuity and transversality are supplied by `hV` and `htrans`. The theorem is local and therefore applies to each correction before the separate periodic gluing step.
TorusEuler.divergence_completedWaveOn.summary: Completed oscillation is divergence free on a chart

TorusEuler.divergence_curl.text: The divergence of the ordinary spatial curl vanishes at a point where the potential is twice continuously differentiable. The named hypothesis `hQ` is `ContDiffAt ℝ 2 Q x`; no global regularity or periodicity is needed. The proof uses symmetry of the second Fréchet derivative. Applied after the profile graph chain rule, this is the geometric cancellation underlying the divergence-free completed velocity.

TorusEuler.divergence_endpointPhysicalLa.text: A jointly smooth lift of a solenoidal half-Holder curve has zero pointwise spatial divergence at every slab time. Weak gradient annihilation is converted to the classical divergence identity.
TorusEuler.divergence_endpointPhysicalLa.summary: The smooth recovered label velocity is divergence free

TorusEuler.divergence_eq_trace_fderiv.text: Divergence in the Euclidean lift is the trace of the spatial derivative.
TorusEuler.divergence_eq_trace_fderiv.summary: Divergence is the trace of the spatial derivative

TorusEuler.divergence_eq_zero_of_tendsto.text: At a fixed spatial point, convergence of the approximating Fréchet derivatives to the actual derivative of the limit preserves zero divergence. The proof passes to the finite sum of coordinate diagonal entries. The convergence hypothesis already identifies the limiting operator with `fderiv u`; the theorem does not obtain derivative convergence from convergence of velocities.
TorusEuler.divergence_eq_zero_of_tendsto.summary: Convergence of spatial derivatives preserves zero divergence

TorusEuler.divergence_firstWaveLocalized.text: The localized first-wave velocity has zero divergence at every time and spatial point under the stated regularity parameter conditions. The proof applies divergence of curl to the smooth potential slice. It certifies the completed field, not the uncorrected leading oscillation, whose label-dependent envelope can create divergence.
TorusEuler.divergence_firstWaveLocalized.summary: The completed first wave has zero divergence

TorusEuler.divergence_free_lift_realVect.text: An even scalar symbol sends a smooth divergence-free torus field to a cutoff field with zero classical divergence everywhere on the lift. The proof translates the input to solenoidal Fourier coefficients, uses scalar multiplication to preserve each transverse mode space, and translates back. The zero mode is retained within the Fourier characterization.
TorusEuler.divergence_free_lift_realVect.summary: The real even cutoff preserves incompressibility

TorusEuler.divergence_gradient_cutoffPre.text: The pressure difference satisfies the difference of the two gradient-square traces, minus $\operatorname{div}R_V$. The assumptions `hP` and `hR` are the Poisson equation for $p$ and the approximate momentum equation for $(V,\Pi)$. The time-derivative field `W` is differentiable and divergence free by `hW` and `hdivW`. Lean states the trace-square difference before expanding it into the two cross terms involving $v_\Lambda=u-V$.
TorusEuler.divergence_gradient_cutoffPre.summary: Poisson equation for the pressure difference

TorusEuler.divergence_gradient_endpointF.text: For any finite set of frequencies and complex vector coefficients, the Laplacian of the real Fourier pressure potential equals the divergence of the real synthesized vector field. Smoothness follows from finite synthesis. Conjugate symmetry is not assumed: both sides consistently take real parts before the final real identity.
TorusEuler.divergence_gradient_endpointF.summary: The real finite potential solves its Poisson equation

TorusEuler.divergence_gradient_meanPress.text: Assume the displayed linearized momentum identity, twice differentiable velocity fields and pressure, a differentiable time-derivative placeholder `W`, and divergence-free `U`, `V` and `W`. The pressure Laplacian equals forcing divergence minus twice the mixed gradient trace. The divergence-free time derivative is an explicit hypothesis in this spatial lemma.
TorusEuler.divergence_gradient_meanPress.summary: Taking divergence gives the mean-pressure Poisson equation

TorusEuler.divergence_gradient_truncated.text: Assuming `A` has no Fourier coefficients outside radius `r`, proves that the Laplacian of its slice pressure equals minus the divergence of its entire Euclidean lift. The band condition allows exact finite Fourier reconstruction. Without that condition the definition only sees the retained modes, and this full-source conclusion is unavailable.
TorusEuler.divergence_gradient_truncated.summary: The band hypothesis recovers the full pressure source

TorusEuler.divergence_linearizedAdvectio.text: For two twice continuously differentiable divergence-free vector fields, the divergence of the sum of the two linearized advection terms equals twice the trace of the product of their gradients. The second-derivative terms vanish because each divergence is identically zero. This is the algebra behind the mean-pressure Poisson source.
TorusEuler.divergence_linearizedAdvectio.summary: The two cross-advection divergences give twice the mixed trace

TorusEuler.divergence_momentumTensorDive.text: For a $C^2$ divergence-free vector field, the divergence of the divergence of its self-momentum tensor equals $\operatorname{tr}((Df)^2)$. The proof first identifies tensor divergence with advection, then uses the incompressible advection identity. The matrix square is composition of the velocity derivative, not its squared operator norm.
TorusEuler.divergence_momentumTensorDive.summary: The second momentum divergence is the gradient-square trace

TorusEuler.divergence_phase_piola.text: For a volume-preserving deformation with a differentiable local inverse, the sum of spatial divergence and phase-direction divergence is preserved under pushforward. The transformed phase vector is `G.adjoint k`. The assumptions include the symmetric second derivative, local inverse identity, determinant one, and separate label and phase derivatives of `c`; no global flow conclusion is asserted.
TorusEuler.divergence_phase_piola.summary: Piola transformation preserves the combined phase divergence

TorusEuler.divergence_piola.text: For a differentiable deformation `X`, local inverse `Y`, and label vector field `v`, the divergence of $F(Yx)v(Yx)$ at `X a` equals the label divergence of `v`. The assumptions include a symmetric derivative `DF`, local determinant one, and an eventual local inverse identity `hYX`. It is a pointwise Piola identity, not a global diffeomorphism theorem.

TorusEuler.divergence_piola_of_contDiffA.text: The Piola identity gives $\operatorname{div}_x(Fv\circ Y)(X(a))=\operatorname{div}_av(a)$ when $Y$ is a local inverse of $X$ and $\det DX=1$ near the label. The binders `hX`, `hY`, `hYX`, `hdet` and `hv` supply these local derivative and inverse hypotheses. The theorem states the full divergence identity, not only preservation of zero divergence. It therefore applies directly to the solenoidal label velocity in the endpoint construction.
TorusEuler.divergence_piola_of_contDiffA.summary: Divergence under a volume preserving deformation

TorusEuler.divergence_slabVelocityTimeDe.text: The time derivative of an incompressible velocity on a closed slab is incompressible, including at the endpoints.
TorusEuler.divergence_slabVelocityTimeDe.summary: Time differentiation preserves incompressibility on the closed slab

TorusEuler.divergence_stationaryShear.text: The stationary shear is divergence free at every point for every real parameter. Its velocity varies only in the second spatial coordinate, while its second component is zero. The Lean proof computes the trace of the already established derivative, so the statement uses a genuine smooth gradient.

TorusEuler.divergence_transportedHierarc.text: The physical divergence of a transported vector profile is the trace of its label derivative composed with the inverse-label derivative, plus the transported covector paired with its phase derivative. The theorem assumes genuine derivatives of both the label map and profile at the graph point. It does not require the field to be divergence free.
TorusEuler.divergence_transportedHierarc.summary: The transported divergence is a slow trace plus a fast contraction

TorusEuler.dyadicDerivativeWeight_sum_le.text: For $\rho>0$ and every truncation length $N$, bounds $\sum_{j<N}2^{4j}(1+2^j\rho)^{-5}$ by $18\rho^{-4}$. The estimate is uniform in $N$: the proof divides at the first scale with $2^j\rho\ge1$ and uses geometric series on either side. It is a finite-sum estimate; convergence of the operator series is supplied elsewhere.

TorusEuler.dyadicEuclideanMultiplierKern.text: The grade `j` Euclidean kernel is the inverse Fourier transform of the Schwartz symbol rescaled by $2^j$, including the dimension-three volume factor. It is the basic smooth term that will be translated across the lattice and then summed over scales. Every dyadic scale is positive.
TorusEuler.dyadicEuclideanMultiplierKern.summary: One inverse Fourier kernel at a dyadic scale

TorusEuler.dyadicMultiplierCutoff.text: Choose the standard smooth bump centered at zero with inner radius one and outer radius two. This fixed scalar cutoff is used both for the annular partition and the Bernstein estimate. Its radius inequalities are supplied in the construction; smoothness, unit values, and vanishing outside are then exposed by separate lemmas.
TorusEuler.dyadicMultiplierCutoff.summary: A fixed smooth cutoff between radii one and two

TorusEuler.dyadicMultiplierCutoff_smooth.text: The chosen scalar cutoff is smooth of all orders on Euclidean frequency space. This is inherited from the `ContDiffBump` construction with its valid radii. The theorem supplies the smoothness hypothesis needed to build Schwartz kernels and globally smooth annular localizations of symbols that may be singular at zero.
TorusEuler.dyadicMultiplierCutoff_smooth.summary: The fixed dyadic cutoff is smooth at every order

TorusEuler.dyadicMultiplierCutoff_unit.text: If the frequency norm is at most one, the fixed dyadic cutoff has value one. The proof translates the norm condition into membership in the bump’s closed inner ball. This property makes the difference cutoff vanish near zero and ensures the dyadic partition telescopes to one on nonzero lattice frequencies.
TorusEuler.dyadicMultiplierCutoff_unit.summary: The cutoff equals one on the closed unit ball

TorusEuler.dyadicMultiplierCutoff_zero.text: At every frequency of norm at least two, the fixed cutoff is zero, including the boundary sphere. This precise closed inequality is used in annular support and telescoping arguments. It provides a compact frequency region for Fourier inversion rather than a decay estimate outside that region.
TorusEuler.dyadicMultiplierCutoff_zero.summary: The cutoff vanishes at and beyond radius two

TorusEuler.dyadicPeriodicMultiplierBlock.text: The periodic block at one fixed scale sums all lattice translates of the corresponding Euclidean kernel. Rapid spatial decay makes this sum and its derivatives convergent under the later completeness hypotheses. It is a single-scale object, unlike the full kernel that also sums over all dyadic grades.
TorusEuler.dyadicPeriodicMultiplierBlock.summary: One dyadic kernel is repeated over the lattice

TorusEuler.dyadicPeriodicMultiplierKerne.text: The full kernel is the double infinite sum over nonnegative dyadic grades and integer translations. Its intended smooth interpretation is established only off the singular lattice, where every derivative has a common summable majorant. The raw expression is defined at lattice points too, but no kernel regularity there is claimed.
TorusEuler.dyadicPeriodicMultiplierKerne.summary: The full periodic kernel sums scales and lattice translates

TorusEuler.dyadicSeries_halfHolder.text: For Banach-valued blocks on a metric space, assume supremum decay $C2^{-j/2}$ and Lipschitz growth $C2^{j/2}$. The partial sums converge uniformly to their infinite sum, whose norm is at most $4C$ and whose increment is at most $14C\sqrt{d(x,y)}$. Completeness and nonnegative `C` are explicit; convergence is proved from the block hypotheses.
TorusEuler.dyadicSeries_halfHolder.summary: Dyadic size and slope bounds give half-Hölder convergence

TorusEuler.dyadicSeries_holderWith.text: Under the same geometric block bounds, now with nonnegative-real constant `C`, the infinite sum satisfies `HolderWith (14*C) (1/2)`. This repackages the preceding increment estimate in Mathlib's Hölder predicate. The Banach target is complete, and the summability needed to interpret the sum follows from the size hypothesis.
TorusEuler.dyadicSeries_holderWith.summary: The dyadic sum is a bundled half-Hölder function

TorusEuler.endpointBoundaryDerivative.text: The expression combines $\langle\xi,M_t\xi+M\xi_t\rangle$ and $\langle\xi_t,M\xi\rangle$. It is the algebraic product-rule expansion of the derivative of $\langle\xi,M\xi\rangle$. Arguments `Mt` and `dξ` are arbitrary supplied values; actual derivative hypotheses are required when this expression is integrated in the energy identity.
TorusEuler.endpointBoundaryDerivative.summary: The derivative of the quadratic boundary term

TorusEuler.endpointClosedTimeNorm.text:
The supremum of $\|f(t)\|$ for $t\in[0,T]$, written as `sSup` of the image of the closed interval. The definition has no continuity hypothesis and uses the norm of the supplied target space. When that target is a spatial Hölder space, this is the time supremum used in Appendix A; bounds using the supremum require boundedness, supplied later by continuity on the compact interval.

Default-value audit (b5): On an empty interval or when the norm image is unbounded, the real supremum has Lean's default value zero. Continuity on a nonempty compact interval gives the intended supremum; nonnegativity alone does not certify a valid norm bound.
TorusEuler.endpointClosedTimeNorm.summary: Supremum norm on the closed time interval

TorusEuler.endpointClosedTimeNorm_endpoi.text: For a continuous Banach-valued curve on a nonnegative interval, the closed-time norm of its primitive is at most the duration times the curve's closed-time norm.
TorusEuler.endpointClosedTimeNorm_endpoi.summary: The time primitive costs at most the duration

TorusEuler.endpointClosedTimeNorm_le.text: On a nonempty closed interval of nonnegative duration, a uniform upper bound for the norm of a curve also bounds its closed-time supremum. Continuity is unnecessary when the uniform bound is already supplied.
TorusEuler.endpointClosedTimeNorm_le.summary: A uniform bound controls the closed time norm

TorusEuler.endpointClosedTimeNorm_le_of_.text: A source word equal to the negative primitive of a continuous force word has closed-time norm at most duration times the force norm. This is the estimate used after differentiating the integrated mean equation.
TorusEuler.endpointClosedTimeNorm_le_of_.summary: The differentiated force primitive has the duration bound

TorusEuler.endpointClosedTimeNorm_nonneg.text: For nonnegative duration, the closed-time norm is nonnegative, even if the image is unbounded. In the latter case Lean's real supremum is the default zero, so this theorem alone does not certify boundedness.

TorusEuler.endpointCoefficient_halfHolde.text: Suppose the spatial diameter is bounded by $R^2$, with `M,R ≥ 0`, and coefficient increments are at most $M d(a,b)$. Then they are at most $MR\sqrt{d(a,b)}$ on the same time slab. The square-root diameter factor is explicit; no special numerical diameter of the torus is assumed inside this lemma.
TorusEuler.endpointCoefficient_halfHolde.summary: A diameter bound turns Lipschitz control into half Hölder control

TorusEuler.endpointComplexifyContinuous.text: The definition embeds each real vector value of a continuous torus field in the complex Euclidean space. Continuity follows from the bounded linear complexification map. It changes the target scalar representation for Fourier analysis while preserving the underlying real coordinates; it does not add a new independent imaginary component.
TorusEuler.endpointComplexifyContinuous.summary: Regard a continuous real field as a complex field

TorusEuler.endpointComplexifySpatialOper.text: Apply the concrete Euclidean complexification to every real spatial coefficient operator, bundled as a real continuous linear map between operator spaces. This is the finite-dimensional version used by fixed-time frozen symbols. Its operator inputs may be singular; extension itself does not construct their inverse.
TorusEuler.endpointComplexifySpatialOper.summary: Extend spatial coefficient matrices to complex velocities

TorusEuler.endpointComplexifySpatialOper.text: The imaginary part of the extended spatial operator output is the original real operator applied to the input imaginary part. No symmetry or coercivity is needed for this algebraic identity. It complements the real-part formula when transferring real quadratic estimates to complex Fourier amplitudes.
TorusEuler.endpointComplexifySpatialOper.summary: Spatial extension acts correctly on imaginary components

TorusEuler.endpointComplexifySpatialOper.text: Apply an extended spatial operator to an embedded real vector; the result is the embedding of the original real action. This specialization makes the abstract extension compatible with actual three-dimensional coefficients. It is used when complex Fourier calculations are translated back to the real Euler variables.
TorusEuler.endpointComplexifySpatialOper.summary: Spatial extension agrees with the real coefficient action

TorusEuler.endpointComplexifySpatialOper.text: The real part of the output of an extended spatial operator equals the original operator applied to the input real part. The identity holds for every complex input vector, not only real embeddings. This component formula underlies the real-part transfer of multiplier identities.
TorusEuler.endpointComplexifySpatialOper.summary: Spatial extension acts correctly on real components

TorusEuler.endpointComplexifyTimeOperato.text: For a chosen interval endpoint `T`, complexify bounded real operators on the full time L² space. The map between operator spaces is real-linear and continuous. It lets the frozen Fourier analysis act on paths as its coefficient values, while preserving quantitative bounds independently of time-path dimension.
TorusEuler.endpointComplexifyTimeOperato.summary: Extend operators acting on whole time paths

TorusEuler.endpointComplexifyTimeOperato.text: The imaginary projection commutes with an extended time-path operator in the expected real sense. Namely, project the output to imaginary part or first project the input and then apply `A`; both give the same real L² path. This identity does not require `A` to act by pointwise multiplication.
TorusEuler.endpointComplexifyTimeOperato.summary: Extended path operators preserve the imaginary component action

TorusEuler.endpointComplexifyTimeOperato.text: For a real time-path operator `A` and real path `v`, applying the complex extension to the embedded path equals embedding `A v`. The identity is in time L² for the restricted measure. It ties the complex path operator directly to the original real endpoint coefficient operator.
TorusEuler.endpointComplexifyTimeOperato.summary: Time path extension agrees with embedded real action

TorusEuler.endpointComplexifyTimeOperato.text: The real part of an extended time-path operator output equals the original real operator applied to the real part of the input path. This is an equality of time L² classes, with no pointwise-in-time action assumed for `A`. It supports the mixed Fourier inverse on entire path spaces.
TorusEuler.endpointComplexifyTimeOperato.summary: Extended path operators preserve the real component action

TorusEuler.endpointComplexify_angularLer.text: At every integer frequency $k$, complexifying the real angular Leray operator at the associated lattice vector gives the existing complex Leray mode projection. The proof checks coordinates using the decomposition into real and imaginary parts. The equality includes $k=0$, where the spatial Leray convention is the identity rather than the removal of the mean.
TorusEuler.endpointComplexify_angularLer.summary: Complex angular projection equals the Fourier mode projection

TorusEuler.endpointCompressedCoefficient.text: Given `hP`, which says the supplied strong and weak projections agree after embedding, the compressed coefficient equations also agree. The input is a strong solenoidal field. This theorem is conditional on projection compatibility; it does not construct either projection or infer that arbitrary projected operators coincide.
TorusEuler.endpointCompressedCoefficient.summary: Compatible projections give compatible coefficient equations

TorusEuler.endpointCutoffPressure_of_pro.text: For a continuous `g` with zero weak Leray projection, any supplied cutoff function `ψ` and scale `Λ` produce a smooth periodic zero-mean pressure whose gradient is the real cutoff field. No regularity or positive-scale hypothesis is needed for this finite algebraic construction. Approximation to the original field requires the later smooth-cutoff convergence assumptions.
TorusEuler.endpointCutoffPressure_of_pro.summary: Every finite cutoff of a zero projection field has a pressure

TorusEuler.endpointDisplacementDerivativ.text:
Define M applied to Fz plus Fv, the derivative of the physical displacement Fz when the deformation satisfies F-prime equals MF and z-prime equals v. The formula alone does not impose those derivative identities.

Default-value audit (b5): This is a total algebraic expression for arbitrary F, M, z, and v. Interpreting it as a displacement derivative requires the separate equations F-prime equals MF and z-prime equals v.
TorusEuler.endpointDisplacementDerivativ.summary: The displacement derivative from label variables

TorusEuler.endpointDisplacementEnergy_co.text: The sharp factor $1-T^2/2$ in the endpoint energy estimate for a path vanishing at $T$. The hypotheses require continuous derivatives and a continuous operator $H$ satisfying $\langle Hx,x\rangle\le\|x\|^2$. Symmetry of $H$ and initial vanishing are unnecessary. The theorem integrates in time for one path. The paper’s space-time inequality follows by applying it at each label and integrating over labels; that extra integration is not in this declaration.
TorusEuler.endpointDisplacementEnergy_co.summary: An upper Hessian bound yields displacement coercivity

TorusEuler.endpointFiniteFourierPressure.text: The definition takes the real part of a finite Fourier sum whose scalar coefficients are obtained by `pressureCorrectionMode` from the supplied vector modes. It is defined for any finite frequency set and coefficients. Being a potential for a particular vector sum requires the gradient-mode compatibility hypotheses proved separately.
TorusEuler.endpointFiniteFourierPressure.summary: Build a real pressure from finitely many potential modes

TorusEuler.endpointFourierPotential.text: For a bounded real-linear functional `L` on complex scalars, applying it to a Fourier character yields a bundled smooth periodic real potential. Real and imaginary coordinate functionals provide the usual cosine and sine tests. These potentials connect weak real divergence constraints with complex Fourier coefficients.
TorusEuler.endpointFourierPotential.summary: Real Fourier characters provide smooth periodic test potentials

TorusEuler.endpointGradientMode_eq_coeff.text: If the continuous field `g` has zero weak spatial Leray projection, each complex Fourier coefficient equals the gradient mode of its pressure-correction coefficient. This includes the zero mode: its coefficient must vanish because Leray preserves the mean. The hypothesis `hPg` is essential; an arbitrary continuous field need not have a periodic scalar potential.
TorusEuler.endpointGradientMode_eq_coeff.summary: Every coefficient of a zero projection field is a gradient mode

TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderCaps_of_lif.text: Uniform value and spatial derivative bounds for a lift give the torus half-Holder norm bound C plus twice L and Lipschitz constant twice L. Close lifts of torus labels account for the numerical factor two.
TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderCaps_of_lif.summary: Lift bounds control the torus Holder coefficient

TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderSolenoidal.text:
Define the solenoidal half-Holder space as the inverse image of the weak spatial L2 solenoidal subspace under the natural embedding. This does not require classical derivatives of a half-Holder field.

Default-value audit (b5): Membership is inherited from weak L2 gradient tests, so no totalized classical derivative is used to define divergence of a rough Holder field. The zero field is included and no mean-zero spatial condition is imposed.

TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToContinuou.text: This bounded real linear map sends a half-Hölder torus field to its continuous value field. It discards the stored difference-quotient component and uses the supremum norm on the target. The construction allows the pressure residual to be differentiated in a continuous-function space, where the spatial potential recovery theorem applies.
TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToContinuou.summary: Forget the Hölder quotient while retaining a continuous field

TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToContinuou.text: After converting a half-Hölder field to a continuous torus field, its value at every label is exactly the original `HalfHolder.eval`. This identity exposes the common pointwise function behind the two bundled types. It is used to connect the temporal residual formula to the spatial pressure-gradient statement.
TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToContinuou.summary: The continuous conversion preserves pointwise values

TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToContinuou.text: Embedding the continuous conversion of a half-Hölder field into spatial $L^2$ gives exactly `endpointHalfHolderToL2 f`. The equality follows from agreement of their almost-everywhere evaluations. It ensures that moving to a continuous-function space for pressure reconstruction preserves the weak projection constraint already proved for the Hölder field.
TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToContinuou.summary: Both continuous and Hölder embeddings give the same Hilbert class

TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToL2.text:
Send a half-Holder torus field to its spatial L2 class through the bounded continuous representative. The map is linear and bounded; subsequent lemmas identify its almost-everywhere values.

Default-value audit (b5): A bounded continuous torus representative is automatically square integrable on normalized finite Haar measure. The map produces its equivalence class without selecting exceptional point values.
TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToL2.summary: Embedding a Holder field into spatial integral space

TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToL2_apply_.text: The spatial $L^2$ element obtained from a half-Hölder field agrees almost everywhere with its pointwise evaluation. The input has a continuous bounded representative, whereas the output is an equivalence class. This lemma supplies the precise representative relation used in weak divergence tests.
TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToL2_apply_.summary: The Hilbert image represents the same Hölder field

TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToL2_coeffi.text: Embedding a pointwise half-Hölder product into spatial $L^2$ gives the same class as first embedding the vector field and then applying the weak coefficient multiplier. The coefficient `K` and field `v` are both bundled half-Hölder objects. The proof compares their almost-everywhere representatives, ensuring compatibility without choosing matching values everywhere.
TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToL2_coeffi.summary: Strong and weak coefficient multiplication agree

TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToL2_inject.text: If two half-Hölder fields have the same spatial $L^2$ image, they are equal as half-Hölder elements. Full support of Haar measure makes almost-everywhere equality of continuous representatives imply equality everywhere. The quotient component is then determined by field values, so it introduces no extra ambiguity.
TorusEuler.endpointHalfHolderToL2_inject.summary: The Hölder to Hilbert embedding loses no field information

TorusEuler.endpointHessian.text:
The operator $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$ along a fixed particle label. The argument `Mt` is a supplied operator; identifying it with the time derivative of `M` is a hypothesis of the lemmas that use this definition. Composition is written `M.comp M`. No symmetry is imposed on $M$ or $H^\#$, which permits a parent that does not solve the Euler equations.

Default-value audit (b5): The supplied Mt is not required by the definition to equal an actual derivative. The formula is total for arbitrary operators and can be nonsymmetric; the energy theorems separately provide the derivative identity and quadratic upper bound.

TorusEuler.endpointHessian_eq_pressureHe.text: Along a parent trajectory, $H^\#$ equals the pressure Hessian minus the spatial derivative of the momentum residual. The hypotheses are `hu`, joint $C^2$ regularity on the closed slab, `hX`, the trajectory equation at the time under consideration, and `hp`, differentiability of the pressure gradient there. The parent need not solve Euler. The formula uses the time derivative of the gradient at fixed label, exactly as in the manuscript.
TorusEuler.endpointHessian_eq_pressureHe.summary: Effective Hessian equals pressure curvature minus residual gradient

TorusEuler.endpointIntegral.text:
Define time integration as a bounded linear map from the finite-interval L2 path space to its target space. Its bound is the square root of the interval measure, by Cauchy-Schwarz.

Default-value audit (b5): The restricted measure is finite for every real T; at nonpositive T it is zero and the integral map is zero. L2 elements are represented only up to almost-everywhere equality, which is respected by this integral.
TorusEuler.endpointIntegral.summary: Integrating a square integrable time path

TorusEuler.endpointIntegral_angularTimeL.text: For positive `hT`, every path in the output of the combined angular-time projection has zero time integral. The spatial operator commutes with integration, and mean subtraction gives zero before it is applied. This identifies the path subspace on which the endpoint coefficient is assumed coercive.
TorusEuler.endpointIntegral_angularTimeL.summary: The combined projection has zero time integral

TorusEuler.endpointIntegral_apply.text: Applying `endpointIntegral T` to an $L^2$ path returns its Bochner integral against Lebesgue measure restricted to $(0,T]$. This is the defining evaluation identity for the continuous linear map. The path is an almost-everywhere equivalence class, so the integral is independent of the chosen representative.
TorusEuler.endpointIntegral_apply.summary: Evaluating the bounded time integration map

TorusEuler.endpointIntegral_subtractMean.text: On a positive interval, the integral of the mean-subtracted $L^2$ path is zero. Completeness of the target space is present in this part of the module. The identity is the analytic reason that integrating such a velocity produces a displacement with the same value at both endpoints.
TorusEuler.endpointIntegral_subtractMean.summary: Mean subtraction enforces the terminal condition

TorusEuler.endpointInverseCommonScale_le.text: Assume $D\ge1$, $0\le M\le D$, and nonnegative coefficient constants. The sum of the two coercivity reciprocals and zeroth- and first-order kinetic and vorticity costs is bounded by $(13+C_K+C_\Omega+4L_K+4L_\Omega)D^9$. This arithmetic packages all low-order inputs under one common parent scale before applying the polynomial inverse cap.
TorusEuler.endpointInverseCommonScale_le.summary: Low-order coefficient inputs fit a ninth-power bound

TorusEuler.endpointJointCoefficient_ae_b.text: The uniform bound `hKsup` gives $\|K(q)\|\le M$ almost everywhere in the product time-torus measure. The first-coordinate projection carries almost every product point into the restricted time interval. This provides the joint essential bound used when comparing mixed coefficient multiplication with the joint L² multiplier.
TorusEuler.endpointJointCoefficient_ae_b.summary: A closed slab bound controls the joint multiplier

TorusEuler.endpointJointConstraintProjec.text:
Define the joint L2 orthogonal projection onto fields satisfying weak spatial divergence freedom and zero time mean. This Hilbert-space projection is compared with the Fourier-defined mixed projection separately.

Default-value audit (b5): This is the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a proved closed constraint subspace, not a chosen inverse. At zero time measure its ambient L2 space is trivial.
TorusEuler.endpointJointConstraintProjec.summary: The orthogonal projection onto endpoint constraints

TorusEuler.endpointJointConstraintProjec.text: On an inserted real Fourier mode, the joint orthogonal projection acts by applying `angularTimeLeray` to the time-path amplitude. `hT : 0 < T` makes mean subtraction the orthogonal time-mean projection. The proof identifies the projected part and shows that the discarded constant and longitudinal parts are orthogonal to the endpoint space.
TorusEuler.endpointJointConstraintProjec.summary: The joint projection acts by the combined mode symbol

TorusEuler.endpointJointModeInsert.text: Lift a time L² path to the joint space, then multiply by a continuous real spatial character. The resulting bounded linear map represents $(t,a)\mapsto\chi(a)w(t)$. Its construction combines measure-preserving pullback with a bounded multiplier, avoiding an unproved assertion about jointly measurable representatives.
TorusEuler.endpointJointModeInsert.summary: Insert a time path with a spatial character

TorusEuler.endpointJointModeInsert_apply.text: The L² representative of an inserted mode equals the spatial character times the time-path representative almost everywhere in the product measure. This is the formula used for testing against joint velocities. It does not identify representatives at every time and label, where quotient choices may differ.
TorusEuler.endpointJointModeInsert_apply.summary: Inserted modes have the separated product representative

TorusEuler.endpointJointRealFourierCoeff.text: Define the real time-valued Fourier coefficient as the Hilbert adjoint of insertion of the character with frequency `k` and phase `c`. This produces a bounded map from joint L² to time L² without immediately choosing spatial slice integrals. A later theorem proves the expected almost-everywhere Bochner integral formula.
TorusEuler.endpointJointRealFourierCoeff.summary: Time valued Fourier moments are adjoints of mode insertion

TorusEuler.endpointJointRealFourierCoeff.text: The time-path coefficient defined by adjointness agrees almost everywhere with integrating the real character against each spatial slice of `v`. The proof compares integrals over arbitrary measurable time sets and uses Fubini. This supplies the expected Bochner formula without assuming all spatial slices are well behaved at every time.
TorusEuler.endpointJointRealFourierCoeff.summary: The joint coefficient is the spatial slice integral almost everywhere

TorusEuler.endpointJointRealFourierCoeff.text: If `v` belongs to the weak endpoint space and `T > 0`, every real Fourier coefficient has zero time integral and is transverse to its spatial frequency almost everywhere in time. The proof observes that `v` is fixed by the joint projection, then applies the fixed-space characterization of the mode symbol.
TorusEuler.endpointJointRealFourierCoeff.summary: Admissible joint fields have constrained Fourier amplitudes

TorusEuler.endpointJointRealFourierCoeff.text: Embed a half-Hölder field of time paths into joint L² and extract a real Fourier coefficient. The result is the Haar Bochner integral of the spatial character times the original path field. The formula is an equality of time L² elements; it avoids choosing a common pointwise time representative for every label.
TorusEuler.endpointJointRealFourierCoeff.summary: Mixed Fourier moments agree with joint coefficient extraction

TorusEuler.endpointJointRealFourierCoeff.text: For positive `T`, taking a real time-valued Fourier coefficient after the joint projection equals applying the corresponding angular/time-mean symbol to the incoming coefficient. Adjointness of coefficient extraction and mode insertion transfers the preceding mode identity. Symmetry of both projections is used to move them across the inner products.
TorusEuler.endpointJointRealFourierCoeff.summary: Joint projection multiplies each time valued Fourier coefficient

TorusEuler.endpointJointRealFourierCoeff.text: For positive `T`, the Fourier coefficient of the joint projection of an embedded mixed field equals the combined symbol applied to its path-valued spatial Fourier moment. This combines coefficient compatibility with the joint projection formula. It is the precise relation later used to compare strong and weak realizations of the projection.
TorusEuler.endpointJointRealFourierCoeff.summary: Projected mixed fields obey the combined Fourier symbol formula

TorusEuler.endpointJointSpatialProjectio.text: The spatial solenoidal projection and subtraction of the temporal mean commute on joint $L^2$ fields. The only explicit length hypothesis is `hT : 0 < T`. Both operators act on the same Hilbert space, and subtraction of the mean preserves the spatial solenoidal subspace. `Commute` asserts equality of the two operator compositions. This is the Hilbert-space form of the commuting projections used in the endpoint argument.
TorusEuler.endpointJointSpatialProjectio.summary: Spatial projection commutes with time mean removal

TorusEuler.endpointJointSpatialSolenoida.text: This submodule consists of joint $L^2$ fields annihilated by every bounded measurable time test η and smooth periodic scalar potential p. The kernels express weak spatial divergence zero. The definition imposes no zero time mean and no continuity in time. Its intersection-of-kernels form makes closedness available from continuity of each test functional.
TorusEuler.endpointJointSpatialSolenoida.summary: Joint fields with zero spatial divergence

TorusEuler.endpointJointSubtractMean.text: On the joint $L^2$ space, this defines $Q=I-T^{-1}J^*J$, where J is time integration, not the primitive from zero to a variable time. Thus $J^*J$ lifts the time integral back as a constant path. The definition accepts hT : 0 ≤ T; later projection and range results impose strict positivity when cancelling the slab length.

TorusEuler.endpointJointSubtractMean_app.text: Applying the mean-removal operator to u expands to $u-T^{-1}J^*(Ju)$. This is an equality of joint $L^2$ elements, proved by unfolding the definition. The hypothesis is only hT : 0 ≤ T. Representative formulas and the conclusion that the result has zero integral are separate declarations, so this rewrite alone supplies neither.

Mean removal agrees almost everywhere with $u(t,a)-T^{-1}(Ju)(a)$. Here Ju is the spatial $L^2$ class obtained by integrating in time, and its chosen representative appears on the right. The theorem assumes $0\le T$, unlike the strict-positive projection theorem, because it only identifies two representatives of the same total operator.

TorusEuler.endpointJointSubtractMean_end.text: For a spatial half-Hölder family w of $L^2$ time paths, subtracting the mean after embedding into joint $L^2$ equals embedding after subtracting the mean at every label. The binder hT : 0 ≤ T is sufficient. The proof compares almost-everywhere slices and their integrals; it does not promote an $L^2$ path to continuity in time.
TorusEuler.endpointJointSubtractMean_end.summary: Mean removal respects the mixed embedding

TorusEuler.endpointJointSubtractMean_isS.text: For a positive slab, mean removal is idempotent and symmetric for the real $L^2$ inner product. The result packages those properties as LinearMap.IsSymmetricProjection; it does not yet identify the range. Idempotence uses the zero integral of the projected field, while symmetry follows from the adjoint expression $I-T^{-1}J^*J$.

TorusEuler.endpointJointSubtractMean_pre.text: Subtracting the time mean keeps a jointly solenoidal field inside the same submodule. The integral is spatially solenoidal, its adjoint lift is jointly solenoidal, and submodule closure handles the scaled subtraction. The statement allows hT : 0 ≤ T; it proves preservation even before the stricter hypothesis used to identify $Q$ as a projection.
TorusEuler.endpointJointSubtractMean_pre.summary: Mean removal preserves zero spatial divergence

TorusEuler.endpointJoint_eq_of_slices.text: Two joint L² fields are equal if their time slices agree almost everywhere at almost every spatial label. The proof uses measurability of the equality set and exchanges the order of the almost-everywhere quantifiers. This is the uniqueness principle that makes the subsequent chosen joint representative construction canonical as an L² class.
TorusEuler.endpointJoint_eq_of_slices.summary: Almost everywhere agreement of paths determines a joint field

TorusEuler.endpointJoint_eq_zero_of_four.text: If every real time-valued Fourier coefficient of `v` vanishes for all frequencies and complex phases, then `v = 0` in joint L². The proof uses only phases giving cosine and sine and a countable family of frequencies to obtain simultaneous almost-everywhere slice identities. Spatial Fourier uniqueness then applies at almost every time.
TorusEuler.endpointJoint_eq_zero_of_four.summary: Time valued Fourier coefficients determine a joint L² field

TorusEuler.endpointL2Complexification.text: Assemble the real embedding and both projections into an `EndpointComplexification` for L² vector fields over `μ`. All required identities have been proved on equivalence classes, including squared-norm splitting. This permits the same operator-extension machinery to treat the finite-dimensional spatial case and the infinite-dimensional time-path case.
TorusEuler.endpointL2Complexification.summary: Entire vector valued L² spaces admit complexification

TorusEuler.endpointL2Energy.text: The integrated label energy on the $L^2$ velocity space, with the displacement represented by the primitive. The kinetic term is $\|Fv\|_{L^2}^2$; the second term pairs $\Omega v$ with $z$. The binders `cF` and `cM` require coefficients continuous on the closed time interval. These give bounded multiplication operators, allowing the energy to be continuous in the $L^2$ velocity and hence to pass to limits.
TorusEuler.endpointL2Energy.summary: The label energy on square integrable velocities

TorusEuler.endpointL2Energy_coercive.text: The label energy controls the full $L^2$ velocity norm with constant $[2D^2(1+L)^2]^{-1}$. The binders `hGF`, `hGbound`, `hMbound` and `hupper` give the inverse, coefficient bounds and Hessian upper bound, together with the coefficient derivative hypotheses. The velocity is arbitrary in $L^2$ subject to `hv : endpointIntegral T v = 0`. The proof first establishes the estimate for smooth mean-zero velocities, then uses their density and continuity of the quadratic form.

TorusEuler.endpointL2Energy_eq_integral.text: If `g` agrees almost everywhere with the $L^2$ path `v`, the quadratic energy equals the integral of the label energy evaluated at `g` and its time primitive. The hypothesis `hT : 0 ≤ T` fixes the orientation of the interval integral. Multipliers and primitives are compared almost everywhere, so the statement is independent of the chosen representative.
TorusEuler.endpointL2Energy_eq_integral.summary: The Hilbert-space energy equals the label integral

TorusEuler.endpointL2Multiplier.text: Construct a continuous linear map from one $L^2$ space to another by multiplying by an almost-everywhere strongly measurable, essentially bounded operator field. The field is first bundled in $L^\infty$, then the Hölder bilinear map acts on it. The construction respects equivalence classes rather than assigning a canonical pointwise output everywhere.
TorusEuler.endpointL2Multiplier.summary: Pointwise coefficient multiplication on the L² quotient

TorusEuler.endpointL2Multiplier_apply_ae.text: For any $L^2$ input, a representative of the bundled multiplier output equals the coefficient applied to the input representative almost everywhere. This is the precise link between the quotient-space operator and the pointwise formula. It makes no claim about equality at every time, which would depend on chosen representatives.
TorusEuler.endpointL2Multiplier_apply_ae.summary: The quotient multiplier agrees almost everywhere with pointwise action

TorusEuler.endpointL2Multiplier_apply_to.text: For a representative `v` with proof `hv` of square integrability, applying the bundled coefficient multiplier to `hv.toLp v` equals bundling the pointwise product using its established integrability proof. The equality is in the $L^2$ quotient. It removes differences between two ways of constructing the same equivalence class.
TorusEuler.endpointL2Multiplier_apply_to.summary: Bundling before or after multiplication gives the same class

TorusEuler.endpointL2Operator.text: This is the fixed-label operator $B=K-J\Omega$ on $L^2$ time paths. Here $K=F^*F$, $\Omega=F^*(M^*-M)F$, and J is the forward time primitive. The assumptions cF and cM give continuity on the closed slab, making the multipliers bounded. The operator acts on all paths before restriction to zero time mean.

TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy.text: For arbitrary bounded operators `F` and `M`, form the label energy $\langle F^*Fv,v\rangle+\langle F^*(M^*-M)Fv,z\rangle$. In the application, `F` is the flow derivative and `v` is the label velocity. The definition itself assumes no flow equation or coercivity; those hypotheses belong to subsequent identities and estimates.
TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy.summary: The kinetic and vorticity terms in label coordinates

TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy_coercive.text: The $1/2$ coercivity bound for the label energy when $0\le T\le1$. The inputs satisfy the deformation and gradient evolution equations, and the label displacement vanishes at both endpoints. The effective Hessian is `endpointHessian M Mt`; its quadratic form must be bounded above by the identity. The proof identifies the label energy with the physical displacement energy and applies terminal Poincaré. The stated integrals are at one spatial label, before integrating over labels.
TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy_coercive.summary: Half the displacement energy is controlled on short intervals

TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy_coercive_.text: Under the flow derivative equations, both endpoint conditions for `z`, $0\le T\le1$, `D ≥ 1`, and `L ≥ 0`, obtain the lower bound $[2D^2(1+L)^2]^{-1}\int\|v\|^2$. `hGF` is the explicit left-inverse relation; `hGbound`, `hMbound`, and `hupper` supply inverse, gradient, and Hessian bounds. This is a one-label C¹ estimate, before density gives the weak formulation.
TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy_coercive_.summary: The endpoint form controls the label velocity energy

TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy_eq.text: The label energy equals $|\xi_t|^2-\langle H^\#\xi,\xi\rangle$ minus the algebraic expression for the boundary derivative. Here $\xi=Fz$ and the symbol for $\xi_t$ is defined as $M\xi+Fv$. This theorem is purely algebraic: the supplied `Mt` need not yet be a derivative. The following integrated theorem adds the derivative hypotheses and removes the boundary term using the two zero traces.

TorusEuler.endpointMixedCoefficient.text: Turn a jointly indexed coefficient into a spatial half-Hölder field of bounded operators on time L². Time measurability at every label, uniform value and spatial increment bounds on the slab, and `hM : 0 ≤ M` are explicit inputs. The output acts on entire time paths by multiplication at each label.
TorusEuler.endpointMixedCoefficient.summary: Bundle the coefficients as a half Hölder operator field

TorusEuler.endpointMixedCoefficientMul_r.text: Suppose `hΩ` identifies a mixed operator field with multiplication by the joint coefficient `ω` on every time path, almost everywhere in labels. If `hw` represents the input joint field, then mixed multiplication represents the joint $L^2$ multiplier output. Both representation assumptions are retained explicitly; regularity of the operator field is not proved here.
TorusEuler.endpointMixedCoefficientMul_r.summary: Mixed multiplication represents the joint coefficient action

TorusEuler.endpointMixedCoefficientSolve.text: This specialization builds the mixed coefficients from `K` and `Ω`, using their time-slice measurability, nonnegative uniform bounds, and spatial half-Hölder bounds. With positive `T`, the combined Fourier law for `P` turns a projected mixed solution into the joint weak solution. The coefficient hypotheses are supplied here rather than inferred from arbitrary measurable fields.
TorusEuler.endpointMixedCoefficientSolve.summary: Concrete coefficient data produce the same weak solution

TorusEuler.endpointMixedCoefficient_appl.text: Evaluating the mixed coefficient at a label and applying it to a time path agrees almost everywhere with the original matrix field acting pointwise in time. This identifies the bundled path-operator field with `K`. It allows later mixed-space algebra to be compared directly with the original joint endpoint equation.
TorusEuler.endpointMixedCoefficient_appl.summary: The mixed coefficient still acts by timewise multiplication

TorusEuler.endpointMixedCoefficient_hasS.text: If two coefficient curves form a spatial derivative pair at every slab time, their derivative curve has a uniform half-Hölder bound, and the mixed operators have the prescribed time actions at every label, the mixed coefficient fields form the same spatial derivative pair. The proof controls difference quotients in temporal operator norm, rather than relying only on pointwise convergence.
TorusEuler.endpointMixedCoefficient_hasS.summary: Pointwise coefficient jets become mixed operator jets

TorusEuler.endpointMixedCorrection.text:
Sum coefficient-times-velocity products over all ordered derivative-word pairs in which at least one derivative acts on the coefficient. The coefficient-free highest velocity derivative is excluded from this correction.

Default-value audit (b5): The empty word has zero correction because its pair list is empty. The formula is a total finite sum for arbitrary word-indexed coefficient and field families; derivative meaning is supplied by later hypotheses.

TorusEuler.endpointMixedCorrectionPairs.text:
Enumerate pairs of ordered derivative words in which the coefficient word is nonempty. The recursion preserves repeated terms, so it retains the multiplicities needed by iterated product differentiation.

Default-value audit (b5): The empty word gives the empty list. Repeated derivative directions can yield repeated pairs, which are intentionally retained as product-rule multiplicities rather than removed.
TorusEuler.endpointMixedCorrectionPairs.summary: Ordered product rule terms with a coefficient derivative

TorusEuler.endpointMixedCorrectionPairs_.text: Adding back the principal undifferentiated-coefficient term gives exactly $2^{|w|}$ choices in the ordered product rule. This public theorem exposes the private list-counting result to later estimates. It counts the actual correction list, so repeated coordinate directions retain the multiplicities required by differentiation.
TorusEuler.endpointMixedCorrectionPairs_.summary: All Leibniz choices include one principal term

TorusEuler.endpointMixedCorrectionPairs_.text: Membership in `endpointMixedCorrectionPairs t` implies that the coefficient word is nonempty, the two word lengths add to `t.length`, and the unknown word is strictly shorter. This is the structural fact making the derivative recursion triangular. It identifies which terms may already be known when constructing the next derivative.
TorusEuler.endpointMixedCorrectionPairs_.summary: Every commutator term has a lower order unknown

TorusEuler.endpointMixedCorrectionPairs_.text: Both words in any correction pair are sublists of the original derivative word. Consequently a correction of a sorted word uses sorted subwords, with no new coordinate directions. This combinatorial fact allows the physical derivative recurrence to be restricted to canonical multi-indices while retaining the exact Leibniz multiplicities.
TorusEuler.endpointMixedCorrectionPairs_.summary: Correction words remain within the original multi-index

TorusEuler.endpointMixedCorrectionPairs_.text: Separate the first new coefficient derivative from the two ways to differentiate each existing correction term. This finite-sum identity supports induction on derivative-word length.
TorusEuler.endpointMixedCorrectionPairs_.summary: The next product rule correction from the previous one

TorusEuler.endpointMixedCorrection_hasSp.text: Differentiate every correction term by the product rule under the supplied coefficient and lower-velocity derivative hypotheses. Ordered word multiplicities are preserved rather than simplified combinatorially.
