The conclusion `IsEulerSolution` includes smoothness, periodicity, mean-zero pressure, momentum, and incompressibility. The momentum equation uses vanishing time derivative and self-advection. Thus the residual is zero as well as the chosen pressure.
TorusEuler.isEulerSolution_stationaryShe.summary: The stationary shear solves Euler with zero pressure

TorusEuler.isEulerSolution_zero.text: For every real T>0, the velocity u(t,x)=0 and pressure p(t,x)=0 satisfy IsEulerSolution T u p. All regularity, periodicity, gauge and equation fields are supplied explicitly. This is a useful check that the basic solution predicate is inhabited. It does not satisfy EulerSingularityWitness: it extends to longer intervals and its vorticity and both time integrals remain zero.

TorusEuler.isOpenQuotientMap_toUnitTorus.text: The map from real Euclidean coordinates to the unit three-torus is an open quotient map. The proof combines coordinate quotient maps with the Euclidean product homeomorphism. This topological property permits continuity of a torus field to be inferred from continuity of its periodic Euclidean lift.
TorusEuler.isOpenQuotientMap_toUnitTorus.summary: The Euclidean quotient map is open and surjective

TorusEuler.isOpen_offOrigin.text: The set `offOrigin` is open because it is the complement of the closed integer lattice. On the Euclidean lift, removing the torus origin removes every lattice representative, not only the vector zero. This permits local smoothness arguments on neighborhoods away from the singular torus point.

TorusEuler.isSelfAdjoint_kineticForm.text: The kinetic operator F-adjoint F is self-adjoint for every bounded operator F. Invertibility is unnecessary for this symmetry statement.

TorusEuler.iteratedDerivWithin_bilinear.text: For a continuous bilinear map `B`, smooth functions `f,g` on a set `S`, and `hS : UniqueDiffOn ℝ S`, the $q$th within-derivative of their bilinear product is the usual binomial sum at `t ∈ S`. This formulation includes nondegenerate closed intervals. The uniqueness condition prevents arbitrary choices of within-derivatives from entering the product identity.
TorusEuler.iteratedDerivWithin_bilinear.summary: The time Leibniz formula on a differentiable domain

TorusEuler.iteratedDerivWithin_timeSlice.text: For a smooth field on `I × O`, with unique differentiation on both factors, the one-variable within-time derivative of order `n` equals the full product derivative evaluated repeatedly on `(1,0)`. Both the time and space points belong to their domains. This converts boundary data from normal multilinear jets to ordinary time derivatives.
TorusEuler.iteratedDerivWithin_timeSlice.summary: Time jets are full derivatives in the normal direction

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_phaseMean_const.text: View the phase mean of a smooth one-periodic profile as a constant function of phase. Its derivative of order `j` equals the mean of the corresponding derivative of the original profile. At order zero this preserves the mean; at positive orders both sides vanish by periodicity.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_phaseMean_const.summary: Phase differentiation commutes with a constant mean field

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_phaseOscillatio.text: For a smooth one-periodic function, taking any iterated phase derivative commutes with removing the phase mean. At positive orders the derivative of the subtracted constant is zero and the derivative itself has zero mean. This equality therefore works uniformly at order zero and at every higher order.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_phaseOscillatio.summary: Phase derivatives commute with subtracting the mean

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_phasePrimitive_.text: A smooth one-periodic profile with `hmean : phaseMean f = 0` has a normalized primitive that commutes with every phase derivative. The zero-mean assumption is essential to the periodic primitive identity and is explicitly carried by this theorem. The conclusion is equality of functions of phase, for each derivative order `j`.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_phasePrimitive_.summary: Phase derivatives commute with the periodic primitive

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_terminalBorelAt.text: At a positive scale, the derivative of order `k` of the degree-`n` atom at zero is one when `k=n` and zero otherwise. Local equality with the normalized polynomial proves the assertion. It holds for every natural derivative order, including zero, and supplies the diagonal jets of the Borel series.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_terminalBorelAt.summary: Exactly one prescribed derivative at zero

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_waveSwitch.text: For every natural order `q` and arbitrary real `t₀,r,t`, differentiating the affine-clock switch gives $r^q$ times the same derivative of `smoothTransition` at $r(t-t_0)$. No positivity assumption on `r` is needed for this chain-rule identity. Positive rate is required later when the physical switching interval is identified.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_waveSwitch.summary: Each switch derivative contributes one physical rate factor

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_waveSwitch_zero.text: If `q > 0`, `r > 0`, and `t` lies outside `[t₀,t₀+1/r]`, the `q`th derivative of the physical switch vanishes. The affine clock maps such a point outside `[0,1]`, where the smooth transition is locally constant. The restriction to positive order matters because the switch itself remains one after activation.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_waveSwitch_zero.summary: Switch derivatives vanish beyond the closed switching interval

TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_waveSwitch_zero.text: For `q > 0` and `r > 0`, the switch derivative vanishes outside the open interval `(t₀,t₀+1/r)`, including both endpoints. The proof extends vanishing from the complementary open half-lines to their closures using continuity of the differentiated smooth switch. This is a stronger endpoint statement than support in the closed interval alone.
TorusEuler.iteratedDeriv_waveSwitch_zero.summary: Switch derivatives are flat at both endpoints

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_angularLeray_p.text: For positive scale `hc` and nonzero `hξ`, the $n$th derivative at $\xi$ equals $c^n$ times the derivative at $c\xi$. Thus the derivative has degree $-n$. The proof differentiates the degree-zero symbol identity through a scalar linear map on the punctured space.

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_comp_sub_linea.text: The derivative of a composition, after its linear highest-derivative term is removed, is a sum over ordered partitions with at least two blocks. The assumptions `hn`, `hf` and `hg` give a positive order and the corresponding differentiability. Each term differentiates the outer map once per block and the inner map by the block sizes. This is the multilinear form of the paper's sum defining $N_\beta$.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_comp_sub_linea.summary: The nonlinear terms in the differentiated composition

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_endpointParity.text: For a field smooth through order `m`, gives the order-`m` iterated derivative of the reflection average. The reflected term is multiplied by `sign * (-1)^m`. This parity alternation is what permits uniform treatment of every derivative order in the finite half-Hölder norms, rather than checking just the velocity itself.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_endpointParity.summary: Each spatial derivative contributes one reflection sign

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_fourier_schwar.text: For a Schwartz kernel, the order-`j` Fourier derivative at zero in directions `v` equals $(-2\pi i)^j$ times the integral of the kernel multiplied by the corresponding product of inner products. The statement also allows `j = 0`, despite its positive-degree docstring wording. Schwartz decay ensures all moments used are integrable.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_fourier_schwar.summary: Fourier derivatives at zero encode signed moments

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_id_eq_zero_of_.text: At every point, the identity map has zero iterated Fréchet derivative of order at least two. The order condition `hn` excludes its nonzero first derivative. Applied to a flow initially equal to the identity, this supplies zero initial data for every higher variational equation.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_id_eq_zero_of_.summary: Higher derivatives of the initial identity vanish

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_liftConvolutio.text: For any continuous torus field, every derivative of its smooth spectral cutoff is convolution of the input lift with the corresponding derivative of the dilated kernel. Smoothness of the input is not assumed: the cutoff has finite Fourier support. Positive scale and smooth compact support of the symbol supply the kernel realization.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_liftConvolutio.summary: Differentiate the cutoff by differentiating its convolution kernel

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_liftConvolutio.text: For a complete complex normed target, an integrable kernel, and `hf : ContDiff ℝ j f`, convolution commutes with the order-`j` Fréchet derivative. The family `hM` bounds every derivative from order zero through `j`, not only the top derivative. Induction repeatedly applies differentiation under an integrable majorant.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_liftConvolutio.summary: All bounded derivatives through the chosen order pass through convolution

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_liftConvolutio.text: For a Schwartz kernel and a finite Fourier input, every iterated derivative of the convolution equals convolution with the corresponding iterated kernel derivative. The proof compares the two finite Fourier formulas. Completeness of the complex target supports the Bochner integrals; finiteness of the Fourier sum avoids any series-limit issue.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_liftConvolutio.summary: Derivatives of polynomial convolutions move to the kernel

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_lift_finiteFou.text: For arbitrary finite Fourier synthesis and a list of derivative directions, the iterated derivative multiplies each amplitude by the product of the corresponding directional frequency factors. The target is any complex normed space. Smoothness is automatic for the finite synthesis, so no separate input regularity hypothesis is needed.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_lift_finiteFou.summary: Repeated derivatives act by products of frequency factors

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_phaseMean.text: Every parameter derivative of the phase mean equals the phase mean of the corresponding parameter derivative, provided the original profile is jointly smooth. The order `k` is arbitrary and phase is integrated over one unit interval. This statement does not require periodicity because it is an identity for a fixed interval integral.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_phaseMean.summary: Parameter differentiation commutes with phase averaging

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_phaseOscillati.text: For a jointly smooth parameterized profile, subtracting the phase average commutes with every iterated parameter derivative. Both sides are evaluated at the same parameter `x` and phase `s`. The result transfers derivative estimates to the oscillatory part without assuming that the original profile already has zero phase mean.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_phaseOscillati.summary: Parameter derivatives commute with removing the mean

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_phasePrimitive.text: For a jointly smooth parameterized profile, taking its normalized phase primitive commutes with all parameter derivatives. The identity includes the constant removed to normalize the primitive's phase mean. It is an algebraic-integral commutation statement; periodic primitive properties require the additional periodicity and mean conditions used elsewhere.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_phasePrimitive.summary: Parameter derivatives commute with the normalized primitive

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_scaledPhasePro.text: For a smooth profile, an iterated derivative of its rescaled version evaluated on coordinate directions equals the unscaled derivative at the scaled point, multiplied by the product of coordinate weights. Each label slot contributes `ℓ` and each phase slot contributes `h`. No nonzero assumption is needed for this forward scaling identity.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_scaledPhasePro.summary: Mixed derivatives acquire the product of their scales

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_slabPath_unifo.text: On a compact parameter set, every parameter derivative of order $m\le n$ of a $C^n$ path-valued map is uniformly bounded at all slab times. The bound is on the operator norm of the full multilinear derivative. Compactness bounds the path-space derivative and the evaluation operator costs at most one.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_slabPath_unifo.summary: Compact parameter sets give uniform jet bounds in time

TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_terminalBorelA.text: Evaluating the atom’s `k`th Fréchet derivative at zero on directions `v` gives their product times the indicator of `k=n`. The scale must be positive. This is the multilinear form of the scalar derivative identity, used when controlling joint time-space derivatives rather than only one-variable derivatives.
TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_terminalBorelA.summary: The full derivative of a scalar atom at zero

TorusEuler.kineticForm.text:
Define the nonnegative kinetic coefficient K as the deformation adjoint composed with the deformation. It may be degenerate when the deformation is singular; quantitative positive ellipticity requires a bounded left inverse and is proved separately.

Default-value audit (b5): A singular F gives a degenerate nonnegative quadratic form, and F zero gives K zero. The definition itself does not justify a positive inverse ellipticity constant.
TorusEuler.kineticForm.summary: The kinetic coefficient in label coordinates

TorusEuler.kineticForm_elliptic.text: If $GF=I$, $D>0$ and $\|G\|\le D$, then $\langle F^*Fv,v\rangle\ge D^{-2}\|v\|^2$ for every vector. The proof starts from $v=G(Fv)$ and uses the operator norm. It requires only a bounded left inverse, not a parent flow or a differential equation. Applying it to the actual deformation yields the ellipticity used in both inverse applications in Theorem 4.2.
TorusEuler.kineticForm_elliptic.summary: Ellipticity from a bounded inverse deformation

TorusEuler.kineticForm_identity.text: The identity deformation has identity kinetic coefficient. In the flow application this identifies K at initial time and helps recover the initial correction from the constant field.
TorusEuler.kineticForm_identity.summary: The kinetic coefficient of the identity deformation

TorusEuler.kineticForm_inverse.text: If `G` is a two-sided inverse of `F`, witnessed by both `hGF` and `hFG`, then $GG^*$ is a two-sided inverse of the kinetic form $F^*F$. The conclusion explicitly gives both compositions as the identity. This statement uses a supplied inverse rather than relying on a totalized inverse definition.
TorusEuler.kineticForm_inverse.summary: The inverse deformation gives a two sided kinetic inverse

TorusEuler.kineticForm_quadratic_upper.text: The kinetic pairing of `v` is at most $\|F\|^2\|v\|^2$. This follows by identifying it with $\|Fv\|^2$ and applying the operator norm bound. The result is an upper estimate for any bounded deformation operator; ellipticity and a lower estimate require distinct assumptions.
TorusEuler.kineticForm_quadratic_upper.summary: The deformation norm bounds the kinetic quadratic form

TorusEuler.labelFlow_firstVariation.text: The derivative of the perturbed flow with respect to its velocity perturbation solves $\xi_t=M\xi+b\circ X$ and starts at zero. The binder `hX` supplies flows of $U+\varepsilon b$ for every real $\varepsilon$. The hypotheses `hUlip`, `hDlip`, `hblip`, `hbnd`, `hbc` and `hD` give the uniform bounds and continuity used in the parameter differentiation. The conclusion identifies the solution with the actual derivative at $\varepsilon=0$, rather than merely defining a variational equation.
TorusEuler.labelFlow_firstVariation.summary: First variation with fixed initial labels

TorusEuler.labelPhaseScale.text:
Scaling the label by the envelope radius and the phase by the profile width makes the weighted coordinate derivatives into the ordinary derivatives of a rescaled profile.

Default-value audit (b5): If either scale is zero the linear map collapses the corresponding coordinates. Results recovering unscaled derivatives assume the positive scales used by the construction.

TorusEuler.labelPhaseScale_apply.text: The rescaling map sends (a,s) to (ℓa,hs). The label radius and phase width are independent scalar factors; positivity or invertibility is needed only when later results undo the scaling.

TorusEuler.labelPhaseScale_phaseCoordina.text: Applying the label-phase scaling map to a coordinate direction multiplies that direction by its assigned weight. The equality holds for arbitrary real scales, including zero. It is the linear algebra input that attaches one envelope factor or one phase-width factor to each slot of a mixed derivative.
TorusEuler.labelPhaseScale_phaseCoordina.summary: Scaling acts diagonally on the four directions

TorusEuler.labelPhaseSlope.text: Map a label increment `v` to its scaled label component and the corresponding scaled phase increment: $(\ell^{-1}v,h^{-1}\langle k,v\rangle)$. This continuous linear map records both derivative costs in evaluating a phase profile along a graph. The definition allows arbitrary real scales; inverse identities later require them nonzero.
TorusEuler.labelPhaseSlope.summary: Label increments on the scaled phase graph

TorusEuler.labelPhaseSlope_apply.text: Evaluating `labelPhaseSlope` gives the explicit pair of scaled label and phase components. The equality is definitional for every real scale and vector. In applications, the first component costs the reciprocal envelope radius and the second costs the wave-vector magnitude divided by the phase width.

TorusEuler.labelWaveVector.text:
The local wave vector along a trajectory, defined as the adjoint derivative of the reverse flow applied to the initial covector `k`. The parameters `s`, `a`, and `t` specify the starting time, particle label, and current time. The reverse transition is evaluated at `X s t a`. This is the formal expression for $(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$ once the inverse-flow derivative identities have been established.

The raw definition itself imposes neither the flow equation nor nonvanishing of the carrier.

Default-value audit (b5): The definition uses the derivative of an arbitrary candidate inverse-label map. Smoothness, invertibility and nonzero launch data are supplied by the parent-flow lemmas before the covector receives its physical interpretation.
TorusEuler.labelWaveVector.summary: Wave covector transported by the inverse flow derivative

TorusEuler.labelWaveVector_smul.text: Multiplying the launch covector $k$ by a real scalar $c$ multiplies its transported wave vector by the same scalar. This is linearity of the inverse deformation transpose in the covector argument. No flow equation or invertibility assumption is imposed here; those hypotheses are needed when interpreting this algebraic expression as transport.
TorusEuler.labelWaveVector_smul.summary: Transport preserves the launch covector scale

TorusEuler.laplacianMode.text: The Laplacian symbol is $-(2\pi)^2|k|^2$, regarded as a complex scalar. It corresponds to the sum of second derivatives for the unit-torus Fourier normalization. The negative sign is the usual Laplacian convention, which determines the sign of the pressure inverse used below.
TorusEuler.laplacianMode.summary: The Laplacian multiplier has negative frequency square

TorusEuler.laplacianMode_mul_inverseLapl.text: Multiplying the Laplacian symbol by its inverse gives zero at zero frequency and one at every other frequency. This explicit case distinction prevents treating the pressure inverse as an unrestricted inverse. It is the coefficient-level statement that a periodic Poisson solution recovers the source minus its mean.
TorusEuler.laplacianMode_mul_inverseLapl.summary: The pressure inverse recovers every nonconstant mode

TorusEuler.laplacianMode_ne_zero.text: If `hk` says the integer frequency is nonzero, its Laplacian symbol is nonzero. Positivity of the squared frequency length and the nonvanishing of $2\pi$ justify this statement. The lemma provides the scalar cancellation guard for the inverse Laplacian at nonzero modes.
TorusEuler.laplacianMode_ne_zero.summary: The Laplacian symbol is invertible away from zero frequency

TorusEuler.laplacianMode_zero.text: The Laplacian symbol at zero frequency is zero. This follows directly from the sum of squared frequency coordinates. It records the constant-mode obstruction to inverting the periodic Laplacian and supplies the base case for the deliberately zero-mean pressure inverse.
TorusEuler.laplacianMode_zero.summary: The Laplacian annihilates the constant frequency

TorusEuler.laterPhysicalWindow_fits_pare.text: The scheduled half-length shrinkage and a crossing in the old first half imply strict separation of the new endpoint from the old endpoint, together with containment of the whole new slab. The hypotheses refer to adjacent induction half lengths. The statement does not itself prove the shrinkage or locate the crossing.
TorusEuler.laterPhysicalWindow_fits_pare.summary: The scheduled next interval stays strictly inside its parent

TorusEuler.latticeVector.text:
For a function n : Fin 3 → ℤ, latticeVector n embeds its three coordinates into ℝ³. WithLp.toLp 2 supplies the Euclidean-space wrapper and each integer is coerced to a real number. These are exactly the translations used by SpatiallyPeriodic; the map is not a rounding operation or a choice of fundamental representative.

Default-value audit (b4): Only integer coercions and the Euclidean wrapper occur. There is no inverse, limiting operation, derivative or integral, and no degenerate branch to exclude.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.

TorusEuler.le_exp_integral_of_volterra.text: If continuous $u$ and nonnegative continuous $k$ satisfy $u(t)\le c+\int_a^t k(r)u(r)\,dr$, then $u(t)\le c\exp(\int_a^t k)$. The proof differentiates an integrating factor and shows it decreases. Neither $u\ge0$ nor $c\ge0$ is assumed; their usual nonnegativity in the norm application is not needed for this abstract inequality.
TorusEuler.le_exp_integral_of_volterra.summary: An exponential bound from the integral inequality

TorusEuler.lemma31_waveProfile.text: The explicit profiles and normalized primitives satisfy all conclusions of Lemma 3.1 for every $0<h\le1$. The proof chooses $C=1/2$, combines smoothness, parity, periodicity and the primitive identity, and imports a separate constant for each derivative order $j\ge2$. The family is fixed before the scale is quantified. Thus this theorem supplies both the witnesses and the uniformity needed by the new statement, while its conclusion still allows an existential positive constant.
TorusEuler.lemma31_waveProfile.summary: Uniform bounds for the explicit profile family

TorusEuler.length_hierarchyLeibnizSplits.text: The ordered Leibniz list for a word of length $m$ contains exactly $2^m$ entries. Each derivative is assigned to either the first or second factor. Repeated coordinate letters retain their multiplicities, so this counts product-rule terms rather than distinct pairs of resulting words.
TorusEuler.length_hierarchyLeibnizSplits.summary: There are two choices for each derivative

TorusEuler.lerayMode.text: The coefficient $a$ is sent to $a-(k\cdot a)|k|^{-2}k$, using complex coordinate arithmetic. For nonzero frequency this removes the component parallel to $k$. At zero frequency, totalized division makes the correction vanish and preserves the constant vector mode, as required for the periodic Leray projection.

TorusEuler.lerayModeProjection.text: This continuous complex-linear map is the orthogonal projection onto `transverseModeSpace k`. It is a Hilbert-space realization of the earlier coordinate Leray formula. Subsequent lemmas identify the two realizations and obtain the operator norm bound needed to extend the projection to square-integrable fields.
TorusEuler.lerayModeProjection.summary: The bounded orthogonal projection onto transverse coefficients

TorusEuler.lerayModeProjection_toLp.text: Applying the bounded orthogonal projection to a Euclidean-wrapped coefficient gives the wrapper of `lerayMode k a`. The proof expands the projection onto a one-dimensional span and matches the inner product and squared norm. This identity includes the intentional identity action at frequency zero.
TorusEuler.lerayModeProjection_toLp.summary: The orthogonal projection equals the explicit Leray formula

TorusEuler.lerayModeProjection_zero.text: At zero frequency, the continuous linear Leray projection equals the identity operator. This is operator equality, extending the earlier coefficientwise identity. It ensures that the Hilbert-space construction retains constant vector fields rather than projecting onto a mean-zero spatial subspace.
TorusEuler.lerayModeProjection_zero.summary: The bounded zero frequency projection is the identity

TorusEuler.lerayMode_eq_angularLeray_com.text: For an arbitrary complex coefficient, the Leray output is reconstructed from the angular projection of its real coordinate vector and that of its imaginary coordinate vector. The formula uses the same real frequency for both. This permits real Hilbert-space coercivity estimates to be applied to complex Fourier coefficients.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_eq_angularLeray_com.summary: Leray acts separately on real and imaginary parts

TorusEuler.lerayMode_eq_sub_gradient.text: The Leray-projected coefficient equals the original coefficient minus the gradient of `pressureCorrectionMode`. This identity holds at zero and nonzero frequencies, using the chosen zero-mean inverse Laplacian. It ties the geometric transverse projection to the pressure formulation needed in the endpoint equation.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_eq_sub_gradient.summary: The Leray correction is a pressure gradient

TorusEuler.lerayMode_idempotent.text: The Leray symbol is idempotent at every frequency. Its first application produces a transverse coefficient, and the preceding fixed-point lemma shows that the second application preserves it. The identity includes the zero mode, where the symbol is already the identity.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_idempotent.summary: Applying the Leray symbol twice changes nothing

TorusEuler.lerayMode_ofRealVector.text: Applying the coordinate Leray symbol to a real vector cast into complex coordinates is the same as applying the angular Leray operator at the real frequency and then casting its result. This holds for all integer modes, including zero. It verifies compatibility of the real and complex formalizations.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_ofRealVector.summary: The complex Leray formula agrees with the real symbol

TorusEuler.lerayMode_of_transverse.text: If the frequency contraction of `a` is zero, the Leray symbol fixes `a`. The hypothesis `h` expresses transversality; it automatically holds at zero frequency. The result requires no norm estimate and directly identifies vectors in the symbol range as fixed points.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_of_transverse.summary: Transverse coefficients are unchanged by Leray projection

TorusEuler.lerayMode_tensorDivergenceMod.text: At every Fourier mode, Leray-projected tensor divergence equals the original tensor divergence plus the gradient mode of the normalized pressure symbol. The formula includes the zero mode consistently. It identifies the nonlocal pressure contribution used when the source is separated from the observation region.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_tensorDivergenceMod.summary: Projected tensor divergence splits into local and pressure parts

TorusEuler.lerayMode_zero.text: The zero-frequency Leray symbol is the identity on every coefficient vector. This is proved from the actual totalized formula, not assumed as a separate branch. Preserving the constant mode is necessary for the spatial projection to retain divergence-free mean fields used in the endpoint problem.
TorusEuler.lerayMode_zero.summary: The Leray projection preserves the constant mode

TorusEuler.liftConvolution.text: Define the convolution at `x` by integrating the scalar kernel value times the field at $x-y$ over Euclidean three-space. The field can be a periodic lift, but periodicity is not built into the definition. Analytic integrability conditions are supplied by the subsequent bounded-field lemmas.
TorusEuler.liftConvolution.summary: Convolving the periodic lift with a scalar kernel

TorusEuler.liftConvolution_cutoffSchwart.text: Convolving the periodic lift of a continuous torus field with the scaled inverse Fourier kernel equals its finite spectral cutoff. The target is a complete complex normed space. The symbol must be smooth and vanish outside the radius-two ball, and the scale must be positive. Equality of torus Fourier coefficients identifies the two realizations. This theorem supplies the passage from the multiplier definition to physical kernel estimates.

For a smooth compactly supported cutoff symbol and positive frequency scale, convolution of any finite torus Fourier sum with the dilated constructed Schwartz kernel equals the prescribed cutoff. This combines Fourier inversion with the preceding polynomial identity. Extending the conclusion to larger function spaces requires the later boundedness and density arguments.
TorusEuler.liftConvolution_cutoffSchwart.summary: The constructed Schwartz kernel realizes the cutoff

TorusEuler.liftConvolution_fourierMode.text: Convolving a scalar lifted Fourier character by `K` multiplies that character by the Fourier transform of `K` at the lattice frequency. This is the scalar specialization of the vector-valued mode identity. It fixes the torus multiplier convention before finite Fourier sums are treated term by term.

TorusEuler.liftConvolution_fourierMode_s.text: For a complex Banach-valued coefficient `a`, convolution of its Fourier mode by `K` multiplies it by the whole-space Fourier transform of `K` at the corresponding lattice vector. The declaration has no explicit integrability hypothesis: it is an identity of total integral expressions. Concrete kernel applications later establish integrability and continuity.
TorusEuler.liftConvolution_fourierMode_s.summary: Each Fourier mode is a convolution eigenfunction

TorusEuler.liftConvolution_lift_finiteFo.text: For an integrable kernel, convolving a finite torus Fourier sum on its Euclidean lift multiplies each coefficient by the kernel's Fourier transform at that lattice frequency. The finite sum can be interchanged with integration directly. This establishes the convolution representation first on trigonometric polynomials, before any density argument.
TorusEuler.liftConvolution_lift_finiteFo.summary: Convolution acts mode by mode on a finite Fourier sum

TorusEuler.liftConvolution_scaledLiftKer.text: An integrable Euclidean kernel whose Fourier transform is the prescribed compactly supported real symbol realizes the torus cutoff after positive dilation. The equality is proved for arbitrary finite Fourier sums. The symbol-transform identity `htransform` is an explicit input, so this theorem does not itself construct the kernel.
TorusEuler.liftConvolution_scaledLiftKer.summary: The dilated kernel realizes the periodic cutoff on polynomials

TorusEuler.lift_lerayMode_eq_sub_gradien.text: The synthesized Leray field equals the original vector polynomial minus the gradient of its synthesized pressure correction. This is a pointwise identity on the Euclidean lift. It combines the modewise algebraic decomposition with the exact gradient formula for finite Fourier sums.
TorusEuler.lift_lerayMode_eq_sub_gradien.summary: Finite Leray projection subtracts the pressure gradient

TorusEuler.linearFundamental_parameterDe.text: A parameter-dependent fundamental solution with uniformly bounded norm has a parameter derivative satisfying the inhomogeneous variational equation. The inputs include a global parameter Lipschitz bound on `A`, its derivative at the selected parameter, continuity of that derivative in time, and parameter continuity of `F`. Differentiation under a dominated integral proves the derivative instead of assuming it.
TorusEuler.linearFundamental_parameterDe.summary: Differentiate the fundamental solution through its coefficient

TorusEuler.linearODEWordFactor.text: Defines the recurrence $F(0)=1$ and $F(n+1)=1+2^{n+1}qF(n)$. In applications, `q` is the product of homogeneous stability, time length, and the positive-order coefficient bound. The recurrence records dependence on differentiation order explicitly, without claiming that this factor is uniform in order.
TorusEuler.linearODEWordFactor.summary: Order-dependent factor for the coefficient commutator

TorusEuler.linearODEWordFactor_mono.text: If $0 \le  q \le  r$, then the recurrence factor at every fixed order is no larger at `q` than at `r`. The proof combines induction with nonnegativity of the earlier factor. This allows a uniform cap on stability times duration times coefficient size to replace the actual product.
TorusEuler.linearODEWordFactor_mono.summary: Increasing the coefficient cost increases the order factor

TorusEuler.linearODEWordFactor_nonneg.text: For $q \ge  0$, every value of the order recurrence is nonnegative. Induction uses its constant one and the nonnegative product in the successor step. This sign control is needed when the factor multiplies initial-data and forcing budgets or is replaced by a larger commutator cap.
TorusEuler.linearODEWordFactor_nonneg.summary: Nonnegative commutator cost gives a nonnegative factor

TorusEuler.linearODE_exists_Icc.text: For `hab : a ≤ b`, continuous bounded-linear-operator coefficients on $[a,b]$, and arbitrary initial data, constructs a path satisfying $x\prime=A(t)x$ there and $x(a)=x_0$. The ambient real normed space must be complete. Derivatives are taken within the closed interval, allowing endpoint data; the function is defined on all real times but the ODE is asserted only on this interval.
TorusEuler.linearODE_exists_Icc.summary: Solve a linear equation from the left endpoint

TorusEuler.linearODE_exists_Icc_of_mem.text: A continuous homogeneous linear ODE has a solution on the full closed interval, with initial data at any point of the interval.
TorusEuler.linearODE_exists_Icc_of_mem.summary: Solving a linear equation from any slab time

TorusEuler.linearODE_forced_norm_le.text: For a continuous linear equation on a Banach space, the bound `hStable` on all forward homogeneous trajectories controls a supplied forced trajectory. Its norm is at most $M\|z(a)\|+\int_a^t M\|f(r)\|\,dr$. The proof constructs fundamental and inverse solutions and applies variation of constants. Stability is an explicit hypothesis, not a consequence of continuity alone.
TorusEuler.linearODE_forced_norm_le.summary: A stable homogeneous flow bounds the forced solution

TorusEuler.linearODE_fundamental_comp_in.text: Proves the reverse composition $\Phi(t)\Psi(t)=I$ from the normalized fundamental and inverse equations. This direction additionally assumes `hA : ContinuousOn A J`. The product solves the commutator equation $X\prime=AX-XA$, and uniqueness identifies it with the identity. The result applies to normed real spaces without a finite-dimensional or completeness hypothesis.

TorusEuler.linearODE_inhom_exists_Icc.text: Constructs a solution of $x\prime=A(t)x+g(t)$ for continuous $A$ and $g$ on a closed interval, with data prescribed at any member `t₀`. Completeness of the ambient space is required. The proof adjoins a scalar coordinate equal to one and solves a homogeneous equation on the product space; it asserts no uniqueness or bounds beyond existence.
TorusEuler.linearODE_inhom_exists_Icc.summary: Solve a forced linear equation on a closed interval

TorusEuler.linearODE_inv_comp_fundamenta.text: If operator paths $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ solve $\Phi\prime=A\Phi$ and $\Psi\prime=-\Psi A$ within an order-connected set, and both equal the identity at a point of that set, then $\Psi(t)\Phi(t)=I$ throughout it. Product differentiation gives zero derivative. No continuity assumption on $A$ is needed for this order of composition, because the resulting equation is constant.
TorusEuler.linearODE_inv_comp_fundamenta.summary: The inverse flow cancels the fundamental flow

TorusEuler.linearODE_ne_zero_of_mem.text: A solution of a homogeneous linear differential equation cannot reach zero if it is nonzero at one time. The interval is order-connected (`hJ`), its operator coefficient is continuous (`hA`), and `hx` is the equation. Uniqueness against the zero solution proves the conclusion throughout the interval. Applied to the wave vector and then the amplitude operator, it prevents either vector from vanishing.

TorusEuler.linearODE_parameters_joint_co.text: A supplied family of solutions is jointly continuous in time and a pseudometric parameter if coefficients, forcing, and initial data have the stated uniform Lipschitz bounds. The size assumption `hX` controls the solution itself by nonnegative `C`. The conclusion also produces one parameter Lipschitz constant for the whole slab; no existence assertion is hidden here.
TorusEuler.linearODE_parameters_joint_co.summary: Uniform coefficient bounds give continuous parameter dependence

TorusEuler.linearODE_perturbation_bounds.text: Assume the unperturbed Banach-space flow has forward bound $M\ge0$, the continuous matrix error has norm at most continuous $\rho$, and $x,y$ solve the perturbed and unperturbed equations. With $D=\int_a^t\rho$, the theorem bounds growth by $M\|x(a)\|e^{MD}$ and the comparison error by $M\|x(a)-y(a)\|+M^2\|x(a)\|e^{MD}D$. No smallness condition is imposed; later estimates make the exponential harmless.
TorusEuler.linearODE_perturbation_bounds.summary: Growth and error under an integrated matrix perturbation

TorusEuler.linearODE_unique_of_mem.text: Two solutions of a continuous linear ODE on an interval agree everywhere if they agree at any time in the interval.
TorusEuler.linearODE_unique_of_mem.summary: A continuous linear equation has unique trajectories

TorusEuler.linearODE_variation_of_consta.text: A forced linear equation has the representation $z(t)=\Phi(t)z(a)+\int_a^t\Phi(t)\Psi(r)f(r)\,dr$. The hypotheses `hA` and `hf` give continuous coefficients and forcing, while `hΦ`, `hΨ`, `hΦ₀`, and `hΨ₀` specify normalized fundamental and inverse equations. `hz` is the forced equation and `ht` places the observation time in the interval. Taking zero initial data gives the integral used for the amplitude error.
TorusEuler.linearODE_variation_of_consta.summary: Variation of constants for a linear equation

TorusEuler.linearODE_weightedHierarchyWo.text: Specializes the localized weighted word estimate to $x(l)=0$. Under the same closed-support, smoothness, positive-weight, stability, and commutator-cap assumptions, the resulting constant is the order factor times $K\cdot (r-l)\cdot H$. The proof verifies a zero initial word bound and invokes the general theorem, so support propagation remains part of the argument.
TorusEuler.linearODE_weightedHierarchyWo.summary: Zero initial data removes the initial-value contribution

TorusEuler.linearODE_weightedHierarchyWo.text: On $[l,r]$, initial data and forcing vanish outside a closed set `S`, while weighted homogeneous stability and positive-order coefficient estimates are required only on `S`. Smoothness, a strictly positive time weight, and a cap on $K\cdot (r-l)\cdot C$ yield a global finite-word bound for the weighted solution. Outside `S`, uniqueness gives zero solution and closedness gives zero derivatives.
TorusEuler.linearODE_weightedHierarchyWo.summary: Localized initial data and forcing give a global word bound

TorusEuler.linearODE_wordBounds.text: On a positive slab $[0,T]$, assumes smooth coefficients, forcing, and solution, a strictly positive differentiable weight, weighted homogeneous stability on `S`, and initial, forcing, and positive-order coefficient bounds through order `N`. Every solution word through that order is bounded by $\mathrm{linearODEWordFactor}(KTC,N)\,K(B+TH)$. Independence from other parameters requires a separate uniform bound on $K\cdot T\cdot C$.
TorusEuler.linearODE_wordBounds.summary: Control all parameter words through a prescribed order

TorusEuler.linearODE_wordBounds_Icc.text: For $l < r$, gives the same all-word estimate on $[l,r]$, replacing time length `T` by $r-l$ and initial data at zero by data at `l`. All smoothness, positive-weight, homogeneous-stability, and coefficient hypotheses are stated on that interval. The proof translates the problem to a zero-start slab and translates solutions back.
TorusEuler.linearODE_wordBounds_Icc.summary: The weighted word estimate allows any launch time

TorusEuler.lipschitzOnWith_halfHolder_of.text: If every label evaluation has the stated within-interval time derivative and the derivative fields have half-Hölder norm at most `B ≥ 0`, the entire field curve is `B`-Lipschitz in the half-Hölder norm. The proof controls values and spatial increments separately. A pointwise value bound on derivatives alone would not establish this norm-level conclusion.
TorusEuler.lipschitzOnWith_halfHolder_of.summary: Uniform derivative control gives a Lipschitz Hölder-space curve

TorusEuler.lipschitzWith_toUnitTorus.text: The map from Euclidean space to the unit torus is Lipschitz with constant one. It packages the preceding distance comparison as a `LipschitzWith` statement, supplying continuity and quantitative control for translated curves. This concerns the quotient map, not a discontinuous choice of real representatives of torus points.

TorusEuler.localizedCoefficient_holderHa.text: For a cutoff with bounded values, support through radius $2r$, and Lipschitz bound `hχlip`, the localized difference $\chi(x)(B(a)-B(x))$ has supremum $O(rL)$, Lipschitz constant $O(L)$, and half-Hölder seminorm $O(\sqrt rL)$. The remaining inputs are positive `r`, nonnegative constants `hC`, `hL`, and the coefficient bound `hBlip`. This supplies the smallness used to absorb the near source without differentiating the cutoff.
TorusEuler.localizedCoefficient_holderHa.summary: Small Hölder norm of the localized coefficient difference

TorusEuler.localizedCompletedWave_proper.text: The curl of the localized wave potential is smooth, periodic, and divergence free, and agrees inside the label cell with the leading graph plus its slow curl correction. The assumptions explicitly include smooth inverse labels `hA`, lattice equivariance `hperiod`, a positive boundary collar `hδ`, `hδ'`, smooth potential `hQ`, and collar vanishing `hzero`. The hypotheses `hκ`, `hk`, and `htrans` identify a nonzero transported covector and impose transversality. The wave vector remains an arbitrary real vector.
TorusEuler.localizedCompletedWave_proper.summary: Smooth periodic divergence free localized waves

TorusEuler.localizedCurl_properties.text: Assume the inverse label is smooth and lattice-equivariant, the evaluated potential is smooth, and it vanishes in a collar of width $0<\delta\le1/2$. Its localized curl is smooth, periodic, and divergence free. Where inverse labels lie in the cell interior, it agrees exactly with the curl of the unperiodized transported potential.
TorusEuler.localizedCurl_properties.summary: A collar supported potential gives a smooth periodic solenoidal wave

TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile.text: The cellwise graph $a\mapsto f(t,a,k\cdot a)$ is first extended by `periodizeCentered`, then composed with the inverse label map `A t`. The definition accepts every real vector `k` and every target type `F`. Smoothness is not part of the definition: it is supplied by vanishing in a collar of the cell boundary. This order of operations explains how the localized construction avoids requiring an integral wave vector.
TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile.summary: Periodic extension of a localized profile graph

TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile_e.text: Assume the forward flow `X` is a left inverse of the label map, is lattice-equivariant, fixes zero and is `L`-Lipschitz. If the profile vanishes outside the centered label radius `r`, then its transported value vanishes at any point farther than `L*r` from every lattice point. This is the support statement before applying the Fourier cutoff.
TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile_e.summary: Transported support stays near lattice translates of the origin

TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile_e.text: Assume the inverse label is continuous at `x`, its value lies in the interior centered cell, and the profile vanishes in the stated positive-width collar. Then localized periodized graph evaluation agrees with ordinary transported evaluation near `x`. This local equality transfers derivatives without differentiating the discontinuous representative globally.
TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile_e.summary: The localized and ordinary profiles agree near interior labels

TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile_r.text: Assume an odd spatial label map `A t` and a profile whose simultaneous label-phase reflection is given by a continuous linear map `L`. With a positive radial envelope contained within the cell, its localized transported realization obeys the same output reflection at $-x$. Both the label and the graph phase change sign under oddness of `A t`.
TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile_r.summary: Odd inverse labels carry reflection to physical space

TorusEuler.localized_couplingDifference_.text: Bounds the change in $\langle k,Ma\rangle$ when the covector and amplitude have relative error at most `δ`, while the gradient has absolute operator error at most `δ`. With $D\ge1$, $0\le\delta\le1$ and $\|M\|\le D$, the error is at most $4D\delta\|k_0\|\|a_0\|$. The three-term expansion separates the covector, amplitude and gradient contributions.
TorusEuler.localized_couplingDifference_.summary: The coupling changes linearly with relative errors

TorusEuler.localized_coupling_positive.text: Assume nonzero reference covector and amplitude, central raw coupling at least $D^{-1}\|k_0\|\|a_0\|$, and the stated relative and gradient errors with $0\le\delta\le(8D^2)^{-1}$. Both perturbed norms remain within factors one half and two. The raw coupling stays strictly positive and above $(2D)^{-1}$ times the reference norm product, while its normalized value is at least $(8D)^{-1}$.
TorusEuler.localized_coupling_positive.summary: Positive central coupling survives a small spatial perturbation

TorusEuler.localized_norm_bounds.text: A perturbation satisfying $\|x-x_0\|\le\delta\|x_0\|$ with $\delta\le1/2$ has norm between half and twice the reference norm. The proof uses only the triangle inequality in a normed additive group. A separate assumption that `δ` is nonnegative is unnecessary for this conditional statement; the later seed application supplies it through its nonnegative error budget.
TorusEuler.localized_norm_bounds.summary: Relative closeness preserves the vector size

TorusEuler.localized_normalized_coupling.text: Identifies the contraction of the normalized covector and normalized amplitude with $\langle k,Ma\rangle/(\|k\|\|a\|)$. This algebraic identity holds for arbitrary vectors, including zero vectors under Lean’s totalized normalization and division. It does not assert positivity or a meaningful direction at zero; those facts enter through the nonvanishing hypotheses of the coupling theorem.
TorusEuler.localized_normalized_coupling.summary: Normalized coupling is the raw contraction quotient

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_advection_eq_ze.text: If the continuous torus velocity `g` is supported in the $2\Lambda$ band and `A` agrees with its self advection after lifting, every coefficient of `A` outside the $4\Lambda$ band is zero. Spatial differentiation preserves frequencies; multiplying the differentiated field by `g` adds two frequencies. The equality assumption `hA` identifies the supplied representative.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_advection_eq_ze.summary: Self advection doubles the parent frequency band

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_compactSymbolDy.text: The blocks inside `compactSymbolDyadicBlocks` act on each input Fourier coefficient by evaluating the compact symbol at the scaled lattice frequency. Packing the blocks with decay certificates does not change their convolution action. This formula is used when summing annular pieces to recover the desired nonzero-frequency multiplier.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_compactSymbolDy.summary: The certified blocks keep the original sampled symbol formula

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_complexPressure.text: For every integer frequency, the Fourier coefficient of the complex multiplier output is the pressure symbol applied to the input coefficient. Positive homogeneity supplies the hypothesis of the general multiplier theorem. This identifies the constructed operator mode by mode, including frequency zero, rather than merely asserting an operator-norm bound.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_complexPressure.summary: The multiplier has the prescribed Fourier coefficients

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_complexPressure.text: The Fourier coefficient of the complex pressure multiplier equals negative inverse Laplacian mode times the double derivative contraction of the tensor coefficient. Homogeneity of the symbol validates the dyadic Fourier law. The identity also holds at zero, where the output coefficient is zero by normalization.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_complexPressure.summary: Every pressure coefficient has the exact Poisson multiplier

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_conj.text: The coefficient at $k$ of the complex-conjugated field is the conjugate of the original coefficient at $-k$. The sign reversal comes from conjugating the Fourier character. This identity supports the proof that a real, even multiplier preserves real-valued fields despite using complex Fourier notation.

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_coordinateDeriv.text: For a continuously differentiable lifted torus vector field, a continuous field representing its coordinate derivative has Fourier coefficient equal to $2\pi i k_i$ times the original coefficient. The actual derivative representation `hd` is required. The result uses the unit-torus frequency normalization and includes the zero mode, whose derivative coefficient vanishes.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_coordinateDeriv.summary: Fourier coefficients identify a vector coordinate derivative

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_coordinate_hess.text: For continuous torus representatives `g` and `h` of a periodic $C^2$ complex field and one of its Hessian entries, the Fourier coefficient of `h` is the coefficient of `g` times the two coordinate derivative symbols. The hypotheses `hg` and `hh` are exact representation equalities, not automatically supplied by their types.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_coordinate_hess.summary: Transfer the Hessian formula to torus representatives

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_finiteFourierSu.text: In a complete complex normed space, the coefficient of a finite Fourier sum at $k$ is the assigned value when $k$ belongs to the synthesis set, and zero otherwise. Character orthogonality proves the result. This identifies a polynomial exactly, rather than approximately, through its finite coefficient list.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_finiteFourierSu.summary: A finite synthesis has exactly its assigned coefficients

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_halfHolderDyadi.text: The Fourier coefficient of the multiplier output is the sum of the Fourier coefficients of its dyadic blocks. The blocks are summable in the continuous-function supremum norm, and coefficient extraction is continuous in that norm. No claim about summability in the full half-Hölder norm is needed for this interchange.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_halfHolderDyadi.summary: Fourier coefficients pass through the uniformly convergent block sum

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_homogeneousHalf.text: Assume `hhom` makes `A` invariant under positive scaling away from zero. Then every Fourier coefficient of the constructed multiplier output is `A(k)` applied to the corresponding input coefficient. At nonzero frequencies the annular partition telescopes; at zero the separate constant term gives the prescribed value. This is where symbol identification is actually proved.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_homogeneousHalf.summary: With homogeneity the constructed operator has the prescribed symbol

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_inner_latticeVe.text: If `hv` places a real spatial $L^2$ field in the weak solenoidal subspace, the Fourier coefficient of its contraction with a frequency vector vanishes at that frequency. The proof uses real and imaginary Fourier potentials as smooth tests. This establishes a consequence of weak divergence freedom without differentiating the velocity.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_inner_latticeVe.summary: Weak solenoidality annihilates longitudinal Fourier coefficients

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_neg_of_parity.text: If a torus field satisfies `hg : g (-z) = c • g z` for a real scalar `c`, its Fourier coefficients satisfy the corresponding relation at opposite frequencies. The proof changes variables by the measure-preserving negation map. This statement does not require a finite Fourier expansion.

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_operatorTorusCo.text: For a continuous integrable operator kernel and continuous input, the Fourier coefficient of the convolution equals the Euclidean Fourier transform of the kernel at the lattice frequency applied to the input coefficient. Completeness of both value spaces and joint integrability justify Fubini and operator interchange. The kernel need not be scalar.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_operatorTorusCo.summary: An operator convolution applies its sampled symbol to each coefficient

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_realVectorFouri.text: For an even symbol, each Fourier coefficient of the complexified real cutoff is the input coefficient multiplied by $\psi(\Lambda^{-1}k)$ inside the closed band of radius $2\Lambda$, and zero outside it. The conditional band test is part of the finite-synthesis definition. The identity holds without a positivity assumption on `Λ`; physical cutoff estimates impose one separately.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_realVectorFouri.summary: The real cutoff has the prescribed finite Fourier coefficients

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_real_coordinate.text: For a periodic real $C^2$ field and exact continuous torus representatives of it and a mixed derivative, complexified Fourier coefficients differ by the two coordinate derivative factors. The assumptions `hg` and `hh` tie the representatives to the actual field. This is a Fourier identity, with no Hölder-norm estimate yet.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_real_coordinate.summary: The real Hessian has the complex Fourier derivative formula

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_real_hessian_eq.text: For a periodic $C^2$ potential and exact representatives of its Hessian entry and Laplacian, the Hessian coefficient equals two derivative factors times `inverseLaplacianMode` times the source coefficient. The zero mode is handled separately; inversion occurs only when `k ≠ 0`. No zero-mean normalization of the potential is required, since its Hessian ignores constants.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_real_hessian_eq.summary: Recover Hessian coefficients from the Laplacian source

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_real_laplacian.text: For a periodic real $C^2$ field, the coefficient of its represented Laplacian equals `laplacianMode k` times its represented scalar coefficient after complexification. Exact lift identities are required for both torus functions. This provides the equation used to eliminate the potential’s coefficient in favour of its Laplacian source.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_real_laplacian.summary: The real Laplacian obeys the Fourier symbol identity

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_smoothFourierCu.text: For positive `hΛ` and a symbol vanishing when its argument has norm greater than two, the cutoff coefficient at $k$ is $\psi(\Lambda^{-1}k)\widehat g(k)$. Completeness of the target space is assumed. The support hypothesis ensures that frequencies omitted by finite synthesis would also have zero multiplier.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_smoothFourierCu.summary: The cutoff multiplies Fourier coefficients by the scaled symbol

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_smoothFourierCu.text: If `hk` places the frequency strictly beyond radius $2\Lambda$, its Fourier coefficient in the cutoff output is zero. The result uses only the finite synthesis band, so no smoothness or support assumption on `ψ` is required. Completeness is needed for the coefficient-recovery theorem used in the proof.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_smoothFourierCu.summary: Frequencies beyond the cutoff band vanish

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_timeDerivative_.text: A jointly smooth family supported in one fixed finite band has its supplied time derivative supported in that same band throughout $[a,b]$. The strict inequality `hab` makes within derivatives unique at the endpoints. The proof differentiates the finite Fourier representation; `hd` identifies the continuous torus field `d` with the actual derivative.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_timeDerivative_.summary: Time differentiation preserves a fixed Fourier band

TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_torusLiftConvol.text: For a Schwartz kernel and continuous torus field, the Fourier coefficient after convolution is the input coefficient multiplied by the Euclidean Fourier transform of the kernel at the lattice frequency. Joint integrability justifies swapping the Euclidean and torus integrals. Haar translation invariance and the character law then separate the coefficient.
TorusEuler.mFourierCoeff_torusLiftConvol.summary: A convolution coefficient is multiplied by the sampled transform

TorusEuler.mFourier_neg_arg.text: Evaluating the torus character at the negative spatial point is the same as evaluating the character with negative frequency at the original point. This group-character identity applies directly on the quotient torus. It supplies the change of variables in the coefficient and polynomial parity arguments.

TorusEuler.materialAcceleration.text:
The Eulerian material acceleration on a time slab.

Default-value audit (b5): Both time and spatial derivatives are totalized. The PDE interpretation requires time regularity within the specified slab and spatial differentiability; an empty time set must not be used as a classical evolution domain.

TorusEuler.materialAcceleration_restrict.text: For a jointly continuously differentiable velocity, identifies material acceleration computed within a smaller closed interval with that computed within the enclosing interval. The smaller interval must have positive length, and the evaluation time must lie inside it. Unique within derivatives justify the equality even at the smaller interval’s endpoints.
TorusEuler.materialAcceleration_restrict.summary: Material acceleration agrees on a positive smaller slab

TorusEuler.meanCoefficient_radius_condit.text: If $D,B\ge1$, $A\le BD^a$, and $\ell\le(BD^{a+9})^{-2}$, then $\ell D^6\le1$ and $AD^9\sqrt\ell\le1$. The displayed theorem does not assume a positive radius or nonnegative $A$; negative radii satisfy these algebraic conclusions under Lean's square-root convention. Applications needing a geometric radius must supply positivity separately.
TorusEuler.meanCoefficient_radius_condit.summary: One radius restriction satisfies both smallness conditions

TorusEuler.meanDerivativeLifting.text: Assume a wordwise inverse recurrence, nonnegative solution sizes, weighted forcing bounded by $M$, and positive-order coefficient costs satisfying $A\ell^{|s|}B_s\le C$. Then every word through order $N$ obeys $\ell^{|s|}V_s\le AM(1+2^NC)^{|s|}$. The induction uses strictly shorter solution words; the inverse factor $A$ is retained only once outside the order-dependent constant.
TorusEuler.meanDerivativeLifting.summary: Keep a single low-order inverse cost through differentiation

TorusEuler.meanPressureHessian_closedSla.text: The actual mean pressure Hessian on the closed slab has its uniform spatial Hölder bound and its supremum bound from the linearized momentum.
TorusEuler.meanPressureHessian_closedSla.summary: The mean pressure Hessian has a uniform bound

TorusEuler.meanPressureHessian_halfHolde.text: Assume a smooth periodic pressure satisfies the stated Poisson equation with periodic half-Hölder coefficient fields. Its Hessian then belongs to the order-zero half-Hölder space, with norm bounded by $48\lVert\mathrm{pressureHessianMultiplier}\rVert$ times the forcing-gradient norm plus the product of the velocity-gradient norms. This is a two-sided norm estimate for the mean component, unlike the signed leading-pressure estimate.
TorusEuler.meanPressureHessian_halfHolde.summary: The periodic Poisson multiplier controls the mean Hessian

TorusEuler.meanPressureHessian_rate_abso.text: The mean velocity and source estimates give the same frequency decay for the mean pressure Hessian after a polynomial parent loss is absorbed into the parameter threshold. This is an estimate for the selected mean correction, not the full pressure.
TorusEuler.meanPressureHessian_rate_abso.summary: Absorbing the parent factor in the mean pressure bound

TorusEuler.meanPressurePoissonSource.text: Given half-Hölder fields representing the two velocity gradients and the forcing gradient, this defines the scalar field obtained by tracing the forcing gradient and subtracting twice the trace of the gradient composition. The construction is made inside the half-Hölder space. Its identification with a physical pressure Laplacian requires the later representation and momentum hypotheses.
TorusEuler.meanPressurePoissonSource.summary: The forcing divergence minus twice the mixed gradient trace

TorusEuler.meanPressurePoissonSource_eva.text: At any point, the bundled Poisson source is the trace of `Df` minus twice the trace of `DU.comp DV`. The theorem unfolds the linear trace and Hölder composition definitions. It is an exact formula for the defined field and does not assume that the three operators are actual gradients.
TorusEuler.meanPressurePoissonSource_eva.summary: Evaluate the scalar Poisson source pointwise

TorusEuler.meanPressurePoissonSource_lif.text: Assume the three torus half-Hölder fields lift to the actual derivatives of `U`, `V` and `f`. Then the lift of the defined source equals forcing divergence minus twice the trace of the two velocity gradients. This connects the torus functional-space construction to the Euclidean formula used by the Poisson identity.
TorusEuler.meanPressurePoissonSource_lif.summary: The torus source lifts to the physical divergence formula

TorusEuler.meanPressure_poisson_closedSl.text: For twice jointly differentiable divergence-free parent and mean velocities, assume the linearized momentum equation uses `derivWithin` on the positive closed slab. Then the mean-pressure Poisson identity holds at every slab time, including both endpoints. The proof obtains zero divergence of that within-time derivative from the joint regularity and divergence constraint.
TorusEuler.meanPressure_poisson_closedSl.summary: The Poisson identity also holds at temporal endpoints

TorusEuler.meanScalarBudget_le_power.text: The scalar costs in the mean estimate combine into the single power $\mathsf D^{a+2b+2s}$. The hypothesis `hAinv` bounds the inverse, and `hBudget` contains two coefficient factors and one source factor involving $\ell_*^{-1/2}$. Nonnegativity and $\mathsf D\ge1$ allow these factors to be enlarged and collected. The result isolates the dependence on the fixed radius exponent $s$.
TorusEuler.meanScalarBudget_le_power.summary: Combining the coefficient costs into one fixed power

TorusEuler.meanScalarRadius_absorbs_inve.text: The product $A\mathsf D^9\sqrt{\ell_*}$ is at most one if $A\le\mathsf D^a$ and $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-s}$ with $s\ge2(a+9)$. The binders `hAinv` and `hs` state those two conditions, and `hD` gives $\mathsf D\ge1$. This scalar estimate explains how choosing the envelope exponent once controls derivative terms without increasing the scale exponent with the measured order.
TorusEuler.meanScalarRadius_absorbs_inve.summary: A small radius absorbs the inverse constant

TorusEuler.memLp_endpointL2Mul.text: An almost-everywhere strongly measurable operator field with an almost-everywhere uniform bound sends an $L^2$ representative to another $L^2$ representative by pointwise application. The bound `hbound` is measure-dependent and need not hold on an exceptional null set. This is the integrability result behind the bundled endpoint multiplier.
TorusEuler.memLp_endpointL2Mul.summary: Bounded measurable coefficients preserve square integrability

TorusEuler.memLp_endpointPrimitive.text: An interval-integrable velocity has a square-integrable primitive on a nonnegative finite interval. Continuity of the primitive on the compact slab supplies the bound needed for its $L^2$ membership. This allows time integration to be bundled as an operator between quotient spaces, even when the original velocity is only integrable.

TorusEuler.memLp_endpointTimeIntegral.text: For nonnegative `T`, integrating a joint $L^2$ field over $(0,T]$ in time gives an $L^2$ function of the label. Fubini and the finite time interval provide the required bound. The statement establishes integrability of the resulting label function before it is bundled into its quotient space.
TorusEuler.memLp_endpointTimeIntegral.summary: Partial time integration gives a square-integrable label field

TorusEuler.memLp_realBanachFourierCutoff.text: If `g` belongs to `MemLp` at exponent infinity on the finite torus measure, so does its real convolution cutoff. Essential boundedness provides integrability, then continuity and compactness bound the output. This declaration establishes membership only; the dimension-independent norm inequality is a later result.

TorusEuler.memLp_realVectorFourierCutoff.text: Every output of `realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunction` belongs to `MemLp` at exponent infinity on the torus. The argument uses continuity of the finite reconstruction and compactness of the torus. This proves boundedness and measurability of the output, not a norm estimate in terms of an arbitrary input.
TorusEuler.memLp_realVectorFourierCutoff.summary: The finite vector cutoff is essentially bounded

TorusEuler.mem_endpointHalfHolderSolenoi.text: A half-Holder field is solenoidal exactly when its continuous representative has zero integral pairing with every smooth periodic gradient.
TorusEuler.mem_endpointHalfHolderSolenoi.summary: The Holder divergence condition through gradient tests

TorusEuler.mem_endpointJointSpatialSolen.text: Membership in the joint solenoidal submodule is equivalent to the vanishing of endpointTorusDivergenceTest T η p u for every pair of tests. The theorem unfolds the intersection of kernels and has no time-length hypothesis. It is a criterion in weak form; it does not assert that a classical divergence exists for u.

A joint field is weakly solenoidal exactly when, for each smooth potential p, its spatial pairing with the gradient of p is zero for almost every time. Read the quantifiers literally: the statement is ∀ p, followed by an almost-everywhere equality in time. It does not itself produce one exceptional null set valid simultaneously for every potential.

TorusEuler.mem_endpointSpatialSolenoidal.text: A spatial L2 field belongs to the weak solenoidal subspace exactly when it annihilates every smooth periodic potential gradient under integration.
TorusEuler.mem_endpointSpatialSolenoidal.summary: The weak solenoidal space through gradient tests

TorusEuler.mem_endpointTorusSpace.text: A joint $L^2$ path belongs to the endpoint subspace exactly when all coordinate mean-test integrals and all separated divergence-test integrals vanish. This expands the intersection-of-kernels definition. It does not by itself upgrade the path to a continuous velocity or assert pointwise endpoint values.
TorusEuler.mem_endpointTorusSpace.summary: Membership means that both families of tests vanish

TorusEuler.mem_endpointTorusSpace_iff_fo.text: For positive `T`, joint membership in the weak endpoint space is equivalent to zero time mean and transversality of every real Fourier coefficient. The converse compares `v` with its orthogonal projection and uses Fourier separation to show their difference vanishes. This is a full characterization, not merely a necessary condition on modes.
TorusEuler.mem_endpointTorusSpace_iff_fo.summary: Endpoint constraints are equivalent to constraints on every Fourier path

TorusEuler.mem_endpointTorusSpace_iff_sl.text: Membership in the joint constraint space is equivalent to zero time integral at almost every label and vanishing gradient pairing at almost every time for each smooth periodic potential. A common exceptional set for all tests is obtained separately.
TorusEuler.mem_endpointTorusSpace_iff_sl.summary: The endpoint constraints expressed through slices

TorusEuler.mem_freezingFixedSpace.text: A vector belongs to the fixed subspace exactly when the operator leaves it unchanged. This converts the kernel definition into the equation used by compressed inverses.

TorusEuler.mem_freezingFixedSpace_iff_we.text: Suppose the fixed vectors of `Q` are exactly a Hilbert submodule `V`, and `P` intertwines with `Q`. A half-Hölder field is fixed by `P` exactly when its Haar embedding lies in `V`. This turns the abstract projected-space condition into the weak divergence and, where applicable, time-mean constraints.
TorusEuler.mem_freezingFixedSpace_iff_we.summary: Recognize projected fields by the weak constraint

TorusEuler.mem_frequencyBand.text: An integer frequency belongs to the band of radius R exactly when the Euclidean norm of its lattice vector is at most R. This is the defining spectral cutoff condition.
TorusEuler.mem_frequencyBand.summary: A Fourier-band index has bounded lattice length

TorusEuler.mem_frequencyBand_neg.text: A frequency belongs to the closed finite ball of radius `R` exactly when its negative does. The radius is any real number, including negative values where both membership assertions fail. This symmetry permits reindexing finite Fourier sums by frequency negation when proving parity and reality.
TorusEuler.mem_frequencyBand_neg.summary: Frequency balls are invariant under sign reversal

TorusEuler.mem_hierarchyAdmissibleWords.text: A word belongs to the canonical finite list exactly when its length is at most n and its letters are nondecreasing. This avoids counting permutations as separate mixed multi-indices.
TorusEuler.mem_hierarchyAdmissibleWords.summary: Admissible words are sorted and have bounded length

TorusEuler.mem_periodicComplexSolenoidal.text: A complex $L^2$ field belongs to the Fourier solenoidal subspace exactly when its inner product with every inserted longitudinal mode vanishes. It suffices to test generators because the pairing is linear on their span. This characterization includes the harmless zero-frequency test.
TorusEuler.mem_periodicComplexSolenoidal.summary: Solenoidality can be tested against individual longitudinal modes

TorusEuler.mem_periodicComplexSolenoidal.text: A complex spatial $L^2$ field belongs to the Fourier solenoidal subspace precisely when every Fourier coefficient lies in its transverse mode space. This translates the longitudinal testing definition into a coefficientwise condition. It includes zero frequency, where the transverse space is the whole coefficient space.
TorusEuler.mem_periodicComplexSolenoidal.summary: A Hilbert field is solenoidal exactly when its coefficients are

TorusEuler.mem_transverseModeSpace_iff.text: A complex coefficient, placed in the Euclidean wrapper, belongs to the transverse mode space exactly when its frequency contraction vanishes. The statement includes zero frequency, where all coefficients qualify. It translates algebraic divergence-free conditions into the closed subspace language used for Hilbert-space projection.
TorusEuler.mem_transverseModeSpace_iff.summary: Orthogonality is exactly zero frequency contraction

TorusEuler.mem_transversePlane.text: A vector belongs to `transversePlane k` exactly when its inner product with `k` is zero. This unfolds the kernel of the continuous linear functional defined by `k`. The statement holds in any real inner-product space; when $k=0$ the kernel is the whole space, not a two-dimensional plane.
TorusEuler.mem_transversePlane.summary: Membership in the transverse space means orthogonality

TorusEuler.mixedPhaseJet.text: First differentiate the profile `j` times in phase, then take its `k`th Fréchet derivative in the parameter at fixed phase. The value is a continuous `k`-multilinear map, written `P [×k]→L[ℝ] E`. In applications the parameter is the label and time is fixed, so this represents one mixed derivative from the finite profile norm.
TorusEuler.mixedPhaseJet.summary: Phase derivatives followed by parameter derivatives

TorusEuler.momentumResidual.text:
The residual $R=\partial_tU+DU\,U+\nabla p$ on the chosen time set. The time derivative is taken within that set, so the same expression is used on a closed parent slab, including its endpoints. A zero residual is the unforced momentum equation. This definition specifies the actual defect of a velocity and pressure, rather than an independently prescribed forcing unrelated to those fields.

Default-value audit (b5): The momentum residual combines totalized derivatives. Smoothness and nondegeneracy of the time slab are proved before residual identities are read as the Euler equation.

TorusEuler.momentumResidual_restrict_Icc.text: Extends the material-acceleration restriction identity to the momentum residual for the same pressure. The smaller closed slab is positive and contained in the original one, and the velocity is jointly continuously differentiable there. The pressure term is identical in both expressions, so no extra pressure differentiability is needed for this equality.
TorusEuler.momentumResidual_restrict_Icc.summary: The physical residual is unchanged by valid slab restriction

TorusEuler.momentumResidual_transportedH.text: Adding a transported velocity and pressure profile to a parent gives the parent residual plus profile time evolution, parent strain, self-advection, and the transported pressure gradient. The inverse-label transport identity cancels the parent material derivative. All derivatives and geometric identities are supplied at the point; unique within-set time differentiation covers closed-slab endpoints.
TorusEuler.momentumResidual_transportedH.summary: The physical residual splits into parent and profile contributions

TorusEuler.momentumTensor.text:
The rank-one momentum tensor with column `i` equal to `v i • u`.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.momentumTensor.summary: The rank-one tensor formed from two velocities

TorusEuler.momentumTensorColumn.text:
Select one column of a continuous torus tensor field and bundle it as a continuous vector field. The column map is used to apply the vector Fourier cutoff to a tensor.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.momentumTensorColumn.summary: One continuous column of the momentum tensor

TorusEuler.momentumTensorDivergence.text:
Tensor divergence adds the derivative of the `i`th column in coordinate `i`.

Default-value audit (b5): Finite sums and index sets are defined at zero order or empty ranges as well. The paper use supplies the intended order and level restrictions.
TorusEuler.momentumTensorDivergence.summary: Divergence of a tensor by differentiating its columns

TorusEuler.momentumTensorDivergence_appl.text: Tensor divergence is the sum over i of the derivative in coordinate direction i of column i. This fixes the convention used when converting self-advection into a tensor divergence.
TorusEuler.momentumTensorDivergence_appl.summary: The coordinate formula for tensor divergence

TorusEuler.momentumTensorDivergence_self.text: For a divergence-free velocity, tensor divergence is the Euler advection term.
TorusEuler.momentumTensorDivergence_self.summary: Tensor divergence equals advection for incompressible velocity

TorusEuler.momentumTensorFourierCutoff.text:
The real tensor cutoff operates on the columns of a physical momentum tensor.

Default-value audit (b5): The tensor cutoff is built from explicit complexification and real-part maps. Approximation and derivative bounds use the symbol conditions and positive scale of the cutoff lemmas.
TorusEuler.momentumTensorFourierCutoff.summary: Fourier truncation of each momentum-tensor column

TorusEuler.momentumTensorFourierCutoff_a.text: The i-th column of the tensor Fourier cutoff is the vector Fourier cutoff of the i-th original column. This identity lets the proof commute truncation with tensor divergence by a finite sum.

TorusEuler.momentumTensor_apply.text: The `i`th column of `momentumTensor u v` is the scalar component `v i` multiplied by the vector `u`. This fixes the tensor convention used by the residual expansion. For $u=v$, taking the column divergence gives the usual Euler momentum transport once incompressibility is supplied separately.
TorusEuler.momentumTensor_apply.summary: The momentum tensor stores velocity-product columns

TorusEuler.momentum_realFourierCutoff_eq.text: Given continuous representatives of velocity, its proposed time term, tensor divergence, pressure term, and residual, an exact input momentum identity yields the tensor formula for the truncated residual. The cutoff velocity must be divergence free. The field `u_t` is only assumed to equal the cutoff time representative here; actual time differentiation and the gradient character of the pressure term are established elsewhere.
TorusEuler.momentum_realFourierCutoff_eq.summary: Rearrange truncated momentum into the residual tensor

TorusEuler.mul_endpointClosedTimeNorm_le.text: For positive label scale, a bounded weighted derivative-word value set controls the closed-time norm of its actual half-Holder representative up to a factor square root two. Positivity is needed when dividing by the scale power.
TorusEuler.mul_endpointClosedTimeNorm_le.summary: Weighted lift bounds control recovered Holder norms

TorusEuler.mul_le_of_meanCoefficientThre.text: If $B\le C D^9\sqrt\ell$ and $A D^9\sqrt\ell\le1$, then $AB\le C$, provided $A,C\ge0$. This is the scalar absorption used after the low-order inverse norm multiplies a differentiated coefficient bound. The theorem assumes the two quantitative bounds and does not derive the coefficient estimate or choose the radius.
TorusEuler.mul_le_of_meanCoefficientThre.summary: The low-order inverse absorbs a coefficient derivative

TorusEuler.mul_norm_halfHolder_le_of_hie.text: If a torus half-Hölder field represents the unweighted spatial derivative word, its norm multiplied by $\ell^{|w|}$ is bounded by $\sqrt2$ times the weighted word supremum. Nonnegative radius and spatial smoothness justify moving the weight into the field. This supplies coefficient estimates in the torus Banach space from label-side bounds.
