This evaluation identity makes the representation concrete. It is used when comparing real divergence pairings with complex longitudinal inner products.

TorusEuler.periodicFarMultiplierJet.text: At target `x` and source `y`, this operator takes the order `d` derivative of the periodic kernel at `x-y` and applies the chosen real output action. It is the derivative kernel used in far pressure integrals. The analytic derivative interpretation is guaranteed only when the difference avoids the integer lattice.
TorusEuler.periodicFarMultiplierJet.summary: A far kernel derivative acts on a source density

TorusEuler.periodicFarPressure.text: This real scalar field integrates the periodized pressure kernel against a complex tensor density over `S` intersected with the half open fundamental cell. Separation is not part of the raw definition. Later theorems prove that integrable sources separated from the target make this the actual smooth far pressure contribution.
TorusEuler.periodicFarPressure.summary: The actual pressure kernel is integrated over a separated source

TorusEuler.periodicHierarchyProfile.text: This physical field combines `mean t ∘ A t` with a localized periodic extension of the difference between the profile and `mean`. The definition itself does not prove that `mean` is the phase average or that the extension is smooth. Subsequent theorems require periodicity of the mean and agreement in a collar near cell faces.
TorusEuler.periodicHierarchyProfile.summary: The mean plus the periodic extension of the oscillation

TorusEuler.periodicHierarchyProfile_hold.text: Under the inverse-chart and cell-collar hypotheses for periodization, a nonnegative jet bound `M` through order `m + 1` yields spatial periodicity, `SpatialHolderHalf m`, and half-Hölder norm at most $3(m+1)M$. The extra derivative controls increments of the order-`m` derivatives. The estimate is conditional on the raw graph jet bound.
TorusEuler.periodicHierarchyProfile_hold.summary: One extra bounded derivative gives the periodic Hölder estimate

TorusEuler.periodicHierarchyProfile_jetB.text: For a smooth inverse-label map with a continuous two-sided inverse and affine lattice equivariance, a smooth profile agreeing with a periodic mean in a positive cell-face collar has a smooth periodic physical extension. Any jet bound on the raw graph evaluation transfers with the same constant. Continuity extends the interior estimate to the closed cell faces.
TorusEuler.periodicHierarchyProfile_jetB.summary: Periodization preserves smoothness and the exact jet constant

TorusEuler.periodicImagPartVector.text: Take the imaginary part of every complex coordinate and repackage the result as a real Euclidean three-vector. The resulting map is real-linear and continuous. It supplies the imaginary projection of the concrete spatial complexification, complementing the previously defined real-part map.
TorusEuler.periodicImagPartVector.summary: Coordinatewise imaginary parts of complex velocities

TorusEuler.periodicImagPartVector_apply.text: The `i`th coordinate of `periodicImagPartVector v` equals `(v i).im`. This definitional identity removes the Euclidean-space conversion maps from subsequent calculations. It allows reconstruction and norm splitting to be proved by the elementary real and imaginary coordinate identities for complex numbers.
TorusEuler.periodicImagPartVector_apply.summary: The imaginary projection acts coordinate by coordinate

TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient.text: The bounded Fourier coefficient map is defined as the Hilbert adjoint of inserting one mode. It maps a spatial $L^2$ field to its complex Euclidean coefficient. This operator definition is convenient for transferring self-adjoint projection identities; a later theorem identifies it with the usual integral coefficient.
TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient.summary: Fourier extraction as the adjoint of mode insertion

TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_eq_mFou.text: The bounded adjoint-based coefficient map equals the standard integral Fourier coefficient of the chosen $L^2$ representative. The proof compares all coefficient inner products and commutes a bounded linear functional with the integrable Fourier expression. This establishes that the Hilbert construction uses the expected sign and normalization.
TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_eq_mFou.summary: Adjoint coefficient extraction equals the Fourier integral

TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_leray.text: For every spatial $L^2$ field and integer frequency, the Fourier coefficient after Leray projection is the Leray symbol applied to the original coefficient. Self-adjointness and the single-mode action prove the formula. No claim of pointwise convergence of a Fourier series is needed.
TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_leray.summary: The all-field Leray operator acts coefficient by coefficient

TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_realLer.text: At lattice frequency `k`, the Fourier coefficient of the complexified real projection equals the mode projection of the original complexified coefficient. This is the explicit multiplier formula for the real weak operator. It includes the zero mode, whose projection is defined as the identity rather than being removed.
TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_realLer.summary: Every Fourier coefficient receives the Leray mode projection

TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_sub_rea.text: Every Fourier coefficient of $v-\mathbb Pv$ is a gradient coefficient with pressure multiplier $\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$. The input $v$ is a real $L^2$ vector field on the torus, complexified to read its Fourier coefficients. This theorem expresses the familiar Leray formula in Fourier coordinates. The scalar correction has zero mode zero, which is the zero-mean normalization. The tie also includes the multiplier identity that identifies the pressure coefficient.
TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_sub_rea.summary: The removed Leray component is a pressure gradient

TorusEuler.periodicL2Mode.text: This bounded complex-linear map sends a coefficient vector to the spatial $L^2$ class of the corresponding Fourier character times that coefficient. It provides a genuine Hilbert-space mode rather than an unevaluated formal series. The following lemma identifies the represented field almost everywhere.
TorusEuler.periodicL2Mode.summary: Inserting one vector Fourier coefficient into L2

TorusEuler.periodicL2Mode_apply_ae.text: The $L^2$ mode insertion agrees almost everywhere with the torus character multiplied by its Euclidean coefficient. This statement gives the representative formula for a Hilbert-space element. It is used to compute inner products and to relate mode insertion to integral Fourier coefficients.
TorusEuler.periodicL2Mode_apply_ae.summary: A Hilbert mode represents its character times coefficient

TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift.text:
The actual half-Hölder Leray projection, expressed as a map on periodic Euclidean lifts.

Default-value audit (b5): The underlying halfHolderProjectionLift explicitly returns the zero function unless the input is both spatially periodic and of finite zeroth half-Hölder regularity. The paper applications establish those predicates before using the projection identities. See PeriodicLerayHolderLift.lean, lines 313–320.
TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift.summary: The periodic Leray projection on Euclidean lifts

TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_add.text: For two periodic order-zero half-Hölder fields, the lifted Leray projection of their sum equals the sum of their projections. The proof descends both fields and uses linearity of the actual torus operator. Both domain hypotheses matter because the total lifted definition returns zero on inadmissible inputs.
TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_add.summary: The Leray lift is additive on its stated domain

TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_add_c.text: The periodic Leray projection removes the Fourier-truncated pressure gradient.
TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_add_c.summary: The Leray projection removes the truncated pressure gradient

TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_eq_se.text: A smooth periodic vector field whose divergence vanishes is fixed by the concrete periodic Leray lift. Smooth periodicity first supplies a genuine half-Hölder torus representative. The divergence identity then places that representative in the solenoidal subspace, where the bounded projection acts as the identity.
TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_eq_se.summary: The projection fixes smooth solenoidal fields

TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_gradi.text: The actual Euclidean lift of the periodic Leray projection sends the gradient of an `EndpointSmoothPotential` to zero. The proof first establishes that this gradient is periodic and half-Hölder, then uses its orthogonality to the solenoidal subspace. The conclusion therefore follows inside the intended projection domain, rather than from the lift’s zero fallback for inadmissible inputs.
TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_gradi.summary: The lifted Leray projection removes smooth periodic gradients

TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_holde.text: The periodic Leray Hölder bound used in the estimate of (5.58).
TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_holde.summary: The order-one Hölder bound for the Leray projection

TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_pullb.text: On the lift of a torus half-Hölder field, the projection is its actual torus Leray projection.
TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_pullb.summary: The lifted projection agrees with the torus projection

TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_slice.text: The within time derivative of a jointly smooth periodic divergence-free velocity on a nondegenerate closed slab is fixed by the actual periodic Leray projection. The proof differentiates its pairing with gradients of test potentials. Smoothness and periodicity put the derivative in the valid half Hölder domain, including at both time endpoints.
TorusEuler.periodicLerayHolderLift_slice.summary: The time derivative of a solenoidal field is projected identically

TorusEuler.periodicPoissonPressure_uniqu.text: Two smooth periodic pressures with equal Laplacians and zero spatial mean are equal. The assumptions `hp`, `hq`, `hpper`, `hqper`, `hpmean`, `hqmean` and `hEq` state precisely those conditions. Their difference has zero gradient by the periodic Poisson identity, hence is constant; zero mean removes the constant. The theorem applies at each time to the pressure selected in Proposition 5.11 and allows any common Poisson source.
TorusEuler.periodicPoissonPressure_uniqu.summary: Uniqueness of the normalized periodic Poisson pressure

TorusEuler.periodicProjectedEuler_of_sta.text: On a positive closed prefix, smooth periodic approximants with uniformly converging values and every spatial jet, a uniformly vanishing residual, and the actual stage evolution yield the integrated projected equation, its within derivative, and joint smoothness of the limit. Smooth spatial slices of the limit are also assumed. This theorem does not yet introduce pressure.
TorusEuler.periodicProjectedEuler_of_sta.summary: Stage limits satisfy the actual projected evolution smoothly

TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentum.text: The bilinear expression is $-\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(u\otimes v)$ on the Euclidean lift, formed by differentiating the momentum tensor and applying the periodic Leray lift. The minus sign matches the evolution equation. This raw definition accepts arbitrary functions; agreement with an actual analytic projection requires its periodic Hölder domain.
TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentum.summary: The signed projected tensor divergence drives Euler evolution

TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumJets.text: The bounded bilinear momentum map extends from genuine smooth tuples to their closure, mapping two order `m+2` inputs to an order `m` output. Density and completeness justify the extension. On embedded smooth velocities it returns the actual signed projected tensor divergence, as the following agreement theorem proves.
TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumJets.summary: Momentum extends to completed compatible derivative data

TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumJets.text: For smooth periodic inputs, each component of the extended momentum output equals the actual derivative of the signed projected tensor divergence. The index ranges through order `m`, while the two inputs are stored through `m+2`. This is the exact interpretation needed by the integrated jet bootstrap.
TorusEuler.periodicProjectedMomentumJets.summary: The extended map returns the actual momentum derivatives

TorusEuler.periodicRealLeray.text: Define the real spatial Leray operator as the orthogonal projection onto the closed subspace annihilating all smooth gradient tests. Its codomain is the ambient real L² space, so ordinary operator composition is available. The later theorems identify this weak definition with the familiar Fourier-symbol projection.
TorusEuler.periodicRealLeray.summary: The real orthogonal projection onto solenoidal fields

TorusEuler.periodicRealLeray_realPart_eq.text: Projecting the real part of a complex spatial L² field equals taking the real part after the complex Leray projection. The proof characterizes orthogonal projection by range membership and orthogonality of the discarded part. The real/complex inner-product identity supplies the orthogonality transfer.
TorusEuler.periodicRealLeray_realPart_eq.summary: Taking real parts commutes with the Leray projection

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2.text: Apply the coordinatewise real-part map to complex vector-valued spatial L² fields. The result is a real continuous linear map between the corresponding Haar L² spaces. It is defined on equivalence classes using the bounded pointwise map; its representative formula is established separately and holds almost everywhere.
TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2.summary: Real parts of spatial square integrable fields

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_apply_ae.text: The L² representative of the real-part map agrees almost everywhere with taking the coordinatewise real part of the input representative. This is the compatibility provided by `compLpL`. It allows later inner-product calculations to use ordinary pointwise complex algebra while preserving the quotient-space meaning of the operators.
TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_apply_ae.summary: Real parts agree almost everywhere with pointwise evaluation

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_complexify.text: Complexify a real spatial L² field and then take its real part; the original L² field is recovered exactly. The equality is between equivalence classes and follows from almost-everywhere coordinate calculations. It supplies a left inverse for complexification, so no information is lost when passing to Fourier coefficients.
TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_complexify.summary: Taking real parts recovers an embedded real field

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_leray_mem_.text: The real part of the complex Leray projection of any spatial L² field belongs to the weak real solenoidal subspace. It is first proved on Fourier modes, whose projected amplitudes are transverse, then extended by density through each continuous gradient-testing functional. No smoothness of the original L² field is assumed.
TorusEuler.periodicRealPartL2_leray_mem_.summary: Projected complex fields have solenoidal real parts

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartVector.text:
Coordinatewise real part on the complex Euclidean spatial vector.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.periodicRealPartVector.summary: Taking real parts of complex Euclidean vectors

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartVector_apply.text: The `i`th coordinate of `periodicRealPartVector v` is the real part of the `i`th complex coordinate of `v`. This pointwise identity identifies the bounded map with the usual real-part operation, despite the different Euclidean-space wrappers used for the real and complex vectors.

TorusEuler.periodicRealPartVector_comple.text: Complexification followed by real projection recovers the original vector.

TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJets.text: This function is the canonical completed jet tuple of a smooth periodic velocity. It is the evaluation of `periodicVelocityJetsLinear`, so all components still equal actual derivatives of the same field. The completed space is needed for integration and time regularity arguments, while these particular inputs remain smooth.
TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJets.summary: A smooth velocity enters the completed jet space

TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJets_apply.text: For a smooth periodic input, evaluating any component of its completed jet tuple gives the corresponding actual iterated Fréchet derivative. The index `i : Fin (m + 1)` limits the order to the stored range. Completion has changed the ambient space, not the value of an embedded smooth tuple.
TorusEuler.periodicVelocityJets_apply.summary: Completed smooth tuples still evaluate to actual derivatives

TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump.text: The scaled bump is evaluated after subtracting the nearest integer, implemented by $\lfloor s+1/2\rfloor$. The formula is one-periodic for all scales. Smoothness and evenness across the cell seams are proved under $0<h\le1$, where the bump vanishes well before those seams.
TorusEuler.periodicWaveBump.summary: Repeating the scaled bump in each unit phase cell

TorusEuler.periodic_iteratedDeriv_phase.text: If a function is periodic with period `τ`, every iterated derivative has the same period. No smoothness hypothesis is present in this declaration because Lean's derivative is a total function and translation preserves its definition. In applications to smooth profiles, these total derivatives agree with the ordinary analytic derivatives.

TorusEuler.periodic_odd_of_pointwise_lim.text: If each vector field is spatially periodic and odd and the sequence converges pointwise, its limit has both symmetries. The proof compares limits at translated points and at $x$ and $-x$. No smoothness or uniform convergence is assumed here; these are purely closed symmetry identities in a normed target.
TorusEuler.periodic_odd_of_pointwise_lim.summary: Periodicity and oddness survive pointwise convergence

TorusEuler.periodic_periodicWaveBump.text: Adding one to the phase leaves the periodic bump unchanged because the nearest-integer floor also increases by one. The theorem holds for every real scale, even degenerate scales. It is an algebraic periodicity statement; smoothness at the wrapping points requires the separate admissible-scale hypotheses.

TorusEuler.periodic_phaseOscillation.text: If a profile is one-periodic, subtracting its phase mean gives another one-periodic profile. This proof only uses that the subtracted mean is constant in the phase; continuity and integrability are not hypotheses. It does not assert that the resulting profile has zero mean, which is proved separately under the appropriate integration assumptions.
TorusEuler.periodic_phaseOscillation.summary: Subtracting the mean preserves the phase period

TorusEuler.periodic_phasePrimitive.text:
The normalized phase primitive is one-periodic when its input is continuous, one-periodic, and has zero phase mean. These assumptions appear as the named binders `hf`, `hper`, and `hmean`. The result explains why the inverse phase derivative in the paper is well-defined on the mean-zero oscillations used for the wave potential. A nonzero phase average would instead create a nonperiodic linear drift in an ordinary primitive.

The derivative identity and zero-average normalization of the primitive are supplied by separate declarations.

TorusEuler.periodic_wavePotential.text: For continuous one-periodic $V$ with zero phase mean, proves one-periodicity of `wavePotential κ V`. The proof transfers the mean through the fixed cross-product operator and uses the periodic primitive theorem. It does not require $\kappa\ne0$ or transversality; these conditions enter the separate fast-curl recovery theorem.
TorusEuler.periodic_wavePotential.summary: The wave potential has the prescribed phase period

TorusEuler.periodic_wavePressurePrimitiv.text: The normalized pressure primitive is one-periodic under the named scale hypotheses `hh` and `hle`. The proof applies `periodic_phasePrimitive` to the continuity, periodicity, and zero phase mean of the constructed velocity profile. This verifies the compatibility needed for a periodic pressure, rather than merely choosing an arbitrary primitive. Its zero additive mean is a separate normalization proved by `phaseMean_wavePressurePrimitive`.

TorusEuler.periodic_waveProfile.text: The integrated profile has period one for every scale satisfying `hh : 0 < h` and `hle : h ≤ 1`. The proof shifts an integral over one period and uses the zero phase mean of the normalized slope. The result complements oddness: an even derivative alone would not make its primitive periodic. This declaration corresponds to the periodicity step in the profile construction.

TorusEuler.periodizeCentered.text:
Extend a label profile periodically using its values on the centered cell.

Default-value audit (b5): Periodicity is automatic, but continuity across cell faces is not. The construction uses profiles vanishing near the boundary before claiming smooth periodic extension.
TorusEuler.periodizeCentered.summary: Periodic extension from the centered cell

TorusEuler.periodizeCentered_eq_on_cente.text: The periodic extension agrees on the whole closed cell when the profile vanishes near its boundary.
TorusEuler.periodizeCentered_eq_on_cente.summary: The periodic extension agrees on the closed cell

TorusEuler.periodizeCentered_neg_equivar.text: If a profile transforms under reflection by a map `L` fixing zero and vanishes on the negative cell walls, its centered periodic extension obeys the same reflection law. No continuity is assumed. The wall hypothesis handles points where negation does not commute with the half-open centered representative; away from those walls the representatives are exact negatives.
TorusEuler.periodizeCentered_neg_equivar.summary: Periodic extension preserves reflection when cell walls vanish

TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateDirection.text:
The label coordinate directions and the separate phase direction.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateDirection.summary: Three label directions and one phase direction

TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateWeight.text: Assign the envelope scale `ℓ` to each label-coordinate direction and the profile width `h` to the phase direction. Products of these weights encode the mixed derivative factors in the finite profile norm. The definition records scaling alone; positivity and smallness are separate assumptions in estimates.
TorusEuler.phaseCoordinateWeight.summary: Each derivative receives its own geometric scale

TorusEuler.phaseDirectionalDerivative.text:
A coordinate derivative, with a direction field allowed to vary with the base point.

Default-value audit (b5): A raw fderiv value is zero at nondifferentiability points. Smoothness is supplied separately in the word-calculus theorems; a numerical bound for this expression alone is not a differentiability theorem.
TorusEuler.phaseDirectionalDerivative.summary: Differentiation along a possibly varying direction field

TorusEuler.phaseDirectionalDerivative_je.text: For smooth coefficient field `D` and profile `f`, bounds through orders `n` and `n+1` give a bound $2^nCM$ through order `n` for the derivative of `f` in direction `D`. The nonnegative constants are explicit. Time weights can stay inside `M` because every derivative here acts only on the profile domain.
TorusEuler.phaseDirectionalDerivative_je.summary: One directional derivative obeys the weighted product bound

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_bilinear_produc.text: Two smooth functions with jets through order `N` bounded by nonnegative constants `A` and `B` have a bilinear product bounded by $2^N\cdot A\cdot B$, provided the bilinear operator has norm at most one. The same bound covers every derivative order below `N`. This is the explicit finite Leibniz factor used for coframes, amplitudes, and potential coefficients.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_bilinear_produc.summary: A bilinear product has a finite Leibniz bound

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_comp_left_contr.text: Postcomposing a smooth function with a continuous linear map of norm at most one preserves its finite Fréchet-jet bound. The order and the numerical bound are unchanged.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_comp_left_contr.summary: A linear contraction preserves a finite derivative bound

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_normalizedPress.text: For a positive frequency and a smooth nonvanishing covector, assumes finite jet bounds for the normalized covector, strain, and normalized reciprocal squared norm. Their product gives smoothness and an explicit bound $2\cdot 2^N\cdot \mathrm{BQ}\cdot 2^N\cdot \mathrm{BK}\cdot \mathrm{BM}$ for the normalized pressure-amplitude coefficient. All three budgets are nonnegative; no frequency-independent estimate follows until their sizes are supplied.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_normalizedPress.summary: Normalized pressure coefficients inherit three product budgets

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_normalizedPress.text: Assumes a positive frequency and radius, $D \ge  1$, radius smallness $\ell\cdot D^{16} \le  1$, and prescribed raw jets of strain, normalized covector, and reciprocal squared norm. The normalized pressure-amplitude coefficient after label scaling is smooth and has finite jet budget $2\cdot 2^{2\cdot N}\cdot C^3\cdot D^7$. The exponent seven is independent of the derivative order; the prefactor is not.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_normalizedPress.summary: Scaled pressure coefficients cost seven parent powers

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaledPhasePote.text: For positive frequency, nonnegative radius, $D \ge  1$, and $\ell\cdot D^{16} \le  1$, assumes raw jet bounds for the normalized covector and reciprocal squared norm through order `N`. The scaled potential coefficient is smooth and has jet bound $2^N\cdot C^2\cdot D^6/\mathrm{freq}$. The covector must be smooth and nonvanishing; the bound isolates an inverse frequency before the later slow curl costs a label derivative.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaledPhasePote.summary: Scaled potential jets retain an inverse frequency factor

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_labelDiv.text: For a smooth profile and positive envelope radius, a second-order bound on the rescaled profile gives a first-order bound $3\ell^{-1}M$ on its label divergence. One derivative is spent to form divergence and three coordinates contribute the constant. The result tracks the envelope cost separately from phase differentiation.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_labelDiv.summary: Label divergence costs one envelope reciprocal

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_longitud.text: The combined divergence identity `hdiv` replaces the large phase derivative of $\langle k,c\rangle$ by label divergence. With positive scales, smooth one-periodic data, a second-order oscillation bound, and a first-order mean bound, the longitudinal first-order bound is $(2+h)3\ell^{-1}M_{\rm osc}+\|k\|M_{\rm mean}$. The full wave-number factor applies only to the mean.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_longitud.summary: Divergence cancellation controls the longitudinal phase velocity

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_periodic.text: For a smooth, one-periodic, zero-mean profile and nonzero phase scale, a scaled jet bound through order `n` gives a bound $2\cdot B$ for its normalized phase primitive through the same order. Derivatives may involve both label and evaluation phase. The proof translates the integrand and applies a mixed-jet integral estimate; the nonzero phase scale permits division in that translation.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_periodic.summary: A normalized periodic primitive preserves the jet order

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_phasePri.text: For a smooth one-periodic profile of zero mean at every label, an order-one bound on its rescaled profile gives an order-one bound $(2+h)M$ for the rescaled normalized primitive. The phase width is positive and `hprim` supplies differentiability. Label integration costs at most two, while phase differentiation recovers the input with a factor `h`.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_phasePri.summary: The phase primitive gains one phase-width factor

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_slowCurl.text: For a positive label radius and smooth potential and inverse coframe, assumes potential jets through order $n+1$ and radius-weighted coframe jets through `n`. The scaled slow curl is smooth and has budget $\lVert \mathrm{curlOfDerivativeCLM}\rVert \cdot \ell^{-1}\cdot 2^n\cdot \mathrm{BP}\cdot \mathrm{BG}$. The extra derivative and inverse radius are explicit, so a two-jet activation estimate requires three potential jets.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_slowCurl.summary: A slow curl uses one extra potential derivative

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_wavePote.text: For a smooth periodic zero-mean profile, smooth potential coefficients, and nonzero phase scale, bounds the exact wave potential from profile and coefficient budgets through the same order `n`. The resulting budget is $2\cdot 2^n\cdot \mathrm{BK}\cdot \mathrm{BV}$, and joint smoothness is also proved. One finite Leibniz factor comes from applying the coefficient; the factor two comes from the normalized primitive.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_scaled_wavePote.summary: The actual wave potential inherits a product jet bound

TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_sum_of_level_bo.text: For every level from two through `P`, assume the profile is differentiable to order `n` and satisfies the stated jet bound. The finite sum then has the sum of those constants as a jet bound. An empty higher-level range gives the zero profile, so the lemma also covers shallow truncations.
TorusEuler.phaseJetBound_sum_of_level_bo.summary: Sum the higher pressure profiles at fixed derivative order

TorusEuler.phaseMean.text:
The phase mean of a profile `f` is its vector-valued integral over the interval $[0,1]$. The target `E` is a real normed vector space. This definition keeps time and label fixed when applied to a wave profile. It is the averaging operation used to separate the hierarchy source into a phase-independent forcing and an oscillatory forcing; no spatial averaging or particle-label integration occurs here.

Default-value audit (b5): The integral is totalized on arbitrary phase functions. Continuity or integrability is needed for the usual mean identities; the bundled profiles used in the hierarchy supply it.
TorusEuler.phaseMean.summary: Average of a profile over one phase period

TorusEuler.phaseMean_add.text: The phase mean of the sum of two continuous profiles is the sum of their phase means. Continuity supplies the integrability required by the interval integral.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_const.text: The average of a constant over a phase interval of length one is the same constant. This fixes the normalization of the phase average.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_const.summary: A constant profile equals its phase average

TorusEuler.phaseMean_const_smul.text: A real scalar factor may be moved outside the unit-period phase mean. The scalar is constant in the phase variable.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_const_smul.summary: A constant scalar passes through the phase average

TorusEuler.phaseMean_deriv.text: If f has a continuous derivative df everywhere and period one, the phase mean of df vanishes. The proof is the fundamental theorem of calculus with matching endpoints.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_deriv.summary: A periodic derivative has zero phase mean

TorusEuler.phaseMean_fastSource.text: Assume periodic completion and profile, a continuous phase derivative of the profile, and `hslave` identifying the completion's longitudinal component with the negative primitive of `divV`. Phase integration by parts converts the mean of $(C\cdot\kappa)Y_s$ into the mean of $\mathrm{divV}\,Y$. Periodicity cancels the boundary term; the slaving identity supplies the sign.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_fastSource.summary: Integration by parts removes the fast derivative

TorusEuler.phaseMean_iteratedDeriv_succ.text: For a smooth one-periodic profile, the phase average of every positive-order derivative is zero. The fundamental theorem of calculus reduces that average to equal endpoint values of a periodic lower derivative. The theorem supplies the mean-zero condition needed when the normalized primitive is applied after phase differentiation.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_iteratedDeriv_succ.summary: Positive phase derivatives have zero mean

TorusEuler.phaseMean_meanFastSource.text: The phase average of $(B\cdot\kappa)Y_s$ vanishes when $Y$ is periodic with continuous derivative. Here $B$ and $\kappa$ do not depend on the phase variable. The statement uses the integral of a derivative over one period, and does not require either constant vector to vanish or be transverse.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_meanFastSource.summary: A constant phase coefficient has zero derivative mean

TorusEuler.phaseMean_phaseOscillation.text: For a continuous profile in a complete real normed space, the average of $f-\operatorname{phaseMean}(f)$ over the unit period is zero. Linearity of the integral and the unit interval length give the cancellation. Periodicity is not required for this identity, because only values on the integration interval enter the mean.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_phasePrimitive.text: The phase average of the normalized primitive is zero for every continuous input with values in a complete real normed space. The indefinite integral is continuous, so subtracting its phase average removes precisely its constant component. No periodicity or zero-mean assumption on the input is needed for this identity. Those additional assumptions enter the separate theorem that the resulting primitive has period one.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_phasePrimitive.summary: The normalized primitive has zero phase mean

TorusEuler.phaseMean_reflect_periodic.text: Shows that averaging a one-periodic phase function after replacing phase by its negative gives the original mean. Orientation reversal and periodicity move the integral back to one period. This preserves the normalization used to identify reflected pressure primitives; integrability is supplied in the smooth applications, rather than asserted by this theorem.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_reflect_periodic.summary: Reflection leaves a periodic phase average unchanged

TorusEuler.phaseMean_smul_deriv.text: For a scalar one-periodic weight $u$ and a vector one-periodic profile $v$, both differentiable with continuous displayed derivatives, proves $\langle u v\prime\rangle=-\langle u\prime v\rangle$. The two periodicity hypotheses cancel the boundary term over $[0,1]$. Completeness is required for the vector-valued integral; no spatial derivative or zero-mean hypothesis is included.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_smul_deriv.summary: Move a phase derivative by integration by parts

TorusEuler.phaseMean_sub.text: The phase mean of the difference of two continuous profiles is the difference of their phase means. This is used when separating the mean from the oscillation.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_translate_periodic.text: For a one-periodic phase function, translating its phase argument by any real number leaves the phase mean unchanged. The proof changes variables in the interval integral and uses periodicity. No separate integrability hypothesis appears in this algebraic identity; analytic uses have smooth phase slices so that the integral has its usual meaning.
TorusEuler.phaseMean_translate_periodic.summary: A periodic phase average is invariant under translation

TorusEuler.phaseMean_wavePotential.text: For continuous $V$, the potential defined by taking the mean-adjusted primitive of the cross-product integrand has zero phase mean. This property holds for every fixed $\kappa$, with no transverse, periodic, or zero-mean assumption on $V$. Those stronger assumptions are needed for its intended periodic inverse-curl interpretation, not for the normalization itself.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_wavePressurePrimiti.text: The pressure primitive has zero phase average for each scale with `hh : 0 < h` and `hle : h ≤ 1`. The proof uses the mean-removing definition of `phasePrimitive` and continuity of `waveProfile`. The normalization fixes the otherwise arbitrary constant in the scalar pressure profile. This theorem concerns the phase mean of $P_h$, not the spatial mean of the full localized Eulerian pressure.

TorusEuler.phaseMean_waveProfile.text: For an admissible positive width h ≤ 1, the selected wave profile has zero average over one phase period. This normalization makes the oscillatory profile compatible with the hierarchy.

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord.text:
The first letter of an ordered word is the outermost derivative.

Default-value audit (b5): The empty word is the identity on functions. Nonempty words use totalized Fréchet derivatives; analytic word identities require the stated smoothness of fields and directions.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord.summary: Ordered directional derivatives of a profile

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear.text: Exact ordered Leibniz formula for a real continuous bilinear operator, including application of an operator-valued coefficient to a vector field.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear.summary: The exact ordered Leibniz formula for bilinear products

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear_bo.text: Finite-order sup and difference bounds for a product. The hypotheses need only hold for subwords of the specified derivative.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear_bo.summary: Finite sup and difference bounds for differentiated products

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear_co.text: Subtracting $B(f,D_wg)$ from the full derivative $D_w(B(f,g))$ leaves precisely those Leibniz terms with a derivative on $f$. Smoothness of the direction fields and both factors is explicit. Each remaining second word is shorter than $w$, providing the lower-order terms in the derivative-lifting argument.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_bilinear_co.summary: Remove the highest derivative of the solution

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_const_smul.text: A time weight may be applied to the field before taking any label or phase derivative at fixed time.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_const_smul.summary: A fixed time weight commutes with spatial differentiation

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constantDir.text: Smooth directional derivatives in constant real directions are unchanged by a permutation of the ordered coordinate word.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constantDir.summary: Constant directional derivatives are invariant under permutation

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constant_eq.text: For a smooth function, an ordered word of constant directional derivatives is its iterated Fréchet derivative evaluated on the same ordered directions. This identifies the word calculus with the usual finite derivative norms.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_constant_eq.summary: Constant derivative words equal evaluated Fréchet derivatives

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_eq_jet.text: For a smooth function, successive derivatives in constant directions equal evaluation of the iterated Fréchet derivative on that ordered list. This is the word-to-tensor identification used by the differentiated ODE estimates.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_eq_jet.summary: Constant words evaluate the Fréchet derivative tensor

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_hierarchyLa.text: Each weighted label derivative introduces one factor of the label radius.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_hierarchyLa.summary: Each weighted label derivative contributes the radius

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_jetBound.text: A list `w` of smooth directional operators maps an order-`N` profile bound to an order-`n` bound when `hn` ensures $n+|w|\le N$. Each step contributes at most $2^NC$. The resulting constant is $(2^NC)^{|w|}M$, and the order of the operators is preserved by the list.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_jetBound.summary: A word of derivatives consumes its length in regularity

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_linearODE_t.text: Parameter word derivatives of a linear solve satisfy the time derivative of the differentiated right-hand side, including at both slab endpoints.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_linearODE_t.summary: Spatial derivative words satisfy the differentiated time equation

TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_scaled_dire.text: Replacing each smooth direction field $D_i$ by the constant scalar multiple $r_iD_i$ multiplies the word derivative by the product of its letter weights. The weights depend on the index, not on position. For coordinate directions this accounts for the factors $\ell^m h^j$ in the finite norm.
TorusEuler.phaseOperatorWord_scaled_dire.summary: Coordinate weights multiply along the derivative word

TorusEuler.phaseOscillation.text:
The oscillatory part of `f` at phase `s` is `f s - phaseMean f`. This definition makes precise the source split $H_2-\langle H_2\rangle$ in the introductory hierarchy. The target is any real normed vector space, and the formula makes sense before regularity is assumed. Vanishing average and preservation of periodicity are consequences once the corresponding integrability and periodicity conditions are available.

Default-value audit (b5): This subtracts the totalized unit-period integral. It has the usual zero-mean oscillation interpretation under the integrability assumptions used by the phase-average lemmas.
TorusEuler.phaseOscillation.summary: Oscillatory part obtained by subtracting the phase mean

TorusEuler.phaseOscillation_longitudinal.text: The longitudinal oscillatory velocity equals the negative zero-mean phase primitive of its label divergence. The assumptions `hc`, `hper` and `hdiv` give smoothness, period one and $(\nabla_a+k_*\partial_s)\cdot c=0$. Lean also concludes that the mean label velocity is divergence free. This replaces multiplication by the large carrier in the oscillatory phase velocity with a label derivative and a phase primitive.
TorusEuler.phaseOscillation_longitudinal.summary: The phase velocity is a label-divergence primitive

TorusEuler.phasePrimitive.text:
The primitive is obtained by integrating from phase zero to the current phase and subtracting the phase average of that integral. The definition is written as `phaseOscillation` applied to the indefinite integral. For a continuous period-one input with zero phase average, the accompanying periodicity theorem shows that this primitive is again period one. Its zero-mean normalization removes the freedom to add a phase-independent constant.

Default-value audit (b5): The primitive is formed by an interval integral followed by mean removal. A derivative and a periodic primitive require the corresponding continuity, periodicity and zero-mean hypotheses.

TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_deriv.text: Assuming `hderiv` gives a derivative $df$ of $f$ at every phase and `hdf` makes it continuous, proves $\operatorname{phasePrimitive}(df)=f-\operatorname{phaseMean}(f)$. The primitive starts at zero and then has its own mean removed. The identity does not require periodicity; periodicity is an additional condition when interpreting this operation as the inverse phase derivative.
TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_deriv.summary: A primitive recovers the profile without its mean

TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_wavePotentialT.text: The primitive of the potential time source for `freq • k` is exactly `freq⁻¹` times the primitive for `k`, with positive frequency. The statement is an equality of normalized phase integrals, not a derivative assertion. It combines the source’s algebraic homogeneity with linearity of the primitive.
TorusEuler.phasePrimitive_wavePotentialT.summary: Phase integration preserves the inverse-frequency factor

TorusEuler.phaseProfile_eq_of_hasDerivAt.text: Phase normalization determines the additive constant of a primitive.
TorusEuler.phaseProfile_eq_of_hasDerivAt.summary: The phase mean fixes the primitive constant

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text:
Extend a profile by shifting its phase with its lattice translation.

Default-value audit (b5): The centered representative jumps across cell walls. This raw extension is periodic with the matching phase shift but need not be smooth; compact support away from the walls is used by the smooth-extension theorem.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: Periodic extension with the matching phase shift

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: The extension agrees with the profile on the entire closed cell.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The twisted extension agrees on the closed cell

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: If simultaneous label and phase reflection transforms a profile by a zero-preserving map `L`, and the profile vanishes on every negative cell wall, its twisted extension has the same reflection law. The wall condition handles the centered representative’s half-open boundary convention. The map `L` need not be linear for this algebraic result, only satisfy `L 0 = 0`.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: Wall vanishing preserves reflection through the twisted extension

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: Evaluating the phase-twisted extension at label `A t x` and phase $\langle k,A(t,x)\rangle$ gives exactly the localized transported profile. The phase shift cancels the uncentered label contribution, leaving the graph phase at the centered representative. This is an identity for arbitrary maps, profiles and real covectors; it does not require smoothness, periodicity or an integer frequency.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The twisted profile agrees with its transported phase evaluation

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: If each original label slice has a specified phase period, the twisted periodized profile has that same phase period. The period need not equal one in this general statement.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: Twisted periodization preserves a supplied phase period

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: When the positive envelope radius leaves a strict collar before the cell walls, the twisted extension equals the original enveloped profile at every point of the closed centered cell and every phase. This includes boundary points that have different centered representatives, since the envelope vanishes there. The equality does not require smoothness of the underlying profile.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The twisted extension agrees throughout the closed cell

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: The envelope confines the extension to the translates of its original support ball.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The periodized envelope stays near lattice points

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: For a positive envelope radius with $2\ell\le1/2$, multiplying a profile by the radial envelope preserves any simultaneous label-phase reflection represented by a continuous linear map `L`. The twisted extension inherits that same law. The weak radius inequality suffices because only zero values at the cell walls are needed; smooth gluing elsewhere uses a strict inequality.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The radial envelope preserves a linear reflection law

TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.text: The twisted periodization is invariant when labels and phase are shifted together by the lattice vector and its pairing with k. The identity is valid for the raw extension; smoothness across cell walls is a separate result.
TorusEuler.phaseTwistedPeriodizeCentered.summary: The extension respects simultaneous lattice and phase shifts

TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_graph_cost.text: The combined derivative factor $\ell_*^{-1}+h^{-1}|k_*|$ is bounded by a parent power times $\lambda^{3/2}$. The assumptions `hLabel`, `hWidth` and `hCarrier` specify $\ell_*^{-1}\le\mathsf D^a$, $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$ and $|k_*|\le\mathsf D\lambda$, with $\mathsf D,\lambda\ge1$. This is the scalar cost used by the transported-profile jet bounds; the coframe adds another parent factor.

TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_residual_ho.text: If `RV` is exactly the depth tail plus `chiPrime` times the primary field, and both have the stated two-jet bounds, its first half-Hölder norm is bounded by $C_{step}\lambda^2(\lambda^{-2P/3}+S)$. The hypotheses control $|\chi^{\prime}|\gamma$ by `S` and absorb both numerical constants into `Cstep`. The final power is enlarged from $7/4$ to two.
TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_residual_ho.summary: Depth and activation errors combine in the residual norm

TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_velocity_ho.text: Supplied jets through order `m + 1` yield half-Hölder bounds for both oscillation and mean. With $\lambda\ge1$ and $0\le\gamma\le1$, the oscillation has exponent $3(m+1)/2-5/4$, while the mean retains $-5/2$. The theorem combines exponents and converts jets to norms; it assumes the preceding physical jet estimates.
TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_velocity_ho.summary: Oscillation and mean retain their distinct Hölder frequency rates

TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection.text: The plane wave has zero self-advection at $x$ when `hperp : ⟪k, a⟫_ℝ = 0`. The only regularity assumption is `hF`, the derivative of $F$ at the particular phase $k\cdot x$. The spatial derivative is rank one, so evaluating it on the wave velocity introduces the factor $k\cdot\mathbf a$. No temporal wave equation is needed for this cancellation.
TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection.summary: A transverse plane wave has zero self-advection

TorusEuler.preceding_curl_projection_of_.text: If the newest covector is nonzero, its scale is positive, and its third scaled coordinate in the preceding frame is at least one half, a bound on its scaled length gives a lower bound for its normalized projection against the preceding curl. The formula uses the actual cross product, with its sign retained.
TorusEuler.preceding_curl_projection_of_.summary: The newest direction detects a positive preceding curl component

TorusEuler.preceding_curl_projection_of_.text: Combining coordinate bounds, window length at most $CL^4$, logarithmic loss $L^8\le\mu^{1/8}$, and preceding strength at least $c\mu^{1/4}$ gives a signed curl projection of at least $c\mu^{1/8}/(6C^2)$. Nonzero perpendicular preceding data and positive frequency scales are explicit. The conclusion retains `c` as supplied; its positivity is not assumed here.
TorusEuler.preceding_curl_projection_of_.summary: The projected preceding curl grows as a positive frequency power

TorusEuler.preceding_strength_retained_o.text: The strength $|k(t)|\,|a(t)|$ is at least $e^{-1}$ times its initial value on the short interval. The hypotheses `hshort` and `hB` bound its length by $\mu^{-1/16}$ and the background gradient by $\mu^{1/32}$. The frame is nondegenerate and orthogonal by `hframe`; `hk`, `ha`, and `htrace` supply its evolution and incompressibility. The result makes the paper’s unspecified absolute loss explicit.

TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode.text: The scalar coefficient $\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}a$ at integer frequency $k$. It is the product of the inverse-Laplacian multiplier and the divergence multiplier. Taking its gradient gives the part removed by the Leray projection. The inverse Laplacian sets the zero mode to zero, so this convention produces a mean-zero scalar potential. The definition concerns one Fourier coefficient; the real $L^2$ coefficient theorem connects it to the spatial operator.
TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode.summary: The scalar pressure coefficient removed by Leray projection

TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode_zero.text: The scalar pressure correction at frequency zero is zero for every vector coefficient. This is the Fourier form of the zero-mean normalization for the inverse Laplacian in the Leray formula. The result needs no transversality or regularity hypothesis on the coefficient. It should not be read as saying that the velocity itself has zero average: constant divergence-free velocity modes are retained by the Leray projection.
TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode_zero.summary: The pressure correction has vanishing zero mode

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular.text: Defines the real angular operator $I-\mathbb P(\xi)$, which projects onto the frequency direction for nonzero $\xi$. Its value at zero is zero because the Leray symbol there is the identity. This is the angular part of $D^2\Delta^{-1}$; the definition alone does not identify any field as an actual pressure Hessian.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular.summary: The pressure projection onto the frequency direction

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_apply.text: Applying the angular pressure operator to $v$ gives $(\langle\xi,v\rangle/\|\xi\|^2)\xi$. The formula is valid also at zero under Lean’s total division convention, where both sides vanish. To interpret it as projection onto a one-dimensional direction one must additionally have $\xi\ne0$.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_apply.summary: The pressure projection is the longitudinal component

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_neg.text: The angular pressure operator is even in its frequency argument: replacing $\xi$ by $-\xi$ leaves it unchanged. This includes zero. The identity is used to pair positive and negative Fourier modes when proving the real cosine and sine moment formula; it is not a regularity statement about the symbol.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_neg.summary: Opposite frequencies have the same pressure projection

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_pos_sm.text: For `hc : 0 < c`, the angular pressure operator at $c\xi$ equals that at $\xi$. Thus the operator depends on the frequency direction, not its positive magnitude. The theorem includes $\xi=0$ but excludes a zero scaling factor, which would collapse a nonzero frequency to the distinguished zero mode.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_pos_sm.summary: Positive rescaling leaves the pressure projection unchanged

TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_zero.text: The angular pressure operator is zero at frequency zero. This is the intended Fourier convention for a Hessian, which cannot contain a nonzero constant Fourier mode when obtained by differentiating a periodic potential. The declaration is a symbol identity; the later Poisson comparison proves that the constructed multiplier has the corresponding physical meaning.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianAngular_zero.summary: The pressure Hessian has zero constant mode

TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier.text:
The bounded linear operator $D^2\Delta^{-1}$ from scalar $C^{0,1/2}$ functions on the torus to operator-valued $C^{0,1/2}$ functions. Its type is `HalfHolder Labels ℝ →L[ℝ] HalfHolder Labels RealOp`; the arrow `→L[ℝ]` includes continuity. The definition takes the real part of the corresponding complex Fourier multiplier. The zero Fourier mode is set to zero, as appropriate for the Hessian of a normalized Poisson solution.

Default-value audit (b5): This is a bounded linear map on actual torus half-Hölder fields. Its identification with the Hessian of normalized Poisson pressure uses the appropriate pressure equation and removal of the constant mode.

TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier_eq_.text: If a periodic $C^2$ potential has Laplacian represented by `f` and Hessian represented by the half-Hölder operator field `H`, then the multiplier output is exactly `H`. The theorem requires these representation hypotheses; it does not create the potential or assume an arbitrary source is a periodic Laplacian. Entrywise Fourier uniqueness proves the equality.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier_eq_.summary: Identify the multiplier with the actual pressure Hessian

TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier_rea.text: The real Fourier moment of the Hessian output equals the corresponding scalar input moment multiplied by the angular pressure operator at that frequency. The complex parameter `c` encodes both cosine and sine tests. Evenness of the symbol allows the positive and negative modes to combine, establishing a real-valued identity without selecting a pressure potential.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier_rea.summary: The real multiplier acts on cosine and sine moments

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol.text: At each real frequency, constructs a complex-linear map taking a scalar Fourier coefficient to that coefficient times the complexified angular pressure operator. The result is operator-valued, so its coordinate entries represent the Hessian entries. Boundedness of the resulting periodic operator and agreement with a Poisson solution are later theorems.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol.summary: The complex symbol converts a scalar to a Hessian

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_apply.text: Unfolds the complex symbol as scalar multiplication of the complexified angular projection. This identity is valid for every frequency and complex scalar. It exposes the exact action used in the Fourier coefficient calculations, without requiring the scalar to be real or the frequency to be nonzero.

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_lattice.text: Each lattice-frequency matrix entry of the pressure symbol equals the two Fourier derivative factors times `inverseLaplacianMode` and the scalar input. The proof handles `k = 0` separately before cancelling the nonzero Laplacian eigenvalue. This fixes the sign and the $2\pi$ normalization of the intended operator at every frequency.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_lattice.summary: The symbol equals two derivatives and an inverse Laplacian

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_neg.text: The scalar-to-operator symbol is unchanged when the real frequency is negated. This follows from evenness of the underlying real angular projection and is valid including at zero. It supports the comparison of conjugate Fourier modes needed to recover a real operator from real source data.

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_pos_smu.text: Positive rescaling of the real frequency leaves the complex pressure symbol unchanged. The explicit hypothesis `hc` excludes scaling by zero; no restriction on the scalar input to the symbol is needed. This homogeneity is passed to the periodic half-Hölder Fourier multiplier construction.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_pos_smu.summary: The complex pressure symbol has degree zero

TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_zero.text: At the zero frequency, the complex scalar-to-operator symbol is the zero continuous linear map. This eliminates the constant mode before any Fourier reconstruction. It records a deliberate normalization for the Hessian multiplier rather than a statement that arbitrary sources have zero mean.
TorusEuler.pressureHessianSymbol_zero.summary: The complex pressure symbol vanishes at zero

TorusEuler.pressureHessian_quadratic_upp.text: Let the Hessian operator split into leading, geometric, higher and mean pieces. A signed leading upper bound at scale $\mathrm{freq}^{-1/4}$ and nonnegative norm bounds for the other three pieces at faster decays give a common signed upper bound with summed constants. The theorem never deduces a norm bound for the leading piece or the total Hessian.
TorusEuler.pressureHessian_quadratic_upp.summary: Combine one signed contribution with three norm bounds

TorusEuler.pressureTensorAnnularSymbol.text: The fixed dyadic cutoff localizes the pressure symbol into a compactly supported smooth operator-valued symbol, packaged as a Schwartz map. The cutoff removes the singular frequency origin before the Schwartz construction. Its inverse Fourier transform is the building block for the actual periodic far pressure kernel.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorAnnularSymbol.summary: The pressure symbol is localized to one smooth frequency annulus

TorusEuler.pressureTensorDoubleDivergenc.text: The double divergence of a complex tensor field is $\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j a_{ij}$, expressed using the coordinate Hessian entries. It is the source with a minus sign in the normalized pressure Poisson equation. The definition fixes the coordinate order used in the Fourier symbol and in the real Euler comparison.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorDoubleDivergenc.summary: Contract both spatial derivatives of the tensor source

TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift.text: The real pressure lift is the real part of the complex dyadic pressure sum. For smooth periodic tensor fields it is smooth and agrees with the actual half Hölder pressure multiplier. Its identification with a prescribed pressure additionally requires the periodic Poisson equation and zero spatial mean.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift.summary: Take the real pressure produced by the dyadic series

TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_eq_l.text: If a half Hölder torus tensor `q` pulls back pointwise to a smooth periodic lift `f`, their real pressures agree pointwise after lifting. Finite dyadic convolutions converge both to the block sum and to the bounded multiplier output. The representative premise `hq` is explicit; the theorem does not select an arbitrary torus representative.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_eq_l.summary: The smooth dyadic construction equals the bounded torus multiplier

TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_eq_r.text: For a smooth periodic tensor and a $C^2$ periodic complex pressure solving its Poisson equation with zero mean, the real dyadic lift is exactly the real part of that pressure. Smoothness provides the tensor’s half Hölder torus representative, continuity provides the pressure representative, and Fourier uniqueness identifies them. The equation alone would leave an additive constant.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorDyadicLift_eq_r.summary: The dyadic pressure equals the normalized Poisson solution

TorusEuler.pressureTensorMultiplier.text: This bounded real operator composes the complex pressure tensor multiplier with pointwise real part. It accepts complex tensor fields but returns a real half Hölder field. For tensors built from real velocities, later Fourier Poisson uniqueness identifies this output with the actual normalized Euler pressure.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorMultiplier.summary: The real pressure is the real part of the complex multiplier

TorusEuler.pressureTensorRealOutput.text: This real continuous linear map converts a complex-linear tensor-to-scalar operator into a real-linear one by taking the real part of its output. The input tensor remains complex. This lets the periodized complex Fourier kernel produce real pressure values without changing the source coordinate convention.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorRealOutput.summary: Take the real scalar output of a complex tensor operator

TorusEuler.pressureTensorRealOutput_appl.text: Applying the converted tensor operator to a complex tensor returns the real part of the original complex result. This definitional identity is used to commute the real-output map with integrals and to compare real pressure with its complex Fourier representation. It asserts no symmetry of the input tensor.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorRealOutput_appl.summary: The real output map is pointwise real part

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol.text: The scalar operator sends a tensor to $-\sum_{i,j}\xi_i\xi_j A_{ij}/\|\xi\|^2$. It is the symbol of $-\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}\operatorname{div}$ with zero constant mode. The negative sign is essential for the pressure Poisson equation, and the finite tensor coordinate functionals make the operator continuous.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol.summary: The normalized pressure symbol contracts the tensor twice

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_apply.text: Applying the pressure symbol equals the negative finite double sum of weighted tensor entries. This expands the bundled continuous linear operator into coordinates. The formula is valid at zero as well, where all weights vanish; nonzero-frequency inversion is justified in later Fourier-mode identities.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_apply.summary: The symbol has the explicit double contraction formula

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_lattice_.text: At a lattice frequency, applying the scalar pressure symbol equals negative inverse Laplacian mode times the double-divergence Fourier contraction. The formula holds at zero with the prescribed normalization. This gives the exact modal interpretation of the abstract angular symbol used to build the bounded multiplier.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_lattice_.summary: The pressure symbol solves the Fourier Poisson equation

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_lattice_.text: The pressure symbol applied to a tensor equals the negative scalar pressure-correction mode of its single divergence. This aligns the tensor convention with the existing Leray decomposition. The sign means the projected tensor divergence is the unprojected divergence plus the gradient of this normalized pressure.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_lattice_.summary: The pressure scalar has the opposite complement sign

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_neg.text: Changing the frequency vector to its negative leaves the pressure operator unchanged. Each weight contains two coordinate factors and a squared norm. This parity matches the real pressure operator and is distinct from a parity assumption on the tensor field to which the multiplier is applied.

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_pos_smul.text: Positive scaling of the frequency vector leaves the pressure symbol unchanged. The proof transfers the homogeneity of each angular weight through the finite sum of coordinate operators. This is the degree-zero homogeneity premise needed to identify the dyadically constructed multiplier with its claimed Fourier coefficients.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_pos_smul.summary: The pressure multiplier depends only on frequency direction

TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_zero.text: The pressure symbol at frequency zero is the zero operator. This follows from the chosen coordinate quotient convention and is used to normalize pressure and remove any constant-mode term from the far-kernel formula. It does not invert the Laplacian at zero; it prescribes the missing mode.
TorusEuler.pressureTensorSymbol_zero.summary: The pressure symbol removes the constant mode

TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.text: Defines the scalar half-Hölder field $\operatorname{tr}(U^2)-\operatorname{tr}(V^2)$ from two operator-valued fields. The products are composition of operators, not entrywise multiplication. The definition is algebraic; it becomes the pressure source’s quadratic difference only when `U` and `V` are identified as the two velocity gradients.
TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.summary: Compare the traces of the two gradient squares

TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.text: With `hD : D = U - V`, rewrites the trace-square difference as the trace of $DV+UD$. This exact identity is valid for noncommuting operator fields. It makes the small cutoff-gradient difference appear once in each term, which is the structure needed for the pressure error estimate.
TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.summary: Factor the square difference without commuting matrices

TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.text: At each label, the scalar field evaluates to the difference of the traces of the two operator squares. This exposes the definition’s actual order of composition and trace convention. No assumption that either input is a derivative is used, so the identity remains an algebraic one until the physical representations are supplied.
TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.summary: Evaluate the traces of the operator squares

TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.text: At a fixed label and with `D = U - V`, the trace-square difference equals $\operatorname{tr}(DV)+\operatorname{tr}(UD)$. This is the pointwise form of the field factorization. It neither commutes the operator factors nor identifies `D` as a derivative unless that interpretation is furnished externally.
TorusEuler.pressureTraceSquareDifference.summary: Read the cutoff difference inside the trace

TorusEuler.pressureVelocityTensor.text: The tensor field at $x$ has complex coordinates $v_i(x)v_j(x)$, using the bounded bilinear velocity tensor map on the diagonal. It is the source of the pressure double divergence. Reality and symmetry follow from the diagonal real input, while smoothness and periodicity are established separately from properties of $v$.
TorusEuler.pressureVelocityTensor.summary: Form the quadratic velocity source for pressure

TorusEuler.pressure_sub_at_zero_eq_lineI.text: If `g` is the actual continuous gradient of a scalar field $p$, then $p(x)-p(0)$ equals the integral of $\langle g(sx),x\rangle$ from zero to one. This is the fundamental theorem of calculus along the radial segment. Periodicity and mean normalization are unnecessary for this difference identity.
TorusEuler.pressure_sub_at_zero_eq_lineI.summary: Recover pressure differences along radial lines

TorusEuler.profileFlowCoframeCost.text: The order-`m` cost multiplies $4^m$, the four-direction product constant, and the parent’s finite coefficient-order constant. The factors account respectively for conversion to scaled Fréchet jets, the product estimate, and the inverse-coframe norm. The following lemmas use this fixed-order coefficient when turning a profile seminorm into a pullback derivative bound.
TorusEuler.profileFlowCoframeCost.summary: The finite cost of applying the inverse coframe

TorusEuler.profileFlowJetConstant.text: The common coefficient adds the oscillatory and mean costs and a further $1+C(1)$ allowance for the cutoff tail after applying the inverse coframe. It packages the three contributions without taking another maximum. Under nonnegative coefficient and level costs it is at least one, as the next theorem proves.
TorusEuler.profileFlowJetConstant.summary: One coefficient pays for both profiles and the added tail

TorusEuler.profileFlowJetPower.text: The chosen exponent is six times the hierarchy loss exponent plus eight. It dominates the oscillatory exponent $2r+1$, the mean exponent $6r+1$, and the cutoff-coframe exponent eight. This permits one parent power in the final pullback-jet record while retaining different frequency decay rates for the oscillation and mean.
TorusEuler.profileFlowJetPower.summary: One parent exponent covers both profiles and the cutoff tail

TorusEuler.profileFlowMeanCost.text: The mean coefficient uses the first-order coframe cost, the number of retained levels, and the common level constant. Only one mean term is counted per level, unlike the two oscillatory contributions. Its first-order choice matches the mean field required by the corrected pullback-jet interface used in the deformation argument.
TorusEuler.profileFlowMeanCost.summary: The finite level sum determines the mean cost

TorusEuler.profileFlowOscillationCost.text: The oscillatory coefficient is the second-order coframe cost times twice the number of retained levels and the common level constant. The factor two comes from summing both transverse oscillations and their completion corrections. The count is exactly the cardinality of the natural interval from one through the chosen depth.
TorusEuler.profileFlowOscillationCost.summary: The finite level sum determines the oscillatory cost

TorusEuler.profileWidth_and_seedScale.text: The profile width lies in the range of Lemma 3.1. Its product with the normalized seed scale is the leading velocity scale in §5.
TorusEuler.profileWidth_and_seedScale.summary: The profile width gives the required velocity scale

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertEquiv.text: For a closed Hilbert subspace and a bounded ambient operator coercive there with strictly positive constant, Lax–Milgram gives a continuous linear equivalence of the subspace. Its forward map is later identified with the compressed operator. This construction supplies an actual inverse on the constrained space, not an extension to arbitrary ambient vectors.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertEquiv.summary: Positive coercivity makes the compressed operator invertible

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertEquiv_apply.text: Under the closedness and positive coercivity hypotheses, the continuous linear equivalence produced by Lax–Milgram agrees on every subspace vector with `projectedHilbertOperator`. This links the abstract existence theorem back to the concrete projected equation. The inverse introduced by the equivalence therefore solves that equation on `H`.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertEquiv_apply.summary: The equivalence acts as the original compressed operator

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertOperator.text: Restrict the input of `A` to the closed subspace `H`, apply the ambient operator, and orthogonally project the result back into `H`. Closedness provides completeness of the subspace. This defines the projected operator of the weak endpoint equation before coercivity is used to show that it is invertible.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertOperator.summary: Compressing an operator to a closed Hilbert subspace

TorusEuler.projectedHilbertOperator_eq_p.text: Solving the compressed equation with right-hand side equal to the projection of `f` is equivalent to the ambient inner-product identity against every test vector in `H`. Closedness provides the orthogonal projection. This equivalence needs no coercivity, because it only translates two formulations of the same equation.
TorusEuler.projectedHilbertOperator_eq_p.summary: A projected equation equals testing against the subspace

TorusEuler.projectedMomentum_realFourier.text: The supplied projection converts the unprojected truncated momentum identity into the projected residual formula, provided it removes the cutoff pressure term from this particular momentum expression. The projection is otherwise an arbitrary map; no general linearity or gradient-annihilation theorem is assumed implicitly. The hypotheses retain the exact momentum representatives and incompressibility required by the preceding algebraic identity.
TorusEuler.projectedMomentum_realFourier.summary: Apply a compatible projection to truncated momentum

TorusEuler.projected_residual_of_cutoff.text: The projected residual equals the cutoff of $R_V$ plus the divergence of the two cross terms and the quadratic cutoff tail. The assumptions `hut`, `hCommute`, `hPressure`, `hV` and `hR` express time commutation, divergence commutation, removal of pressure gradients and the two momentum equations. The theorem is an abstract linear-algebra identity for a bilinear tensor map. Its proof preserves the order $(u-V)\otimes u+V\otimes(u-V)$ appearing in the paper.
TorusEuler.projected_residual_of_cutoff.summary: The projected residual after frequency truncation

TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_eq_coordinate_.text: For continuous linear maps `J` and `G`, the curl associated with `J.comp G` is the sum of cross products between the transformed coordinate directions and `J` applied to those directions. This is a purely algebraic derivative-map identity. No claim that `J` or `G` comes from a genuine flow is required.
TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_eq_coordinate_.summary: The pulled-back curl splits into three coordinate cross products

TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_eq_weightedCoo.text: When the label scale `ℓ` is nonzero, the pulled-back curl equals the sum of three weighted label derivatives multiplied by the inverse-scale curl rows. This is an algebraic identity involving the totalized Fréchet derivative. No smoothness hypothesis is needed for this rewrite; analytic bounds later supply genuine differentiability and coefficient control.
TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_eq_weightedCoo.summary: Weighted coordinate derivatives reproduce the pulled-back curl

TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_material_eq.text: The material derivative of a transported curl splits into the curl of the time derivative, a coframe commutator term, and multiplication by the strain. The hypotheses `hJ`, `hG`, and `hI` supply the time derivatives of the spatial jet and inverse coframe and uniqueness of the within-time derivative. Here `hG` is the inverse-coframe equation $G'=-GM$. The middle term in the conclusion is the explicit counterpart of $[\partial_t,\mathbf d\times]Q$.
TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_material_eq.summary: The material derivative of the transported curl

TorusEuler.pulledBackGradient_eq_weighte.text: For nonzero label scale, applying the inverse coframe’s adjoint to the label gradient equals a sum of weighted label derivatives multiplied by the corresponding pressure rows. The scalar derivative is converted to a vector through the inner-product duality map. This is an identity for arbitrary input functions and linear maps, before regularity assumptions are applied.
TorusEuler.pulledBackGradient_eq_weighte.summary: The pressure gradient splits into weighted label coordinates

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope.text:
The radial envelope $g(a)=\chi(|a|/\ell_*)$. This definition chooses the particular smooth cutoff `envelopeCutoff`, namely one minus a translated smooth transition. Its radius is the argument `ℓ`; positivity is required by the subsequent support and smoothness theorems. The paper permits a fixed smooth cutoff with the stated plateau and support, while this declaration makes one admissible choice.

Default-value audit (b5): At radius zero, division by the radius is Lean zero, so this chosen envelope is identically one. For negative radius the radial argument is nonpositive and the cutoff is again in its plateau. The support and smoothness theorems that serve the construction assume a strictly positive radius.

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_one.text: The chosen radial envelope is identically one on the ball $|a|\le\ell_*$. The assumptions are exactly `hℓ : 0 < ℓ` and `ha : ‖a‖ ≤ ℓ`. This is the plateau that preserves the leading wave near the origin. It concerns the spatial cutoff and does not describe when the time cutoff becomes one.
TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_one.summary: The envelope equals one on its inner ball

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_unit_scaled.text: For positive `ell`, the radial envelope at label `a` equals the unit-radius envelope evaluated at $\ell^{-1}\cdot a$. The proof unfolds the envelope and simplifies the norm of scalar multiplication. This identity isolates all radius dependence in a linear rescaling, enabling derivative constants to be chosen from the fixed unit envelope.
TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_unit_scaled.summary: Every positive-radius envelope rescales the unit envelope

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_zero.text: For positive radius, the chosen radial envelope is zero at every point whose norm is at least twice that radius. This is the outer support condition of the localized wave; smoothness is proved separately.
TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_zero.summary: The envelope vanishes outside its outer ball

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_mem_Icc.text: The chosen radial envelope takes values in the closed unit interval for every real radius and every point. This unrestricted range bound does not supply the intended support geometry when the radius is nonpositive.

TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_neg.text: The radial envelope has the same value at a point and its negative, since the norm is even. No positivity or smoothness assumption is needed for this identity.

TorusEuler.radius_power_small.text: The first-order envelope threshold bounds every smaller radius power.
