TorusEuler.radius_power_small.summary: The envelope threshold controls smaller radius powers

TorusEuler.range_endpointJointConstraint.text: The range of the ambient orthogonal projection `endpointJointConstraintProjection T` is precisely `endpointTorusSpace T`. That space combines zero time mean at almost every label with the weak spatial divergence condition. The statement identifies the projection range; it does not separately reconstruct the displacement or its pointwise endpoint values.
TorusEuler.range_endpointJointConstraint.summary: The joint projection range is the endpoint constraint space

TorusEuler.range_endpointJointSubtractMe.text: For hT : 0 < T, the range of time-mean removal equals the kernel of time integration. One inclusion is the zero-integral theorem. For the other, a field with zero integral is fixed by $Q$ and supplies its own preimage. The equality concerns submodules of joint $L^2$, before imposing any spatial divergence constraint.

TorusEuler.range_periodicComplexLeray.text: The range of the bounded complex Leray operator equals the Fourier solenoidal submodule. This equality establishes both that every projected field is solenoidal and that every field in that submodule is attained. It concerns Hilbert-space elements, with no additional pointwise regularity claim.
TorusEuler.range_periodicComplexLeray.summary: The full Leray range is precisely the solenoidal subspace

TorusEuler.range_periodicRealLeray.text: The range of the ambient real Leray operator is precisely `endpointSpatialSolenoidal`. Thus every output passes the weak gradient tests, and every field passing them is attained by the projection. This identifies the subspace intrinsically before later arguments recognize it through transverse Fourier coefficients.
TorusEuler.range_periodicRealLeray.summary: The projection range is exactly the weak solenoidal space

TorusEuler.rankOne_directionProjection_s.text: The longitudinal rank-one projection is invariant under nonzero real rescaling of its direction.
TorusEuler.rankOne_directionProjection_s.summary: Longitudinal projection is unchanged by nonzero rescaling

TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff.text: Defines the real-valued convolution operator by integrating the real part of the finite spectral kernel against a field with values in a real normed space. The Fourier multiplier identification for an even symbol is proved separately by scalar testing. The definition itself accepts arbitrary representatives and does not assert their integrability.

TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_congr.text: Almost-everywhere equality of two real normed-space-valued representatives gives pointwise equality of their real convolution cutoffs. The integrands agree almost everywhere at each fixed output point, so integral congruence applies. The declaration explicitly omits the surrounding `CompleteSpace` assumption; it is only a congruence statement for the total integral.
TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_congr.summary: Real convolution respects almost everywhere equality

TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_scala.text: With an even symbol, an integrable field in a real Banach space, and a continuous real linear functional `l`, scalarization of the real cutoff equals the complex scalar Fourier cutoff of `l ∘ g`. Evenness makes that scalar cutoff real. This identifies the operator’s Fourier meaning, beyond its real-kernel definition.
TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_scala.summary: Testing the real cutoff by a scalar functional

TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_vec_e.text: For an integrable `Vec3`-valued field, the real-kernel convolution equals complexification followed by the complex Fourier cutoff and real projection. The proof commutes the real-part map with an integrable Bochner integral and checks the scalar multiplication coordinatewise. Integrability is essential to this identification as stated.
TorusEuler.realBanachFourierCutoff_vec_e.summary: The real convolution agrees with the velocity cutoff

TorusEuler.realFourierFrequency.text: This definition casts the three integer frequency components to real numbers and places them in the Euclidean vector wrapper. It supplies the real frequency at which the angular Leray symbol is sampled. The associated norm and inner-product lemmas connect this representation to the earlier complex coefficient formulas.
TorusEuler.realFourierFrequency.summary: Integer modes embedded as real Euclidean frequencies

TorusEuler.realFourierScalarization.text:
A real linear measurement viewed as a complex-valued torus function.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.realFourierScalarization.summary: Testing a real Fourier field by a linear functional

TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.text: For a complex operator symbol smooth away from the origin, constructs the fixed-cutoff dyadic operator on half-Hölder fields and realifies it through `X`. The value of the symbol at zero supplies the mean action in the underlying construction. Positive homogeneity is not assumed by this definition; it enters separately when identifying every nonzero Fourier coefficient with the requested symbol.
TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.summary: Construct the real multiplier using a fixed cutoff

TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.text: For a smooth, even, degree-zero homogeneous symbol `P`, the real half-Hölder multiplier acts on every real-character moment by `P` at the lattice vector. The hypotheses `hEven` and `hHom` are explicit, and the conclusion includes the zero Fourier mode. This identifies the constructed real operator with the desired projection symbol.
TorusEuler.realHomogeneousHalfHolderMult.summary: The real multiplier has the prescribed Fourier moments

TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3.text: For arbitrary measure `μ`, lift the coordinatewise real-part map to complex vector-valued L² functions. The result is a real continuous linear map into real vector L². It is one of the projection maps used to build the complexification of the entire time-path Hilbert space.
TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3.summary: Take real parts of vector valued L² paths

TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_I_smul.text: The real part of $i v$ is minus the imaginary part of `v` as an L² equality. Representative compatibility reduces the assertion to the corresponding scalar complex identity in each coordinate. It records the sign convention needed to prove that componentwise real-operator extension is complex-linear.
TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_I_smul.summary: Multiplication by i turns imaginary paths into negative real parts

TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_apply_ae.text: Taking the L² real-part map has the same representative as applying `periodicRealPartVector` pointwise, almost everywhere. The measure is arbitrary and no time-interval assumption is involved. This equality permits integrals and norm identities to use the familiar finite-dimensional real-part formula.
TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_apply_ae.summary: Path real parts agree with pointwise real projection

TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_complexify.text: A real L² path is unchanged by first complexifying it and then taking its real part. This equality holds in the quotient space and is proved by representative comparison. It provides the left-inverse axiom of the concrete L² complexification, ensuring that real data retain their identity under embedding.
TorusEuler.realPartL2Vec3_complexify.summary: Real projection recovers the original real path

TorusEuler.realPart_fourierCoeff_pair.text: For continuous complex-valued-space field `f`, a real-linear map `Re`, frequency `k`, and complex scalar `c`, the real-character moment of `Re(f)` is half of `Re` applied to the combination of coefficients at $-k$ and $k$. The input need not be real-valued. Both opposite modes are required by the real part of the character.
TorusEuler.realPart_fourierCoeff_pair.summary: Real character moments use both opposite Fourier coefficients

TorusEuler.realPart_fourierCoeff_pair_tr.text: Assume `hRe` makes a complex operator compatible with a real operator under `Re`, and `hneg` and `hpos` give the same complex multiplier relation at both opposite frequencies. Then the corresponding real-character moment of `g` is the real operator applied to that of `f`. A single-frequency identity would not suffice for this conclusion.
TorusEuler.realPart_fourierCoeff_pair_tr.summary: Paired Fourier identities transfer a real multiplier action

TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff.text: Defines the scalar cutoff by complexifying a continuous real torus function, taking the finite Fourier sum with symbol `ψ` and scale `Λ`, and extracting its real part. It is defined even for scales and symbols outside the analytic cutoff regime. Approximation estimates and the intended symmetric multiplier interpretation require their own hypotheses.

TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff_diver.text: For a continuously differentiable lifted vector field with a continuous scalar divergence representative, cutting off that representative equals taking the divergence of the vector cutoff. The proof combines the coordinate derivative identities with scalar finite-sum linearity. The statement is valid for arbitrary symbol and scale and does not itself supply norm bounds.
TorusEuler.realScalarFourierCutoff_diver.summary: The real cutoff commutes with vector divergence

TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart.text: Turns a complex-linear operator into a real-linear operator by complexifying a real input and taking the real part of the output. The construction is itself a continuous real-linear map on operators. It is used after Fourier reconstruction to obtain a real pressure Hessian from real scalar source data.
TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart.summary: Restrict a complex operator to real vectors

TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart_apply.text: States the exact evaluation rule for `realSpatialOperatorPart`: complexify the real vector, apply the complex operator, then take its real part. The equality is definitional and holds for every complex operator. No assumption that the operator preserves real vectors is required.
TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart_apply.summary: Evaluate the real part of a complex operator

TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart_press.text: Taking the real operator part of the pressure symbol applied to a complex scalar gives the scalar’s real part times the real angular projection. The identity holds for every frequency. It is the algebraic step that converts paired complex Fourier coefficients into the real cosine and sine moment formula.
TorusEuler.realSpatialOperatorPart_press.summary: Recover the real scalar pressure projection

TorusEuler.realTensorFourierCutoff.text:
The real Fourier cutoff on a tensor field represented in a complex normed space.

Default-value audit (b5): The maps J and R are arbitrary continuous linear maps in the definition. Recovering the original real tensor requires the retraction property R∘J=id, and approximation bounds also require a positive cutoff scale.

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff.text:
The Fourier cutoff on real Euclidean vector fields, obtained by complex Fourier synthesis followed by the coordinatewise real projection.

Default-value audit (b5): The cutoff delegates to finite Fourier synthesis and uses an arbitrary real scale in the raw definition. Positive scale, symbol support and regularity are supplied by the cutoff estimates.

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.text: Complexifies a possibly noncontinuous real velocity field, applies the complex Fourier cutoff, then takes its real part. The definition accepts an arbitrary function on the torus. Subsequent results relate this representative-level construction to continuous fields and to almost-everywhere classes; meaningful analytic estimates use integrability or essential boundedness.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.summary: Applying the real vector cutoff to a representative

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.text: Almost-everywhere equal real velocity representatives give exactly equal cutoffs. The proof passes their equality through complexification, applies the complex cutoff congruence, and then takes real parts. The result is pointwise equality of output functions; it does not require the inputs themselves to have pointwise equal values.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.summary: Real velocity cutoffs ignore null-set changes

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.text: For a continuous real velocity field, the representative-level cutoff agrees with the earlier `realVectorFourierCutoff`. This is an equality of the two operator definitions, not a proof that an arbitrary input is continuous. It allows estimates stated for continuous torus fields to be used with the expanded representative interface.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoffOfFunc.summary: Agreement with the continuous velocity cutoff

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_T1_of.text: With smooth time-dependent Fourier coefficients in the retained band, smooth odd divergence-free input slices and an even symbol, the cutoff is jointly smooth on the specified time set. Every slice is periodic, odd, divergence free and has no frequencies beyond $2\Lambda$. These are the listed admissibility properties; no bound on the residual or deformation is asserted.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_T1_of.summary: Smooth coefficient paths produce an admissible next parent

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_add.text: Real vector cutoff preserves addition of continuous torus fields.

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_gradi.text: For a continuously differentiable scalar torus lift and a continuous vector field representing its gradient, the real vector cutoff of that field is the gradient of the real scalar cutoff. The proof differentiates the finite Fourier sum coordinatewise. This exact identity holds for arbitrary real symbol and scale, independently of the later analytic cutoff bounds.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_gradi.summary: The real cutoff preserves the form of a gradient

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_sum.text: The commutation with finite vector field sums, used in tensor divergence.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_sum.summary: Fourier truncation commutes with finite sums

TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_tenso.text: For a continuous torus tensor whose lift is continuously differentiable, let `d` continuously represent its physical divergence. The real vector cutoff of `d` equals the divergence of the real tensor cutoff. The proof uses each coordinate derivative and a finite sum; no smooth-symbol or positive-scale assumption is needed for this exact identity.
TorusEuler.realVectorFourierCutoff_tenso.summary: The real cutoff commutes with tensor divergence

TorusEuler.real_inner_angularLeray_eq_ze.text: For any real frequency vector `ξ` and vector `z`, the angular Leray projection of `z` is orthogonal to `ξ`. The proof splits off `ξ = 0` before cancellation of its squared norm. At zero frequency the orthogonality statement is automatic and is consistent with retaining every amplitude.
TorusEuler.real_inner_angularLeray_eq_ze.summary: The angular projection removes the frequency component

TorusEuler.realifyHalfHolderMultiplier.text: Given a bounded real-linear operator $L$ on half-Hölder fields valued in the complexification, embeds each real input by `X.ofReal`, applies $L$, and then takes `X.re` pointwise. This yields a bounded real-linear operator on real-valued fields. The construction works for arbitrary $L$ and does not require its outputs on real inputs to have zero imaginary part.
TorusEuler.realifyHalfHolderMultiplier.summary: Transport a multiplier to real Hölder fields

TorusEuler.realifyHalfHolderMultiplier_i.text: If the complex embedding of $v$ equals $F$ applied to the embedded $f$ plus $G$ applied to the embedded $s$, then $v$ equals the sum of the two corresponding realified outputs. Applying the real-part map proves the equality pointwise. The premise supplies the exact embedded identity, so preservation of the real subspace by each operator separately is unnecessary.
TorusEuler.realifyHalfHolderMultiplier_i.summary: Transport an embedded multiplier identity to real fields

TorusEuler.reciprocal_inductive_frequenc.text: The reciprocal frequencies have a geometric tail bound: the sum beginning at index $j$ is at most $2/\lambda_j$. The hypotheses `hinit : 2 ≤ freq 0` and `hstep : ∀ n, freq n ^ 2 ≤ freq (n + 1)` give growth at least by squaring. The declaration states both summability and the quantitative bound, allowing the same estimate to control velocity increments and derivative errors.
TorusEuler.reciprocal_inductive_frequenc.summary: Summable reciprocal frequencies and a uniform tail bound

TorusEuler.referenceCouplingNumerators.text: The reference numerator identities reduce the large terms to $N_\eta=1+4e+2e^2+\varepsilon xs^2$ and $N_\nu=x-\varepsilon+2\varepsilon s^2+2\varepsilon\tau s(1+e)$. The hypotheses `hx`, `hs`, and `hY` are exactly $x=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, $(1+x^2)s^2=1$, and the deviation formula for $Y$. No differential equation or smallness estimate is needed for this cancellation.
TorusEuler.referenceCouplingNumerators.summary: Cancellation in the reference coupling numerators

TorusEuler.relayCrossMap.text: The map sends $v$ to the continuous linear operator $w\mapsto v\times w$. Its norm is controlled by one, so composing it with the normalized wave-vector profile preserves parent derivative bounds. This public construction supplies the same geometric operation needed in the potential and its time derivative.
TorusEuler.relayCrossMap.summary: The cross product as an operator-valued linear map

TorusEuler.relayCrossMap_apply.text: For any vector `v`, evaluation of `relayCrossMap` returns `cross3Left v`. The equality is definitional, exposing the concrete cross-product operator after it has been packaged as a continuous linear map. This allows the jet algebra to be identified with the normalized coefficient formulas used in the relay.

TorusEuler.relayCurlRowCLM.text: The map sends a coframe `G` to $\ell^{-1}(G^*e_i)\times\cdot$, the coefficient paired with one scaled label derivative in the curl. It is linear in `G`, so every label derivative of the row is controlled by the corresponding derivative of `G`. The inverse width is kept explicit.
TorusEuler.relayCurlRowCLM.summary: The linear coefficient of a scaled curl row

TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile.text:
Apply the mean-zero oscillatory pressure construction to the fixed-label strain, covector, forcing and velocity profile. This is a scalar phase profile used by the slow pressure-gradient term.

Default-value audit (b5): This is a normalized phase primitive, not a pressure solution predicate. Smoothness, phase periodicity, nonzero covectors and the transverse momentum equation justify its use as pressure.
TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile.summary: The normalized phase pressure used in the relay

TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile_con.text: The normalized phase pressure is linear under simultaneous scalar multiplication of the velocity and forcing slices. Both terms in its pressure slope scale, and so does their zero-mean phase primitive. The coefficients `M` and `k` are held fixed; the theorem does not describe scaling the wave vector or strain.
TorusEuler.relayPhasePressureProfile_con.summary: Velocity and forcing scale the phase pressure together

TorusEuler.relayPotentialProfile.text:
The actual primitive fields in the relay with the frequency removed from the covector. Each depends only on the indicated fixed-time coefficient and profile data.

Default-value audit (b5): This uses the raw wave potential; nonzero covectors and integrable phase profiles are needed for its physical primitive interpretation. The coefficients and profiles in the construction provide those hypotheses.
TorusEuler.relayPotentialProfile.summary: The normalized primitive profile for the relay

TorusEuler.relayPotentialProfile_const_s.text: Scaling the velocity slice by a constant multiplies its relay potential by that constant. The normalized wave-vector coefficient is a continuous linear map and the centered phase primitive commutes with scalar multiplication. The equality is pointwise in label and phase, so a time-dependent weight may be treated as constant on each fixed-time slice.
TorusEuler.relayPotentialProfile_const_s.summary: The potential is linear under simultaneous scaling

TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile.text:
At fixed label, take the normalized phase primitive of the potential-time source built from M, k, V and f. The definition prepares the primitive used in the linear relay; the solution equation is supplied separately.

Default-value audit (b5): The phase integral is a totalized integral. Smooth phase profiles, the nonzero covector and the time evolution identity must be supplied before identifying this primitive with an actual time derivative.
TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile.summary: The phase primitive of the potential-time source

TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile_con.text: If both the velocity and forcing slices are multiplied by `r`, the potential-time profile is multiplied by `r`. Its integrand is linear in those two inputs through separate coefficient maps. This identity permits amplitude normalization after the physical time derivative has been evaluated, without introducing a derivative of the weight.
TorusEuler.relayPotentialTimeProfile_con.summary: Velocity and forcing scale the potential derivative together

TorusEuler.relayPressureRowCLM.text: This map sends `G` to the scalar-to-vector operator $c\mapsto\ell^{-1}cG^*e_i$. It provides the $i$th pressure-gradient coefficient in label coordinates. Packaging the operation as a continuous linear map lets the same coframe derivative estimate control both the pressure row and the curl row.
TorusEuler.relayPressureRowCLM.summary: The linear coefficient of a scaled pressure gradient

TorusEuler.scalarODE_exists_Icc.text: A continuous scalar vector field, uniformly Lipschitz in its state variable on $[lo,hi]$ for times in $[a,b]$, has a solution starting from `x₀` in that strip. The inward inequalities `hlower` and `hupper` keep it inside. The proof projects the state onto the strip, obtains an equation bounded on the chosen time window, then shows that the projection has no effect along the solution.
TorusEuler.scalarODE_exists_Icc.summary: Solving a scalar equation inside an invariant interval

TorusEuler.scalarODE_exists_Ici.text: An invariant state interval gives a solution on $[a,\infty)$ when the field is continuous and Lipschitz in its state variable, uniformly on each compact time window. The constant may depend on the window through `hlip`. Compact-interval solutions agree by uniqueness and are joined into one path. Values before $a$ are unconstrained; the conclusion gives the within-ray derivative and strip membership.
TorusEuler.scalarODE_exists_Ici.summary: Continuing a bounded scalar solution for all future times

TorusEuler.scalar_le_of_derivWithinAt_no.text: If $y(a)\le c$ and the supplied derivative `dy t` is nonpositive whenever $y(t)\ge c$, then $y\le c$ throughout $[a,b]$. The derivative assumption `hy` includes both endpoints within the closed interval; `hsign` is needed only on $[a,b)$. The proof compares with slightly increasing barriers and lets their slopes tend to zero.
TorusEuler.scalar_le_of_derivWithinAt_no.summary: A constant upper barrier for a scalar path

TorusEuler.scalar_le_of_derivWithinAt_no.text: The same constant upper barrier holds on the entire ray $[a,\infty)$ when the derivative and sign assumptions hold there. At a requested time the proof applies the compact-interval barrier on $[a,t]$. This theorem assumes a path already defined on the ray; it does not supply global existence.
TorusEuler.scalar_le_of_derivWithinAt_no.summary: A scalar upper barrier for all future times

TorusEuler.scalar_lt_of_derivWithinAt_ne.text: Suppose $y$ is differentiable within $[a,\infty)$, $a\le b$, and $y(b)\le c$. If its derivative is strictly negative whenever it equals $c$ at or after $b$, then $y(t)<c$ for every $t>b$. Only the derivative on the boundary is constrained. The theorem provides the strict sign needed after the reference rate crosses zero.
TorusEuler.scalar_lt_of_derivWithinAt_ne.summary: Strict descent after touching an upper barrier

TorusEuler.scaledCoframe_jet_bound.text: If coframe derivatives of order `j` are bounded by $LD^{7j+1}$ and $\ell D^7\le1$, then multiplying by $\ell^j$ leaves the uniform bound $LD$. The assumptions include nonnegative radius and coefficient constant and $D\ge1$. The residual parent power is independent of derivative order.
TorusEuler.scaledCoframe_jet_bound.summary: The label radius absorbs coframe derivative growth

TorusEuler.scaledFlow_differentiable_tra.text: For a finite-dimensional state space, joint smoothness of the scaled field, uniform Lipschitz control, and the smallness bound give differentiability of every transition between allowed times. The two-time trajectory family is supplied by `hInit` and `hTraj`. The conclusion also covers reversed transitions and does not assume their derivatives in advance.
TorusEuler.scaledFlow_differentiable_tra.summary: Smooth scaled flows have differentiable transitions

TorusEuler.scaledFlow_fderiv_and_displac.text: Every transition of the lifted flow has derivative norm at most two when `hSmall` bounds gradient times interval length by $1/2$. The hypotheses `hInit` and `hTraj` specify the two-time flow, `hGrad` bounds the field derivative, and `hProj` bounds its projected derivative. The conclusion also controls the derivative of the projected displacement by $2M|t-s|$. Since both times range freely over the interval, the same estimates apply to inverse transitions.
TorusEuler.scaledFlow_fderiv_and_displac.summary: The scaled flow and displacement have bounded derivatives

TorusEuler.scaledFlow_lipschitz_and_disp.text: For a two-time trajectory family, uniform Lipschitz bounds `K` on the field and `M` on its projection combine with `hSmall` to make each transition Lipschitz with constant two. The projected displacement has Lipschitz constant $2M|t-s|$. The initial and trajectory equations are hypotheses, and the bounds hold in either time direction.
TorusEuler.scaledFlow_lipschitz_and_disp.summary: Small scaled gradients bound transitions and projected displacement

TorusEuler.scaledFlow_restart.text: Any two-time trajectory family for a uniformly Lipschitz field, with the prescribed initial values, satisfies the restart identity $\Phi(t,u)\Phi(s,t)=\Phi(s,u)$ for times in the slab. ODE uniqueness gives the equality. Choosing the final time equal to the first then identifies reverse transitions as inverses.
TorusEuler.scaledFlow_restart.summary: Transitions compose across an intermediate time

TorusEuler.scaledHigherPressureGradient_.text: The coframe adjoint, strain and longitudinal projection have first-order scaled coefficient bounds, while pressure has a second-order bound and force and velocity have first-order bounds. Under the listed smoothness and nonnegativity assumptions, their reconstructed gradient has the explicit first-order bound in the conclusion. The transverse equation has not been assumed here; it is used separately to identify this expression.
TorusEuler.scaledHigherPressureGradient_.summary: Bound the reconstructed gradient before physical differentiation

TorusEuler.scaledLiftKernel.text: Defines $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$ for a complex-valued kernel on $\mathbb R^3$. The power three is the volume factor, which makes the kernel mass invariant under positive dilation. The definition is meaningful for every real scale, but the change-of-variables estimates used in Appendix B assume a positive scale. Decay, integrability and vanishing moments are properties established separately for the Schwartz kernel.

TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel.text: Dilate a Banach-valued Euclidean kernel by evaluating it at `Λ*y` and multiplying by $\Lambda^3$. The cubic factor is the dimension-three volume normalization. This definition works for every real scale, while the integral and Fourier scaling theorems explicitly restrict to positive `Λ`.
TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel.summary: A multiplier kernel at a new frequency scale

TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel_decay.text: The inverse Fourier kernel at any positive scale $\Lambda$ and derivative order `d ≤ 1` satisfies an order-five decay bound with the factor $\Lambda^{3+d}$. The symbol is a Schwartz function; `multiplierDerivativeMass` measures the weighted integrals of its derivatives. Setting $\Lambda=2^j$ gives the scale in Appendix A. The annular localization and the bound for that derivative mass are separate inputs to the application.
TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel_decay.summary: Decay of a dyadically scaled Fourier kernel

TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel_decay_.text: At positive frequency scale $\Lambda$, the weighted order `d` derivative of the rescaled kernel is bounded by $\Lambda^{3+d}$ times the unscaled decay coefficient. Three powers come from volume scaling in dimension three, and each derivative contributes one more. Positivity of the scale is explicit in the chain-rule and norm calculation.
TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel_decay_.summary: Scaling records volume and derivative powers exactly

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseCoefficient.text: Evaluate the coefficient field `B` at $\ell p_1$, ignoring the independent phase coordinate. This expresses a label-dependent inverse differential in the coordinates of the rescaled profile. The definition itself does not assert that `B` is an inverse Jacobian; that identification is supplied by `hB` in the physical chain-rule theorems.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseCoefficient.summary: The inverse differential at the rescaled label

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseCoefficient_jetBou.text: If every label derivative through order `n` obeys $\ell^j\|D^jB\|\le C$ and `B` is smooth, then the rescaled coefficient has `PhaseJetBound n C`. The assumption `hℓ` is nonnegativity of the label scale. Phase directions add no derivatives because this coefficient does not depend on phase.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseCoefficient_jetBou.summary: Weighted label derivatives bound the rescaled coefficient

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseDirection.text: Apply the rescaled inverse-differential coefficient to a spatial basis vector, then send that label increment through `labelPhaseSlope`. The resulting vector field differentiates the enlarged profile in the direction induced by one physical spatial derivative. It includes both the envelope scale and the phase scale without differentiating time.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseDirection.summary: A spatial direction lifted to label and phase

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseDirection_jetBound.text: An order-`n` bound `C` for the rescaled coefficient gives the same derivative order for the lifted spatial direction, multiplied by $\ell^{-1}+h^{-1}\|k\|$. Smoothness of `B` and nonnegative scales are explicit hypotheses. This supplies the coefficient bound used when iterating variable-direction derivatives of a profile.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseDirection_jetBound.summary: The lifted direction inherits the graph cost

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseGraph.text: Compose the label map `A t` with the scaled label-phase slope to embed physical space into the enlarged profile space. Its components are the scaled label and the initial linear phase evaluated at that label. No assumption that `A` is a flow inverse is part of this definition.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseGraph.summary: The transported phase graph in scaled coordinates

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile.text:
The label-phase profile in the coordinates with unit envelope and phase scales.

Default-value audit (b5): The composition is defined for arbitrary scales. At zero scales it loses spatial or phase dependence; invertible rescaling arguments use positive ℓ and h.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile.summary: The profile in unit label and phase coordinates

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_comp_graph.text: With nonzero label radius and phase width, evaluating the rescaled profile on the scaled phase graph gives precisely the transported physical profile. The equality holds for an arbitrary time-dependent profile `f`, without differentiability assumptions. It removes the coordinate rescaling before later spatial chain-rule estimates are interpreted physically.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_comp_graph.summary: Scaled graph evaluation recovers the transported profile

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.text: The normalized finite directional norm itself supplies the graph input. Its boundedness is explicit, since a real supremum requires it.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.summary: Weighted derivative norms control the rescaled profile

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.text: If every weighted mixed coordinate derivative through order `n` is bounded by nonnegative `M`, the rescaled profile has full Fréchet derivative bound $4^nM$. The factor four counts the three label directions and one phase direction. The theorem requires joint smoothness but permits arbitrary real scaling parameters.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.summary: Weighted component bounds give a full profile bound

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.text: A word bound through order `n` gives a scaled Fréchet jet bound with constant $4^nM$ for each smooth slice. Four label-and-phase coordinates account for the counting factor. Smoothness allows arbitrary coordinate words to be sorted without changing their values, so the admissible-word bound controls every multilinear coordinate entry.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.summary: Coordinate-word bounds control all scaled Fréchet derivatives

TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.text: A word bound for profiles divided by `gamma` gives a scaled jet bound for the original profile after multiplication by `gamma t`. Positivity at the selected time is required to cancel the inverse weight. The weight depends only on the auxiliary index, so label and phase derivatives do not differentiate it.
TorusEuler.scaledPhaseProfile_jetBound_o.summary: Restoring the amplitude weight recovers the physical profile size

TorusEuler.scaledPressureLabelGradient_j.text: If `ell > 0`, the pressure is smooth and its scaled profile has a second-order jet bound `B`, then the scaled label gradient has a first-order jet bound `ell⁻¹ * B`. This spells out the single lost label derivative and length factor used in the higher-pressure Hessian argument.
TorusEuler.scaledPressureLabelGradient_j.summary: Two pressure derivatives control one gradient derivative

TorusEuler.scaledSchwartzKernel.text: For `hΛ : Λ ≠ 0`, package $\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$ as a Schwartz function. Nonzero scale makes dilation an invertible linear map, so rapid decay is preserved. The definition allows negative scales and uses the signed cubic factor; the normalized convolution and moment estimates later impose `Λ > 0`.
TorusEuler.scaledSchwartzKernel.summary: Dilate a Schwartz kernel with the cubic scale factor

TorusEuler.scaledSchwartzKernel_apply.text: Evaluating the scaled Schwartz object gives the already-defined raw function `scaledLiftKernel Λ K`. This is a definitional equality for any nonzero scale. It lets proofs use the bundled object for decay and integrability while keeping the explicit $\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$ function in convolution formulas.
TorusEuler.scaledSchwartzKernel_apply.summary: The bundled dilation has the expected kernel values

TorusEuler.scheduledCrossingRatio.text: The ratio at transition `i` is `couplingRatioOfGain (4 * log (freq (i + 3)))`. Index zero represents the transition starting the second wave, so the gain looks three positions ahead in the zero-based frequency sequence. The definition alone imposes no growth or positivity assumption on that sequence.
TorusEuler.scheduledCrossingRatio.summary: The ratio prescribed for the next physical crossing

TorusEuler.seminorm_word_le_appendixExac.text: Under pairwise commutation of the derivative maps, the seminorm of a word is bounded by the sum over admissible words of exactly its length. Sorting provides a representative of that same length. This sharper version avoids introducing lower-order coefficient terms in the slow-coefficient bound of the lifting proof.

TorusEuler.slabAdvection.text: For velocity fields `v` and `w`, this is $D_xv(t,x)[w(t,x)]$, so `w` is the advecting direction and `v` is the differentiated field. The argument order matters when the binomial rule splits time derivatives between two copies of the velocity. The abbreviation itself asserts neither smoothness nor an Euler equation.
TorusEuler.slabAdvection.summary: Advection with the differentiated field first

TorusEuler.slabAdvection_periodic.text: If `v` is differentiable and both spatial fields are periodic, then $x\mapsto Dv(x)[w(x)]$ is periodic. The proof uses periodicity of the derivative of `v` and then periodicity of `w`. There is no time variable or equation hypothesis here; this supplies the spatial periodicity needed to pass differentiated advection to torus norms.

TorusEuler.slabSpatialHolderHalfNorm.text:
The time-uniform spatial half-Hölder norm on the closed slab.

Default-value audit (b5): The slab supremum is a real supremum. Actual upper and lower norm bounds require boundedness of the spatial Hölder norms over a nonempty slab; smooth periodic closed-slab inputs supply it in the applications.
TorusEuler.slabSpatialHolderHalfNorm.summary: The uniform spatial Hölder norm on a time slab

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet.text: The $q$th time derivative with the spatial point held fixed. The abbreviation applies `iteratedDerivWithin q` to `fun r => f r x` on `Icc a b`, which is the closed interval $[a,b]$. It does not differentiate along a particle trajectory and does not hold a Lagrangian label fixed. The definition itself assumes no regularity; the accompanying smooth-slab lemmas provide the differentiability and endpoint interpretation needed when it is used for the constructed fields.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet.summary: Eulerian time derivatives at a fixed spatial point

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_cutoffResidual_ra.text: The differentiated residual after cutoff is bounded pointwise by the next frequency to the power $-5/2$. The theorem assumes the analytic residual estimate `hR`, the approximate residual bound `hApprox`, and `hNext : next = freq ^ k`. Its numerical reserve is `hk : 16 + 2*exponent ≤ k`, with nonnegative exponent and controlled cutoff constants. It converts those explicit assumptions into the final decay; the scheduled hierarchy supplies them at sufficiently large stages.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_cutoffResidual_ra.summary: The cutoff residual reaches the next-frequency decay

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_endpointTimeParit.text: For a jointly smooth velocity on a positive-length slab, time differentiation at a fixed point commutes with `endpointTimeParityPart σ` for every real $\sigma$. The statement is an exact equality at each time in the slab. A contraction estimate would require a separate restriction on the parity coefficient; this theorem only gives commutation.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_endpointTimeParit.summary: Taking a parity part commutes with every time derivative

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_eq_of_subset.text: For a smooth field on $[a,b]$, its jets agree with those computed on a contained interval $[c,d]$ whenever both intervals are nondegenerate and `t ∈ Icc c d`. The equality includes the smaller interval endpoints. `hsub`, `hab`, and `hcd` are what allow finite-stage estimates on different time slabs to be compared without changing their time derivatives.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_eq_of_subset.summary: Restrict time jets to a smaller closed interval

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_normContinuity.text: If `f` is jointly smooth on a positive closed slab and spatially periodic at every slab time, each fixed time jet is continuous there in both the spatial supremum norm and every half-Hölder norm. The proof uses uniformly continuous spatial jets on the torus through one order above the requested Hölder order. It establishes continuity, not a quantitative size bound on the jet.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_normContinuity.summary: Smooth periodic time jets are continuous in spatial norms

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_periodic.text: If every time slice is spatially periodic on the chosen closed interval, each total within-time jet is periodic at times in that interval. Unlike the smoothness lemmas, this identity needs neither joint smoothness nor a nondegenerate interval. The proof differentiates equal periodic slices; interpreting the resulting jets as classical derivatives requires the separate regularity hypotheses.

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_periodicLerayHold.text: For a jointly smooth periodic velocity on $[0,T]$ with `hT : 0 < T`, each fixed-position time jet commutes with `periodicLerayHolderLift`. The proof represents the jets as smooth curves in the torus half-Hölder space and differentiates a continuous linear map there. This is the analytic justification for moving time derivatives through the projected residual.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_periodicLerayHold.summary: The periodic Leray projection commutes with time jets

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_realVectorFourier.text: Given a smooth field and representatives `g` satisfying `hg` for every time jet, the $j$th time derivative of its fixed Fourier cutoff equals the cutoff of `g j t`. The multiplier and radius are independent of time. The statement holds on the closed slab using `hT : 0 < T`; it does not cover cutoffs whose frequency radius moves with time.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_realVectorFourier.summary: Fixed Fourier cutoffs commute with time differentiation

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_slabAdvection.text: Under `hT`, `hv`, and `hw`, the $q$th fixed-position time derivative of $D_xv[w]$ is the binomial sum of advections of the time jets of `v` and `w`. The identity holds at every `t` in the closed interval, including both endpoints. Commutation of spatial and within-time differentiation justifies differentiating the first factor.

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_slice_smooth.text: For a jointly smooth field on a nondegenerate closed slab, the spatial field obtained from any time jet at `t ∈ Icc a b` is smooth on all of $\mathbb R^3$. The proof composes joint smoothness with the fixed-time inclusion. It gives spatial regularity at the endpoints as well as in the interval interior.

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_smooth.text: If `hab : a < b` and `hf` gives joint smoothness on $[a,b]\times\mathbb R^3$, every time jet is jointly smooth on that same set. The proof inducts using the within-slab slice derivative theorem. The strict interval inequality is part of the mathematical content, ensuring the derivative behavior used at both endpoints is well determined.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_smooth.summary: Time jets remain jointly smooth on the closed slab

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_succ.text: The jet of order `q + 1` equals `derivWithin` of the order-`q` jet at the fixed spatial point, using the same closed interval. This is an unconditional identity between total derivative operations. It does not assert that the field has a classical derivative; later lemmas supply joint smoothness and a nondegenerate interval.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_succ.summary: Differentiate the preceding time jet within the slab

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_succ'.text: The jet of order `q + 1` can also be written as the order-`q` jet of the first within-time derivative. This functional identity keeps the spatial coordinate fixed throughout. It reorganizes derivative induction and product recurrences; by itself it supplies no regularity or endpoint uniqueness beyond the meaning of the total derivative operators.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_succ'.summary: Iterate time jets after the first within-derivative

TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_zero.text: At time order zero, `slabTimeJet a b` is exactly the original field as a function of both time and space. The statement has no smoothness, interval-ordering, or membership hypothesis. It is a definitional starting case used when the time induction returns to already established spatial estimates for the unmodified construction.
TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_zero.summary: The zeroth time jet is the original field

TorusEuler.slowFastDivergence_curlComple.text: Assume the potential is twice differentiable, the completed field differentiable, and its fast curl and slow-curl decomposition are the supplied `V` and `W`. For a twice differentiable label map and phase with gradient `κ`, the slow-plus-fast divergence of `W` vanishes at any chosen phase. Shifting the physical phase graph makes it pass through that phase.
TorusEuler.slowFastDivergence_curlComple.summary: A curl completion has zero total divergence at every phase

TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff.text:
The cutoff is a finite Fourier synthesis over frequencies of size at most $2\Lambda$, multiplying each coefficient by $\psi(\Lambda^{-1}\xi)$. The definition uses complex normed-space-valued Fourier coefficients. Under the paper’s support assumption on $\psi$, the explicit finite band agrees with multiplying every Fourier mode by the prescribed symbol. The definition itself neither asserts boundedness nor preservation of divergence; those are separate results.

Default-value audit (b5): The scale inverse is total at Λ=0 and the selected frequency set can degenerate. The cutoff theorems impose a positive scale and the required symbol properties before asserting approximation or decay.

TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff_conj.text: For the real-valued symbol `ψ` with evenness `hψ`, applying the cutoff to the conjugated scalar field equals conjugating its output. The proof pairs opposite frequencies in the finite band. The conclusion is purely algebraic and does not require input smoothness or a positive cutoff scale.
TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff_conj.summary: A real even cutoff commutes with conjugation

TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff_eq_integr.text: For an integrable torus function `g`, the finite Fourier cutoff at `x` equals the integral of `appendixCutoffKernel ψ Λ x z • g z`. The proof interchanges a finite sum with the integral and expands Fourier coefficients. It establishes this representation for arbitrary symbol and scale; the uniform analytic estimate comes later.

TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff_neg_arg.text: If `hψ` makes the cutoff symbol even and `hg` gives a real-scalar parity relation for the input, the output satisfies that same relation. The scale may be any real number. This algebraic assertion establishes parity preservation independently of the analytic cutoff estimates requiring positive scale.

TorusEuler.smoothPeriodicVelocity.text: This submodule consists of Euclidean vector fields that are smooth and spatially periodic. Closure under addition and real scalar multiplication is proved in the definition. It provides the common algebraic domain for the momentum construction. Neither divergence freedom nor odd parity is part of membership.
TorusEuler.smoothPeriodicVelocity.summary: Smooth periodic fields form the velocity domain

TorusEuler.smoothPeriodicVelocityJets.text: The map sends a smooth periodic field to all its bounded spatial derivatives through order `m`. It is linear because differentiation preserves sums and scalar multiplication on smooth inputs. Including the zeroth derivative makes the tuple remember the original velocity, which is used to prove injectivity.
TorusEuler.smoothPeriodicVelocityJets.summary: A smooth velocity determines its finite jet tuple

TorusEuler.smooth_slabAdvection.text: Given `hT : 0 < T` and jointly smooth `v` and `w` on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, their advective product is jointly smooth on the same closed slab. The proof first differentiates `v` spatially within the slab calculus and then applies that linear-map field to `w`. It preserves endpoint regularity needed by subsequent time derivatives.

TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord.text:
The usual ordered coordinate partials of a field on the lift.

Default-value audit (b5): The word map is defined using totalized derivatives. Permuting words or identifying them with classical partial derivatives uses separate smoothness hypotheses.

TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_comp.text: The chain rule iterated along a coordinate word, for a graph with a supplied direction field over each of its Eulerian coordinate derivatives.
TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_comp.summary: The chain rule along a transported derivative word

TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_endpoin.text: For a smooth field and an ordered word of coordinate derivatives, identifies differentiation of the parity part with selecting sign `sign * (-1)^w.length` after differentiating. The word order remains unchanged. This converts the abstract iterated Fréchet derivative formula into the coordinate-word notation used for hierarchy estimates.
TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_endpoin.summary: Coordinate derivatives alternate the selected parity

TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_eq_iter.text: A spatial derivative word agrees with evaluating the actual Fréchet derivative in the corresponding ordered coordinate directions.
TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_eq_iter.summary: Spatial words evaluate the actual derivative tensor

TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_transpo.text: Under nonzero scales, smooth profile and coefficient fields, and the identification `hB` of `B` with the label-map derivative, every ordered spatial derivative word of the physical profile is the corresponding lifted profile word evaluated on the graph. The list records order explicitly. No commutation of variable-coefficient derivatives is presumed.
TorusEuler.spatialDerivativeWord_transpo.summary: Physical derivative words become profile derivative words

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm.text:
Sum the uniform norm and half-Holder seminorm of all iterated Frechet derivatives through the specified order. It is used together with the spatial Holder predicate, which ensures that every supremum is finite and the derivatives have their intended meaning.

Default-value audit (b5): The formula is total even when derivatives are not meaningful or their supremum ranges are unbounded, because iterated derivatives and real suprema are total. The SpatialHolderHalf predicate is the intended validity condition. Order zero contains the value and increment terms.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm.summary: The higher spatial Holder norm on the lift

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffP.text: The Hessian of $p-\Pi$ is bounded in $C^{0,1/2}$ by a velocity-gradient difference times the two velocity-gradient sizes, together with the $C^{1,1/2}$ residual norm. The hypotheses include smooth periodic pressures, their Poisson and momentum equations, and solenoidality of the approximate velocity and its time derivative. The proof applies the bounded periodic pressure Hessian multiplier to the scalar source. The residual contribution cannot be omitted when $\Pi$ is an expansion pressure.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffP.summary: The pressure error is controlled by velocity tail and residual

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffP.text: For a smooth symbol equal to one on the unit ball and zero beyond radius two, assumes cutoff scale at least one, depth `P ≥ 2`, and `SpatialHolderHalf P` for the input lift. It bounds the order-one tail norm times the sum of the old and new order-one velocity norms by $C(2+C)$ times the truncation error. Evenness is not required here.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffP.summary: The quadratic pressure tail has the cutoff decay

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffT.text: For $s\le M$, proves that the periodic cutoff tail has order-`s` half-Hölder regularity and norm at most $C_M\Lambda^{s-M}$ times the order-`M` input norm. The exponent is an integer power, and positive `Λ` justifies its reciprocal form. Unlike the paper’s setup `Λ ≥ 1`, this statement allows any positive cutoff scale.

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffV.text: The difference $S_\Lambda V-V$ has $C^{m,1/2}$ norm at most a cutoff constant times $\Lambda^{m-P}\|V\|_{C^{P,1/2}}$. The assumptions `hψ`, `hs` and `hunit` specify the smooth cutoff, `hΛ` requires positive scale, and `hm : m ≤ P` fixes the derivative range. The result also supplies half-Hölder regularity of the difference. Its range includes the paper’s orders $s\le2$ when $P\ge2$.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffV.summary: The cutoff velocity difference gains the Fourier-tail factor

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_endpoin.text: For a field carrying `SpatialHolderHalf m`, proves the same regularity certificate after reflection averaging and a nonincreasing full finite norm when `|sign| ≤ 1`. Derivative parity alternates with order, but each sign still has absolute value at most one. Both differentiability and bounded quotient sets are preserved.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_endpoin.summary: Selecting parity costs no half-Hölder norm constant

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_le_of_u.text: Uniform derivatives through order $m+1$ bound the full $C^{m,1/2}$ norm. The hypotheses are `hg : ContDiff ℝ ∞ g`, `hB : 0 ≤ B` and `hjet`, which bounds each derivative by $B$. The conclusion gives both half-Hölder regularity and the explicit norm bound $3(m+1)B$. Interpolation of a bounded function with its bounded first derivative supplies the half-Hölder seminorm at each order.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_le_of_u.summary: One extra derivative controls the half-Hölder norm

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_one_eq.text: The order-one lift norm is exactly the order-zero norm of the field plus the order-zero norm of its Fréchet derivative. This follows by expanding the two derivative levels and using the isometric first-derivative encoding. The identity supports separate estimates for the projected field and its projected derivative columns.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_one_eq.summary: The first-order norm separates value and derivative

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_realTen.text: For real and complex tensor spaces linked by continuous real-linear maps `J` and `R` with `R(J q)=q`, the real tensor cutoff tail obeys the usual $\Lambda^{s-M}$ estimate. The constant gains the factor $\|R\|\|J\|$. The retraction identity is essential: it makes the projected complex tail equal the original real tensor error.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_realTen.summary: The Hölder tail estimate extends to real tensors

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_realVec.text: The real vector cutoff error has $C^{s,1/2}$ norm at most the explicit kernel constant times $\Lambda^{s-M}\|f\|_{C^{M,1/2}}$. The assumptions `hsM` and `hf` give $s\le M$ and input regularity. The symbol is smooth, supported in radius two, and one on the unit ball. Unlike the paper’s displayed range, this declaration allows every positive scale `hΛ : 0 < Λ`.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_realVec.summary: The real velocity cutoff has the full Hölder tail bound

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_succ_eq.text: The implemented order-$m+1$ norm is the order-zero norm of `f` plus the order-$m$ norm of `fderiv f`. This is an exact algebraic equality for the finite sum defining the norm. It holds without regularity hypotheses; interpreting each real supremum as a genuine bound still requires the separate `SpatialHolderHalf` predicate.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_succ_eq.summary: Split the higher Hölder norm at order zero

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_zero_eq.text: The lift norm at order zero equals the sum of the field’s real supremum norm and half-Hölder seminorm. This equality is definitional up to the isometric encoding of zero-argument multilinear maps. No boundedness hypothesis is present in the identity; interpreting either real supremum as a norm still requires the appropriate boundedness condition.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_zero_eq.summary: The order-zero norm is supremum plus seminorm

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfQuotient.text:
Define the norm of a field increment divided by the square root of the increment length. The quotient uses the lifted field on Euclidean labels and is formally zero at a zero increment by totalized division.

Default-value audit (b5): At zero increment both numerator and denominator are zero, and total division gives zero. This harmless convention adds an equal-point quotient without affecting a genuine seminorm; nonzero increments are needed for reciprocal manipulations.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfQuotient.summary: The half Holder quotient of a spatial increment

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfSeminorm.text:
Take the real supremum of the increment quotients over all base points and increments. Boundedness of this range is a separate part of the spatial Holder predicate.

Default-value audit (b5): The quotient at zero increment is zero. The real iSup has a default value when its range is unbounded, so boundedness must be supplied before treating it as a finite Holder seminorm.

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_add.text: A spatial half-Hölder sum estimate for an arbitrary normed target.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_add.summary: Adding fields preserves finite spatial Hölder regularity

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_add_exact.text: If both vector fields have the specified finite half-Hölder regularity, their sum has it too and its norm is bounded by the sum of the two norms. The derivative order is unchanged.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_add_exact.summary: The half-Hölder norm obeys the triangle inequality

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_bilinear.text: A continuous bilinear map preserves $C^{m,1/2}$ regularity and satisfies the product estimate with constant $3(m+1)2^m\|B\|$. The inputs `hf : SpatialHolderHalf m f` and `hg : SpatialHolderHalf m g` give the two factors. The binder `B : E →L[ℝ] F →L[ℝ] G` allows scalar multiplication, vector products and tensors. This is the form used to control the quadratic tensors in the truncated residual.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_bilinear.summary: The half-Hölder norm controls bilinear products

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_comp_clm.text: Continuous linear maps preserve finite spatial half-Hölder regularity.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_comp_clm.summary: Linear maps preserve finite spatial Hölder regularity

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_contraction.text: Contracting a first spatial derivative, as for a tensor divergence, loses one Hölder order.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_contraction.summary: Tensor divergence costs one spatial Hölder derivative

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_halfHolderP.text: A bounded torus operator commuting with actual line derivatives preserves every finite lifted half-Hölder order. The norm factor remains $2\sqrt{2}\|P\|$, independent of the order `m`. The input must be periodic and satisfy `SpatialHolderHalf m`; induction uses the derivative operator’s norm bound and the exact splitting of the higher norm.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_halfHolderP.summary: Bound every Hölder order of the projected lift

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_of_bounded_.text: Uniform adjacent spatial jet bounds control the lift half-Hölder norm.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_of_bounded_.summary: Adjacent derivative bounds control the half-Hölder norm

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_of_contDiff.text: A smooth periodic lift has finite spatial half-Hölder norm at every order.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_of_contDiff.summary: A smooth periodic lift has finite Hölder regularity

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_one_halfHol.text: If `P` preserves all torus line-derivative relations, its guarded lift maps periodic order-one half-Hölder fields to the same class. The norm bound is $2\sqrt2\|P\|$ times the input norm. The proof separately controls the field and reconstructed derivative columns; the periodicity and regularity hypotheses select the meaningful branch of the lifted definition.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_one_halfHol.summary: A derivative-preserving operator is bounded on first-order lifts

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_one_iff.text: A field has first-order half-Hölder regularity exactly when it is $C^1$ and both the field and its Fréchet derivative have order-zero half-Hölder regularity. The explicit $C^1$ condition prevents a totalized derivative value from being mistaken for genuine differentiability. This decomposition is used to establish the projected field’s regularity.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_one_iff.summary: First-order regularity is regularity of value and derivative

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_periodicLer.text: The actual periodic Leray projection preserves every spatial half-Hölder order.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_periodicLer.summary: The Leray projection preserves every spatial Hölder order

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_sub_le_of_u.text: If smooth fields differ by at most a nonnegative $\delta$ in every derivative through order `m+1`, their difference belongs to $C^{m,1/2}$ and its norm is at most $3(m+1)\delta$. The extra derivative controls the half Hölder quotient. The theorem supplies the regularity predicate as well as the numerical norm bound.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_sub_le_of_u.summary: Uniform derivative errors control the full Hölder difference

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_succ_iff.text: Order $m+1$ half-Hölder regularity is equivalent to differentiability of `f`, order-zero regularity of `f`, and order-$m$ regularity of its Fréchet derivative. The order-zero clause retains control of the original function as well as its derivatives. This equivalence includes bounded derivative norms and Hölder quotients, not merely a formal derivative identity.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_succ_iff.summary: Separate the first derivative from higher regularity

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_iff.text: Order-zero half-Hölder regularity is equivalent to continuity of the field, boundedness of its norm range and boundedness of its increment-quotient range. The theorem makes the finiteness requirements explicit. It is the entry criterion for descending a periodic Euclidean field into the bundled quotient half-Hölder space.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_iff.summary: Order zero means continuity and two finite bounds

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_of_con.text: A continuously differentiable periodic lift belongs to the spatial half-Hölder domain.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_of_con.summary: A differentiable periodic field has zeroth Hölder regularity

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_of_hal.text: Pulling back a bundled half-Hölder torus field gives order-zero half-Hölder regularity on Euclidean space and lift norm at most twice the bundled norm. The factor two comes from adding the separate supremum and seminorm contributions. This is a norm comparison, not equality or an isometric identification of the two spaces.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_of_hal.summary: A quotient Hölder field has a controlled lift norm

TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_of_uni.text: If $f$ is differentiable everywhere and its value and Fréchet derivative have uniform bounds $A$ and $B$, then $f$ has spatial half Hölder regularity and norm at most $3A+B$. Small displacements use the derivative estimate; large displacements use the value estimate. The hypotheses themselves imply $A,B\ge0$, and zero displacement is handled separately.
TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_zero_of_uni.summary: Supremum and gradient bounds imply half Hölder control

TorusEuler.spatialSupNorm.text:
Define the real supremum of the pointwise norm over all Euclidean labels. It acts as the intended uniform norm only when the range is bounded above; the definition itself imposes no boundedness.

Default-value audit (b5): This is a real iSup, not an extended-real supremum; unbounded norm ranges can take Lean's default zero. Only bounded-above ranges support the intended pointwise norm comparison.

TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift.text: This bounded real linear map takes a bounded operator on three-vectors to its pointwise action on $L^2$ time paths over $(0,T]$. The result is an operator on equivalence classes of paths. Its almost-everywhere evaluation lemma supplies the precise connection with the informal pointwise description.
TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift.summary: A spatial operator acts at every time along a path

TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift_apply_ae.text: The path obtained by applying the lifted operator agrees almost everywhere with $t\mapsto A(v(t))$. Equality is deliberately almost everywhere because $L^2$ paths are equivalence classes. This evaluation identity is used to prove symmetry, idempotence, and commutation with time integration.
TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift_apply_ae.summary: The lifted spatial action is pointwise almost everywhere

TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift_commutes_endp.text: Any fixed bounded spatial operator, lifted to time paths, commutes with the mean-subtraction map. The identity follows because the operator preserves constant paths and commutes with integration. There is no positivity hypothesis on `T` in this algebraic statement; orthogonality of mean subtraction is established separately.
TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift_commutes_endp.summary: Spatial action commutes with subtracting the time average

TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift_isSymmetricPr.text: If `hA` makes the spatial operator a symmetric projection, its lifted action is a symmetric projection on the real $L^2$ path space. Idempotence holds almost everywhere and symmetry is integrated through the path inner product. No positive-duration assumption is needed for this lifting statement.
TorusEuler.spatialTimeLift_isSymmetricPr.summary: A symmetric spatial projection remains one on paths

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_centeredLab.text: The coordinatewise centered-label representative is unchanged when an integer lattice vector is added. This follows from periodicity of the fractional-part operation. The result is a statement about values only: the representative jumps at cell boundaries, so it is not by itself a smooth map.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_centeredLab.summary: The centered representative is invariant under lattice translation

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_closedSlab_.text: Smooth periodic slices of velocity and pressure give a periodic momentum residual at each slab time, with velocity periodicity assumed over the full time interval to handle the time derivative.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_closedSlab_.summary: The momentum residual remains spatially periodic

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_curl.text: The curl of a spatially periodic vector function is also spatially periodic. The statement itself has no differentiability assumption because Lean’s total derivative respects translation identities even outside the differentiable case. Classical smoothness and the divergence-of-curl identity are established separately before physical applications.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_curl.summary: Curl respects the periodic translation identity

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_dyadicPerio.text: The double dyadic and lattice kernel expression is spatially periodic by reindexing the lattice translates. No separate convergence argument is part of this theorem. Its analytic use together with smoothness requires the later off origin summable-majorant estimates.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_dyadicPerio.summary: The full kernel respects the unit periods

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_endpointFin.text: The real pressure formed from the finite Fourier sum is spatially periodic for every frequency set and coefficient family. Its argument passes through the unit torus, so integer lattice translations do not change the value. This is a periodicity assertion independent of whether its gradient reconstructs a chosen vector field.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_endpointFin.summary: Finite Fourier pressures have the prescribed periods

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_endpointPar.text: If a field is invariant under integer lattice shifts, its reflection average has the same periodicity for any real sign. Reflection sends a lattice shift to the opposite shift, which is still available in the periodicity hypothesis. This result does not require the sign to be a genuine parity value.

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_firstWaveLo.text: The constructed first-wave velocity is periodic for every real choice of its scalar parameters and every time. Centered periodization gives periodicity of the potential, and the inverse shear map respects lattice translations. This algebraic periodicity statement is weaker than the separate smoothness theorem and does not require its collar hypotheses.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_firstWaveLo.summary: The completed first velocity is spatially periodic

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_firstWaveSm.text: For every shear ratio `s`, amplitude scale `c`, and time `t`, the vector seed is spatially periodic. Its label dependence enters through the periodic sweep. The result concerns the unlocalized seed; localization and the twisted periodization used for the physical oscillation are separate constructions.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_firstWaveSm.summary: The explicit seed is periodic in its label

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_fourierMode.text: For every integer frequency, the lifted Fourier mode is invariant under translation by an integer lattice vector. The proof uses equality in the torus quotient. This connects the library character with the periodicity predicate used throughout the Euler formalization on Euclidean space.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_fourierMode.summary: Integer Fourier characters are spatially periodic

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_halfHolderP.text: For any input function and any bounded torus operator, `halfHolderProjectionLift` is spatially periodic. On its admissible branch it is evaluation through the torus quotient; otherwise the definition returns zero. This unconditional periodicity theorem therefore does not certify that the input had a valid half-Hölder descent or that the output is its mathematical projection.

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_liftConvolu.text: If the input field is invariant under all lattice translations, its convolution has the same periodicity for any kernel. The proof compares the integrands pointwise after a lattice shift. No convergence assumption is needed for this identity of total integral expressions; the analytic existence of convolution is established separately.

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_lift_realVe.text: The real vector Fourier cutoff, composed with the quotient map, is a spatially periodic field. Periodicity follows from being a function on the torus, regardless of approximation estimates.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_lift_realVe.summary: The truncated torus field lifts periodically

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_lift_smooth.text: The Fourier cutoff composed with the quotient map is invariant under integer lattice translations. This periodicity holds for arbitrary symbol, scale, and input because the output is defined on the quotient torus. Separate hypotheses establish norm estimates or agreement with a prescribed smooth multiplier.

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_localizedTr.text: The cellwise extended graph is periodic for every real wave vector `k`. The hypothesis `hA` requires the inverse label map to commute with each lattice translation. Periodicity then follows from the centered-cell periodization itself, without any condition on the profile values at the boundary. Boundary vanishing is needed separately for smoothness, so this theorem alone should not be read as constructing a smooth localized wave.

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_modOne_line.text: The circle-valued phase $a\mapsto k\cdot a\pmod1$ is invariant under all integer label translations if and only if $k$ is an integer lattice vector. The forward implication tests the coordinate lattice translations to show every component is integral. The reverse implication uses that the inner product of two lattice vectors is an integer. This is the exact obstruction removed by evaluating a localized profile on one cell and then extending it periodically.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_modOne_line.summary: The phase is periodic exactly for lattice vectors

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_operatorLif.text: A spatially periodic input field remains periodic after convolution with any operator-valued kernel. The identity follows from periodicity of the integrand under lattice translation of the output point. It is valid as an equality of total integral expressions; convergence and norm estimates are separate assertions.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_operatorLif.summary: Operator convolution preserves the lattice period

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_periodicLer.text: Specializes the unconditional periodicity property of the general projection lift to the spatial Leray operator. It remains true for inadmissible inputs because the underlying definition then returns zero. The theorem should be read as a property of the total extension; meaningful projection and regularity claims require the hypotheses supplied by the neighbouring estimates.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_periodicLer.summary: The Leray lift is periodic for every input

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_periodizeCe.text: Extending a function by evaluating it at the centered representative produces a spatially periodic function. This statement alone does not assert continuity at cell walls.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_periodizeCe.summary: The centered extension is spatially periodic

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_stationaryS.text: The stationary shear is spatially periodic for every real parameter. Translating the second coordinate by an integer changes its sine phase by an integer multiple of $2\pi$, leaving the velocity unchanged. This verifies the periodicity requirement for the initial parent on the torus.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_stationaryS.summary: The sinusoidal shear is periodic under integer translations

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_transported.text: Affine lattice equivariance of the inverse-label map and the corresponding joint label-phase shift law for the profile imply spatial periodicity after graph evaluation. This statement works for any target type and needs no smoothness or integrality of the carrier vector. Compatibility of the profile absorbs the carrier’s phase shift.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_transported.summary: A compatible phase twist produces a periodic physical field

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_truncatedPa.text: Shows that the slice pressure is invariant under every integer spatial translation, for every radius and input. Each Fourier mode is periodic, so the finite synthesis has the same property. This supplies the periodicity needed to package the potential for the Leray and pressure-recovery arguments.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_truncatedPa.summary: The finite pressure respects lattice translations

TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_tsum_lattic.text: The double sum over dyadic grades and all integer translations is spatially periodic for any family `K`. Translating the observation point simply reindexes the lattice by a bijection. This identity holds for Lean’s totalized infinite sum without a summability premise; later estimates are needed to interpret it as a convergent kernel.
TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_tsum_lattic.summary: Summing all lattice translates gives a periodic expression

TorusEuler.stage_spatial_jets_of_joint_s.text: A jointly smooth velocity on a nondegenerate closed time slab has smooth spatial slices and jointly continuous spatial derivatives of every order, including at the time endpoints. The proof restricts the joint within derivative to spatial directions. This supplies the continuity assumptions required before passing stage jets to a uniform limit.
TorusEuler.stage_spatial_jets_of_joint_s.summary: Closed slab smoothness controls all spatial jets

TorusEuler.stationaryInductiveEulerStage.text: Builds the full stage-zero record using the sine shear tilted by the scheduled gain ratio, zero pressure and the explicit two-time shear flow. It assumes that the ratio has absolute value at most one and that the initial frequency is at least $1+4\pi$. These hypotheses justify the velocity, Fourier, deformation and residual bounds.
TorusEuler.stationaryInductiveEulerStage.summary: The scheduled stationary shear supplies the zero stage

TorusEuler.stationaryInductiveEulerStage.text: Computes the velocity field of the constructed zero stage as the explicit stationary shear with the scheduled ratio. The equality holds pointwise for every real time and spatial point because that stage is time independent. The same parameter hypotheses required by the constructor remain arguments of this identity.
TorusEuler.stationaryInductiveEulerStage.summary: The base-stage velocity is the prescribed tilted shear

TorusEuler.stationaryShear.text: The initial periodic shear $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+s e_3)$. Lean indexes coordinates from zero, so `x 1` is the paper’s $x_2$ and `seedDirection s` is $e_1+s e_3$. The definition permits every real $s$; positivity and smallness of $s$ enter later amplification estimates. Its velocity points perpendicular to the coordinate on which it depends, making the advective acceleration vanish.
TorusEuler.stationaryShear.summary: The stationary sine shear starting the construction

TorusEuler.stationaryShearComplexTorus.text: This torus field is the finite Fourier sum over the positive and negative second-coordinate unit frequencies with the prescribed sine coefficients. It is a complex Euclidean-valued representation of the stationary parent. The lift theorem proves that its values are exactly the complexification of the real sinusoidal shear.
TorusEuler.stationaryShearComplexTorus.summary: Synthesizing the stationary parent from its two Fourier modes

TorusEuler.stationaryShearComplexTorus_l.text: The complex torus field evaluated on a Euclidean label equals coordinatewise complexification of the stationary sinusoidal shear at that label. The proof expands both distinct frequencies and uses the sine identity. Thus later Fourier support statements refer to the actual parent velocity, not an unrelated model field.
TorusEuler.stationaryShearComplexTorus_l.summary: The two mode field is the actual stationary shear

TorusEuler.stationaryShearDeformation_in.text: For every real scalar `c`, the operators $I+cD$ and $I-cD$ are two-sided inverses when $D$ is the stationary shear gradient. The proof uses $D^2=0$. No smallness of `c` or bound on the shear parameter is required for these exact algebraic inverse identities.
TorusEuler.stationaryShearDeformation_in.summary: The shear deformation inverse reverses its nilpotent correction

TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow.text: The trajectory $X_0(t,a)=a+tU_0(a)$, defined for every real `s` and `t`. Since the second label coordinate stays fixed, the velocity evaluated along the trajectory equals its initial value. The definition alone gives the formula; the derivative, inverse, and Jacobian identities are separate declarations used to establish its flow properties.

TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_inverse.text: Composing the explicit shear flow for time `t` with the same flow for time `-t` returns the initial label. Velocity is constant along each trajectory, so the two increments cancel exactly. This establishes a concrete inverse without invoking a general inverse-function construction or restricting the time size.
