TorusEuler.torusLInf.text:
The torus $L^\infty$ norm, defined as the essential supremum with respect to Lebesgue measure restricted to the centered fundamental cell. Its value lies in the extended nonnegative reals `ℝ≥0∞`. The definition works for any normed additive target, including continuous linear maps when applied to the velocity derivative. It does not assume periodicity or continuity itself; those properties come from the surrounding Euler-solution hypotheses. For a continuous periodic field, the essential supremum agrees with the usual spatial supremum; this interpretation uses continuity and the positive measure of neighborhoods, not the definition alone.

Default-value audit (b4): The codomain is ℝ≥0∞, and eLpNormEssSup uses the extended order. An unbounded essential range can be ⊤; it is not silently replaced by a real zero. No ENNReal.toReal conversion occurs here. Changes on null sets can be invisible, so an isolated point value alone does not lower-bound this norm without continuity. The fixed cell has positive volume. In EulerSingularityWitness, smooth spatial slices provide continuity; the finite velocity bound is explicitly a bound by ENNReal.ofReal C.
TorusEuler.torusLInf.summary: Essential supremum over the fundamental cell

TorusEuler.torusLInf_curl_le.text: The curl essential supremum is at most the operator norm of the curl map times the gradient essential supremum. The field `v` is arbitrary; the statement uses Lean’s total derivative operation. In the smooth setting of the paper, this is the familiar pointwise linear estimate integrated into an essential-supremum inequality. The coefficient is the fixed finite norm `‖curlOfDerivativeCLM‖`, independent of the velocity.
TorusEuler.torusLInf_curl_le.summary: The gradient bounds the curl essential supremum

TorusEuler.torusLInf_stationaryShear_le_.text: If `hs : |s| ≤ 1`, the torus essential-supremum norm of the stationary shear is at most two, expressed through `ENNReal.ofReal`. The bound follows from the pointwise velocity estimate. No representative or exceptional null set is needed because the estimate already holds everywhere.
TorusEuler.torusLInf_stationaryShear_le_.summary: The parent velocity has essential supremum at most two

TorusEuler.torusLiftConvolution.text: For integrable scalar kernel `K` and continuous torus field `g`, define the continuous field obtained by integrating $K(y)g(z-[y])$. Compactness bounds `g`, and the L¹ kernel provides an integrable dominating function. The complete complex target ensures the Bochner integral has its usual value.
TorusEuler.torusLiftConvolution.summary: Convolve a torus field using a Euclidean kernel

TorusEuler.torusLiftConvolution_toUnitTo.text: Evaluating the torus convolution at the image of `x` equals the Euclidean lift convolution applied to $z\mapsto g([z])$ at `x`. The equality follows from the quotient subtraction identity. It connects the torus operator to the real-space kernel estimates without changing the actual integrand.
TorusEuler.torusLiftConvolution_toUnitTo.summary: Torus convolution agrees with convolution of the periodic lift

TorusEuler.trace_deriv_comp_inverse_eq_z.text: At a point `a`, assume `F` is differentiable with derivative `DF`, has local determinant one, and admits the stated left inverse `G`. Then the trace of the directional variation `DF w` composed with `G` is zero. This extracts the cancellation needed when differentiating a volume-preserving pushforward.
TorusEuler.trace_deriv_comp_inverse_eq_z.summary: Differentiating a unit determinant gives zero trace

TorusEuler.trace_endpointPhysicalMean_eq.text: For a volume-preserving label map, a divergence-free label velocity gives a mean with zero coframe divergence. The binders `hF` and `hB` identify $F=D_aX$ and $B=Fv$, while `hGF` supplies the inverse coframe. The hypotheses `hX`, `hdet`, `hv` and `hdiv` give two spatial derivatives, unit Jacobian determinant, differentiable $v$, and $\operatorname{div}_a v=0$. The trace conclusion is exactly $\mathbf d\cdot B=0$.

TorusEuler.trace_piola_coframe.text: Assume `F` has a symmetric spatial derivative, determinant one near `a`, and a left inverse `G` at `a`. The trace of the derivative of $Fv$, composed with `G`, equals the divergence of `v`. The extra derivative of `F` has zero trace by the determinant identity, while cyclicity of trace cancels the inverse in the remaining term.
TorusEuler.trace_piola_coframe.summary: A volume preserving coframe preserves divergence

TorusEuler.trace_piola_coframe_of_contDi.text: For a twice differentiable spatial map `X`, determinant one in a neighborhood and a left inverse of its derivative give the coframe divergence identity for a differentiable field `v`. Second derivative symmetry is obtained from `hX`, rather than assumed separately. The result is pointwise at the label `a` and does not assert global invertibility of `X`.
TorusEuler.trace_piola_coframe_of_contDi.summary: The flow deformation gives the divergence identity

TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_joint_contDi.text: In finite-dimensional parameter and state spaces, a jointly continuous family solving a smooth vector-field ODE with a smooth initial map is jointly smooth on a positive closed slab. The proof bootstraps using the spatial variational equation and the combined time-parameter derivative. It is a regularity theorem for an existing family, not a global existence result.
TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_joint_contDi.summary: A continuous smooth-flow family is jointly smooth

TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_spatialDeriv.text: For a finite-dimensional trajectory family of a smooth time-dependent ODE, assume joint continuity `hYc`, the trajectory equation `hYt`, and smooth initial data `hY₀`. Every time slice is then spatially differentiable; its derivative is jointly continuous and solves the first variational equation within $[0,T]$. The theorem derives regularity of an existing family rather than constructing trajectories.
TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_spatialDeriv.summary: A trajectory family has a continuous variational derivative

TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_spatialJets.text: Under smooth finite-dimensional ODE data, joint continuity of the trajectory family, and smooth initial values, the spatial derivative of any order `n` exists continuously across the slab. Both the trajectory derivative and the differentiated right-hand side are jointly continuous. The time derivative of the former is exactly the latter, expressed as a within-interval derivative.
TorusEuler.trajectoryFamily_spatialJets.summary: Every spatial derivative satisfies its differentiated ODE

TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyMean_freq.text: For a phase-independent mean, transporting through a smooth inverse chart increases only the explicit parent-parameter power in its jet bound. The input frequency exponent `alpha` remains unchanged. Positive frequency suffices; there is no carrier-size or phase-width assumption. The estimate depends on supplied scaled mean jets and weighted derivatives of the actual coframe.
TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyMean_freq.summary: The mean preserves its frequency exponent under transport

TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyMean_jetB.text: A phase-independent mean composed with the inverse labels has the same chain-rule estimate with no carrier term. The input supplies scaled jets of the mean, weighted coframe jets, and a number `Q ≥ 1` bounding the label cost alone. The proof specializes the general transported-profile estimate to zero carrier and unit amplitude.
TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyMean_jetB.summary: Phase-independent fields incur only the label derivative cost

TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyProfile_f.text: With width $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$, carrier length at most $D\lambda$, and inverse label scale bounded by $D^a$, a scaled profile bound of frequency exponent `alpha` gives graph jets with exponent $3n/2+alpha$. Smooth chart and coframe identities and weighted derivative bounds are required. The theorem keeps an explicit parent exponent and restores `gamma` after differentiation.
TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyProfile_f.summary: Every physical derivative adds the explicit carrier cost

TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyProfile_j.text: Given a smooth inverse-label map, its actual coframe field, a bound on weighted coframe jets, and scaled profile jets bounded by `gamma * M`, graph evaluation has a uniform finite jet bound. The supplied number `Q ≥ 1` bounds the combined label and phase cost. The explicit order constant and $Q^n$ record repeated spatial differentiation.
TorusEuler.transportedHierarchyProfile_j.summary: A profile jet bound becomes an Eulerian jet bound

TorusEuler.transportedProfile.text: The graph of a profile $f(t,a,s)$ through an inverse label map `A`. At a spatial point $x$, the definition substitutes $a=A(t,x)$ and $s=k\cdot A(t,x)$. The parameter `k` is an arbitrary real three-vector, and the target `E` is unrestricted. No periodicity or support condition is built into this definition; those conditions enter when the graph is extended from a label cell to a periodic velocity.
TorusEuler.transportedProfile.summary: Profile evaluated at the transported phase

TorusEuler.transportedProfile_chainRule.text: The spatial derivative splits into a slow label derivative and a fast derivative in phase, and the material derivative equals the profile time derivative. The hypotheses `hA` and `hf` give joint within-set derivatives, while `htransport` states $A_t+D_xA\,u=0$. The binders `ht` and `hI` ensure the time lies in a set with a unique derivative. Thus the theorem also covers closed-slab endpoints, provided these derivative hypotheses hold there.
TorusEuler.transportedProfile_chainRule.summary: Spatial and material derivatives of profile graphs

TorusEuler.transportedProfile_neg_equiva.text: If the inverse-label map is odd and the profile transforms by a supplied map `R` under simultaneous label and phase negation, its graph evaluation transforms by the same `R` under spatial reflection. The result is algebraic and allows an arbitrary target type and transformation, beyond the later even and odd specializations.
TorusEuler.transportedProfile_neg_equiva.summary: Spatial reflection reflects both label and phase

TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_traject.text: Evaluating the transported graph on a particle trajectory returns the original profile at the label and its fixed phase. The sole hypothesis `h` is the pointwise inverse relation $A(t,X(t,a))=a$. The theorem does not require a flow equation or differentiability. With the scalar profile $f(t,a,s)=s$, the same identity gives the introductory definition of the transported phase; with the leading profile, it gives the stated trajectory formula for the wave.
TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_traject.summary: Profile graph along a particle trajectory

TorusEuler.transverseModeSpace.text: This complex subspace is the orthogonal complement of the complex line spanned by the real wave vector embedded in Euclidean coefficient space. At nonzero frequency it is the transverse plane. At zero frequency the span is zero and the transverse space is the whole coefficient space.
TorusEuler.transverseModeSpace.summary: Coefficients orthogonal to the frequency span

TorusEuler.transversePlane.text:
The real linear plane transverse to a wave vector.

Default-value audit (b5): At k=0 the kernel of the zero functional is the whole ambient space. The intended codimension-one transverse plane requires k≠0.

TorusEuler.transversePressureIdentity.text: At one time, the wave-vector and forced amplitude derivative equations, together with hperp, the zero derivative of their inner product, imply $\|\kappa\|^2p_s=\langle\kappa,f\rangle-2\langle\kappa,MV\rangle$. The theorem works in any complete real inner-product space. It neither divides by $\|\kappa\|^2$ nor requires a nonzero wave vector, so it does not by itself determine a unique pressure when $\kappa=0$.

TorusEuler.truncatedEulerLerayProjectedR.text: Inserts the proved periodic Leray estimate into the abstract time-uniform residual theorem. It obtains one nonnegative residual coefficient `Cr` before choosing depth `P`, and a tail coefficient `Ct` that may depend on `P`. The inputs require bounded time-indexed Hölder norm ranges. The output estimates the defined projected residual expression; its equality with the physical Euler residual is proved separately.
TorusEuler.truncatedEulerLerayProjectedR.summary: The actual Leray residual obeys the uniform truncation bound

TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.text:
The projected cutoff residual in (5.58) with the Euclidean momentum tensor and its divergence.

Default-value audit (b5): The tensor operations are fixed to the physical ones, but the projection remains an arbitrary function parameter. The actual residual identification chooses the periodic Leray projection and proves its domain conditions.
TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.summary: The projected residual with the physical momentum tensor

TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.text: Specializes the abstract residual bound to the actual Euclidean momentum tensor and its column divergence. A first-order bound for the chosen projection is still an explicit hypothesis. The result controls the second-order cutoff error and first-order residual expression with the common tail budget, while keeping the coefficient of the input residual independent of expansion depth.
TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.summary: The momentum residual has a uniform Hölder estimate

TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.text: For any nonempty index type, applies the slice estimates with one common set of constants and takes real suprema over the family. Boundedness of the input velocity and residual norm ranges is required explicitly. The index can represent time, but no temporal derivative or time continuity is assumed by this norm-aggregation theorem.
TorusEuler.truncatedEulerProjectedResidu.summary: The residual estimates hold uniformly over an index family

TorusEuler.truncatedParentProjectedResid.text:
The right-hand side of (5.58), formed using the real velocity and tensor cutoffs.

Default-value audit (b5): The projection, tensor pairing and contraction are parameters. This expression is the physical residual only after their concrete identities and the smooth cutoff hypotheses are supplied; it is not a PDE assertion by definition.
TorusEuler.truncatedParentProjectedResid.summary: The residual after velocity and tensor truncation

TorusEuler.truncatedParentProjectedResid.text: Assuming a first-order Hölder bound for `proj`, a bilinear tensor product, a derivative contraction and compatible real-complex maps, obtains uniform bounds for the second-order velocity tail and first-order projected residual. The error is $\Lambda^{2-P}(1+\|V\|_P)^2$ with `P ≥ 2`. The coefficient on the supplied residual is independent of `P`; this theorem estimates the defined expression, not its identification with a PDE residual.
TorusEuler.truncatedParentProjectedResid.summary: The abstract projected residual satisfies the truncation estimate

TorusEuler.truncatedParentSlicePressure.text: Takes the negative real Fourier pressure potential of the coefficients of a continuous torus vector field `A`, retaining the finite band of radius `r`. In the child construction `A` represents advection. Smoothness and zero mean hold for every input, but the equation with the full divergence of `A` requires the separate band hypothesis.

TorusEuler.truncatedParentSlicePressure_.text: If the input torus field represents the advection of the stationary shear, its slice pressure is identically zero for every cutoff radius and shear parameter. The shear advects itself trivially, so the represented source and every Fourier coefficient vanish. This confirms the pressure normalization used by the explicit zero-stage construction.
TorusEuler.truncatedParentSlicePressure_.summary: The stationary shear has zero normalized pressure

TorusEuler.truncatedParent_residual_rate.text: If `C ≥ 0` and the next frequency is at least $\max(2,(2C)^2)$, then $C\,\mathrm{next}^{-7/2}+\mathrm{next}^{-5}\le\mathrm{next}^{-3}$. The explicit threshold absorbs the fixed constant and allocates room for both error terms. This is a rate comparison, not an independent bound on any velocity or residual.
TorusEuler.truncatedParent_residual_rate.summary: Two residual terms fit below a third inverse power

TorusEuler.tsupport_radialEnvelope_subse.text: The closed support of the radial envelope lies in $|a|\le2\ell_*$. The assumption `hℓ` makes the radius positive. Together with $\mathsf D\ge2$ and $\ell_*\le\mathsf D^{-3}$, this places the support strictly inside the centered unit cell. The declaration states the support inclusion; the numerical comparison with the cell is a further consequence of the chosen radius.
TorusEuler.tsupport_radialEnvelope_subse.summary: The envelope is supported in the outer ball

TorusEuler.uniformPhysicalEstimates_of_l.text: From a `LaterPrimaryCosts` witness, proves `UniformPhysicalEstimates Unit`. It combines first and later seed estimates, recurrence bounds, pressure geometry, Fourier cutoff constants and residual estimates, then takes maxima and sums to choose common exponents and nonnegative costs. The first case uses zero switches; the later case uses the actual activation profile and its weighted switch bound.
TorusEuler.uniformPhysicalEstimates_of_l.summary: The first and later bounds share one common cost table

TorusEuler.uniqueDiffOn_hierarchyProfile.text: For T > 0, the closed time–label–phase slab satisfies the unique-differentiability condition used by within-set derivatives. The positivity excludes a slab reduced to a single time.
TorusEuler.uniqueDiffOn_hierarchyProfile.summary: The nondegenerate slab determines derivatives uniquely

TorusEuler.unitInverseFourthPowerTail.text: Defines the real constant obtained by integrating $|z|^{-4}$ over the complement of the open unit ball in three-dimensional Euclidean space. This records the finite tail mass used in all later off-support estimates without choosing a numerical spherical-coordinate evaluation. Scaling then gives the radius dependence $r^{-1}$.

TorusEuler.unitInverseFourthPowerTail_no.text: The unit inverse-fourth-power tail constant is nonnegative because its integrand is nonnegative on the integration set. This sign is subsequently needed when multiplying inequalities by the tail constant and replacing Euclidean torus distance by a larger multiple of the product distance. The statement claims neither strict positivity nor an exact numerical value.

TorusEuler.unitTorusMeasure.text:
Product Haar probability measure on the unit three-torus.

Default-value audit (b5): The source builds this object by the explicit algebraic operations or certified restrictions shown in the body. There is no exceptional-input fallback in this declaration; any analytic interpretation still requires the hypotheses of the theorem using it.
TorusEuler.unitTorusMeasure.summary: Probability Haar measure on the unit three-torus

TorusEuler.unitTorusMeasure_closedBall.text: For a nonnegative radius, the Haar measure of the closed ball about any torus point is $(\min(1,2r))^3$, expressed through `ENNReal.ofReal`. The formula uses the product metric on three unit circles. It is not the Euclidean three-dimensional ball-volume formula, and this distinction matters when reading the interpolation constants.
TorusEuler.unitTorusMeasure_closedBall.summary: Small torus balls have an explicit volume

TorusEuler.unitTorus_sup_le_holderHalf_a.text: A continuous field on the unit torus satisfies $\|v\|_\infty\le\varepsilon H+\varepsilon^{-3}\|v\|_{L^2}$ when its half-Hölder seminorm is bounded by $H$. The hypotheses include `hε : 0 < ε`, `hε1 : ε ≤ 1`, and the increment bound `hholder`. Averaging on a ball of radius $\varepsilon^2$ gives the power $\varepsilon^{-3}$ in three dimensions. The theorem uses the product metric and normalized Haar measure.
TorusEuler.unitTorus_sup_le_holderHalf_a.summary: Interpolation between Hölder and spatial energy norms

TorusEuler.velocityPressureTensor.text: This continuous real bilinear map sends two vectors to the complex tensor with entry $u_i v_j$. Its norm is bounded by the product of the two Euclidean norms using coordinate estimates. On the diagonal it supplies the velocity tensor for pressure, while no symmetry is claimed for two different inputs.
TorusEuler.velocityPressureTensor.summary: Real velocities give a bounded bilinear complex tensor

TorusEuler.velocityPressureTensor_apply.text: The entry `(i,j)` of the tensor made from two real vectors is the complex inclusion of `u i * v j`. This definitional identity fixes the coordinate order used in double divergence and the pressure Poisson equation. It introduces no approximation or transpose convention.
TorusEuler.velocityPressureTensor_apply.summary: The velocity tensor has the expected coordinate product

TorusEuler.vorticityForm.text:
The coefficient $\Omega=F^*(M^*-M)F$ that pulls the antisymmetric part of the parent gradient back to particle labels. The arguments `F` and `M` are continuous linear operators on a real Hilbert space. This is an algebraic definition and does not assume the Euler equation, invertibility of $F$, or a spatial curl identity. The later adjoint identity shows that this coefficient is skew adjoint.

Default-value audit (b5): The formula is total without invertibility or smoothness. If M is self-adjoint, the skew part and hence Omega vanish; skew-adjointness holds for every input F and M.
TorusEuler.vorticityForm.summary: The vorticity coefficient in label coordinates

TorusEuler.waveBump.text: The concrete bump is `Real.smoothTransition (1 - 64 * s ^ 2)`. It is even, equals one at zero, lies between zero and one, and vanishes outside $[-1/8,1/8]$, so it is an admissible choice inside the paper's wider interval $(-1/4,1/4)$. The definition selects a witness rather than quantifying over all bumps. Its smoothness, parity, and support are checked by nearby private lemmas, which are not exported as annotation targets.

TorusEuler.waveBump_zero.text: The bump has value one at phase zero because the smooth transition is evaluated at one. This is the normalization needed before subtracting its mean. Dividing the mean-free slope by its value at zero then makes the eventual wave profile derivative equal exactly one there.
TorusEuler.waveBump_zero.summary: The compact bump equals one at its center

TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal.text: If the phase derivative of $\langle\kappa,C\rangle$ equals `-divV`, if `divV` is continuous, and if that scalar component has zero phase mean, obtains $\langle\kappa,C(s)\rangle=-\operatorname{phasePrimitive}(\mathrm{divV})(s)$. The theorem assumes the derivative identity; it does not derive it from commuting spatial operators or a curl construction. No nonvanishing condition on $\kappa$ is needed here.
TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal.summary: Recover the correction along the wave vector

TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal_o.text: The longitudinal component $\langle\kappa,C\rangle$ is the negative normalized primitive of the slow divergence. Here `hderiv` assumes the phase derivative identity, `hdiv` makes the divergence continuous, and `hC` and `hmean` make the vector correction continuous with zero mean. The theorem integrates that identity and fixes its constant. It does not establish the geometric derivative relation by itself; `profileCompletion_longitudinal_derivative` supplies that relation for the actual curl completion.
TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal_o.summary: Longitudinal correction is a normalized primitive

TorusEuler.wavePotential.text:
The vector potential is the normalized phase primitive of $-\kappa\times V/\|\kappa\|^2$. The inputs `κ` and `V` are a fixed covector and a phase profile. Although the definition exists without hypotheses, periodicity of the resulting potential requires a continuous, periodic, mean-zero input; its fast curl recovers $V$ when the covector is nonzero and $V$ is transverse. Keeping these conditions separate prevents the definition from being mistaken for an unconditional inverse curl theorem.

Default-value audit (b5): The inverse squared covector norm and interval primitive are totalized. Nonzero covectors, phase smoothness and the zero-mean condition justify the physical completion identity.
TorusEuler.wavePotential.summary: Normalized primitive of the transverse cross product

TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource.text: The vector inside the phase primitive in the formula for $\partial_tQ[V]$. It combines $(M^T\kappa)\times V$, $\kappa\times MV$, and $-\kappa\times f$, divided by $|\kappa|^2$, with the correction from differentiating that denominator. This is a pointwise definition in `M`, `κ`, `v`, and `f`. A separate derivative theorem supplies the hypotheses under which it is the time derivative of the potential integrand.
TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource.summary: The integrand for the vector potential time derivative

TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_eq_co.text: An algebraic identity splits the potential-time source into its amplitude coefficient applied to v and its vector-potential coefficient applied to the forcing. This does not itself differentiate a time-dependent solution.
TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_eq_co.summary: The potential time derivative separates amplitude and forcing

TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_frequ.text: Replacing the normalized covector `k` by `freq • k` multiplies `wavePotentialTimeSource` by `freq⁻¹`, assuming positive frequency. Strain, velocity, and forcing remain fixed. This is an exact algebraic homogeneity identity, independent of time regularity and valid even for a zero normalized covector because the formula is totalized.
TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource_frequ.summary: The time source scales by inverse carrier frequency

TorusEuler.wavePotential_fast_curl.text: The fast curl $\kappa\times\partial_sQ[V]$ equals $V$ at every phase. The assumptions are a nonzero covector `hκ`, continuity of the phase profile `hV`, and pointwise transversality `htrans`. The proof differentiates the normalized primitive and applies the vector triple-product identity. Periodicity and zero phase mean are unnecessary for this pointwise derivative identity, though they are needed to make the potential a periodic profile in the construction.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_fast_curl.summary: Fast curl recovers a transverse oscillation

TorusEuler.wavePotential_firstWaveLeadin.text: The normalized potential of the explicit first leading profile equals `firstWavePotentialProfile`. The hypotheses `hh` and `hh₁` require $0<h\le1$. The underlying definitions use the radial envelope, `waveProfile`, `wavePressurePrimitive`, the first smooth seed, and its transported covector. Algebraically this has the paper's form $gP_h(\mathbf a\times\kappa)/\|\kappa\|^2$. The statement is confined to the first-wave data and does not quantify over arbitrary seeds, envelopes, or odd profiles.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_firstWaveLeadin.summary: Explicit vector potential of the first wave

TorusEuler.wavePotential_frequency_scale.text: The vector potential can be factored as $\lambda^{-1}$ times a primitive involving the normalized covector $\kappa/\lambda$ and coefficient $\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2$. The hypothesis `hf : 0 < freq` permits the frequency rescaling. This identity separates the small factor from the parent coefficients before applying product and primitive estimates. It is a scaling identity for the potential, not yet the derivative bound for the completed velocity.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_frequency_scale.summary: The vector potential carries one inverse frequency

TorusEuler.wavePotential_neg_reflected.text: The normalized potential of the reversed, negated velocity is the reversed potential of the original velocity.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_neg_reflected.summary: Reflection of the normalized vector potential

TorusEuler.wavePotential_zero_of_profile.text: If the input profile vanishes at every phase, its normalized vector potential vanishes at every phase as well. The named hypothesis `hV` is the full pointwise statement $V(s)=0$ for all $s$. No continuity, periodicity, or nonzero-covector assumption is needed for this elementary identity. Applied at a fixed inactive label, it shows that taking a phase primitive does not spread spatial support.
TorusEuler.wavePotential_zero_of_profile.summary: Zero phase profiles have zero vector potential

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient.text:
The scalar coefficient $c_{\mathbf a}=2\widetilde\chi g\langle\kappa,M\mathbf a\rangle/|\kappa|^2$ in the leading pressure. The argument `cutoff` represents the product $\widetilde\chi g$, while `κ`, `a` and `M` are the covector, amplitude and parent gradient. This definition does not assume a sign. Positivity in the paper comes from the nonnegative cutoff and the positive coupling on the support.

Default-value audit (b5): Division by the squared covector norm is total at κ=0. The pressure sign and size arguments use the nonzero covector and positive coupling supplied by the seed construction.

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_cente.text: For nonzero covector $\kappa$ and amplitude $a$, this identity rewrites the signed pressure tensor as $-2\chi\,\|a\|\|\kappa\|\langle\widehat\kappa,M\widehat a\rangle\,\widehat\kappa\otimes\widehat\kappa$. The factor called cutoff is $\chi$ here. With cutoff one the same normalization explains the new-wave pressure coupling in Section 2. The result is a rank-one tensor identity rather than the displayed scalar formula alone. Both nonzero hypotheses are explicit and protect the norm denominators introduced by normalization; no positivity of the coupling is asserted.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_cente.summary: The pressure tensor in normalized wave directions

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_eq_ne.text: The positive coefficient used to write the leading pressure as $-cP_h$ equals minus the oscillatory pressure slope for zero source and cutoff-scaled amplitude. This is an exact algebraic identity for arbitrary inputs, including a zero covector under Lean’s totalized division. Nonnegativity and geometric use of the coefficient require additional hypotheses.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_eq_ne.summary: The leading pressure uses the opposite slope sign

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_first.text: When `freq ≠ 0`, substituting the transported covector, explicit seed, and stationary-shear gradient into the wave-pressure coefficient yields `(c / freq)` times the normalized coefficient. The shear ratio cancels. Nonzero frequency is needed for the inverse-length calculation; the theorem does not extend its stated factorization by removing that hypothesis.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_first.summary: The first pressure separates scale and frequency

TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_mul_n.text: The coefficient is nonnegative and satisfies $c_{\mathbf a}|\kappa|^2\le2|\kappa|\,|M|\,|\mathbf a|$. The hypotheses are `hκ : κ ≠ 0`, `hcutoff : cutoff ∈ Set.Icc 0 1` and `hν : 0 ≤ ⟪κ, M a⟫_ℝ`. In the paper, the cutoff argument is $\widetilde\chi g$ and the sign follows from the positive coupling on its support. The proof then uses Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator norm of $M$.
TorusEuler.wavePressureCoefficient_mul_n.summary: Sign and size of the leading pressure coefficient

TorusEuler.wavePressurePrimitive.text:
The pressure profile $P_h$ is defined by applying the normalized phase primitive to `waveProfile h`. Its additive constant is chosen so that its mean over one period is zero. The scale binder `h` is unrestricted in the definition; the useful derivative and periodicity statements require $0<h\le1$. This distinction matters because the definition alone does not assert that an arbitrary-scale profile is a valid periodic pressure primitive.

Default-value audit (b5): This is the normalized primitive of the raw wave profile. Its derivative, smoothness, period-one behavior and zero mean are established for the admissible width range.
TorusEuler.wavePressurePrimitive.summary: Normalized pressure primitive of the wave profile

TorusEuler.wavePressure_hessian_quadrati.text: If a total operator decomposes into four contributions, a one-sided quadratic bound for its leading part and operator norm bounds for the other three add to a one-sided bound for the total. Symmetry is not assumed or needed for this inequality. The theorem preserves the favorable sign of the leading pressure instead of replacing it by its norm.
TorusEuler.wavePressure_hessian_quadrati.summary: Combine one signed bound with three norm bounds

TorusEuler.wavePressure_hessian_upper_of.text: Combines a leading quadratic bound at order $N^{-1/4}$ with norm bounds for geometric, higher oscillatory and mean terms at orders $N^{-3/4}$, $N^{-5/12}$ and $N^{-5/2}$. Since $N\ge1$, all three faster decays are bounded by the quarter power. The nonnegative constants `b`, `c` and `d` justify these exponent comparisons.
TorusEuler.wavePressure_hessian_upper_of.summary: All pressure contributions fit the quarter power upper bound

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_center_le.text: A nonnegative pressure coefficient makes the quadratic form of $-c\,\kappa\otimes\kappa$ nonpositive in every direction. The proof reduces it to minus a nonnegative scalar times a square. This sign statement concerns only the leading rank-one contribution; the geometric remainder is bounded separately in operator norm.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_center_le.summary: The central rank one contribution is nonpositive

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian.text: The Hessian of $-c(x)P_h(\phi(x))$ separates into the signed rank-one phase term, two mixed terms, the phase-curvature term and the coefficient Hessian. The assumptions are `hh : 0 < h`, `hh₁ : h ≤ 1`, `hc : ContDiff ℝ 2 c` and `hphase : ContDiff ℝ 2 phase`. Lean uses $\kappa=\nabla\phi$ and $g_c=\nabla c$; expanding the paper’s slow derivatives gives the same product-rule formula.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian.summary: The five terms of the leading pressure Hessian

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian_c.text: If the transported phase vanishes at the origin, the leading pressure Hessian there is $-c(0)\kappa\otimes\kappa-P_h(0)D^2c(0)$. The mixed and phase-curvature terms vanish because $F_h(0)=0$, while the slope is one. The coefficient-Hessian term remains: a zero-mean primitive need not vanish at phase zero.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_hessian_c.summary: The central Hessian retains a slow coefficient term

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u.text: The leading rank-one tensor has quadratic form at most $(h/2)c|\kappa|^2|v|^2$. The hypotheses `hh : 0 < h`, `hh₁ : h ≤ 1` and `hc : 0 ≤ c` specify the phase width and sign. The bound uses the lower estimate on `waveSlope h s`, so it controls only the upper side of the Hessian. Large negative curvature is compatible with this conclusion.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u.summary: The signed rank-one Hessian gains the phase width

TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u.text: For $N\ge1$, cutoff in $[0,1]$, nonnegative coupling and a nonzero covector, the scale bounds on $\kappa$, strain and amplitude yield a quadratic upper bound $2D^3N^{-1/4}|v|^2$. The profile width is fixed to $N^{-1/2}$. This bounds the largest quadratic contribution, not the operator norm of a potentially large negative rank-one tensor.
TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u.summary: The signed leading Hessian has quarter power decay

TorusEuler.waveProfile.text:
The profile $F_h(s)$ is the integral of `waveSlope h` from zero to `s`. The choice of base point fixes $F_h(0)=0$. The definition accepts all real scales, while the useful smoothness, parity, periodicity, and estimates are proved under $0<h\le1$. Evenness and zero phase mean of the slope make this primitive odd and periodic, which is why no second normalization constant is needed for the velocity profile.

Default-value audit (b5): This raw interval integral is defined for arbitrary h. The intended smooth periodic wave and quantitative estimates are proved for 0<h≤1.
TorusEuler.waveProfile.summary: Odd profile obtained by integrating the slope

TorusEuler.waveProfile_zero.text: The profile defined by integrating its slope from zero has value zero at zero for every real scale. The equality uses the integral over a degenerate interval. It is the base-point condition that combines with oddness and unit central derivative in the localized wave construction.
TorusEuler.waveProfile_zero.summary: The primitive profile vanishes at phase zero

TorusEuler.waveSlope.text: The slope is the periodized scaled bump minus its phase mean, divided by one minus that mean. The parameters `h` and `s` are the scale and phase. This formula matches the paper's $(\psi(s/h)-c_h)/(1-c_h)$ on the centered period, with `c_h` represented by `phaseMean (periodicWaveBump h)`. The definition has no positivity hypotheses; the subsequent theorems impose $0<h\le1$ to control the denominator and prove its normalized bounds.
TorusEuler.waveSlope.summary: Mean subtraction and normalization of the slope

TorusEuler.waveSwitch.text: The switch is the smooth transition evaluated at $r(t-t_0)$. The definition accepts arbitrary real $r$; activation after $t_0$ with duration $1/r$ requires the positive-rate hypotheses in later lemmas. This scalar factor multiplies the leading wave and its divergence correction without changing their spatial cancellation.

TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_of_activati.text: The time switch equals one when `hr : 0 < r` and `ht : t₀ + 1 / r ≤ t`. The hypothesis translates the condition $\tau\ge1$ into physical time. The conclusion includes equality at the end of the switching interval, which is used when a later crossing is known to occur beyond that interval.
TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_of_activati.summary: The switch is complete after one normalized unit

TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_sub_envelop.text: The time switch is exactly $1-\chi(1+r(t-t_0))$, with `envelopeCutoff` denoting the cutoff used by the paper. This algebraic identity holds for all real `t₀`, `r`, and `t`. The companion zero-before-activation result supplies the second branch of the piecewise description when the physical rate is positive.
TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_one_sub_envelop.summary: The time switch uses the prescribed cutoff

TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_zero_of_le.text: The time switch equals zero whenever `ht : t ≤ t₀` and `hr : 0 ≤ r`. The statement includes the activation endpoint itself. It follows because the smooth transition is zero for nonpositive arguments. This is the precise property needed when later oscillations are asserted to vanish through their activation times.
TorusEuler.waveSwitch_eq_zero_of_le.summary: The time switch vanishes before activation

TorusEuler.waveSwitch_weighted_derivativ.text: There is one nonnegative constant controlling $|\widetilde\chi'\gamma|$ by $CrG$ whenever `γ` is bounded by `G` on the switching interval. The assumptions include $r>0$, $G\ge0$, and the stated pointwise bound for `γ`. The derivative vanishes outside that interval, so no global bound on `γ` is needed.
TorusEuler.waveSwitch_weighted_derivativ.summary: The weighted switch derivative costs one growth rate

TorusEuler.weightedLabelWord_holderQuoti.text: Under the same positive-word and adjacent-jet assumptions, dividing the increment by $\sqrt{\operatorname{dist}(x,y)}$ gives the stated Hölder quotient bound. The hypothesis `hxy : x ≠ y` makes the denominator strictly positive. This theorem covers distinct labels; the jet-range proofs handle equal labels separately using the total division convention.
TorusEuler.weightedLabelWord_holderQuoti.summary: Divide the increment estimate at distinct labels

TorusEuler.weighted_endpointIntegratedFo.text: For positive duration and radius, assume smooth coframe and force, bounded Hölder jet sets, and actual torus derivative words for their product whose negative primitives equal the source words. Each weighted source time norm is bounded by $T\sqrt2$ times the finite product estimate. The argument includes both integration duration and the Euclidean-to-torus Hölder comparison.
TorusEuler.weighted_endpointIntegratedFo.summary: The integrated source is bounded by the coframe product

TorusEuler.weighted_fixedTransverse_forw.text: The physical center growth estimate gives the fixed-coordinate estimate on the same slab. Reading and lifting coordinates cost the two deformation bounds, so a physical constant `D` becomes `D^3` when both are at most `D`.
TorusEuler.weighted_fixedTransverse_forw.summary: Fixed transverse coordinates cost two deformation bounds

TorusEuler.weighted_homogeneous_jetBound.text: On a nondegenerate interval, assumes a smooth homogeneous linear ODE, a strictly positive differentiable weight, weighted homogeneous stability on a parameter set, initial jets through order `N`, and positive-order coefficient jets. It bounds all solution jets through `N` by $\mathrm{linearODEWordFactor}(K(r-l)C,N)\,KB\,g(t)$. Finite-dimensional parameter and target spaces allow word estimates to yield operator norms.
TorusEuler.weighted_homogeneous_jetBound.summary: Homogeneous stability controls every prescribed parameter jet

TorusEuler.weighted_linearODE_forced_nor.text: The weighted forward estimate for a forced linear ODE in fixed coordinates, with the exact time integral of the normalized forcing.
TorusEuler.weighted_linearODE_forced_nor.summary: Weighted variation of constants for forced linear evolution

TorusEuler.weighted_linearODE_perturbati.text: For a positive differentiable weight, a continuous perturbation bounded by `ρ` changes the weighted forward estimate by $e^{KD}$, where $D$ is the integral of `ρ` up to the observation time. A second conclusion bounds the difference from an unperturbed solution, including the initial mismatch. Both constants and the actual perturbed equations are explicit hypotheses.
TorusEuler.weighted_linearODE_perturbati.summary: An integrated coefficient error controls weighted propagation

TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_differenc.text: Compares solutions of the center operator `A` and a nearby operator `A₁` using a positive differentiable weight `g`. If every center solution has weighted growth at most `K`, the interval has length at most one, and the operator gap is at most `d` with $Kd\le1$, the relative error is bounded by the propagated initial mismatch plus $eK^2d$ times the initial relative size.
TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_differenc.summary: Nearby solutions remain close relative to the center

TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forced_no.text: The nearby forced solution is controlled by its launch amplitude and the integral of the weighted source. The hypotheses `hCenter`, `hchange`, and `hT` are the same central propagator, reciprocal coefficient-difference, and unit-duration bounds used for the homogeneous estimate. The equation appears in `hx` as $x'=A_1x+f$. The conclusion has $eK$ multiplying $|x(a)|/g(a)+\int_a^t|f(u)|/g(u)\,du$, exactly the form used before taking spatial and phase suprema.
TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forced_no.summary: The nearby forced solution satisfies a weighted integral bound

TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forward.text: A homogeneous solution at a nearby label has amplitude ratio bounded by $eK$ times its initial ratio. The hypotheses `hCenter` and `hchange` give the central weighted propagator bound $K$ and coefficient difference at most $K^{-1}$; `hT` bounds the interval length by one. The positive differentiable weight is `g`, with continuous derivative `dg`. Applied with $K=\mathsf D^3$, this yields the near-label Gronwall estimate in the proof.
TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_forward.summary: The central propagator controls nearby homogeneous solutions

TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_stability.text: A uniform coefficient comparison with the center gives stability at a label for every pair of ordered times on the slab.
TorusEuler.weighted_near_label_stability.summary: Near-center coefficient control gives weighted stability

TorusEuler.weighted_stability_restrict_I.text: For continuous linear coefficients on $[l,r]$, a weighted stability estimate for every solution on that interval also holds for solutions launched at any $a \in  [l,r]$. The proof extends the later solution backward using linear ODE existence and identifies the extensions by uniqueness. Positivity or regularity of the weight is not separately needed because the comparison is already assumed.
TorusEuler.weighted_stability_restrict_I.summary: Restrict weighted stability to a later launch time

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: For a hierarchy-regular seed at an active time, a scaled jet bound for the unwrapped unswitched leading wave transfers unchanged to its centered skew-periodization. The wrapped profile is jointly smooth in label and phase, one-periodic, and has zero phase mean. Envelope support inside the centered cell supplies boundary smoothness; phase translation preserves the mean, and the centered-cell jet theorem transfers the budget.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: Centered wrapping preserves the unswitched leading jet budget

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: Defines the continuous linear operation that sends a derivative on label-and-phase space to its composition with the inclusion $v \mapsto  (v,0)$. It extracts label differentiation while holding phase fixed. The operation is used to express the unscaled slow curl in terms of derivatives of the jointly scaled potential.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: Restrict a joint derivative to label directions

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: The linear operation restricting a joint derivative to label directions has operator norm at most one. The proof bounds composition with the inclusion $v \mapsto  (v,0)$, whose norm is at most one for the product norm. This prevents an extra coefficient when extracting label derivatives from the scaled phase profile.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: Forgetting the phase direction does not increase operator norm

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: Proves that the operator-valued cross-product map has norm at most one by applying the usual cross-product norm inequality twice through operator-norm bounds. The estimate has no nonzero-vector hypothesis and includes the zero operator. It supplies the unit operator cost used when differentiating the potential coefficient.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: Cross-product insertion has operator norm at most one

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: For any one-periodic vector function, translation of the phase leaves its mean over one period unchanged. The proof changes variables in the interval integral and applies periodicity. No continuity hypothesis appears in this identity; it is used to preserve the zero-mean condition when the centered wrapping introduces a label-dependent phase translation.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: A phase translation preserves the periodic mean

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: For a continuous one-periodic function with zero phase mean, the normalized primitive of its phase translate evaluated at zero equals the original normalized primitive at the translating phase. The proof compares derivatives and uses the zero mean of the primitive. This formulation turns a moving evaluation phase into a parameter of the integrand.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: The normalized primitive commutes with phase translation

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: Packages $v \mapsto  (x \mapsto  v \times  x)$ as a continuous linear map from vectors to continuous linear operators. Linearity follows from the cross product identities, and continuity follows from the estimate $\lVert v \times  x\rVert  \le  \lVert v\rVert \cdot \lVert x\rVert$. This representation lets iterated derivative estimates treat the potential coefficient through ordinary operator composition.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: The cross product as an operator-valued linear map

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.text: For a smooth label-and-phase potential and nonzero label scale, its ordinary label derivative at the scaled label equals $\ell^{-1}$ times the label restriction of the derivative of the scaled profile. The phase scale may be arbitrary. Uniqueness of the derivative compares two chain-rule expressions; the nonzero radius is essential when cancelling the scale.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationPrimaryJet.summary: Recover a label derivative from the scaled joint derivative

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationProfiles.0.text: If `hs` excludes $s$ from $[0,1]$, the derivative of the smooth transition is zero. The proof uses local constancy on the left and right plateaus. The endpoints themselves are excluded from this statement, although the underlying transition is smooth there as well.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationProfiles.0.summary: The transition derivative vanishes outside its interval

_private.TorusEuler.ActivationProfiles.0.text: There exists a nonnegative real constant bounding the absolute derivative of the smooth transition at every real input. Compactness supplies a maximum on $[0,1]$, and the preceding plateau lemma handles the complement. The bound is existential; no numerical value or optimality is claimed.
_private.TorusEuler.ActivationProfiles.0.summary: One constant bounds the transition derivative

_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationAssembl.text: Deduces $T\delta\le1$ from the window hypotheses $T\ge2$, $\delta\ge0$ and $240\delta T^6\le1$. The proof compares the first and sixth powers of $T$. This estimate is used in the logarithmic strength calculation to convert an integrated older-strain bound into a small relative change of the preceding shear.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationAssembl.summary: The window budget controls integrated older strain

_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationCouplin.text: For two continuous three-dimensional vector paths on the same set, proves continuity of their cross product. There are no nonzero, length or perpendicularity assumptions. The coordinate formula makes each component a difference of products, and the Euclidean-space wrapper preserves continuity. Applied to normalized wave directions, it provides continuity of the third new-frame axis.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationCouplin.summary: Crossing continuous paths gives a continuous path

_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationCouplin.text: If a vector path is continuous on `J` and nonzero at every member of `J`, its normalized direction is continuous there. The nonvanishing assumption ensures continuity of the reciprocal norm. This does not extend the direction continuously through zero vectors; such values remain defined by Lean but are excluded from the theorem’s domain of control.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationCouplin.summary: A nonvanishing vector path has a continuous direction

_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationCouplin.text: Introduces $\kappa=(64C+143)T^{p+9}\delta$ and shows it dominates the wave-vector error, inverse-shear contribution and amplitude-ratio error while remaining at most $1/2$. It assumes the stated lower bounds on $C_0$ and the polynomial smallness condition. This is finite arithmetic bookkeeping for the coupling comparison; it supplies no wave or coupling equation on its own.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationCouplin.summary: One error allowance controls coordinates and coupling inputs

_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationTimeRes.text:
With positive $r,\sigma,
u$ and the defining relation $r^2=2\sigma
u$, proves $(\sigma/r)(1/r)=1/(2
u)$. This is the conversion $S/r=1/(2
u)$ used to measure the matrix error against the older coupling. All three positivity assumptions appear in the source, although the equality is algebraic once the relevant denominators are nonzero.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplificationTimeRes.summary: The shear factor converts growth rate to coupling

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeDenominator.text: For positive real numbers `a` and `b`, the absolute difference of their reciprocals equals $|a-b|/(ab)$. Both positivity assumptions matter when removing the absolute value from the denominator. The identity is the algebraic step that turns lower denominator bounds into reciprocal stability estimates.

For $T\ge2$, $0\le\tau\le T$, $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, and total coordinate error at most $d\le1/2$, the actual coordinates satisfy $|X|,|Q|\le T^2$ and $|Z|\le3/2$. The reference first coordinate is also bounded by $T^2$, while $|\varepsilon\tau|\le T$. This is a scalar consequence of `hclose`, before any wave equation is used.

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.text: Evaluating a matrix entry built from formal multivariate variables at real coordinates `χ` gives the corresponding entry built directly from `χ`. The proof splits the four matrix positions and simplifies polynomial evaluation. This connects the generic polynomial theorem to the concrete reduced amplitude matrix.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.summary: Evaluate a formal amplitude entry at real inputs

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.text: Given values `χ` for the combined strain and scalar index, this definition feeds the two nine-entry blocks and six scalars into `scaledMatrix`. It is valid over any commutative ring. The last three scalars are independent inputs here; only later substitutions identify them with physical reciprocals.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.summary: Build the amplitude matrix from all coordinates

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.text: Packing two strain arrays and six scalar inputs with `scaledAmplitudeInputs`, then reading them through `matrixFromCoordinates`, gives exactly `scaledMatrix` with those arguments. This is a definitional equality proved by `rfl`. It certifies the bookkeeping used to apply polynomial bounds, without adding positivity or denominator assumptions.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.summary: Packing the inputs leaves the matrix unchanged

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.text: There exist a common nonnegative constant $C$ and natural exponent $n$ such that every matrix entry changes by at most $CM^nd$ on a coordinate box of radius $M\ge1$. The proof combines the four individual polynomial estimates by summing constants and taking the largest exponent. The input differences are hypotheses, not conclusions of this helper.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudePolynomialB.summary: One polynomial bound controls every matrix entry

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeScaledStrai.text: In an orthonormal frame, omitting the error strain leaves the older matrix plus a single entry $S\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ratio}}$ in position $(1,0)$. The theorem is pointwise and accepts any continuous linear map `B`. It uses the rank-one form of the preceding wave’s gradient and does not assume an evolution equation for `B`.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeScaledStrai.summary: The preceding shear changes one matrix entry

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeScaledStrai.text: The full reference matrix equals the older reference matrix plus the elementary matrix with unit entry at $(1,0)$. The proof checks the nine possible positions. This exact decomposition mirrors the no-error physical strain identity and makes the strength-ratio error easy to isolate.

For $S\ne0$, the full no-error strain has the same scaled entries as the older strain except at $(1,0)$, where it adds $\sigma_{\mathrm{ratio}}$. This identity uses an orthonormal frame and cancels the shear factor only under `hS`. It isolates the single changing strength coefficient in the amplitude comparison.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeScaledStrai.summary: Rescaling turns the shear entry into a strength ratio

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: This map sends a vector $w$ to $(-S\langle E_1,w\rangle,\langle E_2,w\rangle)$. It uses the sign convention $U=-\alpha_1$ and $V=\alpha_2$. Its norm estimate later costs a factor $S$, explaining how a small physical strain error enters the reduced amplitude equations.

The vector is $(-u/S)E_1+vE_2+((xu-qv)/(Sz))E_3$. Here $u$ corresponds to $U=-\alpha_1$ and $v$ to $V=\alpha_2$. For nonzero $S,z$ this is the amplitude determined by transversality to the coordinate wave. The definition itself does not enforce those hypotheses or orthonormality.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: An amplitude reconstructed from two transverse coordinates

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: For any frame vectors and continuous linear map `E`, the pairing with axis `i` is the linear combination of the three matrix entries weighted by the reconstructed amplitude coefficients. No orthonormality or nonzero denominator hypothesis is needed for this expansion. It prepares the pressure pairing for the added-strain calculation.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: Apply the strain to each amplitude component

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: For nonzero $S$ and $z$, pairing the coordinate wave with `E` applied to the coordinate amplitude gives $(\mathrm{pressureU}\,u+\mathrm{pressureV}\,v)/S$. The result uses the entries of `E` in the supplied frame. It does not require orthonormality because it expands the same pairings on both sides.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: The reconstructed pressure pairing has two coefficient rows

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: The vector is $xE_1+(q/S)E_2+zE_3$, without the physical frequency factor $\lambda$. It is defined for any three vectors `e`, and orthonormality is supplied by the lemmas computing its pairings and norm. This reconstruction isolates the wave direction used to estimate the added strain.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: A wave vector reconstructed from scaled coordinates

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: For an orthonormal frame, pairing the reconstructed wave with its three axes returns $x$, $q/S$ and $z$. Orthogonality cancels all cross terms. No nonzero shear hypothesis is required for this algebraic identity, so its interpretation remains consistent with the total definition at $S=0$.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: Pairings recover the reconstructed wave components

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: The difference between the full amplitude error operator and the operator with `E=0` equals the raw matrix generated by `E` alone with zero older strain. The reference matrix cancels. This identity holds for arbitrary coordinates and parameters because the strain contribution is linear, even before nondegenerate physical interpretation is imposed.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: Subtracting the zero-error operator isolates the added strain

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: For an orthonormal frame and $S\ge1$, the maximum norm of the extracted amplitude pair is at most $S\|w\|$. Each inner product is bounded by the vector norm, and the first component carries the shear factor. This is the reverse coordinate cost in the added-strain estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: Extracting raw coordinates costs one shear factor

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: When the frame is orthonormal, $S\ge1$, $|x|,|q|\le S$ and $z\ge1/2$, the reconstructed amplitude has norm at most $6\|(u,v)\|$. The pair norm is the maximum norm. The proof bounds the three physical coefficients separately, so no Riccati equation or growing-mode assumption is used.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: Reconstruction has a uniform amplitude bound

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: With an orthonormal frame, the squared norm of `coordinateWave` equals `normFactor x q z S`. The proof uses its three pairings and the inner product of the vector with itself. This is an equality of total expressions for all $S$; positivity comes separately from the third coordinate.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: The reconstructed wave has the expected squared norm

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: The vector $-w+2\langle k,w\rangle k/\|k\|^2$ has exactly the same norm as $w$. Lean identifies it with reflection in the span of $k$. The equality also covers $k=0$: the totalized correction term vanishes and the result is $-w$, whose norm is unchanged.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: The pressure reflection preserves vector length

_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.text: Assuming an orthonormal frame and nonzero $S,z$, the raw matrix with zero older strain acts on $(u,v)$ by reconstructing an amplitude, applying `E`, reflecting the result across the wave direction, and extracting its two components. The squared wave norm is proved nonzero from $z\ne0$. This identity makes the operator estimate geometric.
_private.TorusEuler.AmplitudeStrainError.summary: The error matrix acts by reflection and projection

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: At a nonzero frequency `hξ`, the angular Leray map has every requested differentiability order `n`. The reciprocal norm in the normalized-frequency formula is smooth only away from zero. The result is local ambient smoothness; it does not assert continuity at the separately assigned zero-frequency value.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: The angular projection is smooth away from zero

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: For each order $n$, there is a nonnegative constant bounding the derivative norm by $C/\|\xi\|^n$ at every nonzero frequency. Compactness bounds derivatives on the unit sphere, and homogeneity transfers the bound to other radii. The theorem supplies existence of constants, not explicit numerical values.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: Angular derivative bounds decay with frequency order

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: The $L^2$ inner product of a constant vector path with `v` equals the vector inner product of that constant with the time integral of `v`. The restricted interval has finite measure. This identity proves symmetry of the operation that removes the time average.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: Pairing with a constant path extracts the time integral

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: For positive `hT`, the operator-valued lift that also subtracts time means has norm at most one. The proof combines the contractive spatial lift with the norm-one bound for the orthogonal time projection. This estimate is uniform in duration and is used in angular derivative transfer.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: Adding time mean subtraction does not increase operator norm

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: The real inner product of the embedded integer frequency with a vector equals the sum of its integer coordinates times the vector coordinates. This unfolds the Euclidean representation. It is used to show that restricting the complex Leray symbol to real coefficients agrees with the real angular operator.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: The real frequency pairing is a coordinate contraction

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: The squared Euclidean norm of the embedded real Fourier frequency equals the sum of the squared integer coordinates, `frequencyNormSq k`. This is the real counterpart of the complex Euclidean identity. It ensures that both versions of the Leray formula use exactly the same denominator.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: The real frequency norm matches the coordinate sum

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: Applying the lifted spatial operator to a constant $L^2$ path gives the constant path with the transformed value. This is equality of path-space elements, proved from their almost-everywhere representatives. It supports the algebraic commutation between spatial action and subtraction of the time average.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: Constant paths remain constant under spatial operators

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: Time integrating the path after applying a fixed bounded spatial operator gives the operator applied to the original time integral. The path belongs to $L^2$ on a finite measure interval, hence is integrable. This identity is the key reason the spatial action preserves the zero-time-mean condition.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: Spatial operators commute with path integration

_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.text: This bounded linear map sends a spatial operator to its lifted action composed with the time mean projection. It isolates all time-path structure from the frequency-dependent angular symbol. Consequently angular differentiation can be transferred by postcomposition with one fixed bounded linear map.
_private.TorusEuler.AngularLeraySymbol.0.summary: Lifting a spatial operator together with time mean subtraction

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: The positive and negative shear Fourier modes are the exponentials with phases $\pm2\pi i x_2$. The result expands the general integer-character formula at the specific unit frequency. It fixes the signs needed to reconstruct the real sine shear from its pair of complex coefficients.
_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.summary: The two shear characters are opposite complex exponentials

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: The Euclidean norm of the real lattice vector corresponding to the stationary shear mode is one. It is exactly the second coordinate unit vector. This numerical identity ensures that both active frequencies fit within the initial frequency band once the chosen base frequency is sufficiently large.
_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.summary: The initial shear frequency has unit length

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: For positive envelope scale `hr`, if some coordinate lies beyond the stated collar threshold, the radial envelope is zero. The threshold simplifies to twice the scale. A coordinate absolute value is bounded by the Euclidean norm, so the outer-radius cutoff lemma applies.
_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.summary: A coordinate outside the envelope radius forces the cutoff to vanish

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: This is coordinatewise complexification of the vector with first component one, second component zero, and third component `s`. The same direction multiplies both sine Fourier coefficients. It keeps the real velocity geometry while allowing the finite complex Fourier synthesis used to certify the parent’s spectral support.
_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.summary: The shear direction embedded in complex Euclidean space

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: The complexified shear direction is nonzero for every real parameter. Its first coordinate is always one, independently of `s`. This ensures both signed sine coefficients are nonzero, so the later Fourier-support theorem identifies exactly two frequencies rather than merely bounding the support.
_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.summary: The Fourier shear direction never vanishes

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: The scalar factor is $1/(2i)$, the coefficient multiplying the positive exponential in the sine identity. The negative frequency uses its negative. The denominator is a fixed nonzero complex number; the next lemma certifies that the resulting coefficient does not vanish.
_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.summary: The coefficient of the positive sine frequency

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: The scalar $1/(2i)$ is nonzero because its numerator and denominator are nonzero complex numbers. This elementary guard combines with the nonzero shear direction to show that each of the two assigned Fourier coefficients is present for every parameter value.

For any complex argument, the positive exponential multiplied by $1/(2i)$ plus the negative exponential multiplied by its negative equals the complex sine. This exact identity is used after evaluating the two shear characters. It confirms the coefficient sign convention before identifying the real parent field.

If `hr` bounds the radius by one half, the open Euclidean ball about zero is contained in the interior of the centered unit cell. Each coordinate is bounded by the vector norm, giving the cell inclusion. The open-ball property upgrades that inclusion to the cell interior; negative radii simply give an empty ball.
_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.summary: A ball of radius at most one half lies inside the cell

_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.text: The positive unit frequency in the second coordinate is not equal to its negative. The proof reads the second component, where the equality would say one equals negative one. This guarantees that finite synthesis over the two signed modes contains two distinct terms.

At every spatial point, composing the shear velocity gradient with itself gives the zero operator. The gradient is a cosine scalar times the same square-zero central rank-one map. This makes the quadratic trace source in the parent pressure Poisson equation vanish identically.
_private.TorusEuler.BaseParentData.0.Tor.summary: The stationary velocity gradient squares to zero everywhere

_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.text: Sum the three coordinate evaluations of a linear map on the matching coordinate directions. This packages the trace as a continuous linear map on spatial endomorphisms, so it can commute with integrals and derivatives. Applied to a vector field's Fréchet derivative, it recovers the divergence used in the phase cancellation.
_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.summary: The trace as a continuous linear functional

_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.text: The label-divergence functional applied to the Fréchet derivative of `c` at `a` equals `divergence c a`. The equality holds for arbitrary `c`, because both sides use the same total derivative expression. Analytic differentiability must still be supplied when this identity is used as a classical divergence formula.
_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.summary: Applying the trace functional gives divergence

_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.text: At a differentiability point of a function on a product of a normed space and one real coordinate, bounds `A` and `B` for the two partial derivatives give the full derivative bound $A+B$. The product derivative is split into its two linear components. This justifies combining label and phase derivative estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.summary: The full derivative is controlled by both partial derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.text: For a function differentiable at a label-phase point, a bound on its full Fréchet derivative also bounds the derivative of the slice obtained by fixing phase. The spatial inclusion has norm at most one. This helper extracts the label derivative estimate without introducing a new geometric scale.
_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.summary: A label derivative inherits the joint derivative bound

_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.text: The operator norm of the functional extracting label divergence from a label-phase derivative is at most three. Each coordinate evaluation has norm at most one, and the triangle inequality sums the three contributions. This numerical constant enters the rescaled divergence estimate used to control the longitudinal phase velocity.
_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.summary: Three coordinate traces cost at most three

_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.text: The sole assumption `hKw` bounds the product `K*w` by one half, which implies $\exp(Kw)\le2$. Neither factor is individually required to be nonnegative. This elementary numerical estimate converts the scaled-gradient smallness condition into the uniform factor-two flow bounds used later.

For the same homogeneous derivative inequality, the norm at `t` is bounded by its value at any allowed `s` multiplied by $\exp(K|t-s|)$. Both times belong to the supplied slab. Reversing time gives the backward estimate needed to control inverse as well as forward transitions.
_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.summary: Exponential growth between any two allowed times

_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.text: A normed-space curve whose within-interval derivative satisfies $\|x'\|\le K\|x\|$ obeys the exponential bound from its value at the left endpoint. The hypothesis `ht` restricts the evaluation time to that interval. This homogeneous Grönwall estimate underlies the stability of the scaled particle trajectories.
_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.summary: Exponential growth from the left endpoint

_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.text: This continuous linear functional evaluates a label-phase derivative on each of the three label directions, reads the matching output component, and sums. The phase direction is omitted. It packages label divergence on the enlarged profile space, allowing one fixed norm bound to control all three coordinate contributions.
_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.summary: Trace only the label part of the full derivative

_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.text: The scaled label-divergence functional is exactly the sum of the three diagonal evaluations of a linear map on the label directions with zero phase component. This makes its omission of the phase derivative explicit. The identity is purely linear algebra and holds without regularity assumptions on an underlying profile.
_private.TorusEuler.ChildFlowDeformation.summary: The label trace is the three diagonal evaluations

_private.TorusEuler.CoframeDerivativeBou.text: For a $C^2$ periodic parent flow on a nondegenerate slab, the forward transition derivative is a unit. Its `Ring.inverse` equals the reverse transition derivative evaluated at the transported point. Both times must lie in the slab. This identifies the total algebraic inverse with the geometric inverse before differentiating it.
_private.TorusEuler.CoframeDerivativeBou.summary: The reverse Jacobian is the genuine algebraic inverse

_private.TorusEuler.CutoffResidual.0.Tor.text: This continuous linear map sums the three diagonal coordinate evaluations of an endomorphism of Euclidean three-space. Packaging trace in this way permits it to commute with differentiation and linear combinations in the cutoff-divergence calculation. The definition applies to every operator, regardless of whether it arose as a derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.CutoffResidual.0.Tor.summary: The trace bundled as a bounded linear map

_private.TorusEuler.CutoffResidual.0.Tor.text: For any continuous linear endomorphism, the bundled coordinate functional `traceCLM` agrees with `LinearMap.trace` of the underlying linear map. This identifies the implementation with the coordinate-free trace used in divergence formulas. It is a finite-dimensional algebraic identity and carries no smoothness or invertibility assumptions.
_private.TorusEuler.CutoffResidual.0.Tor.summary: The coordinate functional equals the intrinsic trace

_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.text: The real square-root power of $2^j$ equals $(\sqrt2)^j$ for each natural `j`. Since the base is positive, the real-power convention agrees with the usual positive square root. This converts the multiplier hypotheses into geometric sequences that the series estimates can sum explicitly.
_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.summary: Real half-powers agree with geometric half-scales

_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.text: The negative half-power of $2^j$ is the $j$th power of $1/\sqrt2$. This identity rewrites the high-frequency size bounds into a decreasing geometric sequence. The positive dyadic base ensures that the real exponent and reciprocal conventions have their ordinary analytic meanings.
_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.summary: Inverse half-powers form a geometric decay sequence

_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.text: For a distance `d` strictly between zero and one, choose an index `n` so that the low-frequency contribution $d(\sqrt2)^n$ and high-frequency contribution $(1/\sqrt2)^n$ are both controlled by multiples of $\sqrt d$. The same index satisfies both inequalities, enabling a half-Hölder estimate for the full series.
_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.summary: One frequency split balances both increment estimates

_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.text: The numerical inequality $4/3\le\sqrt2$ supplies a convenient lower bound for the ratio between adjacent half-order dyadic scales. It has no variable hypotheses. Its reciprocal form gives a rational majorant for the decreasing geometric series used to estimate the high-frequency tail.
_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.summary: A rational lower bound for the dyadic ratio

_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.text: The reciprocal dyadic half-scale ratio is at most three quarters. This numerical comparison makes the geometric tail summable with an explicit constant. The square root is the ordinary positive square root of two, so the inverse never encounters a zero-denominator case.
_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.summary: A rational upper bound for the reciprocal ratio

_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.text: The sum of $(\sqrt2)^j$ for indices below `n` is at most three times $(\sqrt2)^n$. This finite geometric estimate controls the low-frequency part of a difference after applying the Lipschitz bound to each block. The same splitting index is used for the complementary decaying tail.
_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.summary: The low-frequency prefix costs one final scale

_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.text: The sequence of powers of $1/\sqrt2$ is summable. This is the scalar convergence input for the uniform majorant of the Banach-valued dyadic blocks. It ensures that the infinite sum used later is a genuine convergent series rather than merely Lean's totalized `tsum` expression.

The sum of all powers of $1/\sqrt2$ is at most four. Together with each block's geometric supremum bound, this yields the uniform size bound for the reconstructed function. Summability is established separately before the infinite-series formula is evaluated in this estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.summary: The decreasing half-scale series is bounded by four

_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.text: For every natural index `j`, the square of $(\sqrt2)^j$ is $2^j$. This exact identity converts between half-order scales and the original dyadic frequency. It is used in the estimates choosing the splitting index for a spatial increment and involves no real-power ambiguity.
_private.TorusEuler.DyadicHolder.0.Torus.summary: Squaring the half-scale recovers the dyadic scale

_private.TorusEuler.DyadicMultiplierKern.text: A Fourier mode evaluated at $x-y$ factors into its value at `x` and the negative-frequency exponential in `y`. The identity uses the whole-space Fourier normalization with $2\pi$. It prepares the calculation in which an operator-valued kernel acts on a single torus Fourier coefficient.
_private.TorusEuler.DyadicMultiplierKern.summary: The translated mode exposes the transform's exponential

_private.TorusEuler.DyadicMultiplierKern.text: For a Schwartz kernel, its norm multiplied by the square root of spatial distance is integrable over Euclidean three-space.
