_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: Time integration preserves joint square integrability

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: The labelwise time integral is strongly measurable as a function of the pair of time and label. The proof inserts the indicator of $0<s\le t$ before integrating in $s$. It applies to the measurable representative supplied by `Lp`, including exceptional slices where the integral is totalized.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: The primitive has a measurable joint representative

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.text: When `T` is nonnegative, the real-valued mass of the whole space for Lebesgue measure restricted to $(0,T]$ equals $T$. This elementary normalization is used after Fubini to obtain the joint primitive bound. At `T = 0`, both sides vanish and the identity remains valid.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpaceOperato.summary: The time measure has mass equal to its length

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialDeriv.text: If the families `v` and `w` agree at every word shorter than `t`, their mixed correction at `t` is equal. The coefficient family `B` is unchanged. The proof uses the strict lower-order property of correction pairs, which ensures that the recursive construction never depends on an unknown derivative of the current order.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialDeriv.summary: Lower order agreement determines the commutator

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialDeriv.text: Assume coefficient derivatives through word length `t.length` and unknown derivatives strictly below that length. Differentiating the mixed correction in direction `u i` gives the sum of the two product-rule terms for each correction pair. The two different length thresholds are explicit and are what allow induction on derivative order.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialDeriv.summary: Differentiate all lower order correction products

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialDeriv.text: For a finite list `l`, if each indexed function has the stated derivative at `s`, the sum of those functions has derivative equal to the list sum of their derivatives. Repeated list elements remain repeated, preserving multiplicities. This is used in the product-rule expansion of the higher spatial commutator.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialDeriv.summary: Differentiate a finite list sum term by term

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.text: Evaluating a half-Hölder derivative field `df` along the path $a+\operatorname{toUnitTorus}(shu)$ is continuous as a function of `s`. The argument composes the continuous value field with the Lipschitz quotient map and a linear path. This continuity permits the fundamental theorem of calculus along each directional segment.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.summary: A derivative field stays continuous along a translated line

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.text: The private translated-field constructor evaluates exactly to the original field at `a+b`. This definitional identity is used to prove linearity and norm bounds for the translation operator. It is a pointwise statement on the torus and involves no almost-everywhere representative choice.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.summary: Evaluate a translated field at the shifted label

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.text: If `hC` bounds the norm of `g` by `C` on $(0,1]$, the norm of its interval integral from zero to one is at most `C`. This norm inequality is used after expressing a directional difference quotient as an averaged derivative. It does not itself identify any function as a derivative or require such an interpretation.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.summary: A unit interval integral inherits its uniform bound

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.text: The norm of the constructed translated field is no larger than the original half-Hölder norm. Translation preserves both value bounds and distances between labels, so the same increment estimate applies. This preliminary inequality is later strengthened to equality by translating back by the negative increment.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.summary: Translation preserves the available Hölder bound

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.text: For each lattice mode, the Fourier character at the sum of two torus points is the product of its values at those points. This is the character homomorphism law. It is the algebraic input that makes translation diagonal on Fourier coefficients and allows Fourier multipliers to commute with spatial translation.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.summary: A Fourier character turns addition into multiplication

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.text: For a torus increment `b`, the constructed field takes the value of `f` at `a+b`. Translation preserves the torus distance, so the same value and square-root increment bounds certify the new bundled field. This is the underlying field construction before it is packaged as a bounded linear operator.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointSpatialRegul.summary: Translate a half Hölder field on the torus

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointStrongWeakAg.text: For positive `T`, suppose `hP` gives the combined angular-time symbol on all real-character moments of the bounded mixed operator `P`. Embedding `P w` into joint $L^2$ then gives the orthogonal joint constraint projection of the embedded field. The Fourier law is the evidence identifying the strong and weak projections.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointStrongWeakAg.summary: The mixed Fourier projection matches the joint constraint projection

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.text: Almost every point for the endpoint product measure lies in the closed time and label slab. The time factor is Lebesgue measure restricted to $(0,T]$, and the label factor is torus Haar measure. The proof projects to time and uses $(0,T]\subseteq[0,T]$; no regularity of a field is involved.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.summary: The product measure stays inside the closed slab

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.text: Continuity of the deformation field `F` on the slab implies continuity of $F^*F$. The proof combines continuity of adjoint with composition of continuous linear maps. No inverse deformation is needed for this regularity statement; positivity bounds are supplied separately when the kinetic coefficient enters the endpoint equation.

Continuous deformation and gradient fields on the slab give a continuous pulled-back vorticity coefficient $F^*(M^*-M)F$. All dependence is through continuous operator algebra. This provides the measurable, bounded coefficient required by the weak product operator, while leaving the flow identities and Hessian upper bound to the coercivity theorem.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.summary: Continuity of the space-time vorticity coefficient

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.text: Continuity of an operator coefficient on the compact slab gives almost-everywhere strong measurability for the endpoint space-time measure. Outside-slab values need no continuity assumption, because that measure is concentrated on the slab. This is the measurability obligation for constructing the bounded product multiplier used in the weak inverse.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.summary: Continuous slab coefficients are strongly measurable almost everywhere

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.text: A coefficient continuous on the closed time and torus slab has an almost-everywhere finite operator-norm bound for the endpoint product measure. The bound is existential and depends on the coefficient and duration. It does not supply the explicit uniform polynomial estimate required later for the physical inverse.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.summary: Continuous slab coefficients have a finite essential bound

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.text: The product of $[0,T]$ with the entire three-dimensional unit torus is compact. This holds for every real `T`, including an empty time interval. It supplies the compact domain on which continuous kinetic and vorticity coefficients acquire finite bounds before being used as space-time $L^2$ multipliers.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointTorusCoerciv.summary: The closed time and label slab is compact

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: If `hres` makes the joint residual orthogonal to every zero-time-mean solenoidal test, its pairing with each fixed solenoidal `y` equals the pairing with its time average almost everywhere. The strict condition `hT : 0 < T` licenses $T^{-1}$. This theorem fixes one test at a time, before the later simultaneous projection identity.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.summary: An orthogonal residual has constant solenoidal moments

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: Pairing the weak spatial Leray projection of `r` with a vector `y` in the solenoidal subspace gives the original ambient $L^2$ pairing. Membership is carried by the type of `y`. Orthogonality of the projection is the reason pressure and other complementary components disappear in this test.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.summary: Remove a projection against a solenoidal test

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: Pair a joint $L^2$ residual `r` with a spatial $L^2$ field `y` pulled back along the second coordinate. The scalar pairing is integrable for the endpoint product measure. This is an integrability statement, allowing Fubini in the weak argument; it does not assert pointwise continuity of a residual representative.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.summary: The residual pairing is integrable in space and time

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: Under `hT : 0 ≤ T`, integrating the spatial pairing of `r` with `y` over time equals pairing the weak time integral of `r` with `y`. Fubini and bounded linearity of the inner product justify the exchange. The identity is formulated through $L^2$ classes so it is independent of representative choices.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.summary: Move the time integral outside the spatial pairing

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: An essentially bounded scalar time function `η`, certified by `hη`, may multiply an arbitrary spatial $L^2$ field `y` to give a joint space-time $L^2$ field. The product measure and separated variables are essential here. This builds admissible probes without requiring pointwise regularity of either factor.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.summary: Separate a bounded time test from a spatial field

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: The product of an essentially bounded time function with a weakly solenoidal spatial field belongs to `endpointTorusSpace T` when `hzero` says its time integral vanishes. The proof checks zero time mean and the spatial gradient pairing separately. These tests isolate the time-independent part of an orthogonal residual.
_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.summary: A centered separated test satisfies both constraints

_private.TorusEuler.EndpointWeakInstanta.text: For `hT : 0 ≤ T`, the real mass of Lebesgue measure restricted to $(0,T]$ is exactly $T$. The nonnegative-length condition includes the zero interval. This normalization justifies the time average in the weak endpoint argument; division by $T$ is used later only with a strictly positive length.

_private.TorusEuler.EulerAdvectionBounds.text: The centered periodic cell has strictly positive real volume. The proof exhibits a nonempty interior and uses finite volume of the compact cell. This justifies dividing by the cell volume when subtracting the average from a reconstructed pressure, ensuring that the mean-zero normalization uses a nonzero denominator.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerAdvectionBounds.summary: The normalization cell has positive volume

_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.text: The supplied bounded jets `J` obey the next order derivative relation whenever `hactual` identifies them with the iterated derivatives of a spatially smooth field. Currying the next multilinear derivative turns it into the derivative map of the current jet. This is a representation lemma, not a source of smoothness for the velocity.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.summary: Actual velocity jets satisfy the compatibility equations

_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.text: For a continuous family of bounded continuous functions and a continuous bounded derivative family `D`, the spatial derivative of the evaluated time primitive equals the primitive of `D`. The relation `hx` is assumed at every time in the slab. Compactness in time supplies the domination needed to differentiate under the integral.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.summary: Spatial differentiation passes through the time primitive

_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.text: For a time dependent bounded continuous function, a within time derivative in the uniform norm and a spatial derivative at `x` combine into a joint within derivative on `I ×ˢ univ`. The resulting linear map adds the time contribution and spatial contribution. Uniform control of the time remainder is what makes evaluation at varying spatial points legitimate.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.summary: Time and spatial derivatives combine under evaluation

_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.text: Given a tower smooth in the uniform time norm and compatible under spatial differentiation, the time differentiated tower remains spatially compatible. The hypothesis `hx` supplies the original derivative relation. Difference quotients converge uniformly as bounded continuous functions, allowing the derivative relation to pass to the limit even at closed slab endpoints.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.summary: Spatial differentiation commutes with bounded jet time derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.text: If the tower `U` is continuous in time and successive entries are spatial derivatives, its time primitives satisfy the same derivative relation. The derivative of the order `m` primitive is the curried order `m+1` primitive. Bounded evaluation and currying commute with integration, allowing the previous integral differentiation result to apply.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerJointRegularity.summary: Time integration preserves compatibility of spatial jets

_private.TorusEuler.EulerLimitClosure.0..text: A jointly smooth integrand on a closed convex parameter domain remains $C^m$ after integration over a fixed compact set, for every natural $m$. The hypotheses include unique differentiability of the domain, a proper parameter space and a locally finite measure. Induction differentiates under the integral, supporting the normalized pressure formula at the initial time.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerLimitClosure.0..summary: Compact integration preserves every finite smoothness order

_private.TorusEuler.EulerLimitClosure.0..text: On a closed convex parameter set in a proper normed space, a jointly continuous integrand and supplied continuous parameter derivative over a compact integration set may be differentiated under the integral. The measure is locally finite and the target is complete. The conclusion is a within-set derivative, so it applies at boundary parameters as well.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerLimitClosure.0..summary: Differentiate a compact integral with a continuous derivative

_private.TorusEuler.EulerLimitClosure.0..text: For a smooth integrand on a closed convex parameter domain times the whole integration space, this identifies the derivative of its compact-set integral as the integral of the parameter component of its joint within-derivative. `UniqueDiffOn` fixes that derivative on the domain. The argument inherits properness and local finiteness from the surrounding section.
_private.TorusEuler.EulerLimitClosure.0..summary: Smooth joint integrands supply the compact integral derivative

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: The private level record combines a transverse output, a completion `C` with zero average, and a mean output. It packages exactly the information needed by the recursion. There is no field asserting `C = complete V`; that equality is a property of the constructed levels proved later.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Store one completed oscillation and its mean

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: If `S.average_idempotent` holds and `hR` fixes the parent residual under averaging, then every `meanSource A H parentResidual p` is fixed by averaging. The proof distinguishes $p=2$ from other levels. This gives the exact admissibility proof required by the mean solver.

Assume every `u.B i` is fixed by averaging. Idempotence removes the averaged part of `H`, while `S.average_meanPhaseAdv` makes each supplementary mean-advection term average to zero. The resulting source therefore satisfies the proof argument required by `solveTransverse`, at any indices $P,p$.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: The supplementary source has zero phase mean

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: The dependent family `prior` is available only for indices $i<p$. This definition turns it into a total sequence by using `prior i hi` below $p$ and `zeroLevel` at all other indices. It ensures the preliminary source cannot read unresolved values from the current or later levels.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Expose only the levels already constructed

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: At index one the recursion returns the prescribed leading wave, its completion, and zero mean. At indices $2\le i\le P$ it calls `solveLevel`; every other index receives zero. The leading branch is tested first, so depth zero still stores a leading record even though its finite velocity sum is empty.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Build the finite expansion by strong recursion

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: The recursively defined index-one record is exactly the supplied leading transverse output, its completion under `S.complete`, and `zeroMean`. This identity holds for every depth $P$, because the index-one branch precedes the depth test. It identifies the base data without asserting the leading momentum equation.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: The prescribed leading wave starts the recursion

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: For `hp₂ : 2 ≤ p` and `hpP : p ≤ P`, the recursive level equals the output of `solveLevel` supplied with the same recursion at earlier indices. Strong recursion is unfolded at the current index. This equation enables later proofs to read the mean and transverse equations from the solver output.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Retained correction levels use the ordered solver

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: At positive depth `hP : 1 ≤ P`, any index equal to zero or larger than $P$ is `zeroLevel`. The positive-depth condition excludes the exceptional index-one branch when $P=0$. This supplies the zero conventions needed to close the final interaction sums.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Zero and unretained levels carry no profiles

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: The source for the mean equation is minus the average of the preliminary source `H`, with `parentResidual` subtracted only when $p=2$. The same expression is total at every natural index. Admissibility under averaging requires the separate hypothesis that the parent residual is fixed by the average.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: The mean source includes the parent residual once

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: Taking a level sequence, retaining its values below $p$, and filling the rest with zeros produces profiles that agree with the original profiles before $p$. The proof unfolds the dependent branch for each `i < p`. It justifies discarding provisional padding when rewriting the constructed sources.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: The recursion prefix agrees where it is used

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: A sequence of level records is converted into `HierarchyProfiles` by taking its oscillatory velocity, completion, mean velocity, oscillatory pressure, and mean pressure at each index. This conversion adds no mathematical property. It exposes the recursively constructed records to the algebraic source and cancellation formulas.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Read five profile sequences from the levels

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: This changes only the `B` sequence of a profile family, replacing its value at $p$ by the newly solved mean. Every other sequence and every other mean index is unchanged. The transverse source can therefore include $B_p$ while its oscillatory inputs still come from earlier levels.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Insert the newly solved mean at one level

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: Given earlier levels and a parent residual fixed by averaging, this first solves the mean equation, inserts its velocity at the current index, and then solves the transverse equation with that updated source. The returned subtype records both equations. The completion is obtained by applying `S.complete` to the new oscillation.

This defines the transverse source as $-(H-\langle H\rangle)$ minus the filtered phase-advection contribution of the means. The latter includes the newly computed $B_p$ acting on the leading oscillation. The formula is algebraic; the proof that its phase average vanishes uses compatibility supplied by the solvers.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Subtract the mean and the current mean transport

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: This private record puts zero in the oscillation, both pressures, completion, and mean. Operator linearity discharges its compatibility proofs. It fills indices unavailable to strong recursion and indices outside the retained depth, so source formulas remain total functions on natural numbers.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: The zero level outside the retained expansion

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: This provides the mean-output record with both velocity and pressure equal to zero. Linearity of the hierarchy operators proves all required compatibility fields. It is used at the leading level and in absent levels, rather than as an analytic solution of a nonzero mean source.

If two profile families satisfy `AgreesBefore` at $p$ and `hi : i < p`, their $Y_i$ blocks agree. The proof uses equality of `V i` and `C (i-1)`. Since natural subtraction gives $i-1\le i$, the completion is still among the earlier inputs.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Earlier oscillatory blocks agree with the prefix

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: Agreement of profile families before $p$ gives equality of the full block $Z_i$ for each `hi : i < p`. The earlier $Y_i$ identity supplies the oscillatory part, and the stored equality of `B i` supplies the mean. This lets quadratic source sums use the final family.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Earlier full blocks agree with the prefix

_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.text: Membership in a filtered level sum implies that the first index is at least `shift + 1`, the second is positive, and their sum is `p + shift`. These inequalities justify later uses of natural subtraction and show which profile indices lie before the current recursion level.
_private.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchyConst.summary: Recover the positive indices of one interaction

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: For nonzero `freq`, the first-wave pressure coefficient formed from the explicit seed and material gradient is smooth in the label at any fixed time. The proof rewrites it using the normalized coefficient, whose denominator never vanishes. This checks regularity of the coefficient before its phase primitive and envelope are inserted.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: The raw pressure coefficient is spatially smooth

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: The normalized scalar pressure coefficient is globally smooth as a function of the pair `(t,a)`. The shear rate is a cosine, the sweep is smooth, and the denominator is strictly positive. The result supplies joint regularity before compactness is used to obtain constants independent of time and label.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: The normalized pressure is smooth in time and label

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: For each finite order `n`, the unit radial envelope admits a `PhaseJetBound n C` with $C\ge1$. Its derivatives are bounded on a compact ball and vanish outside the envelope support. The bound controls all orders up to `n`; it is not a single constant for every derivative order simultaneously.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: A fixed envelope has bounded derivatives at every order

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: Fixing a parameter cannot increase the norm of an iterated Fréchet derivative. For globally smooth `f : P × Vec3 → E`, the spatial derivative of `a ↦ f (p,a)` is bounded by the joint derivative at the same point. The proof composes with an isometric inclusion, so the comparison has constant one.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: Spatial derivatives inherit the joint derivative bound

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: This scalar is twice the initial shear rate divided by the square of $1+\mathrm{firstWaveSweep}^2$. The shear ratio and amplitude are absent: they have been separated from the first-wave pressure calculation. Its globally positive denominator makes it suitable for uniform compact-time derivative estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: The pressure coefficient after amplitude normalization

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: If a smooth map satisfies `PhaseJetBound n A`, precomposing it with a continuous linear map of norm at most one preserves the same bound. The chain rule contributes a power of the linear-map norm at each order, which can only decrease the estimate. No invertibility of the contraction is required.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: A linear contraction preserves the derivative budget

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: For a globally smooth function and a list `w` of constant directions, the repeated directional derivative equals the iterated Fréchet derivative evaluated on those directions in the same order. The list length sets the derivative order. This identity converts the coordinate-word representation of hierarchy norms into an operator-norm estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: Ordered constant derivatives equal Fréchet derivative evaluation

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: The cosine factor $\cos(2\pi a_1)$ is unchanged by any integer lattice translation of the label. Lean indexes coordinates from zero, so `a 1` is the second component. This scalar periodicity is the starting point for periodicity of the shear sweep and the explicit first-wave seed.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: The initial shear repeats across the lattice

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: At each fixed time `t`, the scalar `firstWaveSweep t` is spatially periodic. Multiplication of the periodic cosine by its time-dependent scalar preserves every integer translation. This statement places no restriction on time and does not assert periodicity in time; it supplies the spatial hypothesis for later uniform derivative bounds.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: The shear sweep repeats across the lattice

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: At every real time, the normalized pressure coefficient is spatially periodic. The proof combines periodicity of the sweep with periodicity of the cosine in the numerator. This concerns the scalar coefficient before multiplication by the envelope and the phase primitive, rather than the complete physical pressure.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: The normalized pressure repeats across the lattice

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.text: The centered label cell has unique derivatives in the sense of `UniqueDiffOn`. The argument uses convexity and a nonempty interior containing a ball around the origin. This property permits equality of smooth functions on the entire closed cell to identify their ambient derivatives even at its boundary.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveDerivativeB.summary: Derivatives on the closed cell are uniquely determined

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: A time-label field smooth on the slab and spatially periodic at every time is embedded as a phase-independent twisted profile. The carrier `k` is arbitrary because the function ignores the phase shift. The constructor composes with the time-label projection and then takes the established zero-extension representative.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: Insert a periodic material coefficient into the hierarchy

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: At a slab point, the embedded twisted coefficient evaluates to `f p.1 p.2.1`. The phase coordinate disappears because the construction uses only time and label. This equality removes the zero-extension branch using `hp` and makes the original coefficient available in concrete hierarchy equations.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: Read the original time-label coefficient on the slab

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The twisted profile obtained from a global time-label field is phase independent on the slab. Evaluating at any two phases gives the same original field value. This theorem supplies the independence hypothesis used to interpret means and prove cancellation of mean-driven phase advection.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: Embedded material coefficients do not depend on phase

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: If a smooth spatially periodic time-label field is even in labels at each slab time, its phase-independent twisted embedding has joint reflection multiplier one. The phase component contributes nothing because the embedding ignores it. Off-slab zero extension preserves the same symmetry.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: Even material coefficients remain even in the joint coordinates

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The explicit inverse deformation is infinitely differentiable as a function of time and label. The proof combines the smooth material-gradient field with multiplication by time and subtraction from the identity. No inverse-function theorem or determinant lower bound is needed for this explicit polynomial-in-time formula.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The inverse shear deformation is jointly smooth

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The label-dependent material gradient is infinitely differentiable for every shear parameter `s`. It is a smooth cosine factor times a fixed bounded linear map. This coefficient regularity is used when embedding the first-wave hierarchy data into the smooth time-label-phase profile space.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The material shear coefficient is smooth in labels

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The explicit primary pressure is jointly smooth when `freq ≠ 0` and `0 < h ≤ 1`. Nonzero frequency makes the transported covector nonzero everywhere, so its squared norm can be divided into a smooth coefficient. Smoothness of the phase primitive then gives the full pressure regularity.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The unwrapped primary pressure is jointly smooth

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: Under `0 < h ≤ 1`, the primary velocity before localization is infinitely differentiable jointly in time, label, and phase. The smooth seed depends on time and label, while the scalar wave profile depends on phase. Multiplication preserves smoothness, independently of any frequency or support choices.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The unwrapped primary velocity is jointly smooth

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The first-wave material gradient is unchanged by label negation. Its only label dependence is through a cosine of the second coordinate, and cosine is even. This supplies the symmetry of the parent coefficient needed for the hierarchy’s reflection propagation, without imposing a bound on the shear parameter.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The material shear gradient is even in the label

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The explicit amplitude operator, material-gradient term, and pressure-gradient coefficient sum to zero at every label and phase. This is an algebraic identity in the total definitions and requires no nonzero-frequency hypothesis. Analytic identification of its first term with a time derivative is established separately under nonzero frequency.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: Cancel the affine amplitude and pressure terms at one label

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: For `0 < h ≤ 1`, the phase derivative of the localized leading pressure is its phase-independent coefficient times `waveProfile h z`. The radius and frequency are otherwise unrestricted in this derivative statement. It differentiates only the phase primitive, so no covector denominator is being differentiated.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The pressure primitive differentiates back to the wave

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: For nonzero frequency, the time derivative of the localized leading profile is the fixed radial and phase factors times `affineWaveAmplitudeOperator` applied to its seed. The label and phase are held fixed. This supplies the time part of the first-wave momentum identity before lattice wrapping.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The leading velocity evolves by the seed equation

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: This pressure is minus the first-wave pressure coefficient times the mean-zero phase primitive of the wave profile. The coefficient uses the actual transported covector, smooth seed, and material gradient. The radial envelope is omitted here and applied before wrapping the profile into the lattice-compatible space.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The primary pressure before spatial localization

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: This is the scalar wave profile in phase multiplied by the explicit smooth first-wave seed at the chosen time and label. The radial envelope has not yet been applied. The definition also carries no activation switch, because the first wave is fully present at time zero.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The primary oscillation before spatial localization

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: A spatially periodic field has the same value at a label and at `centeredLabel a`. The centered representative differs from the original label by an explicit integer lattice vector. This identity allows wrapped oscillatory profiles to interact with coefficient fields evaluated at the original label.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: A periodic coefficient agrees at its centered label

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: For `0 < h ≤ 1`, the unwrapped pressure has period one in phase. Its coefficient is independent of phase, while the pressure primitive is periodic. The theorem does not require nonzero frequency because it proves periodicity of the total expression, rather than smoothness of its coefficient in the labels.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The unwrapped primary pressure has unit phase period

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: For `0 < h ≤ 1`, the unwrapped primary velocity is periodic in its phase variable with period one. Time and label are fixed, so the smooth seed is a constant vector in this assertion. Periodicity is inherited solely from the scalar wave profile.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The unwrapped primary velocity has unit phase period

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: For `0 < h ≤ 1`, translating the scalar wave profile by any real phase offset preserves its zero phase mean. Integration over a whole period is unchanged by the starting point. This removes the carrier-dependent phase shift when the wrapped leading velocity is averaged.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: A shifted phase profile still has zero mean

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The transported covector is spatially periodic at every time. The inverse-deformation matrix repeats on the label lattice, and its adjoint is applied to the same constant launch covector. This provides ordinary coefficient periodicity before the oscillatory velocity is placed in the carrier-twisted space.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The transported first-wave covector is label periodic

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: At each fixed time, the explicit inverse deformation is spatially periodic in the label. The identity term is constant and the material-gradient term is periodic. This property concerns the derivative matrix; the shear flow itself is lattice equivariant rather than a spatially periodic map.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The inverse deformation repeats with the label lattice

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.text: The material gradient is spatially periodic for every shear parameter. Translating the second label coordinate by an integer changes the cosine angle by an integer multiple of $2\pi$, leaving the matrix unchanged. This periodicity permits the coefficient to be embedded into any carrier-twisted profile space.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveHierarchyIn.summary: The material shear coefficient repeats on the lattice

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: For a nonzero vector `a`, the absolute value of $-\langle a,Ba\rangle/|a|^2$ is at most the operator norm of `B`. Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator norm bound give the numerator estimate. The explicit nonzero assumption guarantees the denominator is positive before cancellation.

A nonzero transverse solution of the affine amplitude equation satisfies $|a(u)|e^{-\|B\|(v-u)}\le|a(v)|$ for ordered slab times. The proof integrates a bound on the logarithmic norm derivative. Unlike the upper estimate, this statement explicitly assumes nonvanishing and perpendicularity at every time through `htrans`.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: A transverse amplitude cannot decay too quickly

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: Any solution of the affine amplitude equation with constant matrix `B` satisfies $|b(v)|\le|b(u)|e^{\|B\|(v-u)}$ for ordered times in $[0,T]$. The reflected-vector identity bounds the derivative norm, and Grönwall gives the estimate. No transversality or nonvanishing hypothesis is required for this upper bound.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: The amplitude grows at most exponentially

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: The local abbreviation denotes the $i$th Euclidean coordinate vector with coefficient one. Lean indexes these three directions by `Fin 3`, so index zero corresponds to the paper’s $e_1$. This supplies the initial wave vector and transverse amplitude in the stationary-shear construction, without making any claim about their subsequent evolution.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: Coordinate directions for the first shear

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: Every coordinate axis used for the initial wave is nonzero. The proof applies the preceding unit-norm identity, so no geometric nondegeneracy assumption is needed. The result discharges the initial-data requirements of the affine wave existence theorem before frequency and amplitude scales are attached.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: The initial coordinate directions are nonzero

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: For a real number between zero and one quarter, its exponential is at most two. The proof uses a quantitative bound on $|e^x-1|$. In the first-wave estimate the argument is twice the accumulated shear norm, so the short-time hypothesis turns exponential comparison into the fixed factor two.

At a point where the amplitude is nonzero and perpendicular to the covector, the derivative of $\log|a|$ is $-\langle a,Ba\rangle/|a|^2$. The amplitude equation is supplied as `ha` on an arbitrary within-set. Transversality cancels the covector correction in the derivative of $|a|^2$, and nonvanishing justifies differentiating the logarithm.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: The logarithmic amplitude has a quadratic rate

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: The chosen Euclidean coordinate vector has norm one for every index in `Fin 3`. The statement concerns the Hilbert-space norm on `Vec3`, not a componentwise bound. It provides the nonzero initial directions and the exact normalization used to compute the first wave’s initial strength and frame.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: Every coordinate direction has unit length

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: The vector $-w+2(k\cdot w)k/|k|^2$ has the same norm as `w`. Lean proves the identity using reflection in the span of `k`. No nonzero hypothesis on `k` appears: at $k=0$, the totalized quotient contributes zero and the expression is simply $-w$, whose norm is still correct.

Given orthonormal vectors `x` and `y`, a linear combination whose coefficients have the same squares as the corresponding components of `z` has norm at most $|z|$. Independent sign changes are allowed. This finite-dimensional estimate controls the moving-frame derivatives by the norm of the shear acting on a unit vector.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: Two signed orthogonal components do not increase length

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.text: The constant gradient matrix of the stationary shear has trace zero for every real shear parameter. The proof expands the trace in the Euclidean basis. This algebraic form of incompressibility allows the affine moving-frame equations to be applied when estimating the first coupling throughout the initial wave window.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveInitializat.summary: The stationary shear matrix has zero trace

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Names the Euclidean coordinate vector with unit coefficient at the chosen `Fin 3` index. The explicit seed formulas use these vectors to separate the rational first two components from the arctangent third component. Indices zero, one and two represent the paper’s first, second and third coordinate directions.

The $j$th component of the $i$th coordinate vector is one when $j=i$ and zero otherwise. This identity unfolds the Euclidean-space representation used by `Vec3`. It lets the explicit stationary-shear calculations work component by component without changing the normed vector space in which the ODE is formulated.

The pointwise cross product of two smooth vector fields on time and label space is smooth. The proof expands each component into products and differences of scalar coordinate functions. This is the elementary regularity step for the numerator of the localized vector potential.

Fixing a time in the jointly smooth first-wave potential gives a smooth spatial vector potential. The assumptions remain nonzero frequency, positive radius, a strict cell collar and $0<h\le1$. This slice result supplies the twice differentiable potential needed for the divergence-of-curl identity.

At a fixed time, the first potential profile is smooth jointly in its label and independent phase. Nonzero frequency controls the inverse-square covector, while positive radius and $0<h\le1$ provide smooth envelope and primitive. A cell collar is unnecessary here because this statement precedes periodization.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: The first potential is smooth in label and phase

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Lists the three components of the first coordinate vector as $(1,0,0)$. The statement uses the zero index in `Fin 3`, corresponding to $e_1$ in the manuscript. These component identities enter the explicit transported-covector formula and the computation of the first component of the smooth seed.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: Components of the first coordinate direction

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Defines the vector with components $cz/(1+z^2)$, $c/(1+z^2)$ and $-sc\arctan z$. Here `s` is the shear parameter and `c` is the initial amplitude scale. The formula supplies a smooth label-dependent solution once the accumulated shear is substituted; its ODE identity is proved later.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: An explicit amplitude in the shear variable

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Expands the vector-valued seed at sweep `z` into its two rational components and its arctangent component. The identity holds for all real parameters, because the denominator $1+z^2$ never vanishes. It is used both in the ODE calculation and in the direct proof that a nonzero scale gives a nonzero seed.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: Read the three explicit amplitude components

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Computes the derivative of the explicit amplitude with respect to `z`: the first two entries have denominator $(1+z^2)^2$, and the third is $-sc/(1+z^2)$. All real parameters are allowed. The time-derivative proof later multiplies this vector by the local shear rate through the chain rule.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: Differentiate the explicit amplitude in the shear variable

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Lists the three components of the second coordinate vector as $(0,1,0)$. This is the initial amplitude direction for the first wave, represented by index one in Lean. The explicit seed’s second component then gives a direct nonvanishing proof whenever its scale is nonzero.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: Components of the initial amplitude direction

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.text: Lists the three components of the third coordinate vector as $(0,0,1)$. The statement supplies the component simplifications for the arctangent term of the explicit seed. This direction carries the shear parameter in the first-wave amplitude, while the transported covector has no component in it.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWaveLocalized.0.summary: Components of the third coordinate direction

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Multiplies the smooth raw coefficient by the smooth radial envelope to obtain smoothness of the localized coefficient at each fixed time. Nonzero frequency and positive radius are explicit assumptions. This is the regularity needed by the pressure product rule; the separate support restriction for its sign is not needed for smoothness.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The localized first pressure coefficient is smooth

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: For a nonzero carrier frequency, proves smoothness in the spatial labels of the first pressure coefficient before multiplication by the radial envelope. The explicit stationary formula has denominator $(1+\mathrm{sweep}^2)^2$, which is everywhere positive. The result is for each fixed time and does not supply a uniform derivative bound.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The uncut first pressure coefficient is smooth

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Chooses a nonnegative constant bounding the coefficient and its first two derivatives after rescaling labels by the envelope radius. For a normalized `FirstWaveOrigin`, positive frequency, radius in $(0,1]$ and a slab of duration at most one, the bound is $K\lambda^{-7/4}$. The constant is selected before the origin, radius and time.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: Two scaled label derivatives retain the pressure decay

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Defines the scalar coefficient multiplying the first pressure primitive, from the radial envelope, transported covector, smooth seed and stationary material gradient. All arguments are arbitrary reals at this definition site. Its sign and smoothness are proved later under explicit carrier and support assumptions; they are not consequences of the name or of the bare formula.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The envelope multiplies the first pressure coefficient

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Factors the radial envelope from the pressure coefficient, leaving the same coefficient evaluated with envelope value one. The statement is an algebraic identity and has no positivity or nonvanishing hypotheses. It allows the subsequent sign argument and scaled derivative estimate to treat the cutoff and raw stationary-wave coefficient separately.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The envelope factors out of the pressure coefficient

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Proves nonnegativity for nonnegative seed scale, positive frequency and radius, with `hfit : 2 * r ≤ 1 / 4`. Outside the envelope the coefficient vanishes. Inside it, the second label coordinate lies where the stationary shear's cosine is nonnegative. This smaller support requirement is stronger than the condition needed merely to periodize the envelope.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The first pressure coefficient is nonnegative on its envelope

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Sets the fixed geometric constant to $(1+8\pi^2)(1+4\pi)$. The two factors bound a derivative of the stationary inverse deformation and the deformation itself on the unit time interval. This is a constant used to estimate the first pressure phase and the rescaled inverse flow, not a bound containing the wave frequency.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: A fixed constant controls the first inverse flow

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: For tilt of absolute value at most one and time in $[0,1]$, bounds the label derivative of the inverse-flow Jacobian pulled back along the forward flow by $1+8\pi^2$. The proof differentiates the explicit cosine factor in the stationary shear. This is a bound for one derivative of the coframe, not for the whole hierarchy.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The first inverse deformation has a uniform label derivative

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Given a smooth coefficient `p`, a smooth inverse-label map `A`, a two-jet bound for the scaled labels and derivative bounds for the scaled inverse map, bounds $p\circ A$, its gradient and Hessian by $2KB^2r^{-2}\lambda^{-7/4}$. Positive radius and frequency make the rescaling identities valid. This theorem is conditional calculus, independent of the choice of first wave.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: Label pressure bounds transfer through the inverse flow

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: For a positive slab of duration at most one, small tilt, positive frequency and radius at most one, bounds the physical phase gradient and Hessian by a fixed constant times frequency. It also controls the first two derivatives of the radius-rescaled inverse flow. These estimates supply the chain-rule factors when the label pressure is read in Eulerian coordinates.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The first pressure phase and inverse labels have two-jet bounds

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Identifies the entire phase-dependent first pressure profile with the negative of the label coefficient times the periodic pressure primitive. This separates slow label dependence from rapid phase dependence. The equality itself is algebraic and holds without the positivity assumptions used later to derive a one-sided Hessian bound.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The first pressure is a signed coefficient times a primitive

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: For times on the closed slab, identifies the graph readout of the typed first pressure profile with its localized transported expression. The inverse-label map `A` is arbitrary here. Positive radius, cell margin, nonzero frequency and phase width in $(0,1]$ are the hypotheses needed by the wrapped pressure representation.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: Reading the first pressure gives the localized pressure

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: Shows that each factor of the chosen inverse-flow constant is at least one, hence so is their product. The estimate allows uniform use of monotonicity for low-order powers in the pressure composition argument. It is a numerical fact about the fixed constant and has no wave or stage hypotheses.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The fixed inverse-flow constant is at least one

_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.text: For a nonnegative coefficient at the point, two derivatives of the coefficient of size $K\lambda^{-7/4}$, and phase derivatives bounded by $B\lambda$, proves an upper quadratic-form bound of order $K\lambda^{-1/4}$. The leading rank-one tensor uses the lower bound for the profile slope. This is one-sided control; it does not bound the absolute Hessian norm by the same rate.
_private.TorusEuler.FirstWavePrimaryPres.summary: The signed pressure product has a small upper Hessian

_private.TorusEuler.FlowDeterminant.0.To.text: Represent a continuous linear endomorphism of three-dimensional Euclidean space by its matrix in the standard coordinate basis. This finite-dimensional conversion allows determinant and trace calculations to use matrix identities before returning to the coordinate-free linear map. No invertibility or determinant condition is built into the definition.

The $(i,j)$ entry of the coordinate matrix is the $i$th component of the image of the $j$th standard basis vector under `A`. This makes the matrix convention explicit and fixes which index is the input coordinate when translating the variational equation to entries.

The coordinate matrix of `A.comp F` is the product of the matrices of `A` and `F`, in that order. This identity holds for arbitrary continuous linear endomorphisms. It lets the vector-space variational equation $F'=MF$ be read as the matrix equation needed by the determinant computation.

If every matrix entry has within-set derivative given by the corresponding entry of $Af(t)$, then the determinant has derivative $\operatorname{tr}(A)\det f(t)$. This three-dimensional identity does not assume the matrix is invertible. It therefore establishes the volume evolution before a determinant-one conclusion is available.

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: A jointly smooth function on $[0,T]$ times a normed spatial domain has a jointly smooth spatial derivative on the same slab, provided `hT` makes the interval nondegenerate. Spatial increments remain inside the domain even at temporal endpoints. The result concerns `fderiv` of each spatial slice, not an arbitrary extension in time.

A jointly smooth field on the product slab remains smooth as a function of space after fixing any time in the slab. The conclusion is `ContDiff` of all orders on the full spatial space. It is stronger than pointwise differentiability but makes no assertion outside the supplied time interval.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: Every time slice retains all spatial derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: Joint smoothness on the time slab implies ordinary differentiability of the spatial slice at every allowed `ht`. Time is fixed before differentiating, so the conclusion is valid on all spatial points and does not require an interior time. This supplies elementary differentiability for the higher variational chain rules.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: Every smooth time slice is differentiable

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: Any ordered partition of a positive number of slots with exactly one block is the explicitly constructed whole-slot partition. The statement is combinatorial and carries the positive-order hypothesis `hn`. It lets the composition expansion remove exactly one linear term, with no ambiguity about its block embedding or ordering.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: A one-block partition is uniquely determined

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: For a strictly positive order `n`, construct the ordered partition with a single block containing all derivative slots. This isolates the term linear in the highest derivative of the inner function in the Faà di Bruno formula. The proof field `hn` guarantees that the sole block is nonempty.

For a positive order `n`, the one-block contribution to composition of formal Taylor series is the first derivative of the outer function composed with the $n$th derivative of the inner function. This is an identity between total derivative expressions. Smoothness assumptions enter later when those formal terms are identified with an actual composition derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: The one-block term is the highest linear variation

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: The Grönwall expression is homogeneous when its initial bound and forcing bound are multiplied by the same scalar `d`. This exact identity includes the zero-rate case. It isolates the size of a parameter increment from the remaining constants in the local trajectory comparison used for spatial differentiability.

Applying a continuous linear map `L` to a curve with within-set derivative `du` gives within-set derivative `L du`. The source and target are arbitrary real normed spaces. This transports ODE identities for operator-valued or multilinear-valued curves to their fixed evaluations without changing the time domain.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: Linear evaluation commutes with time differentiation

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: For a function differentiable on a closed slab, fixing any time in the slab yields a Fréchet derivative in the spatial variable. The derivative is the within-slab derivative composed with the spatial inclusion. This permits higher spatial differentiation without requiring the time coordinate to lie in the interior.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: Fixing time leaves an ordinary spatial derivative

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: On a convex set `s`, differentiability and a Lipschitz derivative bound imply a quadratic first-order Taylor remainder between any two points of `s`. The derivative is an ordinary Fréchet derivative, while `hLip` restricts its Lipschitz estimate to the set. This local form supports the compact-neighborhood argument for differentiating trajectory families.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: Quadratic Taylor control on a convex domain

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: For an ordered partition of `n` derivative slots, summing the sizes of all blocks gives exactly `n`. The covering and disjointness fields of the partition supply this identity. It is the exponent-counting input that turns a product of lower-order deformation estimates into the required bound at order `n`.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: Partition block sizes exhaust the derivative order

_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.text: For a normed-space curve with a within-interval derivative satisfying the stated affine growth inequality, its norm at every allowed time is bounded by the Grönwall expression at the full terminal time `T`. Nonnegativity of `K` and `ε` allows this replacement. The initial norm bound `hinit` is retained as the parameter `δ`.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowHigherVariations.summary: A full-interval bound for vector-valued growth

_private.TorusEuler.FlowSecondVariation..text: Integer lattice translation leaves the Fréchet derivative of a periodic function unchanged. The statement needs no differentiability assumption because it follows from equality of translated functions and the derivative’s translation rule. Later applications separately establish smoothness before interpreting these derivatives as classical spatial gradients.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowSecondVariation..summary: The derivative of a periodic field is periodic

_private.TorusEuler.FlowSecondVariation..text: For operator-valued functions, differentiating $f(q)g(q)$ at a point with $f(p)=0$ needs a derivative only for `f` and continuity for `g`. The derivative is the derivative of `f` postcomposed with the fixed operator `g p`. This removes a circular differentiability assumption when differentiating the fundamental solution’s parameter-difference formula.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowSecondVariation..summary: A vanishing factor needs only continuity of its partner

_private.TorusEuler.FlowSecondVariation..text: For a field differentiable on a closed time slab, its spatial slice at an admissible time has a Fréchet derivative obtained by composing the within-slab derivative with the spatial inclusion. Spatial points are unrestricted. This isolates spatial differentiation from the one-sided time behavior at the slab endpoints.
_private.TorusEuler.FlowSecondVariation..summary: A spatial slice inherits the slab derivative

_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.text: The lifted torus mode at `-y` equals the complex exponential with phase $-2\pi\langle y,k\rangle$. This fixes the sign and normalization matching the whole-space Fourier transform. It is the algebraic bridge between a periodic character and the Fourier multiplier obtained by integrating the Euclidean kernel.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.summary: The reversed character is the Fourier-transform factor

_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.text: The Fourier character at $x-y$ is the product of its values at `x` and `-y`. This identity uses the integer lattice frequency `k` and the exponential definition of the lifted torus mode. It separates the output location from the integration variable in the convolution calculation.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.summary: A translated Fourier mode factors into two characters

_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.text: If a real symbol vanishes whenever the frequency norm exceeds two, its complex-valued version has compact support. The proof contains the support in the closed radius-two ball of Euclidean three-space. This creates the compactness input needed to regard a smooth cutoff symbol as a Schwartz function.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.summary: A bounded support condition survives complexification

_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.text: For positive `Λ`, the integral of $\Lambda^3g(\Lambda y)$ over Euclidean three-space equals the integral of `g`. The declaration is an equality of total Bochner integrals and has no explicit integrability premise. It supplies the change-of-variables identity underlying all normalized kernel scaling formulas.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.summary: Dimensionally normalized dilation preserves the integral

_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.text: For a positive cutoff frequency and a symbol supported in the radius-two ball, applying `smoothFourierCutoff` to a finite Fourier sum multiplies its `k`th coefficient by the symbol at the rescaled lattice frequency. This statement concerns a finite polynomial and does not yet identify a convolution kernel.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierConvolution.0.summary: The cutoff weights each Fourier coefficient by its symbol

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: A finite sum of torus Fourier characters with fixed amplitudes is continuous in any complex normed target. Each term is a continuous scalar character multiplying a constant vector, and finite addition preserves continuity. This supplies the continuous-map packaging used in Fourier uniqueness arguments for spectral cutoffs.

The map from Euclidean three-space to the product unit torus is continuous because every coordinate map to the additive circle is continuous. This structural fact supplies measurability and continuity for lifted or translated torus fields inside convolution integrals. It does not assert differentiability of the quotient map as a Euclidean-valued function.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: The Euclidean to torus quotient map is continuous

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: Two complex continuous torus functions are equal if all their Fourier coefficients agree. The proof embeds them into scalar L² and uses injectivity of Fourier coordinates, then returns to continuous functions using full support of Haar measure. This provides pointwise function equality, not only an almost-everywhere identification.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: Complex continuous torus functions are determined by coefficients

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: The Fréchet derivative of a Euclidean Fourier wave at `x`, applied to `v`, equals the same wave multiplied by $2\pi i\langle k,v\rangle$. The integer frequency is converted by `latticeVector`. This formula links the torus character convention to the real-space kernel derivative symbol.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: Differentiating a Fourier wave yields its directional frequency factor

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: The Euclidean Fourier transform of `K` at lattice frequency `k` equals the integral of `K` multiplied by the negative-frequency torus character of the Euclidean integration variable. The formula fixes the transform sign convention. It is an identity between total integral expressions and does not itself certify integrability of an arbitrary `K`.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: Sampling the Euclidean transform uses the negative torus character

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: For a list of `j` directions, the Fourier transform of the iterated Schwartz-kernel derivative is the original transform times the product of all directional symbols. The empty list gives the original transform. Induction preserves the order convention and supplies the Fourier calculation underlying higher-order Bernstein estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: Repeated kernel derivatives multiply all directional symbols

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: The Fourier transform of a directional derivative of a Schwartz kernel equals its transform multiplied by `kernelDirectionSymbol ξ v`. Schwartz regularity and decay justify the derivative-transform identity. The result tracks the sign and $2\pi$ convention needed when derivatives are moved from a band-limited function to its convolution kernel.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: A directional kernel derivative multiplies the Fourier transform

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: The scalar symbol is $2\pi i\langle\xi,v\rangle$, using the Fourier convention of the paper. It records the factor obtained when differentiating in direction `v`. The definition accepts arbitrary real frequency and direction vectors and contains no projection, denominator, or nonzero-frequency condition.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: The Fourier factor for one directional derivative

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: Differentiate the Euclidean lift of a finite Fourier synthesis in direction `v`. The result is the same finite synthesis with each amplitude multiplied by its directional symbol. The input is a finite set of frequencies, so no convergence or interchange of infinite series is required.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: A directional derivative acts on every finite Fourier amplitude

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: A continuous complex-linear scalar functional applied to a continuous torus field commutes with taking its Fourier coefficient. The proof moves the functional through the Bochner integral and uses complex linearity for the character factor. This reduces vector-valued Fourier uniqueness to scalar Fourier uniqueness.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: Scalar linear functionals commute with Fourier coefficients

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: For each lattice frequency, evaluating the torus character at `z + w` gives the product of its values at `z` and `w`. This character law is used when translating the Haar integration variable in the convolution coefficient calculation. It is an exact algebraic identity valid at every torus point.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: Fourier characters turn spatial addition into multiplication

_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..text: Taking the torus image of `x − y` equals subtracting their torus images. The coordinate quotient homomorphisms supply the equality. This identifies a Euclidean convolution evaluated on periodic lifts with torus translation by the image of its integration variable, without choosing special representatives of torus points.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierCutoffBounds..summary: The quotient map preserves subtraction of spatial points

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: An increment bound $\|f(x+v)-f(x)\|\le D\sqrt{\|v\|}$ with `D ≥ 0` proves both boundedness of the quotient range and seminorm at most `D`. The proof separates the zero-increment case from positive denominators. It converts convolution increment estimates into the formally bundled Hölder bounds.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: A uniform increment estimate bounds the seminorm

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: If `k ≤ M`, the loss-`k` tail constant is bounded by one plus the sum of absolute kernel moments through order `M`. Nonnegativity allows the relevant moment to be selected from the finite sum. This produces one constant valid for every output order below a fixed input regularity.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: One finite moment sum controls every smaller loss

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: The tail constant is nonnegative for every loss order. The proof combines nonnegativity of the absolute kernel moment with the extra zero-order term, which is either zero or one. This supplies a sign needed when comparing the derivative-level norm to the total input norm.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: The loss-dependent tail constant is nonnegative

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: The absolute moment of any order of a Schwartz kernel is nonnegative because both the distance power and kernel norm are nonnegative pointwise. This sign fact permits comparison and summation of the kernel constants in the uniform tail bound. It does not assert strict positivity for a potentially zero kernel.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: Every absolute kernel moment is nonnegative

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: The norm of the `n`th iterated derivative of the `j`th derivative equals the norm at total order `j+n`. The equality uses the isometric currying identifications between multilinear-map spaces. It is stated without differentiability hypotheses, as an identity of Lean’s total derivative operators; substantive derivative estimates still require regularity.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: Nested derivative norms equal the combined-order norm

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: Under $C^{j+n}$ regularity, differences of nested iterated derivatives at two points have the same norm as differences of the derivative of total order `j+n`. The proof applies the norm identity to a translated difference of functions. This preserves the half-Hölder increment estimate when derivatives are regrouped in the cutoff argument.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: Nested derivative increments preserve their norm

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: For a continuous torus field whose lift has order `s+k` half-Hölder regularity, the cutoff tail has order `s` and norm bounded by $C_{s+k}\Lambda^{-k}$ times the input norm. The symbol is smooth, compactly supported and one near zero, while `Λ` is positive. The proof applies the lifted remainder estimate to every derivative through order `s`.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: The tail loses a prescribed number of derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: For `SpatialHolderHalf m f`, the supremum norm plus half-Hölder seminorm of the `j`th derivative is bounded by the full order-`m` norm whenever `j ≤ m`. Every summand is nonnegative because the regularity predicate provides boundedness. This permits a tail estimate at one derivative order to use the common input norm.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: Each derivative level is controlled by the full norm

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: For a field with bounded half-Hölder quotient range, the real seminorm is nonnegative. The zero increment contributes quotient zero, and the conditional supremum is at least this value. This supplies the sign condition needed when multiplying or summing the derivative-level bounds in the tail estimate.

For a smooth cutoff equal to one on the unit ball and supported in radius two, bounds the supremum and half-Hölder seminorm of $g-K_\Lambda*g$ by $\Lambda^{-k}$ times the corresponding top-derivative norm and a kernel moment constant. Positive `Λ`, bounded input, and bounded top derivative and increment quotients are explicit hypotheses. The zero-loss case uses the elementary convolution bound.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: Taylor cancellation bounds the lifted convolution tail

_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..text: For a field with bounded norm range, its real supremum norm is nonnegative. The proof compares the supremum with the norm at the origin. The boundedness hypothesis is kept explicit because the definition uses a conditional real supremum, not an extended-real supremum that automatically records infinity.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierHolderTail.0..summary: A bounded spatial supremum is nonnegative

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: Multiply a Schwartz kernel by a coordinate monomial specified by `ι : Fin j → Fin 3`; the result is integrable. Repeated coordinates are allowed. The proof bounds the absolute product by $\|y\|^j$ and uses Schwartz moment integrability, providing the certificate needed before expanding and integrating Taylor terms.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: Every coordinate monomial is integrable against a Schwartz kernel

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: For the normalized smooth cutoff kernel at positive scale, its product with the finite Taylor polynomial is integrable and has integral `f x`. This theorem does not require smoothness of `f`: every positive homogeneous term cancels regardless of its coefficient, and the degree-zero term is the value. A genuine remainder estimate needs additional regularity.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: Integrating the Taylor polynomial returns the center value

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: For any continuous multilinear map `A`, the function $K(y)A(y,\ldots,y)$ is integrable when `K` is Schwartz. The operator norm bounds the multilinear evaluation by $\|A\|\|y\|^j$. This result applies even when `A` is not the derivative of a function, which is useful for the algebraic Taylor-polynomial integration step.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: Schwartz kernels make every homogeneous multilinear term integrable

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: For a function of class Cⁿ and `j ≤ n`, the `j`th derivative of $t\mapsto f(x+ty)$ equals the `j`th Fréchet derivative of `f` at that point evaluated repeatedly on `y`. The explicit order hypothesis prevents reading total derivative operations outside their justified regularity range.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: Derivatives along a line are repeated directional derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: Form the finite sum through degree `n` of $1/j!$ times the order-`j` Fréchet derivative of `f` at `x`, evaluated on copies of `-y`. This defines the polynomial used to approximate $f(x-y)$. The definition accepts arbitrary `f`; smoothness enters the remainder estimate, not the finite algebraic expression.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: The Taylor polynomial for translating by minus y

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: A continuous `j`-linear map evaluated on `j` copies of `y` equals the sum over all coordinate selections of the corresponding monomial times its basis evaluation. This is a finite algebraic identity with no differentiability requirement. It converts directional Taylor terms into coordinate moments whose cancellation is already available.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: Expand a diagonal multilinear term into coordinate monomials

_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.text: If `f` is Cⁿ⁺¹ and its order-`n+1` derivative has global norm bound `M`, the error in the translated Taylor polynomial is at most $M\|y\|^{n+1}$. The proof reduces to a one-dimensional line segment and discards a favorable factorial denominator. The estimate is valid globally because `hM` is global.
_private.TorusEuler.FourierKernelMoments.summary: A bounded next derivative controls the Taylor remainder

_private.TorusEuler.FrameCouplingVariati.text: An orthonormal frame whose axes have speed at most `2*M`, together with a matrix field bounded by `M` and derivative bounded by `D`, has each frame entry vary by at most $(4M^2+D)(finish-t_0)$. Derivatives are taken within the closed interval. The theorem assumes the frame-speed bounds rather than deriving them from the wave ODEs.
_private.TorusEuler.FrameCouplingVariati.summary: Frame coefficients vary by the gradient and frame-speed budget

_private.TorusEuler.FreezingConcreteMult.text: If $P$ is smooth on a set $s$ and every frozen operator $P(\xi)BP(\xi)+I-P(\xi)$ is a unit there, then its real ring inverse depends smoothly on $\xi$ within $s$. The argument first builds the direct frozen symbol from products and sums, then composes with smooth inversion on the unit set. The unit hypothesis excludes the inverse's default values.

For a symbol smooth away from zero, the constructed real multiplier satisfies an off-support Lipschitz bound when $f$ vanishes on a product-metric ball of radius $r>0$ and the second point lies within $r/4$. The constant is explicit in the annular symbol's derivative mass and the inverse-fourth-power tail. The input factor is the supremum norm $\|f.val.1\|$, not its full half-Hölder norm.
_private.TorusEuler.FreezingConcreteMult.summary: A real multiplier gains local Lipschitz control

_private.TorusEuler.FreezingConcreteSolv.text: For `s ∈ [0,1]`, a pointwise coercivity bound for `B` on one vector `v` gives a bound with constant `min 1 μ` for the affine coefficient on that vector.
