_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Joint continuity gives uniform path continuity within the domain

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: For a convex time set, a jointly continuous family and its supplied continuous time derivative on the unit phase interval may be averaged before differentiation. The resulting within-time derivative is the phase mean of the derivative field. This justifies the mean ODE even at time-domain boundary points, without assuming periodicity.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Differentiate the phase average within the time domain

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: On a convex parameter set, jointly continuous data and jointly continuous supplied parameter derivatives give the within-set derivative of the curried path map. The candidate derivative sends a direction to the path of pointwise derivatives. Convexity controls the remainder uniformly in time, upgrading pointwise differentiability to differentiability in the uniform path norm.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: A continuous derivative field differentiates the path-valued map

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: At a slab point, a jointly continuous time-derivative field and the specified parameter derivative combine into a joint within-slab Fréchet derivative. The time derivative is assumed along every parameter trajectory, while the parameter derivative is needed at the chosen time and point. The proof separates the time increment from the parameter increment without extending beyond the slab.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Combine the time derivative with the parameter derivative

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: For phase-independent continuous operators, a jointly continuous forced ODE solution starting from zero inherits period one and zero phase mean from its forcing. The proof applies uniqueness to the phase-shift difference and to the averaged solution. It allows nonnegative duration and concludes these properties at a specified time of the closed slab.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Zero-start dynamics preserve periodicity and zero phase mean

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: Two profiles that agree on the closed unit interval have equal phase averages. This is an interval-integral congruence, with no continuity or periodicity hypothesis. It is used to compare an actual profile with a clamped continuous-path representative that may have unrelated values outside that interval.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Only the values on one interval determine the average

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: A continuous path of linear maps from the parameter space to the target gives one continuous linear map sending a fixed direction to its time path of images. Its norm is bounded by the uniform norm of the operator path. This is the form of the derivative of a curried time-path family.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: An operator path acts on a fixed parameter direction

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: The construction that turns an operator-valued path into a linear map with path-valued output is continuous linear, with norm at most one. This packages the change in argument order as a bounded operator. It allows regularity of the pointwise derivative field to imply regularity of the derivative in the uniform path space.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Currying operator paths is itself continuous linear

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: At a slab time, the path obtained by applying `slabOperatorPath A` to a direction `p` equals $A(t)p$. This definitional identity identifies the candidate derivative of a path-valued map with the original pointwise derivative. It requires no differentiability or parameter-domain hypotheses beyond the operator path's type.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Evaluate the operator path on its fixed direction

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: This bounded linear map integrates a continuous path on $[0,1]$, using its clamped extension to express the phase-average operation. Its norm is at most one. The compact domain supplies the uniform norm, and the map is used to transfer derivatives through phase averaging.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: Integrate a continuous profile on the unit interval

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.text: If a continuous unit-interval path agrees there with an ordinary real-domain profile, integrating the path gives that profile's phase average. The proof uses equality only on $[0,1]$. It therefore permits the two objects to differ arbitrarily elsewhere and does not require a globally continuous or periodic extension of the profile.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryJointRegu.summary: The path integral equals the original phase average

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.text: If the original generator, weight and specified weight derivative are continuous on `I`, and the weight is strictly positive there, the transformed generator is continuous. Only continuity and positivity are used in this lemma; `dg` is not yet required to be an actual derivative. The result prepares the weighted linear-ODE existence and comparison arguments.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.summary: A positive differentiable weight gives a continuous generator

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.text: A solution of the homogeneous transformed equation becomes a solution of $x′=Ax$ after multiplication by the positive weight. The derivative witness for the weight supplies the cancellation of its logarithmic rate. This converse lets the assumed weighted stability of the original equation control ordinary norms for the transformed equation.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.summary: Multiplying by the weight restores the original equation

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.text: If $x′=Ax+f$ and the positive weight has derivative `dg`, then $x/g$ solves the transformed equation with generator $A-(dg/g)I$ and forcing $f/g$. All identities are within the same set `I` at the point `t`. The strict positivity hypothesis rules out division by a vanishing amplitude weight.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.summary: Dividing a forced solution changes its generator

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.text: For a positive real weight `g`, the norm of $g^{-1}x$ is $|x|/g$. Positivity removes the absolute value in the scalar norm. This identity converts ordinary norm estimates for the normalized solution back into the weighted ratios used throughout the seed comparison.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.summary: A positive scalar weight divides the norm

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.text: Defines the transformed linear generator $A-(g′/g)I$ for the normalized unknown $x/g$. The inputs are the value `g` and its proposed derivative `dg` at a time. The definition itself does not assert that `dg` is a derivative or that the weight is positive; those assumptions enter the transformation theorems.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.summary: The generator after dividing by the amplitude weight

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.text: Assume every homogeneous solution of `A` satisfies the given weighted forward estimate with constant `K`. Then every solution of the transformed generator satisfies the corresponding unweighted norm estimate. The weight is positive and has the stated within derivative throughout the interval, so multiplying back by it and cancelling its values is legitimate.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatoryLabelRegu.summary: Weighted stability becomes ordinary stability after normalization

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatorySolveSymm.text: For a continuous operator coefficient on a nonnegative closed time slab, two solutions of the same inhomogeneous linear equation with equal initial values agree throughout the slab. Subtraction removes the forcing and reduces the claim to homogeneous uniqueness. The theorem allows a zero-length slab, where the conclusion is only equality at the initial point.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatorySolveSymm.summary: Equal initial data give the same forced linear trajectory

_private.TorusEuler.OscillatorySolveSymm.text: The formula for the oscillatory pressure slope is linear in the forcing and velocity when the matrix and covector are fixed. Negating those two inputs therefore negates the scalar slope. This algebraic equality remains valid under Lean’s total division convention and is used inside the separately nondegenerate oscillatory solve.
_private.TorusEuler.OscillatorySolveSymm.summary: Negating velocity and forcing negates the pressure slope

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S53.Lib.text: The scaled derivatives of the wave profile are bounded by `C h` (Lemma 3.1 through `waveProfile_bounds`, replacing the original constants `1/2` and the library bounds). This is a finite derivative estimate for the localized leading profile. The phase width is positive and at most one, and the spatial envelope is kept separate from the central amplitude weight.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S53.Lib.summary: Weighted profile derivatives have size proportional to the width

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S53.Lib.text: With unit label scale, an Appendix D label direction is exactly the corresponding Euclidean coordinate vector. The adjacent sum_coordinate' theorem proves reconstruction by a coordinate sum; the source comment above this theorem describes that different identity.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S53.Lib.summary: Unit label directions are the coordinate vectors

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S53.Lib.text: Coordinate vectors reconstruct every spatial vector. The bridge converts between coordinate word norms in Appendix D and Fréchet derivative bounds used by the fixed-plane construction. The conversion changes constants depending on the order, not the absolute parent exponent.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S53.Lib.summary: Coordinate vectors reconstruct every spatial vector

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S5a.Lib.text: Difference bound for a label-dependent field from its first jet. The first label derivatives of the parent coefficients make the fixed-plane ODE a small perturbation of its value at the origin. A common envelope exponent controls both amplitude comparison and positivity of the physical coupling.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S5a.Lib.summary: A first derivative bound controls differences between labels

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: Let `J m` be continuous curves in complete normed spaces, and suppose each satisfies an integrated equation driven by a bounded bilinear map at index `r m`. On a positive closed interval, every curve is smooth in time. Induction differentiates the integral at successively higher indices; no uniform bound on the derivative loss `r` is assumed.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Integrated quadratic evolution gives every time derivative

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For a family of smooth periodic velocities, continuity of its compatible jet tuple through order two on $[0,S]$ implies continuity of the projected quadratic momentum at each fixed spatial point. The hypothesis `h59` supplies the bounded bilinear map. The conclusion here is continuity in time for the chosen point, not a separate uniform spatial convergence statement.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Continuous second-order jets give a continuous momentum term

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: The inclusion of the smooth jet range has dense range in `PeriodicVelocityJetSpace m`. This follows from defining that space as the topological closure of the range. It asserts density in this particular closed subspace, not density of smooth jets in the entire ambient space of arbitrary derivative tuples.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Smooth jet tuples are dense in the chosen completion

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: This continuous linear map evaluates the zeroth compatible jet at a spatial point and converts its zero-argument multilinear value into a vector. The construction is purely an evaluation map; it asserts no Euler equation or regularity of a time-dependent field. It lets uniform jet convergence imply convergence of the actual nonlinear term at that point.

For smooth periodic `u` and `v`, evaluate the order-zero output of `periodicProjectedMomentumJets h59 0` at `x`. The result is `periodicProjectedMomentum u v x`. This combines the smooth-input compatibility theorem with the identity for the zeroth iterated derivative, connecting Banach-space convergence to the pointwise Euler equation.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Zeroth momentum evaluation returns the physical nonlinear term

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: A continuous spatially periodic function into a normed additive group has a real uniform bound on its norm over all of $\mathbb R^3$. The proof descends it to the compact torus and pulls the compactness bound back. This supplies boundedness of each smooth spatial derivative before it is packaged as a bounded continuous jet.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: A continuous periodic field has a global bound

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: A dense linear isometry `e : E → H` lets every continuous linear map from `E` into a complete space `F` extend to `H`. This definition bundles extension itself as a continuous linear operation on maps. Density gives uniqueness and the isometry controls the norm, preparing the completion argument for periodic momentum on spatial jets.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Extend operators across a dense isometric inclusion

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: Given a bounded bilinear map on `E`, a dense linear isometry from `E` into `H`, and a complete target `F`, this definition extends the operation to two inputs in `H`. It extends in both variables using continuous linear maps. The resulting map agrees with the original operation on the dense domain, as the following theorem records.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Extend a bilinear operation to compatible limiting jets

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: Evaluating the extended bilinear map on `e x` and `e y` returns exactly `B x y`. Both uses of continuous extension are reduced using density and the isometric inclusion. This compatibility identity is what later identifies the completed momentum map with the actual projected tensor divergence for smooth velocity inputs.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The extended operation agrees on original inputs

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: At a fixed point `x`, assume uniform convergence of velocities and second-order compatible jets, continuity of the stage and limit quantities, uniformly vanishing residuals, and the actual stage derivative equation `hStage`. With `h59`, the limit satisfies both the integrated projected equation and its within-time derivative identity on the positive closed prefix. Integration is performed before taking the limit.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The integrated stage equation passes to the limit

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: If `hf : SpatialHolderHalf m f` and `j ≤ m`, then the norm of $D^j f(x)$ is at most `spatialHolderHalfNorm m f`. The boundedness witnesses in `hf` justify taking the suprema, and each seminorm is nonnegative. The theorem therefore applies to genuine Hölder fields, not to arbitrary functions with a totalized norm expression.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The Hölder norm controls each lower derivative

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For a smooth periodic velocity, each derivative of order `i ≤ m` at any point is bounded by the norm of its order-`m` compatible jet tuple. The estimate combines evaluation in the bounded-function norm with the product norm. This supplies uniform derivative bounds before converting tuple control into Hölder control.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The tuple norm bounds each spatial derivative

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: Multiplying a smooth periodic field by a real scalar commutes with its periodic Hölder Leray lift. The proof represents the field in `HalfHolder` and uses linearity of the bounded Leray operator there. This verifies homogeneity on genuine smooth inputs rather than relying on how the total lift is defined for unsuitable functions.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The Leray projection respects scalar multiplication

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For two smooth periodic velocities, this constructs the smooth periodic field $\operatorname{div}(u\otimes v)$. It differentiates their tensor product and contracts the derivative with `momentumTensorDivergence`. Smoothness and periodicity are proved and stored in the output subtype. No divergence-free hypothesis is imposed on either input.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The tensor divergence remains a smooth periodic field

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: This packages $(u,v)\mapsto\operatorname{div}(u\otimes v)$ as an algebraic bilinear map on smooth periodic fields. The product’s bilinearity and linearity of differentiation prove additivity and scalar compatibility in each variable. This declaration supplies no operator-norm estimate; boundedness is established later after the fields are represented by finite jet tuples.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Tensor divergence is linear in each smooth input

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: At a spatial point, the constructed momentum-divergence field is the contraction of the derivative of the tensor product. This definitional equality removes the smooth-field wrapper. It is used to establish additivity and homogeneity without losing the identification with the tensor divergence appearing in the projected Euler equation.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Evaluate the tensor divergence by its defining contraction

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: The pointwise tensor product of two smooth periodic velocity fields is spatially smooth. This follows from the continuous bilinearity of `momentumTensor`, applied to the two smooth functions. The statement itself is a regularity fact; the following constructions add tensor divergence and the Leray projection to obtain the Euler momentum.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The tensor product of smooth velocities is smooth

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: Composing tensor divergence with the negative Leray projection gives an algebraic bilinear operation on smooth periodic velocity fields. On the diagonal it is the nonlinear term in the projected Euler evolution. This map is defined before selecting a finite-jet norm; its continuity and derivative loss are supplied by later estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The projected Euler momentum is bilinear on smooth fields

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: After forgetting the smooth-field subtype, the bundled bilinear momentum equals `periodicProjectedMomentum u v`. The equality is definitional. It connects the algebraic construction used in jet spaces to the actual negative Leray projection of tensor divergence, preventing an abstract bilinear estimate from standing in for an unidentified evolution operator.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The bundled momentum is the actual projected tensor divergence

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: A smooth periodic velocity has Hölder regularity through order `m`, and its Hölder norm is at most $3(m+1)$ times its compatible jet norm through order `m+1`. The proof bounds each derivative and its half-Hölder increment from the next derivative. This is one source of the two-order loss in the later momentum estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: One extra bounded derivative controls the Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For `i : Fin (m + 1)`, this continuous linear map extracts the order-`i` bounded spatial jet from a tuple in `PeriodicVelocityJetSpace m`. The finite index enforces the available range of derivative orders. The map is used to pass integrated evolution and time regularity from whole tuples to individual derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Read one derivative from a compatible tuple

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: This embeds the range of the smooth velocity jet map isometrically into its topological closure, `PeriodicVelocityJetSpace m`. The inclusion does not alter the tuple or its norm. The target contains compatible limits of smooth periodic jets, which is the domain needed for a complete-space evolution argument.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Include smooth jet tuples in their closure

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: The finite jet map is followed by the inclusion of its range into the completed compatible jet space. This gives a real-linear map from smooth periodic velocities to `PeriodicVelocityJetSpace m`. It preserves the actual derivative tuple; the definition performs no limiting process on the velocity itself.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Place a smooth velocity in the compatible jet space

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: This real-linear map sends a smooth periodic field to minus its periodic Leray projection. The output remains smooth and periodic, with its proofs supplied by Hölder estimates at every order. The minus sign is the sign in $u_t=-\mathbb P\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)$; this declaration is not itself an evolution equation.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The negative Leray projection on smooth periodic fields

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For order `m` and a smooth periodic velocity `v`, this packages $D^m v$ as a bounded continuous multilinear-valued function on $\mathbb R^3$. Smoothness gives continuity and periodicity gives a uniform bound. The chosen bound is used only to satisfy the bounded-function type; evaluation still returns the actual iterated derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: A smooth spatial derivative as a bounded continuous field

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: This linear equivalence identifies smooth periodic velocities with the range of their finite jet map. Injectivity comes from the zeroth derivative, and membership in the range supplies a preimage. The equivalence is algebraic; it does not assert a normed-space equivalence on the whole completion or reconstruct a smooth field from an arbitrary limiting tuple.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Recover the velocity from a tuple in the smooth range

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: The bounded-function representation of the order-`m` jet evaluates at `x` to `iteratedFDeriv ℝ m v x`. This is a definitional equality rather than an approximation or convergence statement. It ensures that the subsequent Banach-space estimates remain statements about the original smooth velocity and its derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Evaluating a jet gives the actual spatial derivative

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For a smooth periodic velocity, the derivative of its order-`m` bounded jet is the curried order-`m + 1` jet. The result is a `HasFDerivAt` identity at every spatial point. This compatibility between adjacent derivative orders permits differentiation of the integrated zeroth-order velocity equation in the proof of Proposition 8.1.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Differentiating one spatial jet gives the next

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For every finite order `m`, the map from a smooth periodic velocity to its tuple of derivatives through order `m` is injective. The zeroth component already recovers the original function. The proof evaluates that component, avoiding any claim that higher derivatives alone determine the velocity.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: A finite jet tuple still determines the velocity

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: For `v : smoothPeriodicVelocity`, this theorem extracts invariance under every lattice translation. The smoothness proof stored alongside it is not needed for this projection. Later helpers combine both properties to obtain bounded spatial derivatives on the torus and to define the projected momentum of two such fields.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The chosen velocity type carries spatial periodicity

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: An element `v : smoothPeriodicVelocity` is a function together with proofs of smoothness and periodicity. This theorem extracts the smoothness component as `ContDiff ℝ ∞`. It concerns a single spatial field, with no time variable or Euler equation, and supports the derivative identities used to construct compatible velocity jets.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: The chosen velocity type carries spatial smoothness

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: If a function is spatially periodic, each of its iterated Fréchet derivatives is spatially periodic as well. The declaration allows a general real normed codomain and imposes no smoothness assumption. Translation invariance of the total derivative operation proves the equality; separate regularity hypotheses are used when these derivatives are interpreted as smooth jets.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: Every spatial derivative retains the period lattice

_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.text: Suppose `U` converges uniformly to `u` on a closed interval, and `u` is continuous there. Every bounded bilinear map `B` then sends the diagonal pairs to a uniformly convergent sequence. Compactness bounds the limiting inputs; the estimate controls the two factors separately. The result is generic and imposes no Euler or periodicity assumptions.
_private.TorusEuler.Paper.Proofs.S678b.L.summary: A bounded quadratic operation preserves uniform convergence

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAffineStatement.text: Two solutions of WaveOn J D with the same initial wave vector and amplitude agree on J, provided J is order connected, contains t₀, and D is continuous there. The hypothesis hkn requires the second wave vector to stay nonzero. Linear ODE uniqueness first identifies the wave vectors, then their amplitude coefficients. No nonzero amplitude assumption is required.

If two reference slopes agree on the nonnegative half-line, their exponential integral factors agree there as well. For a nonnegative evaluation time, the entire integration interval lies inside that half-line, so interval-integral congruence suffices. No differential equation or continuity hypothesis is used by this lemma; those enter when identifying the slopes in its callers.

The Euclidean norm of the three-vector with coordinates u, v, and z is bounded by $|u|+|v|+|z|$. The WithLp.toLp 2 wrapper selects the Euclidean norm, unlike the maximum norm on a plain product type. This elementary inequality converts the coordinatewise wave-vector error into the vector error used by the older additive-comparison wrapper.

There is an absolute threshold $N\ge240$. For $C_0\ge N$, a valid amplification window, positive carrier scale, both smallness conditions, the supplied wave equations and prescribed initial data, this theorem identifies that wave with the constructed growing wave. The supplied Y must solve the Riccati equation on the nonnegative half-line with $Y(0)=1$. It gives nonzero transverse data, logarithmic norm comparison, a positive first coupling and late-time coupling-ratio control. ODE uniqueness transfers the estimates to the supplied functions.

Given a physical amplification window with $T\ge2$, threshold $C_0\ge240$, admissible clock hclock, both smallness assumptions, supplied wave equations hWave and initial equalities hk₀ and ha₀, the rescaled functions have the required normalized initial data and satisfy WaveOn on $[0,T]$. The proof uses clock_zero to identify the initial frame and applies the chain rule to both wave equations. This bridge does not itself derive amplitude or coupling estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAffineStatement.summary: Moving the initial data to normalized time

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: If `e` is a continuous linear equivalence equal to the compression of `B` by an idempotent `proj`, then `e.symm f` solves $\mathrm{proj}(Bv)=f$. The second conclusion identifies every competing vector in `freezingFixedSpace proj` with that preimage. The fixed-space restriction is essential: uniqueness is not asserted for arbitrary ambient vectors.

Given an actual continuous linear equivalence `e`, this converts the assumed operator bound on `e.symm` into a bound for every $v$ by $\|e v\|$. Positivity of $\mu$ and nonnegativity of `M`, `S`, and `L` justify enlarging the polynomial base. The exponent is the concrete value $145$, and the prefactor gains $2^{145}$.

For positive coercivity $\mu$ and nonnegative size bounds $S,L$, the base $4+\mu^{-1}+S+L$ is at most twice $2+\mu^{-1}+S+L$. This elementary inequality changes the concrete inverse estimate to the paper’s preferred scale. It gives no inverse or regularity statement by itself.

For an already supplied compressed equivalence `e`, positive coercivity, and an orthogonal translation-compatible projection, order-`N` coefficient regularity yields a constant bounding `e.symm` in the same lifted Hölder norm. The constant is chosen before the datum, so it is uniform in the forcing. It may depend on the coefficient, inverse, projection, and order; this lemma does not assert a universal higher-order polynomial.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Bound the higher norm of the compressed inverse

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: A bounded torus operator `P` commuting with line derivatives and an order-`n` half-Hölder coefficient `B` give a higher Hölder bound for $P(Bv)$ on admissible fixed-space fields `v : freezingFixedSpace P`. The constant is chosen independently of `v`, using the coefficient product estimate and operator norm. Neither idempotence nor coercivity is assumed for this forward bound.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Bound the forward coefficient operator on fixed fields

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: This private lemma restricts order-`n+1` half-Hölder regularity to order one. Both differentiability and boundedness of the required lower derivative quotients are retained. It prepares the first-order coefficient input to the order-zero freezing equivalence before that equivalence is shown bounded in the higher Hölder norm.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Extract first-order control for the inverse

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: The total Fréchet derivative of a spatially periodic function is spatially periodic. Equality of the translated functions gives equality of their derivative expressions. The theorem has no differentiability premise, so its conclusion concerns periodicity only; subsequent Hölder assumptions ensure these expressions represent genuine derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Lattice translations preserve the derivative expression

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: Order $n+1$ half-Hölder regularity implies order-one regularity of the same lifted field. The proof restricts both the smoothness order and the finite family of uniform and increment bounds. This is used to obtain a Lipschitz coefficient before applying the higher inverse theorem; it adds no quantitative estimate of its own.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Retain first-order regularity from a higher order

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: With positive coercivity and nonnegative factors, the polynomial using $S+2M$ is bounded by $2^{145}$ times the polynomial using $S+M$. This absorbs the factor two in the torus Lipschitz estimate into the absolute prefactor. The declaration is a real inequality and contains neither a regularity assertion nor an inverse construction.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Absorb the derivative conversion into the constant

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: This private function evaluates a half-Hölder torus field at the image of a Euclidean point under `toUnitTorus`. It is the periodic Euclidean lift used to compare coordinate derivative words with the usual Fréchet-derivative Hölder class. The definition itself introduces no new differentiability claim.

Starting from a spatially periodic field, any finite word of coordinate derivative operations remains periodic. Induction applies periodicity of the Fréchet derivative at each step and then evaluates a coordinate direction. No regularity is assumed, so this alone does not prove that the derivative word has the analytic meaning or bounds required later.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Every coordinate derivative word is periodic

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: The lift of a half-Hölder torus field is invariant under integer lattice translations. This follows from the quotient map alone and needs no differentiability assumption. It is the periodicity input used when the derivatives of a lifted field are descended back to torus Hölder fields.

If coefficient `B` and field `v` both have lifted order-`n` half-Hölder regularity, applying a derivative-commuting torus operator to their product preserves that class. The proof combines the bilinear product estimate with the projection lift theorem. It assumes neither coercivity nor invertibility and supplies the forward-map half of the higher isomorphism.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Compression preserves the coefficient product’s regularity

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: If `f` has order-`n` half-Hölder regularity and a coordinate word has length at most `n`, the resulting derivative has order $n-|l|$ and no larger Hölder norm. The length bound `hl` matters because subtraction of natural numbers is truncated. Each coordinate direction has unit norm, giving the contraction estimate used in the induction.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: A derivative word consumes its order of regularity

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: Ordinary lifted order-`n` half-Hölder regularity supplies a family of torus fields representing all coordinate derivative words through that order. This private implication discards the quantitative bound furnished by `exists_halfHolderWords_norm_le` and keeps the derivative relations. It is one direction of the equivalence used to restate the higher freezing inverse.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Convert Hölder regularity into derivative words

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: A family satisfying `HasSpatialHolderWords n` yields order-`n` half-Hölder regularity of the Euclidean lift. The successor step reconstructs a Fréchet derivative from the three continuous coordinate derivatives and then applies induction to their remaining words. The hypothesis uses actual torus-line derivatives, which prevents arbitrary named fields from being treated as a derivative hierarchy.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.summary: Recover Hölder regularity from actual derivative words

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAFreezi.text: The correction list for a derivative word of length $n$ contains exactly $2^n-1$ entries, counted with multiplicity. The missing entry is the term with no derivative on the coefficient. This list count, rather than a count of distinct word pairs, controls the finite sum in the triangular derivative estimate.

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAInvers.text: An `EndpointCoefficientC1Bound` gives a half-Hölder norm cap $C_0+2C_1$ and a torus Lipschitz cap $2C_1$ for every time in the normalized slab. The hypothesis includes differentiability, nonnegative constants, and the pointwise derivative bound. This conversion prepares the coefficient sizes needed by the integrated inverse.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAInvers.summary: Convert derivative bounds to Hölder coefficient bounds

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAInvers.text: If two coefficient curves agree on the normalized interval, their coefficient-times-velocity primitives agree at every time in that interval. The integration segment is contained in the interval by `ht`, so pointwise equality suffices. No assertion is made about primitives outside the slab or about agreement of the coefficient extensions there.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAInvers.summary: Equal coefficients give equal integrated moments

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAInvers.text: Starting from an integrated solution whose label velocity is already jointly smooth, smooth coefficient and source lifts imply smoothness of its displacement, constant field, and represented remainder `G`. The equality `hG` identifies that remainder from the integrated momentum; its pressure-gradient interpretation belongs to later results. This lemma transfers smoothness to the remaining outputs and assumes the smooth velocity construction.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixAInvers.summary: Recover smooth displacement constant and momentum remainder

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.text: For a fixed finite set `words` of length-$m$ coordinate words, chooses one nonnegative constant before the real value space, scale and function. The sum of derivative supremums is bounded by $C\Lambda^m\|g\|$ when $\Lambda\ge1$ and the Fourier band is $4\Lambda$. The constant may depend on the chosen words and cutoff symbol.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.summary: Bernstein constants for selected coordinate words

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.text: A real function belonging to `realFourierSpace R` has an infinitely smooth lift along `toUnitTorus`. Membership in the finite span is the essential hypothesis. The proof proceeds through the span operations and smooth Fourier characters; it does not claim that an arbitrary torus function becomes smooth merely by being lifted.

Assumes every continuous real linear measurement of `g` belongs to one finite-dimensional scalar function space `W`. It then writes `g` in the fixed basis of `W` with coefficients in the original normed value space. Separation by continuous linear functionals proves equality. Completeness of that value space is not required by the statement.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.summary: Recovering a vector field from scalar coordinates

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.text: Restricts point evaluation at `z` to a real linear subspace `W` of scalar functions. The output lies in the algebraic dual `Module.Dual ℝ W`. No topology or continuity of evaluation is claimed here; finite dimensionality is introduced only when later expressing arbitrary dual elements by evaluations.

For a finite-dimensional subspace `W` of real functions, every algebraic dual element is a finite linear combination of point evaluations. The finitely supported coefficient function `c` records both the selected points and their weights. This is a representation theorem for the dual; it does not choose a canonical sampling set.

If the continuous real linear functional `l` has operator norm at most one, its complex-valued scalarization of the continuous torus function `g` has supremum norm at most that of `g`. The complex embedding preserves absolute value. This transports scalar Fourier estimates back to real normed-space-valued functions.

For an integer frequency in `frequencyBand R`, selects the real part of its complex character when the Boolean is true and the imaginary part otherwise. These scalar functions span the real finite Fourier space. The definition concerns the torus variable alone and imposes no positivity assumption on the band radius.

Takes the real linear span of the sine and cosine components indexed by the finite frequency band. It is a submodule of all real functions on the torus, not a space completed in a norm. Its finite dimensionality lets the Bernstein proof recover vector-valued functions from finitely many real scalar measurements.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.summary: The real space of bounded Fourier frequencies

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.text: If the continuous real normed-space-valued function `g` has Fourier band `R`, every continuous real linear functional `l` sends it into `realFourierSpace R`. This supplies a finite-dimensional scalar target without complexifying the entire value space. The functional need not have norm at most one for this membership statement.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBBernst.summary: Scalar measurements stay in the Fourier band

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBLInfin.text: A continuous scalar function times an integrable vector-valued function is integrable on the compact torus. The scalar field may be real or complex through `RCLike`. Compactness supplies a finite bound for the multiplier; this helper justifies passing bounded linear maps through the cutoff’s Bochner integral.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBLInfin.summary: A continuous multiplier preserves torus integrability

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBLInfin.text: The coordinatewise complexification of a real vector in `Vec3` has exactly the same Euclidean norm. No function-space assumption is involved. This identity pairs with the real-part contraction to transfer the complex cutoff’s integral estimate to real velocity fields without introducing a dimension factor.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBLInfin.summary: Complexifying a velocity preserves its norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBLInfin.text: The real-part projection from the complex Euclidean three-dimensional space to `Vec3` is contractive. The proof compares squared coordinate norms. This finite-dimensional estimate ensures that converting the complex Fourier cutoff back to a real velocity field does not enlarge the operator bound.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixBLInfin.summary: Taking real parts cannot increase the norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixD.0.Tor.text: For `i ≤ n` and a table whose entries are at least one, bounds `C i` by one plus the sum through order `n`. The proof uses inclusion of the `i`th term and nonnegativity of the rest. This collects finitely many order-dependent coefficient constants without changing the power of the parent parameter.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixD.0.Tor.summary: Each coefficient cost fits the cumulative budget

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixD.0.Tor.text: If every entry of the coefficient-cost table is at least one, then one plus its sum through order `n` is at least one. Only nonnegativity of the summands is needed in the proof. This elementary estimate supplies an admissible enlarged constant for the coefficient calculus.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixD.0.Tor.summary: A finite coefficient budget is at least one

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDCoordi.text: For a continuous $m$-linear map on copies of `Vec3`, bounds its operator norm by the sum of norms of its values on all coordinate tuples. Expanding each argument in the coordinate basis proves the estimate. This comparison accounts for ordered words and allows later coefficient bounds to preserve the exponent of $D$.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDCoordi.summary: Coordinate values control a multilinear operator

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDCoordi.text: Every vector in `Vec3` is the sum of its three scalar coordinates times their coordinate directions. This exact identity supplies the multilinear expansion used to compare operator norms with coordinate evaluations. There are no smoothness, scale or boundedness assumptions because the statement is finite-dimensional linear algebra.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDCoordi.summary: Expanding a vector in coordinate directions

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.text: Defines a function on the label-phase product by averaging `f(x+(0,r))` over one phase period. Keeping the phase translation inside the integrand makes differentiation commute directly with averaging. The definition itself does not assume that `f` is periodic; identifying it with the label-only phase average requires a separate periodicity theorem.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.summary: Averaging translates in the phase variable

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.text: For an infinitely smooth field and a fixed direction `d` in label-phase space, differentiation of the translated average equals the translated average of the directional derivative. The direction is constant, which is material to the commutation. This is the first-order ingredient for the phase-operator estimates of Lemma D.1.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.summary: Averaging commutes with a constant directional derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.text: If each label slice of `f` has period one in the phase, averaging the translated phase interval equals averaging the unshifted phase function at that label. The conclusion holds at every label-phase point. This identifies the smooth translated average used in the proof with the paper’s phase-independent average.

If `f` is infinitely smooth on the label-phase space, its translated phase average is infinitely smooth as well. Integration occurs over a fixed compact phase interval, permitting derivatives under the integral. This result concerns the translated average without yet assuming period one or reducing it to a label-only field.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.summary: Smoothness of the translated phase average

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.text: For smooth `f`, every finite word of constant directional derivatives commutes with the translated phase average. The proof iterates the first-order commutation and preserves smoothness at each step. This moves averaging past arbitrary mixed label and phase derivatives before their supremum bounds are taken.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.summary: Averaging commutes with a derivative word

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.text: For smooth directional fields and smooth function slices, the finite word quantity of `c • f` equals $|c|$ times that of `f`. The `holder` proposition decides whether difference quotients are included. This is a scaling identity for the defined quantity; it does not independently supply boundedness of all derivative-value sets.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDFields.summary: Constant scaling of a finite derivative norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.text: If `L₀` intertwines each input derivative `DE i` with the output derivative `DF i`, it also intertwines every derivative word. Induction on the word proves the equality. This isolates the constant principal part of the linear equation before the proof expands derivatives falling on variable coefficients.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.summary: A commuting linear operator passes through every derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.text: Interchanges a finite sum over the coefficient index with a list sum over derivative correction pairs. Only the additive structure and finiteness of the coefficient index are used. The identity lets the differentiated equation collect all coefficient contributions under one correction-pair sum before taking seminorms.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.summary: Interchanging the coefficient and correction sums

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.text: The finite derivative quantity obtained by summing a seminorm over admissible ordered words is nonnegative. Each summand is nonnegative by the seminorm axioms. No derivative commutation or analytic regularity is needed for this algebraic fact; those assumptions enter when relating arbitrary words to the chosen ordered representatives.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.summary: Nonnegativity of the finite derivative sum

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.text: For a finite index set, the seminorm of its sum is at most the sum of the seminorms. This is the finite-set counterpart of the preceding list lemma. It is used to bound the coefficient-index sum inside each differentiated forcing correction before the derivative-order recursion is applied.

The seminorm of the sum of a mapped finite list is at most the list sum of the individual seminorms. Induction applies the triangle inequality one term at a time. This handles repeated Leibniz correction pairs without requiring the list to contain distinct elements.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.summary: A seminorm bounds a list sum by the termwise sum

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.text: If the linear derivative maps commute, the seminorm of any word of length at most `n` is bounded by the finite derivative norm of order `n`. Sorting the word preserves its value and places it among the admissible summands. The assumptions include a finite, linearly ordered direction type.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDLiftin.summary: Every derivative word fits the finite order norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDMultiI.text: For a smooth coefficient slice, the directional operator word associated with a finite coordinate tuple equals the corresponding evaluation of its iterated Fréchet derivative. The label scale is fixed to one. The proof handles the list length and index casts explicitly, providing the bridge between word and multi-index coefficient encodings.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDMultiI.summary: Coordinate words evaluate the full derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDMultiI.text: At scale one, `hierarchyLabelDirection` is exactly the family of constant coordinate directions. The equality is an immediate scalar-multiplication simplification. It lets the multi-index conversion compare the hierarchy’s weighted directional notation with ordinary spatial derivatives in the unscaled coefficient norm.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperAppendixDMultiI.summary: Unit label scale gives coordinate directions

_private.TorusEuler.PaperFlowBounds.0.To.text: A jointly smooth vector field on the closed time slab has a smooth spatial slice at any time belonging to that slab. The proof composes with the map sending `x` to `(t,x)` and then uses smoothness on the whole spatial space. No differentiability in time outside the slab is asserted.

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.text: The Hessian of a constant scalar multiple of a scalar spatial field equals that scalar times its Hessian. The statement has no differentiability hypotheses: it uses the total Fréchet derivative’s constant-scalar rule over the field. Later analytic applications separately establish pressure smoothness before interpreting these Hessians as classical derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.summary: A constant scalar factors out of the Hessian

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.text: For $T>0$ and a jointly smooth field on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, its ordinary spatial derivative is jointly smooth on the same slab. Unique differentiation of the product identifies the spatial restriction of the within derivative with the usual spatial derivative. The positive-duration hypothesis matters at the time boundary.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.summary: Spatial derivatives vary smoothly throughout the slab

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.text: Any jointly smooth field on the closed slab has an infinitely smooth spatial slice at a slab time. Composition with the fixed-time inclusion proves the assertion. This local helper is used when taking the ordinary spatial gradient and Hessian of the generic pressure, independently of the within-time derivative convention.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.summary: Smooth spatial pressure slices on the slab

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.text: If the approximation’s leading data equal the constructed paper-cutoff input, the slice of its leading and completion switch terms equals the cutoff derivative times `activationPrimary` for that same seed and coframe. The identity holds at every slab time and label-phase point. It is an exact source formula before any norm estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericPhysical.summary: The full activation slice is the derivative times the primary wave

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericSwitchCo.text: Proves `UniqueDiffOn` for the closed centered label cell by its convex geometry and nonempty interior. This supplies uniqueness of derivatives even at the cell faces. It is the necessary justification for differentiating an equality known on the closed cell when computing the curl completion of a wrapped profile.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericSwitchCo.summary: The closed centered cell has unique differentiation

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericSwitchCo.text: Multiplying the phase velocity by a real scalar multiplies its normalized wave potential by the same scalar. The covector and phase point are fixed. The proof uses linearity of the phase primitive and cross product; no nonzero covector hypothesis is needed for this algebraic identity of totalized expressions.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericSwitchCo.summary: A scalar passes through the phase potential

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericSwitchWe.text: A raw field smooth on the active time slab has a smooth label-phase slice at any active time. The proof composes with the fixed-time map and uses that the whole label-phase space is included. This helper provides the spatial derivatives required for the weighted amplitude seminorm, without differentiating the time multiplier.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericSwitchWe.summary: Smoothness of a spatial and phase seed slice

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: If an even-reflection profile agrees on the slab with a label-only function `f`, then `f t` is even for every slab time. Setting the phase to zero converts simultaneous label-phase reflection into ordinary label reflection. This extracts parity of the physical strain and transported covector from the parent-geometry profiles.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Even phase independent profiles give even label fields

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: If a property of time, label and phase is preserved by the specified twisted lattice shifts and holds on the centered cell at every slab time, then it holds throughout the profile slab. The property is arbitrary. The proof moves each label to its centered representative and transports the assertion by the corresponding phase shift.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A centered-cell property extends by lattice shifts

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: Two twisted profiles are equal if their values agree on the centered label cell for every slab time and phase. Twisted lattice periodicity extends the equality to all labels, and both profiles vanish outside the slab. This extensionality result explains why later identities can be proved only on the closed cell.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Equality on the centered cell determines a profile

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: Wraps a raw phase-periodic field by centered twisted periodization and then regards it as a twisted profile on the closed time slab. Smoothness of the periodized field is supplied as `hf`; it is not deduced for arbitrary raw input. The resulting profile has exact phase and lattice compatibility, with the library’s zero extension outside the slab.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Wrapping a smooth profile on the parent cell

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: At a time in $[0,T]$, the wrapped profile evaluates to the centered twisted periodization of its raw input. The theorem explicitly unwraps the nested profile structures. It says nothing about evaluation outside the slab, where `ofSmooth` uses zero; nor does it remove the spatial periodization on an arbitrary label.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Evaluating the wrapped profile inside the slab

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: Defines the scalar leading pressure with its normalized pressure coefficient and phase primitive, but without the radial envelope. The strain, covector and amplitude are evaluated at the same time and label. Factoring out the envelope later makes the support and centered-cell smoothness arguments share the same spatial cutoff.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: The leading pressure before applying the envelope

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: A regular seed has smooth bare pressure on $[t_0,T]$ in time, label and phase. The proof uses smooth strain, covector and amplitude, and the explicit nonzero covector field before dividing by its squared norm. Valid phase-width bounds provide a smooth primitive. Smoothness outside the active slab is not asserted.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: The bare pressure is smooth on the active slab

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: If `c` is smooth on $[0,T]$, vanishes before `t₀`, and `f` is smooth only on the nondegenerate active slab $[t_0,T]$, their product is smooth on the whole slab. The proof first extends `f` smoothly in time, then shows multiplication by `c` removes any dependence on that extension before activation. Completeness of the value space is required for the extension argument.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A vanishing multiplier gives smooth activation

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: Multiplying the seed’s leading wave by a smooth scalar time function that vanishes before activation produces a smooth raw profile on the entire slab. `HierarchyRegularity` supplies the active wave regularity and `t₀ < T`. The preceding extension lemma handles the activation seam; no arbitrary values of the raw seed before activation affect the product.

For a seed with `HierarchyRegularity`, the product of its amplitude and the phase wave profile is smooth on the active time slab. The seed regularity supplies amplitude smoothness and the valid phase width. The spatial envelope and the time cutoff are deliberately absent from this intermediate field.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Smoothness of the unenveloped leading oscillation

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: For the valid phase width supplied by a regular seed, the wave-pressure primitive is even. The proof uses its normalized phase construction and symmetry. This parity is needed with the even label coefficients to show that the leading pressure is unchanged under simultaneous reflection of label and phase.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: The normalized pressure primitive is even

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: The seed’s leading pressure equals its radial envelope times `barePressure`. This is an algebraic identity valid for arbitrary time, label and phase arguments. It separates the compact spatial localization from the smooth active pressure coefficient, allowing the periodization and multiplier lemmas to be applied uniformly.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Factoring the radial envelope from the pressure

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: For a regular seed, the leading wave is zero at any label whose norm is at least twice the envelope radius. The identity holds at arbitrary time and phase because the radial envelope is the factor that vanishes. It establishes spatial support, without claiming the seed amplitude itself is zero there.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: The leading wave vanishes outside its envelope

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: For a phase-periodic raw field whose phase mean is zero at every label, centered twisted periodization also has zero phase mean at every label. The wrapping changes the phase by a label-dependent translation, and integration over one period is invariant under that translation. No spatial derivative estimate is involved.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A wrapped zero-mean phase field still has zero mean

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: Builds the normalized leading pressure profile with a smooth time multiplier vanishing before activation. It factors out the radial envelope, periodizes the smooth supported active pressure, and restricts to the slab. The carrier is the supplied `k`; smoothness and periodicity are proved from the regular seed rather than assumed for arbitrary raw pressure.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A multiplied pressure as a twisted profile

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: At a slab time, the pressure-multiple profile evaluates to the scalar time factor multiplied by the centered periodization of the leading pressure. The formula exposes the underlying field while retaining the spatial wrapping. It does not identify the raw and wrapped values away from the centered-cell support argument.

The leading pressure of a regular seed vanishes at labels of norm at least twice the envelope radius. Its scalar coefficient may remain defined there, but the radial cutoff is zero. The conclusion holds at every time and phase and supplies the same support gap used for the leading velocity’s centered-cell periodization.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: The leading pressure vanishes outside its envelope

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: On the closed slab, the time derivative of the cutoff times the leading seed, plus strain and phase-pressure terms, equals the cutoff derivative times the seed. The proof separates times before activation from the active interval and extends the identity to the seam. The pressure is multiplied by the same time cutoff.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Differentiating the cutoff gives the raw activation equation

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: If a twisted profile has the stated reflection parity at all slab points, then it has that parity as a globally represented function. Reflection preserves the time slab, and outside it both sides vanish by the profile convention. This extension is algebraic; it makes no claim of time smoothness outside the slab.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Reflection on the slab determines global profile parity

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: Builds the twisted velocity profile from `c(t)` times the localized leading seed. The scalar multiplier is smooth on the slab and zero before activation; seed regularity gives a small supported envelope and a valid periodic phase profile. Centered periodization followed by slab restriction supplies the final profile representation.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A multiplied velocity as a twisted profile

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: The wrapped leading velocity multiplied by a smooth active scalar has zero profile phase average. The proof uses the seed’s zero-mean wave profile, invariance of phase integration under wrapping, and zero extension outside the slab. The multiplier may vary in time but not in the phase being averaged.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A time multiple of the leading wave has zero average

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: At every time in the slab, the velocity-multiple profile equals the scalar time factor times the centered twisted periodization of the leading seed. This is an evaluation identity for the wrapped object. The time factor is independent of label and phase, which allows it to be pulled outside periodization.

If the seed amplitude is even in the label on the active slab, its wrapped leading velocity multiplied by a smooth active scalar is odd under simultaneous label-phase reflection. The phase wave is odd and the radial envelope is even. Before activation the multiplier is zero, so no amplitude parity outside the active interval is required.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A time multiple of the velocity has odd reflection parity

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: If the bundled covector profile agrees with the seed’s covector on the slab, the time-multiplied leading velocity is orthogonal to it at every profile point. The proof uses the seed’s transverse amplitude and handles the pre-activation region by zero. The covector identification `hκ` is an explicit assumption.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A time multiple remains transverse to the covector

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: If a raw field vanishes outside radius $2\ell$ and that radius fits strictly inside the centered cell, its centered twisted periodization equals the raw value on the closed cell. The proof treats wrapped boundary representatives using the support gap. This avoids requiring equality only in the cell interior when later taking spatial derivatives.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: Periodization agrees with a supported field on the cell

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.text: If a function is zero at every slab time before `t₀`, its within-slab derivative is zero at any time strictly before `t₀`. The theorem states `HasDerivWithinAt`, using local equality with zero. Strict inequality is essential: it does not by itself identify the derivative exactly at the activation time.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperGenericWaveSwit.summary: A field vanishing before activation has zero derivative there

_private.TorusEuler.PaperGraphReadout.0..text: A smooth spatial slice of the label map `A` turns a twisted profile into a smooth Eulerian graph readout at a time in $[0,T]$. Time membership is explicit because the profile’s regularity is bundled only on that slab. The conclusion is spatial smoothness at the chosen time, not a new jointly smooth flow.

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyDepth..text: For a real loss scale $L\ge1$ and natural exponent `r ≤ 6`, the power $L^r$ is bounded by $L^6$. This elementary monotonicity step places different recurrence losses under the common sixth power used in Theorem 5.6. It supplies no frequency smallness condition by itself.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyDepth..summary: All smaller losses fit the sixth parent power

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyInvers.text: At a launch time in a positive slab, and with `γ t₀ > 0`, the launch seminorm controls every word of the frozen initial profile after division by its launch amplitude. The conclusion is a `HierarchyRelayWordBound` constant in later time. No positive label or phase width is required for this representation-level inequality; the amplitude denominator is explicitly guarded.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyInvers.summary: Launch data enter the weighted word bound

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyInvers.text: Assumes nonzero label and phase widths, a positive multiplier `c`, nonnegative jet bound `B`, positive amplitude weight and smooth active slices. Scaled jet bounds for `c • f` then bound `c` times the weighted finite-word norm by the number of admissible words times `B`. The nonzero widths permit conversion from rescaled derivatives back to the original profile.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyInvers.summary: Scaled jets control the weighted raw profile norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyLeadin.text: For a seed and a phase width satisfying $0<h\le1$, differentiating its leading pressure in phase gives the radial envelope times the wave profile times `oscillatoryPressureSlope`. The time and label are arbitrary here. This explicit identity connects the normalized pressure primitive to the leading transverse momentum equation.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyLeadin.summary: The phase derivative of the leading pressure

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: For the actual parent geometry, a regular seed and representatives agreeing with its unswitched velocity and pressure on the active interval, proves transversality and zero leading material-plus-phase-pressure momentum on that interval. The proof first works on the centered cell, uses within-interval time derivatives, then transfers by twisted periodicity. It does not extend the homogeneous equation to earlier times where the representatives were freely extended.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: The actual unswitched wave satisfies homogeneous active momentum

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: If a typed profile and a raw field agree on the active interval, their weighted finite mixed derivative norms agree at every order. The interval lies in the parent slab, and its amplitude weight is continuous and strictly positive. The proof rewrites equal time slices before differentiating in labels and phase; it does not need the two fields to agree outside the active interval.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: The typed amplitude norm equals the raw active norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: Builds a twisted hierarchy profile from a smooth coefficient and a smooth phase function of period one, after inserting the radial envelope. The positive radius and cell-margin proofs establish smoothness, while periodization supplies the lattice twist. The constructor retains these properties in its output type; it does not assert that the profile solves a wave equation.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: A smooth periodic coefficient produces a wrapped profile

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: For a positive terminal time and the same smooth periodic zero-mean phase function, the typed phase average of the wrapped vector profile equals the zero profile. It promotes the pointwise phase-mean calculation to equality of hierarchy profiles by extensionality on the slab. The conclusion concerns the average, not the original oscillating field itself.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: The wrapped vector profile has zero averaged field

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: At every time in the closed hierarchy slab, evaluation of the constructed profile equals the explicit twisted periodization of the enveloped coefficient and phase function. The coefficient and phase function satisfy the same smoothness, periodicity and radius conditions as the constructor. This is a value identity on the slab, without an assertion about the representative at arbitrary outside times.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: The wrapped profile has its stated slab values

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: If the periodic scalar phase function has zero mean, then every label slice of the wrapped profile also has zero phase mean on the closed slab. The proof writes periodization as a phase translation depending on the centered label. Integrating a periodic function over any unit interval preserves its mean, while the coefficient and envelope remain fixed during that integration.

A globally smooth coefficient and globally smooth scalar phase profile give a smooth twisted periodization after multiplication by the radial envelope. Positive envelope radius and the strict margin $2\ell<1/2$ keep the support away from the centered cell boundary. The conclusion is smoothness on the hierarchy slab, sufficient to build the typed representative.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: The localized twisted periodization stays smooth on the slab

_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.text: For a function vanishing whenever the label norm is at least $2\ell$, its twisted periodization agrees with the original function on the centered cell, provided $2\ell<1/2$. The theorem needs only a zero value in the target type. The support gap provides a collar near every cell face where changing representatives cannot change the value.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperHierarchyUnswit.summary: Periodization leaves the supported central cell values unchanged

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.text: Defines a function on time and torus labels by evaluating `f` at a chosen Euclidean representative of the label. The function is defined for arbitrary `f`; periodicity is not built into the definition. The following lemma proves agreement with the intended Euclidean lift only when the relevant time slice is spatially periodic.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.summary: Choose a Euclidean representative for each label

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.text: For a periodic time slice, descending by a chosen representative and then evaluating at `toUnitTorus a` recovers `f t a`. Two representatives differ by an integer lattice vector, and `hf` removes that difference. This supplies the exact coefficient identities when the parent’s Euclidean deformation data are packaged on torus labels.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.summary: Periodic data are independent of the chosen representative

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.text: If translating the input by a lattice vector translates the output by that same vector, the Fréchet derivative is lattice-periodic. This is the correct symmetry for a flow lift, which is equivariant rather than periodic as a position map. The conclusion concerns the total derivative expression; existence of actual flow derivatives is supplied by separate smoothness results.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.summary: The derivative of an equivariant flow is periodic

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.text: A periodic vector field has a periodic total Fréchet derivative, by differentiating the equality of its lattice translates. This private lemma prepares the parent velocity gradient for descent to the torus. No differentiability premise occurs in the lemma; the flow adapter separately has the smoothness needed to interpret the derivative analytically.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanFlowAdapter.summary: The derivative of periodic velocity is periodic

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..text: On a positive slab, any integrated solution yields a mixed field representing its velocity, fixed by the mixed projection and solving the projected equation. Continuous coefficients and source, exact path-action identities `hKmix` and `hΩmix`, and the source representation `hf` are required. This transfers a candidate solution into the uniqueness domain of the mixed inverse.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..summary: An integrated solution has a mixed representative

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..text: Continuous coefficient curves `K`, `Ω`, source `src`, and solenoidal velocity `g` give continuity of the integrated momentum on the closed slab. The primitive term is treated in the Banach Hölder space, using continuity of coefficient multiplication. This establishes regularity of the expression before it is projected or identified with a pressure gradient.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..summary: The integrated momentum is continuous in time

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..text: For $T>0$, a continuous solenoidal velocity with zero terminal primitive has every mixed representation fixed by the mixed Leray projection. Continuity and `hRep` connect the time-path representative with its spatial slices. The terminal condition becomes zero time mean, while solenoidality supplies the spatial constraint; neither is inferred from the representation alone.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..summary: The represented velocity satisfies both projections

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..text: If a continuous field has the same spatial projection `c` at every time, then the mixed projection of its represented path is zero. The proof tests against fields with zero time mean and solenoidal spatial slices. Positive slab length and the representation hypothesis are explicit, so this is an identification of the concrete projections on the correct function spaces.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..summary: The mixed projection removes a solenoidal constant

_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..text: Two mixed fields solving the same projected equation coincide if both are fixed by the mixed projection and `eM` is the corresponding compression equivalence. The proof sends each field to the same projected source and uses injectivity. Coercivity is not a direct hypothesis here because existence of the actual equivalence has already been supplied.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperMeanStatements..summary: Two projected velocities agree in the fixed space

_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalCutoff..text: If both scalar pressure fields are $C^2$, the Hessian of their difference is the difference of their Hessians at every spatial point. The proof first subtracts gradients and then differentiates that identity. The regularity assumptions ensure this is the classical subtraction rule used in the physical cutoff argument.

Restricts joint smoothness on a closed time slab to spatial smoothness at a specified slab time. This supplies the differentiability needed to compare the pressure of a smooth approximation with its frequency-truncated child. No Fourier or pressure estimate is proved by this fixed-time composition lemma.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalCutoff..summary: Smooth spatial slices for physical truncation

_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.text: A physical parent on a positive closed slab has finite nonnegative bounds for its kinetic and vorticity coefficients and their first spatial derivatives. The proof uses joint smoothness, spatial periodicity, and compactness after passage to the torus. The constants depend on the supplied parent and duration; this is not a uniform estimate over all parents.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.summary: The smooth parent has finite coefficient bounds

_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.text: For a smooth mean solution at a slab time, differentiating $Kv$ gives $\Omega v+F^*f-\nabla q$. The proof combines the physical label momentum equation with the deformation ODE and the inverse identity. The derivative is `HasDerivWithinAt` on the closed interval, so endpoints are included without claiming differentiability of an arbitrary external extension.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.summary: Differentiate the kinetic momentum along a label

_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.text: Joint smoothness on the closed time slab gives a globally smooth spatial slice at any time belonging to the interval. The proof composes with the fixed-time inclusion and removes the universal spatial domain. The membership assumption `ht` is required; the result says nothing about slices outside the prescribed time interval.

Joint smoothness on the product of the closed time interval with all spatial labels yields smoothness, within that interval, of the curve at each fixed label. The conclusion is `ContDiffOn`, retaining the endpoint-sensitive domain. It is used when differentiating the mean equation and applying the fundamental theorem of calculus.

For any time-dependent function on torus labels, its Euclidean evaluation through `toUnitTorus` is periodic at a fixed time. The codomain is arbitrary and no continuity is needed.
