This supplies periodicity of the deformation and gradient lifts when smooth coefficient representations are built for the physical mean inverse.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalMeanSta.summary: Label evaluation gives a periodic physical lift

_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalParentI.text: For a smooth spatial velocity, $D\ge1$ and $R\ge0$, bounds on its first two derivatives by $RD^j$ imply a half-Hölder bound for its gradient, with norm at most $3RD^2$. The first derivative controls the supremum and the second controls spatial increments. This is a local analytic estimate, independent of Fourier truncation once the jet bounds are supplied.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalParentI.summary: Two derivative bounds control the parent gradient Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.PaperSequenceStateme.text: For every natural `j`, proves $t_{j+2}<t_{j+3}$. The next crossing lies after completion of a switch interval of positive length, since its physical rate is positive. The statement deliberately begins at the second activation: the first two wave activation times are both zero.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperSequenceStateme.summary: Activation times strictly increase after the second wave

_private.TorusEuler.PaperSequenceStateme.text: Identifies the velocity stored as the older stage in tip `j` with sequence velocity `U j`. The proof checks the initial and successor index cases directly. This index correspondence is needed when the central crossing's coupling ratio is rewritten in the notation of the paper's common-sequence conclusions.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperSequenceStateme.summary: The preceding tip uses the correct older sequence velocity

_private.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalStateme.text: For inductive stage data whose initial frequency is at least two, every next frequency is at least the square of the current one. The proof uses monotonicity and the stored power recurrence, whose exponent is at least two. This is the growth estimate supplied to the terminal convergence construction; it does not itself prove convergence or divergence of a physical norm.

_private.TorusEuler.PaperTruncatedHierar.text: If $D\ge1$, $0\le A\le B$ and natural exponents satisfy `q ≤ r`, then $AD^q\le BD^r$. Both coefficient and exponent are enlarged using nonnegative powers. This arithmetic helper lets the lengthy truncated-hierarchy estimate combine several compatible coefficient bounds under one selected parent loss.
_private.TorusEuler.PaperTruncatedHierar.summary: Enlarging a coefficient and its parent power

_private.TorusEuler.ParentCoframeEstimat.text: A velocity jointly smooth on the closed slab is smooth in space at any fixed time `t` belonging to that slab. Composition with $x\mapsto(t,x)$ removes the time variable. The statement concerns spatial smoothness on all of $\mathbb R^3$ and does not assert an extension in time beyond the slab.

If `hi : i ≤ n` and all $C_j$ are nonnegative, then $C_i$ is bounded by $1+\sum_{j=0}^{n} C_j$. The proof inserts the chosen index into the finite sum. It allows one derivative-order constant to control all lower orders in the parent composition and inverse estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentCoframeEstimat.summary: The common constant bounds every included derivative

_private.TorusEuler.ParentCoframeEstimat.text: For a nonnegative sequence $C$, the quantity $1+\sum_{j=0}^{n} C_j$ is at least one. The hypothesis `hC` applies to every index. This private inequality supplies positive common constants when several derivative orders are combined in the proof of the parent coefficient bounds.

_private.TorusEuler.ParentPressureParity.text: Derives evenness of the Fréchet derivative from oddness of a vector field, using composition with the linear negation map. The equality is valid without a differentiability hypothesis under the derivative’s total convention. In the physical use, smoothness already holds, so it describes the ordinary velocity gradient.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentPressureParity.summary: The derivative of an odd vector field is even

_private.TorusEuler.ParentResidualEstima.text: The standard coordinate vector in $\mathbb R^3$ has norm one for any index in `Fin 3`. This normalization removes the product of direction norms when evaluating an iterated Fréchet derivative on coordinate vectors. It is a geometric helper for converting full derivative bounds into derivative-word bounds.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentResidualEstima.summary: Each coordinate direction has unit length

_private.TorusEuler.ParentResidualEstima.text: Embedding a real three-vector into the complex Euclidean space preserves its norm exactly. The proof uses the componentwise equality between the complex norm of a real number and its real absolute value. This allows Fourier estimates on the complexified parent residual to retain the original real amplitude bound.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentResidualEstima.summary: Complexification preserves the parent vector norm

_private.TorusEuler.ParentResidualEstima.text: The continuous linear map taking coordinatewise real parts has operator norm at most one. Each real component is bounded by the norm of its complex component, and the Euclidean sum preserves the inequality. This transfers the complex Fourier derivative estimates back to real-valued residuals without enlarging their constants.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentResidualEstima.summary: Taking real parts does not increase the norm

_private.TorusEuler.ParentSeedJetBudgets.text: For any real constant `C`, chooses a natural exponent $A \ge  30$ such that every $D \ge  2$ and positive radius $\ell \le  D^{-A}$ satisfy $2\cdot C\cdot \ell\cdot D^{30} \le  1$. The proof uses an Archimedean power bound at base two. The exponent depends on the fixed constant, while the resulting inequality is uniform in `D` and the radius.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentSeedJetBudgets.summary: One radius exponent absorbs the fixed coframe constant

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: This private definition forgets the quantitative half Hölder bound and retains the underlying continuous real vector field on the torus. Evaluation is unchanged. The conversion allows the Fourier band predicate, which is formulated for continuous maps, to be applied to inputs and outputs of the bounded Leray projection.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: The continuous representative of a half Hölder field

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: A finite sum of torus characters multiplied by arbitrary vector coefficients is continuous. The coefficient space is a complex normed space; no decay condition is needed because `s` is finite. This supplies the continuity hypotheses needed when products of parent Fourier expansions are integrated term by term.

A continuous complex normed space valued field on the compact torus remains integrable after multiplication by the conjugate Fourier character indexed by `k`. Compactness supplies integrability from continuity. This private result justifies finite sum manipulations under the integral defining the parent Fourier coefficients.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Continuous fields have integrable Fourier coefficients

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: For finitely many continuous fields with values in a complete complex normed space, the Fourier coefficient of their sum equals the sum of the coefficients. Continuity is required only for indices belonging to `s`. The proof establishes integrability of each character weighted term before interchanging the finite sum and integral.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Fourier coefficients distribute over finite sums

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: The Fourier coefficient at `k` of one character at frequency `a` times a vector `e` vanishes when `hk : k ≠ a`. The proof integrates the product of the two characters and uses their orthogonality. This is the local calculation behind the finite frequency support argument.

For the product of a scalar finite Fourier sum and a vector finite Fourier sum, the coefficient at `k` vanishes if `k` is unequal to every sum `j + l` from their supports. Expanding the product gives the convolution rule directly. The hypothesis concerns membership in the finite supports, without imposing a radius or symmetry.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Products cannot create unrelated Fourier frequencies

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: For a $C^2$ velocity with nonnegative uniform bounds $M$, $B$, and $H$ on its value, first derivative, and second derivative, the supplied advection field has half Hölder norm at most $2(BM+B^2+HM)$. The representative equality `hA` is essential. The proof combines a Lipschitz estimate at short distances with a supremum estimate at long distances.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Velocity and two derivatives bound half Hölder advection

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: The supremum norm of the underlying continuous torus field is no larger than the bundled half Hölder norm. The result reads the value bound from `HalfHolder.norm_le_iff`. It allows estimates for the Leray projection in the stronger space to serve as amplitude inputs to the parent Bernstein estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Forgetting Hölder control decreases the norm

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: For a $C^2$ spatial velocity, the derivative of $u\cdot\nabla u$ is bounded by $\|Du\|^2+\|D^2u\|\|u\|$ at the chosen point. The product rule differentiates both the velocity and its gradient. This private estimate supplies the Lipschitz part of the later half Hölder bound.

If each of the three coordinate columns of a continuous linear map has norm at most a nonnegative number $M$, its operator norm is at most $3M$. The proof expands an arbitrary vector in the coordinate basis and applies the triangle inequality. It deliberately uses a convenient dimensional constant rather than an optimal one.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Coordinate bounds control the full gradient

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: The map from an integer frequency triple to its Euclidean vector preserves addition. This private coordinate identity makes the frequency arithmetic in products of finite Fourier sums compatible with the Euclidean norm used for the parent band. It contains no assertion about the fields or their regularity.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: Integer frequencies add as Euclidean vectors

_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.text: The Euclidean length of the sum of two integer frequencies is bounded by the sum of their lengths. The preceding embedding identity reduces the claim to the triangle inequality. This is the geometric step that turns two input bands of radius $2\Lambda$ into an output band of radius $4\Lambda$.
_private.TorusEuler.ParentVelocityEstima.summary: A product frequency lies in the summed band

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: For a smooth periodic time family, continuity of its completed jet tuple through order two implies time continuity of the signed quadratic momentum at each fixed point. This follows by continuity of the bounded bilinear extension and the bounded zeroth evaluation map. The conclusion is on the supplied closed time slab.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: Continuity of two spatial orders controls the momentum value

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: This bounded linear map extracts the zeroth component of a completed order zero tuple, evaluates it at `x`, and identifies the zero argument multilinear map with a vector. It lets convergence of completed momentum tuples imply convergence of the actual momentum at a fixed spatial point.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: The zeroth completed jet evaluates to a vector

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: Evaluating the extended order zero momentum tuple of two smooth inputs returns their actual signed projected momentum at `x`. The two inputs are taken through order two. The proof combines the agreement of the extension on smooth tuples with the canonical interpretation of the zeroth derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: Zeroth jet evaluation recovers the momentum value

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: At a fixed spatial point, uniform convergence of velocities, order two jet tuples, and residuals to zero passes the stage equation to the limit. Continuity assumptions justify integration. The result gives both the limiting integral identity and its within time derivative on the closed positive slab, with no remaining forcing term.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: The residual disappears from the integrated momentum equation

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: The finite spatial Hölder norm is nonnegative when `SpatialHolderHalf m f` holds. The proof uses the boundedness premises to justify each real supremum and the zero increment to bound the seminorm below by zero. This premise matters because the norm formula is totalized outside its intended domain.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: Admissible Hölder data have a nonnegative norm

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: Restricting a jointly smooth field on a closed time slab to any time in that slab gives a smooth function of space. The proof composes with the map sending `x` to `(t,x)`. It uses no derivative in time and therefore does not require a strict inequality between the two interval endpoints.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: A jointly smooth slab restricts to a smooth spatial slice

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: Joint smoothness on a closed slab ensures that each fixed spatial value has the within time derivative returned by `derivWithin`. The theorem simply restricts the smooth field along a time line. It does not compute the derivative by an Euler formula; that identification comes from the projected momentum hypotheses.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: A smooth slab supplies its within time derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: A velocity jointly smooth on the half open preterminal slab has smooth spatial slices at every time belonging to that slab. The proof restricts the joint function to a fixed time. This private lemma supplies the ordinary spatial smoothness needed for advection and pressure recovery.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: Preterminal smoothness restricts to every spatial slice

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.text: For a bounded bilinear map `B`, uniform convergence of `U j` to a continuous limit on the compact interval implies uniform convergence of `B (U j) (U j)`. Compactness supplies a uniform bound for the limiting curve. The proof controls the two factors separately, rather than treating a quadratic map as globally uniformly continuous.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerLimit.0.summary: Uniform convergence passes through a bounded quadratic expression

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The momentum operation is transported to the range of genuine smooth jet tuples through order `m+2`, with values in the completed space at order `m`. Injectivity recovers each velocity from its tuple, and the explicit norm inequality makes the resulting bilinear map continuous. The domain remains the exact range at this step.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The momentum estimate gives a bounded map on genuine jets

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: A continuous tower in complete normed spaces becomes smooth in time when each entry satisfies an integrated equation with a bounded bilinear map from a finite higher level. This private variant uses general spaces `X m`, allowing the closed spaces of compatible periodic jets. Induction on the number of time derivatives handles the finite loss function `r`.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Completed jet spaces admit the same time bootstrap

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The inclusion of the smooth jet range into its closure has dense range. This is the topological fact needed by the extension theorem for bounded bilinear maps. It does not assert that every element of the closure is already a smooth jet tuple.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The original jet range is dense in the completed space

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: A continuous periodic field on the Euclidean lift is uniformly bounded. The proof descends it to the compact unit torus, obtains a bound there, and pulls it back. The conclusion gives an unspecified real upper bound, which is enough to bundle actual derivatives as bounded continuous functions.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Continuity and periodicity provide a global bound

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: For a dense linear isometry `e : E → H` and complete target `F`, this construction sends each bounded linear map on `E` to its continuous extension on `H`. The construction itself is a bounded linear operator of norm at most one. Density and isometry provide the extension agreement used later.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Bounded operators extend from a dense isometric subspace

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: A bounded bilinear map on a dense isometric subspace is extended to the ambient space in each argument. Completeness of the target ensures the extensions exist. This is how the momentum map reaches completed compatible jets while retaining bilinearity, without assuming a formula for arbitrary collections of unrelated derivative fields.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: A bounded bilinear map extends in both inputs

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: Evaluating the extended bilinear map at `e x` and `e y` returns `B x y` exactly. The proof applies the continuous linear extension agreement theorem in each argument. This identity ensures that the completed momentum operator computes the original analytic expression on smooth periodic velocities.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The extended map agrees on original inputs

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The explicit coefficient used for the momentum jet estimate is nonnegative at every natural order. This follows from nonnegativity of operator norms, the square root, and positive numerical factors. It supplies the sign assumptions needed to package the subsequent bilinear map as a bounded operator.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The chosen momentum constant is nonnegative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: If `SpatialHolderHalf m f` holds, each actual derivative of order at most `m` is bounded by the full spatial Hölder norm. The premise supplies boundedness for the real suprema and nonnegativity of every summand. The theorem would not follow merely by evaluating the totalized norm formula on an arbitrary field.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: A Hölder norm bounds every stored pointwise derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: For two smooth periodic velocities, the completed norm of their signed projected momentum through order `m` is bounded by the stated constant times the product of their norms through order `m+2`. Tensor differentiation costs one order and the passage from uniform jets to half Hölder control costs another. This is a sufficient boundedness estimate, not an optimal loss claim.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Momentum loses two orders in the uniform jet estimate

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The norm of an actual derivative at any spatial point is at most the completed tuple norm, provided its order is among the stored components. The proof combines evaluation boundedness with the finite product supremum norm. This gives the pointwise inputs for subsequent Hölder and momentum estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Every pointwise derivative is controlled by the tuple norm

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The periodic Leray lift of a real scalar multiple of a smooth periodic field equals the same multiple of its projection. The proof represents the field in the torus half Hölder space and uses the concrete bounded projection there. This domain restriction prevents the raw lift’s fallback branch from obscuring linearity.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Projection commutes with real scaling on smooth fields

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The divergence of the tensor product of two bundled velocities is packaged as another smooth periodic velocity. Smoothness follows by differentiating their smooth tensor; periodicity follows because differentiation commutes with lattice translations. This object is defined before Leray projection and does not require either input to be divergence free.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Tensor divergence remains a smooth periodic field

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The tensor divergence construction is bundled as an algebraic bilinear map on smooth periodic fields. Linearity in each slot uses the derivative rules for sums and scalar multiples of smooth tensors. No operator norm is asserted at this stage; a finite derivative estimate is supplied later on jet tuples.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Tensor divergence is bilinear on smooth periodic velocities

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: Evaluating the constructed smooth periodic momentum divergence returns the contraction of the actual derivative of the pointwise tensor. This definitional equality connects the bundle to the expression used by the projected Euler equation. It remains a tensor divergence formula without a divergence-free premise on the inputs.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The bundled divergence has the expected tensor formula

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: This nonnegative scalar collects the operator norms of Leray projection, tensor divergence, and the momentum tensor, together with the finite product and Hölder comparison constants. It depends on the target order `m`. Its purpose is to prove boundedness of momentum from jets through `m+2` to jets through `m`.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: An explicit constant for the finite jet momentum estimate

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The pointwise tensor formed from two bundled smooth periodic velocities is smooth in space. The proof uses the continuous bilinear tensor map and smoothness of both inputs. Periodicity is not part of this theorem’s conclusion, although it is established in the following divergence construction.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Two smooth velocities have a smooth momentum tensor

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: Composing tensor divergence with negative Leray projection gives a bilinear map on smooth periodic velocities. This package records that the output remains in the same smooth periodic submodule. Its later bounded extension uses finite jet norms; the present definition itself asserts algebraic bilinearity rather than a no-loss estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The smooth momentum operation is an algebraic bilinear map

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: For smooth periodic inputs, forgetting the bundle on the algebraic momentum map yields exactly `periodicProjectedMomentum u v`. This is a definitional equality. It is the bridge from estimates proved for packaged smooth fields back to the explicit signed projected tensor divergence used in the limit equation.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The bundled operation equals the raw momentum expression

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: On the completed tuples of two smooth periodic velocities, the extended momentum map equals the completed tuple of their smooth momentum field. The proof reduces the extensions to their agreement on the dense source. This rules out any change of the intended formula when completion is introduced.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Completion preserves the original smooth momentum calculation

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm of a smooth periodic velocity is at most $3(m+1)$ times the norm of its jet tuple through order `m+1`. Uniform value and derivative bounds yield the half Hölder increment estimate. This is one source of the finite derivative loss in the completed momentum construction.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: One extra uniform derivative controls the Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: This continuous linear map extracts a single bounded spatial jet from a completed compatible tuple. It first forgets the closed subspace membership and then projects onto the chosen finite coordinate. The coordinate index ensures that only an order stored in the tuple can be requested.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: One derivative order is a bounded coordinate projection

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: This linear isometry includes the range of smooth velocity jets in its topological closure. Norms are inherited from the same ambient tuple space, so preservation of norm is definitional. The map supplies the embedding along which the momentum operator will be extended by continuity.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Smooth jet tuples sit densely in their closure

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: This linear map first identifies a smooth periodic velocity with its exact finite jet tuple and then includes that tuple into the closure. It preserves the actual derivative values. The construction is algebraic at this stage; a norm on the original smooth velocity space is not being introduced.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The velocity map into completed compatible jets

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The negative periodic Leray projection is a linear map from smooth periodic fields to themselves. Higher Hölder estimates prove smoothness of the output; Fourier periodicity supplies its lattice invariance. The sign is chosen so composition with tensor divergence gives the right hand side of the Euler evolution.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Negative Leray projection preserves the smooth periodic domain

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The order `m` derivative of a bundled smooth periodic velocity is continuous and periodic, hence uniformly bounded. This definition packages it as a bounded continuous function. The auxiliary chosen bound is used only to establish boundedness; the underlying function remains the actual iterated Fréchet derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Actual derivatives become bounded continuous jet fields

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: Injectivity of the finite jet map identifies the algebraic space of smooth periodic velocities with its range of tuples. This linear equivalence lets the momentum formula be transported from functions to genuine jet tuples before any completion. Its inverse recovers the unique velocity represented by a range element.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: A velocity is equivalent to its exact jet tuple

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The bounded jet constructed from a smooth periodic velocity evaluates exactly to its iterated Fréchet derivative. This is a definitional identity, so the choice of a uniform bound has no effect on values. It is repeatedly used to compare operator estimates in jet spaces with pointwise differential expressions.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Evaluating the bundled jet returns the actual derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The derivative of the order `m` bounded jet field equals the curried order `m+1` jet of the same smooth velocity. The proof invokes its actual Taylor series. This compatibility is necessary for joint regularity; boundedness and continuity of separate tuple entries alone would not establish it.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Successive smooth jets have the required derivative relation

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: Two smooth periodic velocities with identical finite jet tuples are equal, for every order `m`. The proof evaluates their zeroth components and uses the canonical identification of zero argument multilinear maps with vectors. No derivative order above zero is needed for injectivity.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: The zeroth jet recovers the whole velocity

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: This private projection extracts the periodicity proof from a smooth periodic velocity. It permits derivatives and tensor expressions to be moved to the compact torus when bounds are needed. The predicate concerns invariance under all integer lattice translations of the Euclidean lift.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Bundled velocities carry spatial periodicity

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: An element of the smooth periodic velocity submodule carries a proof of smoothness of its underlying function. This private projection extracts that proof. The conclusion concerns a single spatial field and says nothing about time dependence, divergence, parity, or the Euler equation.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Bundled velocities carry spatial smoothness

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.text: The iterated Fréchet derivatives of a spatially periodic function are spatially periodic at every order. Translation commutes with the totalized derivative operator, so no smoothness hypothesis is needed for this identity. Smoothness is supplied separately when these derivatives are used to define the actual periodic jet spaces.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerMomentu.summary: Every spatial derivative retains periodicity

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: The complex Laplacian of a real $C^2$ pressure, viewed as complex-valued, equals the complex inclusion of the divergence of its real gradient. The proof compares each diagonal coordinate derivative and sums them. This prevents a sign or coordinate convention from being hidden in the transition to Fourier Poisson uniqueness.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: The complexified Laplacian is the real pressure divergence

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: For a $C^2$ real velocity, double divergence of its complex pressure tensor equals the complex inclusion of the divergence of its real momentum tensor divergence. The proof expands both coordinate sums and uses commutation of complex inclusion with mixed derivatives. No incompressibility is needed for this representation identity; it is used later to identify tensor divergence with advection.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: The complex source equals real momentum double divergence

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: For a real $C^2$ scalar field, its complex inclusion has coordinate second derivatives equal to the complex inclusion of the original mixed partials. The proof applies the first-derivative compatibility twice, using $C^2$ regularity to make the first coordinate derivative $C^1$. This transfers the real pressure equation to complex coordinates.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: Complex inclusion preserves the mixed coordinate derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: For a $C^2$ field valued in `MomentumTensor`, component $i$ of its tensor divergence is the sum over $j$ of the derivative of component `(j,i)` in direction $e_j$. Coordinate projection commutes with differentiation by the chain rule. The explicit ordering matches the momentum tensor’s column representation.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: Tensor divergence is the sum of coordinate derivatives

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: At a point where a real scalar field is differentiable, the real Fréchet derivative of its complex inclusion evaluated on a vector is the complex inclusion of its real derivative. This is the chain rule for `Complex.ofRealCLM`. The differentiability premise rules out reading a totalized derivative as an unsupported classical derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: Complex inclusion commutes with a real spatial derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: If a smooth periodic vector field is fixed by the periodic Leray lift, its divergence vanishes everywhere. The proof descends the field to the bundled half Hölder space, interprets the fixed point as solenoidality, then uses the smooth gradient-pairing characterization. Smooth periodicity ensures the raw lift is operating on its valid analytic domain.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: A smooth periodic fixed point of Leray is divergence free

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: A jointly smooth field on the half-open Euler slab has a smooth spatial slice at every time in that slab. The proof composes with the map $x\mapsto(t,x)$ and removes the unrestricted spatial domain from `ContDiffOn`. The time may be zero, since no ambient time differentiation is used here.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: Joint smoothness restricts to a smooth spatial slice

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.text: For an Euler solution and a time in `Ico 0 T`, the spatial divergence of its within-time velocity derivative is zero. A nondegenerate closed prefix containing the time allows differentiating the Leray fixed-point relation, including at time zero. Joint smoothness and periodicity of the derivative then convert its fixed-point property to pointwise zero divergence.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerPressur.summary: The within-time derivative remains divergence free

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerUniquen.text: For `h : IsEulerSolution T U p`, choose a positive `S` strictly below `T`. The within-time derivative is continuous jointly in time and space on $[0,S]\times\mathbb R^3$. The proof compares the derivative on this closed prefix with the solution’s half-open time derivative, including the initial face rather than discarding it.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerUniquen.summary: The Euler time derivative is continuous on strict prefixes

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerUniquen.text: If `h : IsEulerSolution T U p` and `r ∈ Ico 0 T`, then the spatial pressure function `p r` is smooth to every order. This follows by composing joint smoothness with the fixed-time inclusion. Despite the short name mentioning continuity, the declaration’s conclusion is full spatial smoothness.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerUniquen.summary: Every preterminal pressure slice is smooth

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerUniquen.text: At a time `t ∈ Ico 0 T`, the Euler equation in `h : IsEulerSolution T u p` gives $u_t=-Du\,u-\nabla p$ pointwise. The theorem only rearranges the existing momentum identity. It is used when subtracting the two Euler equations in the classical uniqueness energy estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicEulerUniquen.summary: The time derivative equals the negative Euler momentum

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.text: This private abbreviation names the three-dimensional unit additive torus used by the higher Leray estimates. It fixes the domain of the Hölder fields and their translations. It adds no regularity, mean-zero condition, or divergence constraint; those belong to the field types, projections, and hypotheses that follow.

For periodic order-zero half-Hölder data, the lifted action of `P` remains in that class and has norm at most $2\sqrt{2}\|P\|$ times the input norm. The constants come from the two conversions between torus and Euclidean-lift norms. This base case does not need derivative commutation, because no spatial derivative is taken.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.summary: Bound the projected field in the base Hölder norm

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.text: The half-Hölder increment quotient of the iterated derivative of `fderiv f` equals the quotient at the next derivative order of `f`. The proof uses the linear isometry that curries multilinear maps, including its preservation of differences. It does not assert that either quotient is bounded; later regularity hypotheses provide that fact.

The norm of the order-`j` derivative of `fderiv f` equals the norm of the order-`j+1` derivative of `f`. This is an equality of real-valued functions, using the isometric currying convention for iterated Fréchet derivatives. It carries no regularity or boundedness assumption and supplies only the algebraic norm identification.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.summary: Successive derivative norms agree under currying

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.text: If `f` is invariant under integer lattice translations, its total Fréchet derivative is invariant under those translations too. The proof uses translation of `fderiv` and equality of the translated functions. No differentiability assumption appears here: this is periodicity of the total derivative expression, not an assertion that an actual derivative exists.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.summary: A periodic function has a periodic derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHigherJ.text: The quotient map from Euclidean space to the unit torus sends a vector sum to the sum of its images. This coordinatewise quotient identity lets a Euclidean line be read as a translated torus line. No regularity or periodicity assumption on a field is involved.

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: Abbreviates the unit three-torus used when comparing bundled quotient half-Hölder fields with periodic Euclidean lifts. The quotient carries the coordinate product metric, while `Vec3` carries its Euclidean norm. The later comparison constants account for this difference; the abbreviation itself asserts no equivalence of norms.

The distance between two quotient labels is at most the Euclidean norm of the difference of their lifts. The proof combines the circle quotient bound with the coordinate-to-Euclidean norm inequality. This provides one direction of the metric comparison used to transfer half-Hölder increment estimates from the torus to the lift.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: The quotient distance is bounded by the lifted distance

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: The quotient of a Euclidean sum equals the sum of the quotient labels. This additive identity expresses a lifted spatial line as a translated torus line. It is used to transport derivative relations between the Euclidean field and its descended half-Hölder representative.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: Translations pass through the quotient map

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: The quotient label of $x-y$ equals the difference of the quotient labels of `x` and `y`. The proof is coordinatewise additivity of the circle quotient. This identity is used to compare torus distances with distances between Euclidean representatives when relating the two Hölder norms.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: Differences pass through the quotient map

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: The first iterated derivative is identified with the Fréchet derivative through the standard one-variable multilinear currying equivalence. The equality holds as an identity of total derivative operators, without a differentiability assumption. It lets norm comparisons move between the paper’s first spatial derivative and Lean’s iterated-derivative representation.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: The first iterated derivative is the curried Fréchet derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: The strong spatial Leray projection commutes with every torus translation on half-Hölder vector fields. The proof uses its exact complex Fourier coefficient law, where translation contributes a scalar phase that commutes with each mode projection. This supplies the invariance needed to pass spatial derivatives through the projection.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: The torus Leray operator commutes with translations

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: The half-Hölder quotient formed from the first iterated derivative equals the quotient formed from the Fréchet derivative. The currying equivalence preserves differences and their norms. This is an encoding identity for the derivative field; it does not independently prove existence or continuity of a classical derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: First-derivative increments have the same Hölder quotient

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.text: The half-Hölder quotient of the zeroth iterated derivative equals that of the original field. Lean stores a zeroth derivative as a zero-argument multilinear map, and the standard currying equivalence preserves norms of differences. This identity removes that encoding when comparing the order-zero lift norm with ordinary field bounds.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayHolderL.summary: The zeroth derivative preserves Hölder quotients

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.text: This private abbreviation names the frequency type consisting of three integer coordinates. It is used uniformly for mode insertion, coefficients, and longitudinal generators in spatial $L^2$. There is no nonzero restriction, so every construction must handle the constant frequency explicitly.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.summary: Three integer indices for spatial Fourier modes

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.text: Pairing the complex frequency vector with the complexified real velocity gives the real Euclidean frequency contraction cast into complex numbers. The integer frequency entries are real, so conjugation in the first inner-product slot changes nothing. This identity connects the two solenoidal-space definitions.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.summary: Complex longitudinal pairing equals the real contraction

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.text: The complex $L^2$ pairing of two inserted modes equals their coefficient inner product when the frequencies agree, and zero otherwise. The proof uses character orthogonality after replacing representatives almost everywhere. This identifies which longitudinal directions must be removed by the all-field Leray projection.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.summary: Hilbert modes have orthogonal frequency components

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.text: Every spatial $L^2$ field is integrable on the probability torus, and multiplication by a Fourier character preserves integrability because its modulus is one. The lemma justifies the Bochner integral defining each coefficient. It applies to arbitrary $L^2$ inputs, with no smoothness assumption.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.summary: Multiplying an L2 field by a character remains integrable

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.text: This private coefficient is the integer frequency embedded in complex Euclidean space. It spans the longitudinal direction for that mode and is inserted into spatial $L^2$ to generate gradient directions. At frequency zero it is the zero vector, leaving constant velocity coefficients unconstrained.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.summary: The frequency vector as a longitudinal coefficient

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.text: This submodule is the complex linear span of all longitudinal mode insertions. A span means finite algebraic linear combinations; it is not declared closed. Its orthogonal complement is nevertheless closed and supplies the solenoidal $L^2$ space used for the orthogonal Leray projection.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayL2.0.To.summary: Finite linear combinations of longitudinal Fourier modes

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: This abbreviation names complex scalar L² over the torus Haar measure. It lets the proof use scalar Fourier density coordinate by coordinate before returning to complex vector fields. There is no zero-mean condition, smoothness condition, or prescribed Fourier support in the type itself.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Scalar square integrable Fourier fields on the torus

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: For any lattice frequency, complex amplitude, and bounded real-linear functional, the Euclidean lift of the scalarized Fourier wave is smooth of all orders. Smoothness comes from the exponential Fourier mode and linearity of `L`. This prepares the classical integration-by-parts argument for its weak solenoidal membership.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: A scalarized torus wave has a smooth lift

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: For a fixed coordinate `i : Fin 3`, project a complex vector-valued spatial L² field to scalar L². The map is complex-linear and continuous because the Euclidean coordinate projection is bounded. It is used to reduce vector Fourier density to the scalar Fourier density theorem.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Extract one coordinate of a complex spatial field

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: The divergence of the Euclidean lift is `L` applied to the Fourier mode multiplied by `divergenceMode k a`. Differentiating each coordinate supplies its frequency factor, and their sum is the divergence symbol. The formula holds before transversality is assumed, so the next lemma can set this contraction to zero.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: The wave divergence is its frequency contraction

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: The real L² inner product of the real part of `u` with `v` equals the real part of their complex L² inner product after embedding `v`. The proof moves the real-part linear map through the integral and uses the vector identity almost everywhere. This is the Hilbert-space compatibility needed for orthogonal projections.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Spatial inner products commute with taking real parts

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: For a complex vector `u` and real vector `v`, pairing the real part of `u` with `v` equals the real part of the complex inner product of `u` with the complexification of `v`. This coordinate identity transfers orthogonality from the complex Fourier space to the real velocity space.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Real pairing equals the real part of complex pairing

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: Insert a scalar spatial L² field into the `i`th coordinate of a three-component complex field, leaving the other coordinates zero. The map is obtained from scalar multiplication by the corresponding Euclidean basis vector. Together with coordinate extraction it reconstructs arbitrary vector fields as a finite sum.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Place a scalar field in one vector coordinate

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: If `hi` says the real part of $-i u$ is zero, then complexifying the real part of `u` recovers `u`. The assumption is exactly vanishing of the imaginary component as an L² class. This reconstruction criterion permits a real-valued conclusion without requiring matching pointwise representatives everywhere.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: A field without imaginary part equals its real embedding

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: Define the complex submodule generated by all torus Fourier waves with arbitrary complex three-vector amplitudes. Elements are finite complex linear combinations of these waves. Density in the whole vector L² space is a later theorem, rather than a property built into the definition.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Finite linear combinations of vector Fourier waves

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: The topological closure of the complex span of all vector Fourier modes is the entire complex spatial L² space. Scalar Fourier density is transferred through coordinate insertion, and the three coordinate components are recombined. This supplies the density step that extends modewise projection identities to arbitrary L² input.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Vector Fourier waves are dense in spatial L²

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: A real continuous linear functional `L` on complex spatial L² vanishes everywhere if `hL` makes it vanish on every vector Fourier mode. Arbitrary complex amplitudes ensure vanishing on complex scalar multiples, despite `L` being only real-linear. Density of the mode span and continuity finish the argument.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: A continuous functional is determined by its Fourier modes

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: For an amplitude `a` belonging to `transverseModeSpace k`, the real part of its vector Fourier mode lies in the weak real solenoidal space. The theorem translates the subspace membership into zero frequency contraction and identifies the representative with a real scalarized wave. It bridges the complex coefficient and real test-function definitions.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Real parts of transverse modes are weakly solenoidal

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: The real part of $-i$ times a complex spatial L² field agrees almost everywhere with its coordinatewise imaginary part. This formula expresses the imaginary projection using the already-defined real-part map. Its representative-level conclusion is enough to show later that a projected embedded real field has no imaginary component.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Multiplication by minus i reveals the imaginary part

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: Complexify a real spatial L² field, multiply it by $-i$, and take the real part: the result is zero. The statement is an L² equality and formalizes vanishing imaginary component of a real embedding. It is used to prove that the complex Leray projection preserves the embedded real subspace.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: An embedded real field has zero imaginary part

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: For a real continuous linear functional `L : ℂ →L[ℝ] ℝ`, apply `L` to each coordinate of a Fourier character times its complex amplitude. The result is a continuous real vector field on the torus. Choosing real or imaginary part gives the real waves used in weak divergence tests.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Real scalarizations of a complex Fourier wave

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: At torus point `z` and coordinate `i`, the scalarized mode is exactly `L (mFourier k z * a i)`. This definitional identity exposes the ordinary complex Fourier wave underneath the real Euclidean-space wrapper. It is used for subsequent smoothness and divergence calculations on the Euclidean lift.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Each scalarized coordinate is the expected Fourier expression

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: If `h` makes the frequency contraction of amplitude `a` vanish, the scalarized Fourier mode, embedded in spatial L², belongs to the weak solenoidal subspace. The proof computes its classical divergence and applies periodic integration by parts. At zero frequency the contraction is automatically zero, so constant fields are retained.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Transverse Fourier waves satisfy the weak divergence condition

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..text: Extract each of the three scalar coordinates of `u`, insert it back into its coordinate position, and sum: the resulting L² class is `u`. The proof combines representative identities with the finite Euclidean basis expansion. This avoids assuming vector-valued Fourier density as an independent library fact.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicLerayReal.0..summary: Summing the coordinate fields reconstructs the vector field

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicMultiplierBo.text: The complex Euclidean inner product with the frequency vector in the first slot equals the algebraic frequency contraction. This works because integer frequency entries are real and unchanged by conjugation. The identity reconciles the coordinate Leray formula with the orthogonal-projection implementation.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicMultiplierBo.summary: Hermitian pairing reproduces the frequency contraction

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicMultiplierBo.text: The integral inner product of two single Fourier terms is the coefficient inner product if their frequencies agree, and zero otherwise. The target is any complex Hilbert space. This transfers scalar character orthogonality to vector or path coefficients before proving finite Parseval identities.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicMultiplierBo.summary: Orthogonality holds for Hilbert valued Fourier terms

_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicMultiplierBo.text: The square of the complex Euclidean norm of the embedded frequency is `frequencyNormSq k`. The calculation uses the reality of integer casts and the sum-of-squares norm formula. It provides the denominator identification needed to compare the explicit Leray coefficient with a singleton-span projection.
_private.TorusEuler.PeriodicMultiplierBo.summary: The Euclidean coefficient norm matches frequency length

_private.TorusEuler.PhaseJetBounds.0.Tor.text: Every scalar coordinate selected from a label-phase pair has absolute value at most the norm of that pair. The product space uses its existing norm, so both label and phase coordinates obey one bound. This estimate is the coordinate-size hypothesis needed to recover multilinear operator bounds from component estimates.
_private.TorusEuler.PhaseJetBounds.0.Tor.summary: Each coordinate is bounded by the product norm

_private.TorusEuler.PhaseJetBounds.0.Tor.text: At a differentiability point of `A t`, assume `hB` identifies the coefficient evaluated at the label with the derivative of `A t`. The graph derivative in a spatial basis direction then equals `scaledPhaseDirection` evaluated on that graph. Only the label scale must be nonzero for the coefficient evaluation to cancel correctly.
_private.TorusEuler.PhaseJetBounds.0.Tor.summary: Differentiating the graph gives the lifted direction

_private.TorusEuler.PhaseJetBounds.0.Tor.text: Scaling by the reciprocals of the label radius and phase width, then by the original scales, returns the same label-phase pair. Both nonzero assumptions `hℓ` and `hh` are essential to this inverse identity. The statement concerns the linear scaling map, independent of flow or profile regularity.

Suppose a finite coordinate family expands every vector and each coordinate is bounded by the vector norm. A multilinear map whose values on all coordinate tuples are bounded by nonnegative `C` has operator norm at most the number of coordinates raised to its arity, times `C`. The hypotheses specify the expansion rather than assume an orthonormal basis.
_private.TorusEuler.PhaseJetBounds.0.Tor.summary: Coordinate evaluations control a multilinear operator norm

_private.TorusEuler.PhaseJetBounds.0.Tor.text: Select one scalar coordinate of a label-phase pair: a spatial component for an index in `Fin 3`, or the phase component for the `Unit` index. The sum type provides exactly four coordinate choices. This is the bookkeeping needed to compare mixed coordinate derivative bounds with a Fréchet operator norm.
_private.TorusEuler.PhaseJetBounds.0.Tor.summary: Coordinates on labels and the independent phase

_private.TorusEuler.PhaseJetBounds.0.Tor.text: Summing each spatial coordinate times its corresponding standard direction reconstructs the original vector in three-dimensional Euclidean space. This identity supplies the coordinate expansion required by the multilinear operator-norm comparison. It involves only finite sums and is independent of smoothness, periodicity, or the flow.
_private.TorusEuler.PhaseJetBounds.0.Tor.summary: Coordinate directions reconstruct each spatial vector

_private.TorusEuler.PhaseJetBounds.0.Tor.text: A label-phase pair is the sum of its four coordinate values times the corresponding label-phase basis directions. The three spatial terms and one phase term are indexed by `Fin 3 ⊕ Unit`. This finite expansion supports the dimension factor in the mixed-derivative operator-norm estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.PhaseJetBounds.0.Tor.summary: Four coordinates reconstruct a label-phase pair

_private.TorusEuler.PhaseProfileEstimate.text: For every nonnegative order `j`, a jointly smooth profile remains jointly smooth after taking `j` derivatives in phase. The statement preserves dependence on the parameter as well as on phase. It enables the subsequent mixed-derivative construction and the exchanges of those derivatives with phase averages and primitives.
_private.TorusEuler.PhaseProfileEstimate.summary: Repeated phase differentiation retains joint smoothness

_private.TorusEuler.PhaseProfileEstimate.text: For a jointly smooth function of a parameter and phase, its iterated Fréchet derivative in the parameter variable remains jointly smooth in both variables. The order `k` is arbitrary. This supplies the regularity needed to differentiate parameter-dependent phase integrals repeatedly, with phase held fixed during each parameter derivative.

The primitive obtained by integrating a jointly smooth profile from phase zero to the variable phase endpoint is jointly smooth in the parameter and phase. The target is complete, and the parameter space has the section's properness assumptions. This is the unnormalized primitive; subtracting its phase mean is a later operation.
_private.TorusEuler.PhaseProfileEstimate.summary: The anchored phase integral is jointly smooth

_private.TorusEuler.PhaseProfileEstimate.text: Joint smoothness in parameter and phase implies joint smoothness of the first derivative in phase. This helper takes a spatially parameterized profile and treats phase differentiation as a component of the full derivative. It prepares repeated phase differentiation before the parameter derivatives defining a mixed derivative are taken.

If the profile and its parameter derivative are jointly continuous and `hderiv` identifies that derivative pointwise, then a phase integral over fixed endpoints has derivative equal to the integral of `df`. The hypotheses justify this exchange. The parameter space is proper and the target complete, as specified by the surrounding section.
_private.TorusEuler.PhaseProfileEstimate.summary: Differentiating a phase integral under the integral sign

_private.TorusEuler.PhaseProfileEstimate.text: For a continuous profile and continuous linear map `L`, taking the phase average after applying `L` equals applying `L` to the phase average. Completeness ensures the relevant Bochner integrals behave as intended. This permits coordinate or multilinear evaluation to pass through the averaged profile.
_private.TorusEuler.PhaseProfileEstimate.summary: Linear evaluation commutes with taking the phase mean

_private.TorusEuler.PhaseProfileEstimate.text: Applying a continuous linear map to a continuous profile commutes with subtracting its phase mean, at every phase `s`. The identity combines linearity with commutation of `L` and the integral. It allows scalar or coordinate bounds to be applied directly to the oscillatory part of a mixed derivative.
_private.TorusEuler.PhaseProfileEstimate.summary: Linear evaluation commutes with the oscillatory part

_private.TorusEuler.PhaseProfileEstimate.text: A continuous linear map passes through both the anchored phase integral and the mean subtraction that defines the normalized primitive. The profile is assumed continuous, so these integrals are well-defined in the complete target spaces. The conclusion is pointwise in phase and does not add periodicity hypotheses.
_private.TorusEuler.PhaseProfileEstimate.summary: Linear evaluation commutes with the normalized primitive

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalAmplificatio.text: If $|u-1|\le\varepsilon\le1/2$, then $|\log u|\le2\varepsilon$. The closeness hypothesis implies $u\ge1/2$, so the logarithm is used on positive values. In the crossing construction this converts relative first-coupling control into a logarithmic bound.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalAmplificatio.summary: A scalar near one has a controlled logarithm

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalAmplificatio.text: For $\tau\in[0,T]$, the physical time `clock τ` belongs to `activeSlab T`. The proof applies monotonicity of the clock and its activation value. This is the forward membership conversion used when moving maxima, nonvanishing and crossing estimates onto the physical slab.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalAmplificatio.summary: A normalized time gives an active physical time

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalAmplificatio.text: A physical time between `clock a` and `clock b` has elapsed normalized time in $[a,b]$. The proof applies monotonicity to both inequalities and simplifies the inverse-clock identities. It is a set-membership lemma, without a claim that either interval lies inside the domain of a physical wave.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalAmplificatio.summary: The inverse clock preserves both interval endpoints

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalAmplificatio.text: Every time in `activeSlab T` has elapsed normalized time in $[0,T]$. This specializes the interval-transport lemma using `clock 0=t₀`. It lets proofs reuse normalized estimates at a physical time whose membership in the active slab is known.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalAmplificatio.summary: An active time lies in the normalized interval

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalAmplificatio.text: Multiplying the strain operator by any real scalar $c$ multiplies the affine amplitude operator’s value by $c$. The pressure correction is linear in the strain just as the transport term is. This algebraic identity also holds for zero wave vectors under the totalized definition, and is used in reversing the clock change.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalAmplificatio.summary: Rescaling the strain rescales the amplitude derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.text: Every Euclidean label equals its centered representative plus the integer vector with coordinates $\lfloor a_i+1/2\rfloor$. This exact decomposition follows from the fractional-part definition. It allows the equivariance of the forward flow to convert a support condition in the centered label cell into a statement near lattice translates in physical space.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.summary: A label splits into its cell point and lattice shift

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.text: Embeds a continuous real vector field on the unit torus into a continuous complex vector field coordinate by coordinate. The resulting bundled continuous map is the input required by Fourier synthesis. It keeps the same values in the real subspace and introduces no differentiability or frequency-support assumption.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.summary: A real torus field as complex Fourier input

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.text: The map from Euclidean three-space to the unit three-torus is a quotient map. The proof combines the open quotient maps for the circle coordinates with the Euclidean product-space homeomorphism. This is what permits a continuous periodic Euclidean field to descend to a continuous torus field used as Fourier-cutoff input.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.summary: The Euclidean quotient map gives the torus topology

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.text: The `m`th directional derivative of the real cutoff lift is the real part of the corresponding derivative of its complex synthesis. The real-part map is continuous linear and the finite Fourier sum is smooth. The identity holds for arbitrary symbol and scale parameters; quantitative estimates add the necessary symbol and scale hypotheses later.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.summary: Real parts commute with cutoff differentiation

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.text: For any real scale `Λ`, the `m`th directional derivative of the scaled kernel equals $\Lambda^m$ times the scaled corresponding derivative of the original Schwartz kernel. The fixed tuple `v` records the directions. This algebraic differentiation identity does not require positive scale; positivity enters the subsequent change-of-variables estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.summary: Kernel derivatives carry one scale factor per derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.text: The coordinatewise complexification of a real Euclidean vector has exactly the same norm. The proof compares the sums of squared coordinate norms. This lets the complex Fourier-kernel estimates apply to real velocities without increasing the input bound when constructing the real vector cutoff.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.summary: Complexifying a real vector preserves its norm

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.text: The coordinatewise real part of a complex Euclidean vector has norm at most the original complex norm. This contraction follows from the coordinate estimates and the Euclidean sum-of-squares formula. It transfers derivative and off-support estimates for complex Fourier synthesis to the real truncated velocity.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.summary: Taking real parts does not increase the vector norm

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.text: If `f` vanishes within positive distance `d` of `x` and is globally bounded by `M`, its convolution at `x` is bounded by $d^{-N}$ times the `N`th absolute kernel moment and `M`. Only integrability of that weighted kernel norm is assumed. The argument separates nearby points, where the input vanishes, from the moment-controlled complement.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.summary: A hole in the support gives a moment bound

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.text: Postcomposing an order-`m` half-Hölder field with a continuous linear contraction preserves its regularity and cannot increase its full lift Hölder norm. The hypothesis is the pointwise inequality `‖L a‖ ≤ ‖a‖`. The proof controls both iterated derivative norms and their increments, enabling transfers between real and complex formulations.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalCutoffEstima.summary: A linear contraction preserves every Hölder order

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalGrowthPropag.text: Given $2\varepsilon\le1$, positive amplitude norm at `u`, a lower reference comparison at `v` and an upper comparison at `u`, the reference growth-factor ratio is bounded by $e$ times the physical amplitude ratio. The lemma needs no time-order assumption or differential equation; it is the algebraic comparison step in the propagator bound.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalGrowthPropag.summary: Reference growth ratios follow physical amplitude ratios

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalGrowthPropag.text: Every `AmplificationWindow T ε S δ` satisfies $T^2\le S$. The proof combines its inverse-shear bound, nonnegative error and polynomial smallness, using $T\ge2$. This recovers the coordinate-scale separation required by the physical-to-normalized amplitude norm bounds directly from the stored window assumptions.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalGrowthPropag.summary: The normalized hypotheses force shear above the squared horizon

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalGrowthPropag.text: The older strain and error strain are continuous by the physical record, while the preceding wave paths are continuous because their within-set derivatives exist. The rank-one product of those paths is continuous as well. Adding the three terms proves continuity of the full physical gradient on `I`.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalGrowthPropag.summary: The complete physical gradient is continuous on its window

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalGrowthPropag.text: This helper transports a physical wave vector and amplitude to $[0,T]$ when their within-set derivatives are known only on `activeSlab T`. It uses the normalized gradient identity and the clock’s membership map. Unlike the earlier `rescale_wave`, it does not require these path equations on all of the larger physical set `I`.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalGrowthPropag.summary: Closed-slab physical paths give normalized closed-slab paths

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalGrowthPropag.text: If a nonzero wave-vector path and an amplitude path satisfy the paired affine equations on $[l,r]$, orthogonality at any $s\in[l,r]$ persists everywhere on that interval. The proof shows the pairing has zero within-set derivative and uses uniqueness. The starting point need not be the left endpoint, so the conclusion includes earlier times.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalGrowthPropag.summary: Transversality propagates from any point of the closed interval

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalHierarchyPro.text: The centered cube is the closure of its interior. Convexity, a nonempty interior containing the origin, and closedness establish the equality. This topological fact allows an estimate proved on interior graph points to extend to cell faces by continuity, so periodization does not lose boundary control.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalHierarchyPro.summary: The closed cell is the closure of its interior

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalHierarchyPro.text: For a smooth label-and-phase function, an ordered word of constant directions equals its iterated Fréchet derivative evaluated on those directions. The empty word corresponds to the zeroth derivative. This identity connects the finite coordinate-word norms with operator-norm jet estimates needed by the physical chain rule.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalHierarchyPro.summary: A constant coordinate word evaluates the corresponding Fréchet jet

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveStageClo.text: For a selected growing crossing with scheduled scale, combines the approximate central rank-one decomposition with a sufficiently small cutoff tail. The child error is $E+D\mathrm{tail}(0)$; the original scale $-1/3$ bound becomes the induction’s $-1/4$ bound. The theorem requires the stated frequency schedule, crossing timing, differentiability, and order-two tail estimate.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveStageClo.summary: Add the cutoff derivative to the central error

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveStageClo.text: A jointly smooth map on a closed time slab has smooth full-space slices at each slab time. Here the domain and target are general normed real spaces, so the helper applies to phase-state pullbacks as well as physical fields. The proof is composition with the constant-time inclusion and makes no assertion outside the slab.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveStageClo.summary: Joint pullback smoothness gives smooth phase slices

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveStageClo.text: Rewrites the frequency two stages ahead as the current scheduled child frequency raised to the next scheduled exponent. The proof uses the defining frequency recurrence twice. This identity aligns the cutoff error estimate, whose parameters are written as powers of the parent frequency, with the induction’s indexed next frequency.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveStageClo.summary: Express the next frequency by two scheduled powers

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveStageClo.text: From an initial frequency at least two, obtains the same lower bound for the parent frequency, monotonicity from the current to the next derivative order, and $\max\{2,\mathrm{order}\}\le\mathrm{depth}$. The depth is six times the next frequency exponent. These inequalities justify using the cutoff tail at order two and at every order required by the induction.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveStageClo.summary: The scheduled depth covers the requested derivative order

_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveStageClo.text: Restricting a jointly smooth field on `[0,T] × Vec3` to a slab time gives a smooth spatial field on all of `Vec3`. The theorem is polymorphic in the target normed space. It supplies differentiability and Hölder regularity inputs for the Fourier cutoff and central-gradient calculations.
_private.TorusEuler.PhysicalWaveStageClo.summary: Smooth physical fields have smooth time slices

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: This private abbreviation names the real continuous linear maps from three-dimensional space to itself. It provides the type for the matrix products and traces in the pressure source comparison. A value of this type need not be the derivative of a velocity field; later representation hypotheses supply that interpretation.
_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.summary: Linear operators representing velocity gradients

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: Defines the complex-linear counterpart of coordinate extraction: apply the operator to coordinate direction `i`, then take component `j`. Being a continuous complex-linear functional allows it to pass through the complex Fourier integral. This is representation machinery, without a hypothesis or conclusion about pressure or symmetry.

Given a periodic $C^2$ potential whose Laplacian equals the represented source, the corresponding entry of the complex multiplier equals the real Hessian entry after complexification. Exact representatives of the potential and entry are hypotheses. Equality of all Fourier coefficients gives pointwise equality of continuous torus functions, including the zero mode.
_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.summary: The constructed entry equals the periodic Poisson Hessian

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: Complexifies a real half-Hölder scalar field, applies the bounded complex pressure multiplier, and forgets the extra Hölder structure to obtain a continuous operator-valued torus function. This representative is used in Fourier uniqueness. The definition itself does not select a scalar potential or solve a Poisson equation.
_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.summary: View the multiplier output as a continuous field

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: The angular pressure operator is smooth on the complement of the zero frequency. The proof subtracts the smooth Leray symbol from the identity on that punctured domain. No smoothness or continuity at zero is asserted; the multiplier construction treats the zero Fourier mode separately.
_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.summary: The pressure projection is smooth away from zero

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: For a real $C^2$ field, either taking two coordinate derivatives before complexification or after complexification gives the same result. The proof applies the first-derivative conversion twice. This allows the complex Fourier integration-by-parts formulas to be used for the real pressure potential.
_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.summary: Complexification commutes with the coordinate Hessian

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: At a point where both vector fields are differentiable, divergence of their sum is the sum of their divergences. The proof expands the Fréchet derivative and finite trace. The differentiability assumptions matter because `divergence` is defined through a total derivative function; linearity is not asserted for arbitrary irregular fields.
_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.summary: Divergence distributes over a differentiable sum

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: At a point where both vector fields are differentiable, divergence of their difference is the difference of their divergences. This uses the derivative subtraction rule before taking the coordinate trace. It supplies the pressure-gradient subtraction step and retains the regularity needed for a meaningful differential identity.
_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.summary: Divergence distributes over a differentiable difference

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: Evaluation of the bundled Hölder product is exactly multiplication of the two evaluated operators in the stated order. The identity is definitional and introduces no smoothness or gradient hypothesis. It lets the source comparison pass between field algebra and matrix algebra at a spatial label.

An entry of the real multiplier output equals the real part of the corresponding entry of its complex continuous lift. The proof unfolds the real-operator extraction and identifies real and complex coordinate vectors. This connects the entrywise complex Fourier uniqueness result to equality of the real operator fields.
_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.summary: The real Hessian entry is the real complex entry

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: At a point where the real scalar field is differentiable, differentiating its complexification and applying a direction gives the complexification of the real derivative in that direction. The argument is the chain rule for `Complex.ofRealCLM`. The explicit differentiability hypothesis prevents interpreting this as an unrestricted chain rule for total derivative expressions.
_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.summary: Complexification commutes with an actual derivative

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: The coordinate Fourier derivative factor at $-k$ is the negative of that at $k$. This follows from the explicit $2\pi i k_j$ convention. It is used when the conjugate test mode in a Fourier coefficient is differentiated, fixing the sign in periodic integration by parts.
_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.summary: Negating frequency negates the derivative factor

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: For arbitrary half-Hölder operator fields `U` and `V`, their pointwise product has both a supremum and an increment bound with common cap $2\|U\|\|V\|$. Splitting the product difference controls the increment. The theorem is about operator fields; no assumption says they are actual velocity gradients or that they commute.
_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.summary: Control the product of two Hölder operator fields

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: Packages pointwise composition of two half-Hölder operator fields as another half-Hölder field. Continuity and the explicit supremum and increment bounds are supplied to `HalfHolder.ofBound`. The order of the two operators is retained, which matters for the noncommutative square-difference identity used in the pressure source.
_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.summary: Multiply the two operator fields in Hölder space

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: Extends the zero cell integral of a periodic coordinate derivative to complex-valued continuously differentiable fields. The proof applies the real statement to the real and imaginary parts, commuting continuous linear maps with the integrable derivative. This prepares integration by parts for complex Fourier modes.
_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.summary: A complex periodic derivative also integrates to zero

_private.TorusEuler.PressureHessianMulti.text: For a real continuously differentiable periodic scalar field, the integral of any coordinate derivative over the centered cell is zero.
